#### **Foreword**

I began my career in cybersecurity in 1987, after graduating with a degree in computer
engineering, when the field itself was still trying to define what "computer security" really
meant. I joined the Computer Security Office at a federally funded research center, working
closely with the National Computer Security Center—now part of the National Security
Agency—during a period when the industry was being encouraged, sometimes gently and
sometimes not, to build operating systems with security designed in from the start rather than
bolted on later as an afterthought.

In the early 1990s, I joined Trusted Information Systems during a formative period for Internet
security. Our team released the TIS Firewall Toolkit and one of the earliest commercial Internet
firewalls, and I had the opportunity to conduct security consulting engagements, perform risk
assessments, and participate in research projects sponsored by ARPA and DARPA. When TIS
was later acquired by Network Associates (McAfee), I eventually served as Vice President of
Product Management overseeing firewall, intrusion detection, and encryption product lines.
That arc reinforced a lesson that has stayed with me: security is never purely technical. It
shows up in operations, in organizations, and in people.

In 2002, my former boss, Steve Lipner, convinced me to join Microsoft's Trustworthy
Computing initiative. Steve argued—correctly, as it turned out—that there was no better place
to drive meaningful security impact than inside a platform used by hundreds of millions of
people and organizations worldwide. It was there that I met Tim Rains.

Tim and I worked together for roughly a decade during a period when Microsoft was reshaping
how large technology companies approached security and trust. We collaborated on bestpractice guidance for securing Windows environments and later on efforts focused on secure
and trusted cloud operations. We also worked closely with Trustworthy Computing leadership
through some of the most challenging moments the industry has faced, including the fallout
from the Edward Snowden disclosures, when questions of trust, transparency, and
government access to data stopped being abstract policy debates and became day-to-day
customer concerns.

We also spent many years contributing to the Microsoft Security Intelligence Report. My role
focused heavily on industry-wide vulnerability analysis, which means I may claim a small
amount of responsibility for inspiring Tim's expanded treatment of vulnerability disclosure
trends in this new edition. Fortunately for readers, he takes those ideas much further and

grounds them in the kind of operational experience you only get from being responsible for
outcomes.

Over the past decade, my own career has shifted toward leading crisis communications and
issues management, and I would not describe myself today as a modern cybersecurity leader.
Tim, however, very much is. He has spent years managing security operations and solving real
problems across some of the largest and most complex enterprise environments in the world.
That difference shows up in the way he writes, and it shows up in what he emphasizes.

Many cybersecurity books do a good job explaining threats. Others focus on frameworks or
technologies. Far fewer capture what it actually feels like to be accountable for defending a
living organization—one constrained by budgets, legacy systems, competing business
priorities, regulatory pressures, and human behavior. Operational security leadership is
constant prioritization, imperfect tradeoffs, and decisions made with incomplete information.
Success rarely comes from adopting the newest tool; it comes from understanding which risks
matter most and then doing the sustained work to reduce them.

One of Tim's defining strengths, which I observed repeatedly while working with him, is his
ability to simplify complex security problems without turning them into slogans. He identifies
the small number of factors that truly drive risk and then focuses teams on practical,
achievable steps. That mindset runs throughout this book.

This edition builds on the foundation of Tim's earlier work while expanding into areas that
now sit at the center of modern security programs. New and updated chapters cover
vulnerability disclosure trends, API security, living-off-the-land techniques, and the rapidly
evolving intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity—both securing AI systems and
using AI to strengthen defense. He doesn't chase buzzwords—he carries the fundamentals
forward into environments that keep getting more interconnected and more complex.

A second strength of the book is how it stays anchored in data. Tim does not rely on anecdotes
or fear-based narratives. Instead, he connects threat intelligence, vulnerability data,
operational experience, and measurable outcomes into guidance you can actually use. You'll
find descriptions of threats, but you'll also find help with the harder questions: how to evaluate
tradeoffs, how to allocate resources, and how to tell whether your security program is getting
better in ways that matter.

Just as important, the book is honest about where security succeeds or fails in the real world:
incentives, leadership decisions, cultural resistance, and the grind of execution over time.
These are not side topics in operational security; they are often the main event. Tim addresses
them with clarity and practicality.

Cybersecurity professionals, executives, and technologists alike will benefit from this
perspective. Those new to the field will gain a grounded understanding of how modern

organizations are attacked and defended. Experienced practitioners will recognize the
constraints and decisions described throughout these chapters and may find language that
helps them explain those realities inside their own organizations.

Having worked alongside Tim during some of the industry's most consequential security
transformations, I have deep respect for his judgment, pragmatism, and commitment to
improving how organizations defend themselves. This book reflects decades of experience, but
more than that, it reflects a disciplined way of thinking about risk and responsibility that
leaders need if they want to make progress without pretending the job is ever "done."

Cybersecurity is not a problem that gets solved once and finished. It is ongoing stewardship
under uncertainty, where progress is measured not by perfection, but by resilience. Books that
help leaders think clearly about that responsibility are rare. This is one of them.

**Jeff Jones, Sr. Director, Microsoft**

#### **Contributors**

###### **About the author**

**Tim Rains** is a cybersecurity leader who has spent more than two decades helping
organizations and governments understand and defend against modern threats. He has held
senior security leadership roles at Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, T-Mobile, and ADT, and
has advised enterprises and public-sector institutions around the world on threat intelligence,
incident response, cloud security, and risk management. Tim also served on a subcommittee of
the National Security Telecommunications Advisory Committee (NSTAC), contributing
national-level guidance to the President of the United States on incentivizing and measuring
the adoption of cybersecurity best practices. His research on vulnerabilities, malware, and
attacker behavior has shaped industry practices, and he brings a practical, data-driven
perspective to helping organizations build security strategies that work in the real world.

_I'd like to thank my family, my wife Brenda and my sons Tristan and Liam, for their support and_
_patience while I wrote this book. Their encouragement during the writing and editing process for this_
_600+ page technical book kept me going. I'd like to thank all my current and former colleagues for_
_allowing me to learn from you. Thank you to our Technical Reviewer, Karen Kent, for her help_
_improving my last two books – I'm grateful for having the benefit of your considerable technical_
_acumen. And finally, thank you to Packt Publishing and their fantastic staff for their help and_
_support getting me through the publishing process for the third time._

###### **About the reviewer**

**Karen Kent** of Trusted Cyber Annex has been helping others communicate high-quality
cybersecurity information for over 25 years. She was formerly a Senior Computer Scientist at
the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and has co-authored more than 150
technical reports and papers for NIST, including the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), the
Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF), and the Common Vulnerability Scoring
System (CVSS). See her full portfolio at `[https://kkentwrites.com](https://kkentwrites.com)` .

#### **Preface**

Imagine you are in a submarine hundreds of feet below the surface, surrounded by dark,
freezing water. The hull is under immense pressure from all directions, and a single mistake in
its design, construction, or operation could spell disaster for the vessel and everyone aboard.

Inside are 150 crew members, several guests, and technologies sourced from 50 different
vendors. Three crew members plan to leave the organization after this voyage and are quietly
collecting copies of files containing their most important work. One crew member, angry about
a promotion he believes he deserved, is plotting how to sabotage the submarine's systems after
the voyage in retaliation. Two others have repeatedly exercised poor judgment in their
operational roles, putting the entire crew at risk. Unbeknownst to anyone, one of the guests is
an agent of a competing organization, searching for sensitive data and intellectual property to
steal, and for opportunities to extort the organization for profit.

Meanwhile, back at the crew's headquarters onshore, third-party consultants and industry
vendors are meeting with executives and members of the Board of Directors, insisting that the
submarine lacks the right technologies and that the captain is not up to the task without their
help. Their claims have led some executives to openly question the captain's leadership and
competency.

Although the submarine is relatively new, the technologies installed onboard are connected by
communications protocols developed in the 1970s. These protocols make integration easy and
enable communication with the public Internet, but they also expose the submarine to tens of
thousands of software and hardware vulnerabilities and hundreds of millions of pieces of
malware. The number of threat actors interested in disrupting the organization's operations
has steadily grown for decades, including nation-state groups that now operate openly on the
public Internet with impunity.

This is the situation the captain and crew find themselves in—and it is analogous to the
challenge that **Chief Information Security Officers (CISOs)** and their teams face today. Their
organizations are surrounded on the Internet by adversaries constantly probing for ways to
penetrate and compromise their IT infrastructures. Their people receive wave after wave of
social engineering attacks designed to trick them into making poor trust decisions that
undermine the controls their security teams have implemented. The specters of ransomware
and data breaches haunt CISOs, **Chief Information Officers (CIOs)**, **Chief Technology**
**Officers (CTOs)**, and Boards of Directors at even the most sophisticated organizations. Driven

_Preface_ xxvi

by the continuous adoption of new technologies, the attack surfaces of modern enterprises
continue to expand faster than proportional investments in cybersecurity programs.

After conducting hundreds of incident response investigations for Microsoft's enterprise
customers, publishing thousands of pages of threat intelligence, and assisting some of
**Amazon Web Services' (AWS)** largest customers, I have had the opportunity to learn from
and advise thousands of businesses and public sector organizations in nearly every country
around the world. I have also had the privilege of leading operational cybersecurity teams at
some of America's best companies. I wrote this book to share some of the insights and lessons
I've learned during my career.

The views and opinions expressed in this book are my own and not those of my current or
former employers.
###### **Who this book is for**

This book is written for cybersecurity leaders, practitioners, and technologists who are
responsible for protecting modern organizations from increasingly complex digital threats. It
serves executives, security teams, IT operators, public-sector leaders, students, and anyone
seeking a deeper, real-world understanding of today's cybersecurity landscape.
###### **What this book covers**

_Chapter 1_, _How Enterprises Get Hacked_, explains how enterprises get hacked by detailing realworld attack scenarios, the five main ways organizations are initially compromised, and the
importance of focusing on cybersecurity fundamentals to build effective strategies.

_Chapter 2_, _What to Know about Threat Intelligence_, provides an overview of **Cyber Threat**
**Intelligence (CTI)**, including its sources, uses, sharing protocols, and guidance for identifying
credible CTI versus industry noise.

_Chapter 3_, _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_, provides an in-depth analysis of industry
vulnerability disclosure trends, examining how leading vendors manage vulnerabilities, and
introduces a framework to help organizations reduce risk and costs through effective
vulnerability management strategies.

_Chapter 4_, _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_, analyzes vulnerability disclosure trends for
popular hardware and software products, evaluates these trends using a vulnerability
improvement framework, and provides practical guidance for enterprise vulnerability
management programs.

_Chapter 5_, _The Evolution of Malware_, provides a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the
evolution, prevalence, and impact of malware, especially ransomware, on global IT

xxvii _Preface_

environments, with practical insights for CISOs and security teams to understand and mitigate
modern cyber threats.

_Chapter 6_, _Internet-Based Threats_, covers the evolution, tactics, and mitigation strategies for
internet-based threats, including phishing, drive-by downloads, and DDoS attacks facing
organizations and individuals today.

_Chapter 7_, _Application Programming Interface Security_, offers a comprehensive look at API
security, covering common vulnerabilities, the evolving threat landscape, secure development
practices, privacy considerations, threat modeling, risk management, and practical mitigation
strategies tailored for CISOs, developers, and security teams.

_Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_, examines how
governments influence cybersecurity as market participants, standards setters, enforcers,
defenders, and even potential threats, and explores the risks and mitigations associated with
government access to data in the context of international regulations, surveillance, and cloud
computing.

_Chapter 9_, _Ingredients for a Successful Cybersecurity Strategy_, explains the essential ingredients of
a successful cybersecurity strategy, emphasizing the importance of governance, risk
management, compliance, mastering cybersecurity fundamentals, protecting high-value
assets, aligning with business objectives, fostering a strong security culture, and overcoming
organizational constraints to effectively defend against evolving threats.

_Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_, provides an in-depth examination of various cybersecurity
strategies used by organizations, evaluates their effectiveness in mitigating common risks
through the Cybersecurity Fundamentals Scoring System (CFSS), and offers guidance on
selecting and combining approaches to build a resilient and effective cybersecurity posture.

_Chapter 11_, _Cybersecurity Strategy Implementation_, provides a practical guide to implementing
the Intrusion Kill Chain cybersecurity strategy in real IT environments, including modernizing
the framework, mapping controls, identifying gaps and investments, and integrating
complementary approaches like the MITRE ATT&CK® framework to strengthen
organizational defenses against traditional network intrusions.

_Chapter 12_, _Measuring Performance and Effectiveness_, shows how CISOs and cybersecurity teams
can use data-driven methods, such as vulnerability management, intrusion reconstructions,
and attack-centric frameworks, to assess the performance of their security strategies,
demonstrate value, identify gaps, and drive continuous improvement.

_Chapter 13_, _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_, explores how cloud computing is
transforming cybersecurity and compliance practices, emphasizing the power of APIs and
automation to modernize security strategies, enhance resilience, and streamline compliance in
cloud environments.

## Part 1
### Introduction to Cybersecurity Strategies and Threat Intelligence

In this opening section, you'll learn how modern enterprises are actually breached. Through
three real-world attack scenarios, you'll see how intrusions unfold and how they can be
mitigated. You'll be introduced to the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, the five primary paths
attackers use to gain initial access, why cybersecurity fundamentals matter more than ever,
and how to apply threat intelligence effectively, while understanding its limits. You'll also trace
the evolution of vulnerabilities, malware, and internet-based threats, giving you the insight
needed to make informed decisions and strengthen your organization's defenses. By the end of
this section, you'll know how to use credible threat intelligence and insights into attacker
tradecraft to build a more effective security program.

# 1
##### How Enterprises Get Hacked

Welcome to _Cybersecurity Strategy for the AI-Driven Era_ . This is the third edition of this book
that I've written. Why write these books? In my career, I have had the opportunity to work as
the most senior cybersecurity advisor at both **Microsoft** and **Amazon Web Services** ( **AWS** ).
I've also had the opportunity to lead operational security teams at some very large, wellknown companies. After advising thousands of commercial and public sector organizations all
over the world and managing large operational cybersecurity teams myself, I concluded that
most organizations do not have a cybersecurity strategy that their security executives or
security teams can articulate. In fact, thinking about all the security briefings I provided and
meetings I had with executives and their teams over the last couple of decades, I recall meeting
fewer than 10 organizations that had a written cybersecurity strategy that the **Chief**
**Information Security Officers** ( **CISOs** ) could **d** escribe and that security team members could
repeat. Instead of discussing cybersecurity domains such as risk management and **Identity**
**and Access Management** ( **IAM** ), I found myself advising CISOs on cybersecurity strategies
almost exclusively. That's not surprising, since industry frameworks and certifications offer
extensive guidance on individual cybersecurity domains, but rarely provide meaningful
direction on strategy itself.

Most of the security teams I advised were approaching cybersecurity as a problem to be solved
by procuring the _right_ combination of tools. But without a clear strategy guiding them, gaps,
areas of over-investment, and areas of under-investment were always the result. Besides,
teams with big budgets and lots of cybersecurity tools still get hacked. If cybersecurity could be
achieved by procuring some tools, it wouldn't be the massive global problem it is today. It is an
inconvenient truth that effective operational cybersecurity is much more challenging than
simply procuring cybersecurity tools.

Given this, I decided to write a book about cybersecurity strategies for CISOs, **Chief**
**Information Officers** ( **CIOs** ), **Chief Technology Officers** ( **CTOs** ), aspiring cybersecurity

_Chapter 1_ 4

executives, cybersecurity teams, and **Information Technology** ( **IT** ) professionals who have
significant cybersecurity responsibilities. _Cybersecurity Threats, Malware Trends, and Strategies_
(Tim Rains) was published by Packt in May 2020. The response to that book in the industry
was very positive, and I wrote a second edition that was published in January 2023. Things
continue to change very quickly in the IT industry: cyberattacks are non-stop, and
cybersecurity strategies continue to garner overwhelming interest. This is why I have written
this third edition.

This chapter will cover the following topics:

The world CISOs live in

Tales from the frontlines: Real-world attack scenarios

How organizations get initially compromised

Focus on the cybersecurity fundamentals

Understanding the difference between attackers' motivations and their tactics

Different types of CISOs: The CISO spectrum

###### **The world CISOs live in**

In 2021, the global cybersecurity industry was estimated to be valued at around $140 billion.
That number ballooned to an estimated $271 billion in 2025 (Grand View Research, 2025).
Combine that with an estimated **Compound Annual Growth Rate** ( **CAGR** ) of 11.9% and this
results in an estimated industry market size that is expected to reach $633.24 billion by 2033
(Grand View Research, 2025). Most of this revenue growth has put immense pressure on
cybersecurity industry vendors' sales and marketing teams. In turn, vendors target roles that
are typically cybersecurity spend approvers or key influencers—CISOs, cybersecurity
executives, and directors of the boards of companies.

To give you an idea of how both the pressure to ensure effective cybersecurity and the rapid
growth of the cybersecurity industry manifest for CISOs, let me share some insights from my
own experience. At one point in my career, I would get, on average, nine calls each weekday

5 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

from cybersecurity vendors trying to sell their products and/or services to me. That's 45 calls
per week or 180 calls per month, on average. In six months, my LinkedIn message inbox
received 643 unsolicited messages from cybersecurity vendors. That's an average of 4
unsolicited messages every day of the week or 129 messages per month, month after month. In
addition to the combined 309 phone calls and LinkedIn messages I received per month on
average, I was also contacted by vendors almost daily through other people on my team or
executives in other parts of the company. These vendors typically want CISOs to meet with
them and explain their priorities and initiatives to determine where their products or services
can help. Most CISOs and security team members already spend a lot of time meeting with the
vendors they already leverage or plan to leverage. Those vendors are constantly looking for
ways to add value and expand their organizations' footprints within their accounts.

Personally, I feel it's impolite if I don't respond to well-meaning industry professionals trying
to represent their organizations and share products they believe in. However, professionally, I
simply could not keep up with the volume of requests from vendors. If you are a vendor that
reached out to me on LinkedIn and didn't get a response, I apologize, but I do hope you
understand. Many of the CISOs I have met share the same challenge.

As the industry grows, more and more cybersecurity vendors use the specter of the "everchanging threat landscape" to market and sell their wares to anxious and often punch-drunk
organizations across every industry. What started out as a relatively simple concept to use
computers to make faster and potentially better business decisions has led to a proliferation of
technologies, regulations, and standards that require an ever-expanding set of people,
processes, and technologies to protect them.

When I started working at Microsoft in the late 90s, they had little to no material revenue from
developing and selling cybersecurity products. In 2021, revenue from Microsoft's cybersecurity
business exceeded $10 billion (Jakkal, 2021), in 2024 it was over $20 billion, and it was
estimated that it will exceed $37 billion in 2025 (Krause, 2024). In 2016, I could walk customers
through Microsoft's relatively large and complicated security reference model crammed into a
single PowerPoint slide. Since then, this has evolved into what they now call **Microsoft**
**Cybersecurity Reference Architectures** ( **MCRA** ), which includes numerous different
reference models. Microsoft writes the following:

_Chapter 1_ 6

_"MCRA describes end-to-end security for the 'hybrid of everything' technology estate_
_spanning legacy IT, multicloud, Internet of Things (IoT), Operational Technology_
_(OT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and more" (Microsoft Corporation, 2025)._

Similarly, when I started working at AWS in 2017, they had around 40 cloud services in their
portfolio. When I left AWS almost four and a half years later, they offered over 300 cloud
services and had a growing portfolio of security services. Besides the introduction of new
services, existing services were constantly improved, and their functionality expanded. Many
IT teams that took the time to evaluate AWS' services before they adopted them would have to
re-evaluate them annually to ensure they still fully understand them.

Combine the growth from just these two vendors with the growth of other major IT and cloud
vendors (Oracle, IBM, Google, etc.) that enterprises typically also leverage, and _thousands_ of
cybersecurity vendors all vying for their business, and you have _a lot_ of options, complexity,
noise, and confusion.

Of course, the backdrop to all this technology proliferation, industry growth, and complexity is
the constant drumbeat of successful cybersecurity attacks. New technologies have enabled
attackers to increase the speed and impact of their attacks. For instance, new ways of
performing very large international financial transactions have enabled attackers to build
sophisticated business models based on extortion and human-operated ransomware.
Similarly, the state of international relations between China, the Democratic People's Republic
of Korea, Iran, and Russia with much of the rest of the world has heightened nation-state
cyberattacks and enabled ransomware gangs and other criminals perpetuating cybersecurity
attacks from these countries to operate in the open with impunity.

As a result, all commercial sector organizations in the Western world have largely been left to
fend for themselves, while governments desperately try to protect their critical infrastructures,
such as the communications and energy sectors, as well as water systems, from attacks.

Subsequently, many of the organizations that I advised would often ask very basic questions:

_Which cybersecurity capabilities are most important?_

_What do we do first? How do you prioritize requirements and capabilities?_

7 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

_What are other organizations in our industry doing?_

_Do you have any threat intelligence from other organizations in our industry? Is there an_
_algorithm that helps us determine the right priorities?_

After having thousands of these discussions and reading between the lines, what they were
really asking me about was a **cybersecurity strategy** . The fundamental question they were
asking me was: _Which cybersecurity strategy or combination of strategies will be most effective for our_
_organization given the industry we are in, the locations where we do business, our regulatory_
_compliance requirements, and the appetite for risk our business has?_

Before we dive into cybersecurity strategies, it is important to level-set our understanding of
the types of threats such strategies are designed to help with. I'll also discuss tactics and
mitigations that many security teams leverage to protect, detect, and respond to modern
cybersecurity attacks. Let's start by looking at how large organizations typically get hacked.
###### **Tales from the frontlines: Real-world attack scenarios**

In my career, I've been involved in literally thousands of **incident response** ( **IR** ) investigations.
I was a technical lead on a team of over 120 IR investigators and engineers at Microsoft that
performed IR investigations for their enterprise customers. I developed most of the tools
(wrote the code) that these teams used to gather and analyze evidence during their
investigations. I also had the opportunity to lead numerous IR investigations at the various
companies I have worked at during my career, working with top-tier IR response teams from
some of the industry's best vendors. I've also spent a considerable amount of time working
with attorneys in the wake of data breaches to comply with various industry breach disclosure
obligations and as a subject matter expert in resulting lawsuits. As difficult and pressurized as
IR typically is, I learned a lot by unraveling and explaining complex attacks in these roles. Let
me share some of the lessons I learned doing IR investigations over the years, to demystify
cyberattacks and shed light on how you can develop effective strategies to counter them.

One of the most difficult tasks that CISOs perform as part of their jobs is informing their
organizations' senior leadership teams that they have had a data breach. Breaking this kind of
bad news to CEOs and potentially many of their direct reports leads to all sorts of questions
that CISOs rarely have the answers to at the beginning of an IR investigation. In fact, most of
the initial assessments made by incident responders will turn out to be inaccurate by the end
of the investigation when more facts have been established.

In a complex IR investigation, the organization's IR team seeks to create a timeline of the
attackers' actions to establish how the attack started and whether it has been contained. This
essentially involves IR investigators hypothesizing about actions attackers could have taken at
each step in their attack and then looking for evidence that their hypotheses are correct. If their

_Chapter 1_ 8

hypotheses are proven untrue, they create new hypotheses based on any new information they
might have received.

_Figure 1.1_ illustrates the contrast between what IR teams think they know versus what they
actually know during a typical complex, high-severity incident investigation. In this notional
illustration, the horizontal axis represents the first 30 days of an investigation in which new
information about the incident was discovered:

_Figure 1.1 – A typical IR investigation knowledge trend_

9 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

An IR **i** nvestigation of a complex incident typically takes time, sometimes weeks or months.
During the investigation, the stakeholders that the CISO keeps informed tend to ratchet up the
pressure for answers to their questions. After all, if they are a publicly traded company, they
likely have numerous disclosure timelines that they must comply with, such as the **Securities**
**and Exchange Commission** ( **SEC** ), potentially US state **Attorneys Generals** ( **AGs** ), business
partners that impose contractual obligations for notifications, and customers that were
impacted. As soon as a company makes an "8-K" disclosure to the SEC, the details become
public knowledge and negative news cycles about the breach typically commence.

Further, news of data breaches tends to travel fast. Based on this news, business partners and
customers naturally want to know whether their data or systems were impacted and
proactively contact the disclosing company with questions of their own. In large, high-profile
data breaches, the combined volume of such requests can disrupt IR investigations, as
cybersecurity teams are forced to shift their focus from the investigation and potentially
containing the attack to communicating with the company's stakeholder community.
Sometimes, business partners disconnect their networks from victim organizations and even
stop accepting emails from them in an attempt to protect themselves from the attack. Industry
vendors, such as threat intelligence providers, start briefing their customers on attacks using
details from the victim's 8-K filings and the resulting news cycles, potentially further
perpetuating inaccuracies.

None of this is helpful for CISOs who are in the midst of a high-severity IR investigation, trying
to gather evidence and determine what happened and whether the attacker has been
contained. All of this can decelerate IR investigations, giving attackers more time to burrow
into the victim's infrastructure, find ways to stay persistent, deploy ransomware, and exfiltrate
data.

Further, CISOs and security teams face the challenge of communicating with their
stakeholders that not all "data breaches" or "cyberattacks" are the same, even though they are
reported in news or threat intelligence briefings the same way, that is, using a set of
underlying, often inaccurate, assumptions. In these scenarios, a key part of the CISO's role is to
provide clear, accurate context to senior executives and stakeholders.

_Chapter 1_ 10

Over-reacting or under-reacting to an incident both have potential consequences; executives
typically prefer a straightforward, accurate assessment of the potential impacts of an incident
over a minimized or overblown rendering.

In this section, I'll describe the following three types of attacks, how they work, how to
mitigate them, and how severe the risk they pose is for enterprise organizations:

Global malware attack

Traditional network intrusion

Data breaches via insecure APIs

I'll refer to these attacks throughout the rest of the book when providing an example of an
attack is helpful. The details I provide are fictional unless otherwise stated.

**Global malware attack: Worms**

Let me paint you a picture of a worst-case scenario based on past successful global worm
attacks. I helped lead Microsoft's IR through more than a few global worm attacks, including
_SQL Slammer_, _Blaster, Sasser_, _MyDoom_, and _Conficker_ . Thankfully, large-scale worm attacks
aren't as common as they used to be, but this doesn't mean CISOs and security teams can
ignore the threat they pose—unfortunately, wormable vulnerabilities are common. Among
worms, there were two predominant types propagating around the internet back in 2003–
2004, when several big global worm attacks occurred. There were worms that exploited
unpatched vulnerabilities and those that exploited design flaws in peer-to-peer and email
platforms. In this example, I'll describe the former type, since the exploitation of unpatched
vulnerabilities is still leveraged today by threat actors and purveyors of malware alike.

11 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

In the past, several global malware attacks started with an attacker discovering a new zero-day
vulnerability in a Microsoft Windows service. This service happens to run by default on the
vast majority of Windows systems in the world.

This vulnerable service uses a well-known **Transmission Control Protocol** ( **TCP** ) port to
listen on the network for connection attempts. There is a default rule in Windows Firewall on
every system that allows network connections directly to the vulnerable service. The attacker
develops a program capable of exploiting this zero-day vulnerability. Technically, this program
is called an **exploit** . Exploits are capable of taking advantage of the specific vulnerabilities they
are designed for, but have no delivery mechanism built into them. The attacker wants to
maximize the number of systems this exploit runs on, so they add the capability for the
program to self-propagate.

This means that when the exploit runs successfully on a vulnerable system, one of the things it
does is use the compromised system to look for other vulnerable systems to compromise and
distribute the exploit program to. This type of malware is called a **worm** . The attacker releases
the worm on the internet by running it on internet-connected systems in several different
locations.

The worm uses the vulnerability to spread before Microsoft is aware of the vulnerability and
before a security update is available to patch it. The default rule in Windows Firewall allows
the worm to talk directly to the TCP port that the vulnerable service is listening on, so there is
nothing preventing the worm from exploiting the vulnerability on virtually every consumer
system running Windows that is directly connected to the internet and that does not have an
additional firewall protecting it. _Figure 1.2_ illustrates how services running on Windows
systems use TCP and **User Datagram Protocol** ( **UDP** ) ports to process network requests. If
those services are not kept up to date with security updates, they become vulnerable to
malware attacks, such as worm attacks. It shows a worm checking whether the **Remote**
**Procedure Call** ( **RPC** ) endpoint mapper service is fully patched, as it accepts network traffic on
TCP port `135` . If the RPC endpoint mapper service is not patched for the vulnerability that the
worm was designed to exploit, it will infect the system and use it to attack other systems.

_Chapter 1_ 12

_Figure 1.2 – A diagram of a Windows-based computer with the services listening on a network using different TCP_

_and UDP ports. A worm is targeting TCP port 135, where the RPC endpoint mapper service is bound_

Anti-malware software doesn't detect the worm because it is brand new, and a sample of it is
yet to be provided to a major anti-malware lab for analysis. Vulnerable Windows systems
behind professionally managed enterprise firewalls wouldn't be safe either, as infected laptops
would introduce the worm into corporate IT environments when they connect via VPN or on
their wireless networks (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). The worm propagates from system to
system around the world in a matter of minutes, and the following takes place:

1. The public internet and most private networks are disrupted and rendered unusable, or
their performance is severely degraded.

13 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

2.

3.

4.

5.

6.

The network traffic generated by the worm as it attempts to propagate and repropagate, from system to system, significantly disrupts legitimate network traffic on
the internet, as well as the private networks it has found its way into.

After a system gets infected, the worm tries to infect all the systems it has network
connectivity with, repeatedly. Hundreds of millions of systems doing this
simultaneously disrupt the global internet and private networks.

When the worm exploits the unpatched vulnerability, it causes the target system to
destabilize, causing a _blue screen of death_, a memory dump, and a system reboot. This
exacerbates the problem because it's hard to disinfect and patch systems that are
constantly rebooting. Additionally, all the systems rebooting generates even more
network traffic.

When each system comes back up, they generate **Address Resolution Protocol** ( **ARP** )
traffic and ask their **Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol** ( **DHCP** ) servers for IP
addresses. When the network segments with DHCP servers get saturated with requests
for IP addresses, the DHCP servers are prevented from giving rebooting systems IP
addresses.

Subsequently, rebooting systems start using automatic private IP addresses that are
typically non-routable ( `169.254.x.x` ). In some cases, these systems can no longer be
reached by management software used to patch them, update their anti-malware
signatures, or deploy possible mitigations or workarounds to them.

Therefore, the damage such an attack could do shouldn't be underestimated. The US
government has identified 16 critical infrastructure sectors deemed critical because if their
network or systems are disrupted, it would have dire consequences on the security, economy,
and public health and safety of the country. These sectors include the following:

The chemical sector

The commercial facilities sector

The communications sector

The critical manufacturing sector

The dams sector

The defense industrial base sector

The emergency services sector

The energy sector

The financial services sector

The food and agriculture sector

_Chapter 1_ 14

The government facilities sector

The healthcare and public health sector

The IT sector

The nuclear reactors, materials, and waste sector

The transportation systems sector

The water and wastewater systems sector (US Department of Homeland Security, n.d.)

If a worm exploits a zero-day vulnerability on vulnerable systems in one of these sectors, the
economy, energy, water, communications, transportation, hospitals, or other critical functions
for society will be disrupted and potentially taken offline. Further, if the attacker includes a
malicious payload with the worm, such as encrypting operating system files or data or
destroying storage media, recovery would be time-consuming, requiring substantial manual
intervention as management software tools and automation systems would be disrupted along
with the networks they are connected to. Additionally, if the underlying storage media on
infected systems also need to be replaced, the damage from such an attack would linger for
years.

Of course, I've painted a picture of a worst-case scenario. But what are the chances that such a
worm attack could actually be perpetrated? To answer the question, let's look at confirmed
_wormable_ vulnerabilities in Windows operating systems disclosed between 2019 and 2025:

_score, description, and currently known exploit availability status_

Each one was assigned a **Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures** ( **CVE** ) ID by the MITRE
Corporation and a **Common Vulnerability Scoring System** ( **CVSS** ) base score quantifying its
severity. I'll discuss both of these in detail in _Chapter 3_ . For now, recognize that the CVSS scores
reflect the seriousness of these vulnerabilities in that the closer they are to 10, the more likely
remote exploitation with no human interaction is—which is exactly what worms need to
execute.

Let's look at some of the vulnerabilities from _Table 1.1_ in more detail. On May 14, 2019,
Microsoft announced the existence of a critical-rated vulnerability (CVE-2019-0708) in
Windows Remote Desktop Services that was wormable (NIST, n.d.). In their announcement,
the **Microsoft Security Response Center** ( **MSRC** ) wrote the following:

_"This vulnerability is pre-authentication and requires no user interaction. In other_
_words, the vulnerability is 'wormable', meaning that any future malware that_
_exploits this vulnerability could propagate from vulnerable computer to vulnerable_
_computer in a similar way as the WannaCry malware spread across the globe in_
_2017. While we have observed no exploitation of this vulnerability, it is highly likely_
_that malicious actors will write an exploit for this vulnerability and incorporate it_
_into their malware." —(Microsoft Corporation, n.d.)_

CVE-2019-0708, the so-called _BlueKeep_ vulnerability, applied to Windows 7, Windows Server
2008, and Windows Server 2008 R2; a third of all Windows systems were still running
Windows 7 in 2019 (Keizer, 2020). This vulnerability was so serious that Microsoft released
security updates even for old, unsupported operating systems, such as Windows XP and
Windows Server 2003, to protect the large number of systems that had never been upgraded
from old, out-of-support operating systems. Protecting these legacy systems, which no longer

17 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

get regular security updates, from a highly probable worm attack leaves less "fuel" for a worm
and results in fewer attacks on supported systems.

Then, on August 13, 2019, Microsoft announced the existence of two more wormable
vulnerabilities (CVE-2019-1181 and CVE-2019-1182). More Windows versions contained these
vulnerabilities, including Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, Windows Server 2012,
Windows Server 2012 R2, Windows 8.1, and all versions of Windows 10 (including Server
versions).

In each of these three cases in 2019, Microsoft was able to find and fix these critical, wormable
vulnerabilities before would-be attackers discovered them.

Unfortunately, there have been other potentially wormable CVEs since 2019. As _Table 1.1_
reveals, there have been at least 11 wormable vulnerabilities in Windows-based systems
between January 2019 and June 2025. In most of these cases, the vulnerabilities had a CVSS
base score of 9.8 or 10 and could enable code execution for attackers without any user
interaction. At least three of these vulnerabilities had public exploit code available at the time
of writing. In 2025, at least two wormable vulnerabilities in Windows were disclosed.

**Mitigating global worm attacks**

The probability and potential **i** mpact of these types of global malware attacks mean that CISOs
and security teams need to have a well-run vulnerability management program. I cover this in
detail in _Chapters 3_ and _4_, which are devoted to vulnerability management. Mitigating highseverity vulnerabilities as quickly as possible makes it harder for attackers to exploit them.
Some IT teams opt to use workarounds instead of security updates to mitigate vulnerabilities.
This helps them avoid the dreaded system reboot requirement that many security updates
impose, which in turn helps them keep their system uptime **Service-Level Agreements**
( **SLAs** ). However, I'm not a fan of this approach to mitigate high-severity vulnerabilities when
security updates are available because, in many cases, it leaves the system one configuration
change away from disaster. The use of workarounds is not typically documented well and
leaves knowledge of their use for the tribe to remember.

_Chapter 1_ 18

Unfortunately, purveyors of malware have evolved their worms over the years to give them a
better chance of compromising as many systems as possible. Back in 2008, variants of the
Conficker worm demonstrated that worms could use a combination of methods to propagate.
It used specific unpatched vulnerabilities (such as MS08-067), it attempted to log in to
network file shares using a hardcoded list of easy-to-guess passwords, and it also used social
engineering via Windows AutoRun feature abuse.

This means that security teams can't simply keep systems patched to mitigate this type of
threat. The following approaches to mitigation can be useful:

Enforcing a policy requiring long, complex, hard-to-guess passwords and using **Multi-**
**Factor Authentication** ( **MFA** ) will mitigate the type of dictionary attack that
Conficker used and other attacks that seek to leverage weak, leaked, or stolen
passwords.

Blocking USB drive use for most users is a best practice to help manage **Data Loss**
**Prevention** ( **DLP** ), as well as malware that attempts to use removable storage media.

Running anti-malware or modern endpoint detection and response software will help
detect infection attempts and potentially prevent systems from being infected by such
malware.

IT teams can't always keep up with the pace of attackers, especially in the case of a
zero-day attack, as described earlier. In such cases, Zero-Trust design principles can be
helpful; for example, **host-based firewalls** such as Windows Firewall, running on all
workstations and servers, are key, as well as network micro-segmentation. If the worm
can't get to the vulnerable service because firewalls are blocking the associated
network ports, it makes it harder for the attack to succeed.

19 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

The stakes are super high. Attackers have further evolved worms to leverage ransomware as
their payloads. Successful worms such as _WannaCry_, _Petya_, and _NotPetya_ demonstrated that
CISOs and security teams must work to mitigate worms or they could result in an extinction
event for their organizations.

Next, let's examine what a traditional network intrusion looks like.

**Traditional network intrusion**

Instead of relying on the randomness of a global malware attack, attackers carrying out
network intrusion attacks tend to target _specific_ victim organizations. This is the type of attack
that the MITRE ATT&CK enterprise matrix (MITRE Corporation, n.d.) and the classic intrusion
kill chain frameworks (Hutchins, E.M., Cloppert, M.J., Amin, R.M., Ph.D., n.d.) seek to help
mitigate. The MITRE ATT&CK framework provides lists of known attacker tactics and
techniques across the stages attackers can leverage during their attacks. These include
**reconnaissance**, **resource development**, **initial access**, **execution**, **persistence**, **privilege**
**escalation**, **defense evasion**, **credential access**, **discovery**, **lateral movement**, **collection**,
**command and control**, **exfiltration**, and **impact** (MITRE Corporation, n.d.).

This type of attack can progress as follows:

1.

2.

3.

4.

5.

Attackers decide which organization(s) they want to victimize and what their
objectives are (I will discuss attacker motivations later in this chapter).

They build, buy, or partner to develop weapons to use in the attack.

They gain initial access to the victim's network, deploy tools, find ways to stay
persistent on the network even after they are discovered, and evade defenders' efforts
to find them.

They use stolen credentials and add their own accounts in order to give themselves
permissions to access network resources and perform reconnaissance to discover
sensitive systems and data that can be collected and exfiltrated from the network.

They typically deploy command and control tools so that they can maintain access to
the network and take actions such as exfiltrating data or deploying ransomware, as
well as other illicit actions that align with their objectives.

_Chapter 1_ 20

_Figure 1.3_ illustrates an example of a traditional network intrusion on an enterprise IT
environment behind a firewall, where attackers deployed ransomware. Initial compromise is
achieved using one or more of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, which I'll discuss in detail
later in this chapter.

_Figure 1.3 – An illustration of a traditional network intrusion where attackers deployed ransomware_

The following subsections paint a more detailed picture of what one of these attacks looks like
by using a specific fictional example. The attack events have been categorized using some of
the tactics defined in the MITRE ATT&CK framework mentioned earlier.

**Initial access and execution**

Attackers use a targeted phishing email campaign to target specific users at a healthcare
organization. They send convincing phishing emails to 10 employees, identified using

21 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

LinkedIn, who are likely to have administrator access to the network, and who are also likely to
have IAM and service desk roles at the victim organization. Four of the 10 employees who
receive the phishing email open it and click on the embedded link. The link takes them to a site
that looks just like the Microsoft 365 portal they are accustomed to logging in to. One of the
four employees is a little more cautious and suspects that it might be a phishing site prior to
entering their credentials into it, while the other three are successfully tricked and enter their
valid login credentials into the web page.

The attackers have scripts that automatically use the harvested credentials to immediately log
in to the legitimate Microsoft 365 portal. All the employees had MFA enabled on their
accounts. Subsequently, when attackers attempt to log in to the employees' Microsoft 365
accounts, their smartphones prompt them to complete the portal login process by granting
approval in an authenticator app. The employees think they are logging in to the legitimate
Microsoft 365 portal, so the MFA prompt they receive is expected behavior, and they approve
the authentication request as they normally do. This gives attackers access to their accounts,
and they immediately add their own burner mobile devices as second factors to the accounts to
enable future logins without the employees' knowledge or participation. Now the attackers
have valid usernames, passwords, and second factors that will enable them to access Microsoft
365 **a** nd other access points to the network, such as via a **Virtual Private Network** ( **VPN** ) and
**Virtual Desktop Infrastructure** ( **VDI** ), anytime.

The attackers can now connect to the victim's network using a VPN connection with one of the
stolen credentials. Attackers perform some reconnaissance on the victim's network by running
legitimate tools (which are used by attackers regularly), such as Nmap, Advanced IP Scanner,
PowerShell, Mimikatz, and PsExec. This helps them identify all the administrator accounts in
the Active Directory and discover information that helps them move laterally on the network.

**Privilege escalation**

Now, the attackers focus on elevating their privileges by compromising some of the
administrator accounts they discovered. To do this, they successfully exploit a vulnerability
(such as CVE-2024-30088) that gives them system-level access to a domain controller that
wasn't patched. This enables them to add new administrator accounts in the Active Directory
for their own use.

**Exfiltration and credential access**

Next, they use a utility that's **i** nstalled by default on the domain controller called `ntdsutil.exe`
to export a copy of the healthcare organization's Active Directory. They upload that file (called

`ntds.dit` ) to a Google Drive account that they had previously compromised. They begin an
offline crack of the passwords that are encrypted in the `ntds.dit` file, which starts yielding
results within minutes. The shortest passwords get cracked almost instantly using virtual

_Chapter 1_ 22

machines with GPUs in the cloud. Now, the attackers have even more credentials to help them
stay persistent, move laterally, get access to sensitive data and exfiltrate it, and deploy
ransomware. This includes the KRBTGT user object that is created by default in every Active
Directory. Once the attackers are able to impersonate this object, they can impersonate any
user object in the Active Directory. At this point, containing the attack and recovering the
Active Directory to a known good state are aspirational goals for the victim organization.

**Impact**

After harvesting accounts and **d** ata from the victim's network for weeks or even months, the
attackers start to encrypt valuable sensitive data and the organization's most valuable systems,
including sensitive patient data, confidential financial data, and valuable intellectual property.
Encrypting only a portion of each file, instead of the entire file, with their ransomware allows
the attackers to devastate the victim's network and core infrastructure before the latter can
understand what is happening. The attackers leave a ransom note behind instructing the
organization to transfer $1.5 million in Bitcoin to them, giving the organization 48 hours to
comply. They pledge to destroy the key that would decrypt and unlock their systems if this
deadline is not met.

The attackers also threaten to publish the terabytes of data they exfiltrated to a victimshaming site that they manage. If this happens, it will make the attack public knowledge
because several media outlets and threat intelligence firms monitor the site for such
disclosures.

The healthcare organization's finance department has no idea how to buy and transfer Bitcoin
if they were to cede to the attackers' demands. Their senior management is hopeful that the
FBI will be able to help them. The likelihood of that happening is low, since the victimshaming
site the attackers referenced contains data from over 100 victims collected across three years,
showing that law enforcement has not been successful in assisting others.

After consulting with a ransomware negotiation firm, the healthcare organization is more
confident that they could pay the ransom and not violate the US Department of Treasury's
**Office of Foreign Assets Control** ( **OFAC** ) regulations or other legal prohibitions, since the
attackers aren't likely to be a known terrorist organization. The company makes the ransom
payment, and the attackers provide a decryption program and key. However, it quickly
becomes evident that it will take more time for the decryption program to decrypt files than
restoring them from backups the company took prior to the attack.

The attackers now issue a second ransom demand for $650,000 in exchange for their promise
not to sell access to the organization's network to other attackers who might perpetrate their
own network intrusions, steal sensitive data, encrypt files, and extort the victim all over again.
The CISO of the healthcare organization cannot guarantee that another threat actor wouldn't

23 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

be able to access their network, given all their credentials were stolen, and the attackers had
months of time to burrow into their infrastructure and systems. The CISO knows that,
according to industry estimates, it takes 290 days to detect and contain these types of breaches
(Okta, n.d.); the reality of the situation is that it will take months of work to contain and
eradicate the attackers' presence on their network.

Samples of the healthcare organization's sensitive data are posted to dark web victim-shaming
sites offering the full dataset for sale. A few hours later, a negative news cycle about the attack
starts with three articles published by different news outlets that saw the posts on dark
websites they monitor. Shortly afterward, the organization's customers and partners start
calling them to find out what is happening, whether their data was stolen, and whether they
need to take steps to protect themselves. The call volume overwhelms their call centers. The
organization struggles to meet the data breach disclosure rules that they need to comply with
because their systems are still mostly down, and they still don't have all the details needed to
explain how the attack happened, what specific datasets were exfiltrated by attackers, and
when the attack started. It only takes a few days before attorneys, threatening class action
lawsuits on behalf of customers, start contacting the organization, although it's still not clear
exactly which customers were impacted.

In the wake of this attack, the CISO and other executives prepare for months of meetings with
attorneys, regulators, auditors, customers, and partners in order to meet all legal and
regulatory requirements, defend themselves from legal actions, retain their customers and
partners, and try to repair the organization's damaged reputation.

**Mitigating traditional network intrusions**

From the description I provided, it should be clear that a traditional network intrusion is
hardly fun or even easy to deal with. This is why most CISOs and security teams focus on
protecting assets in ways that make it harder for attackers to succeed and easier for defenders
to detect their presence on the network as early in the attack as possible.

Mitigating traditional network intrusions in large enterprise environments is very challenging.
If it were easy, cybersecurity would not be a multi-billion-dollar industry growing at double
digits annually. In this attack scenario, a holistic cybersecurity strategy is required because the
attack surface of a typical enterprise is too large for a narrower approach to be successful.
There are several chapters in this book dedicated to helping you understand cybersecurity

_Chapter 1_ 24

strategies and developing a strategy or combination of strategies that will give you the best
chance of success.

Next, let's look at another common type of attack—data breaches caused by insecure APIs.

**Data breaches via insecure APIs**

Today, enterprises use APIs for everything from publishing and consuming data to
provisioning and remotely controlling huge fleets of virtual systems. APIs are everywhere.
Securing APIs can be complicated because it typically requires participation across disciplines
to accomplish; developers and testers, IT systems and infrastructure operators, and
cybersecurity roles all play parts in securing APIs. Attackers know that APIs are everywhere and
that it is challenging to secure them. Subsequently, data breaches due to insecure APIs have
become a common attack vector. Let's look at a fictional but realistic example of such an
attack.

In this scenario, a municipal government department wants to enable self-service for their
customers on their website, for better customer satisfaction while also reducing costs
associated with calls to their call center. The department wants to allow their customers to
request additional garbage cans, reduce the number of garbage cans they pay for, or cancel
their service.

To facilitate this, they publish a web page with instructions for their customers, which includes
a field for customers to enter their municipality account numbers. The account number
entered is used to validate that they are a legitimate customer. Legitimate customers are
redirected to another web page that asks them more questions to prove that they are the
customer they say they are, such as their name, address, phone number, zip code, and date of
birth. People without a known customer account are directed to a web page where they can
open an account if their residence is in the municipality and they qualify for the garbage
pickup service.

One morning, the CISO of the department is approached by a news reporter for comment on
the data breach that they have apparently suffered. The CISO is confused because they are not
aware of any data breach. The CISO gets their **Cyber Threat Intelligence** ( **CTI** ) program
manager to check their CTI vendor's portal for any threat intelligence indicating a data breach.
It is found that a dark website claims that the department has suffered a data breach,
presenting a small sample of "stolen" customer data as evidence. The CISO asks the CTI
program manager to work with the department's database administrator to determine
whether the data is legitimate customer data, and it is found that it is.

25 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

The CISO immediately mobilizes their IR team to start an investigation. They have many
questions:

How did their network get compromised?

Are their key systems going to be encrypted next?

Should they be preparing for a ransom demand? Which user accounts do the attackers
have control of?

What steps should they be taking to contain the attacker?

The department's IR lead traces the data back to a specific database that contains the same
fields as the stolen data. Although it is still too early in the investigation to be conclusive, they
have found no **Indicators of Compromise** ( **IOCs** ) for the database or any of the servers. There
is no indication of any unauthorized access in the log files. Over the next few days, the IR team
performs a painstaking forensic examination of the database and all the servers. At the end of
their analysis, they are convinced that there was no network intrusion. The investigation also
strongly suggests that the data was not stolen by a malicious insider because there were no
abnormal authentication events in the system logs.

The CISO receives an email from one of the network operations engineers who works with the
development team. Her email indicates that she has identified some anomalous network traffic
on the municipality's website a week before the leaked data was discovered on the dark web.
The traffic to the website was normal but showed a sudden spike that lasted a few hours. She
determines that the network traffic spike was due to traffic to and from the new customer selfservice web page. Her analysis shows that a dozen IP addresses in different countries around
the world used that web page. The web page generated queries that were sent to the backend
database via an API. This caused the spike in network traffic.

The network operations engineer shares her findings with the IR team, the development team,
and the IT operations team. From this data, the development team determines that the API was
used to query the database for customer accounts in quick succession, by simply incrementing
the account number for each new query. Each time a query was sent, a response came back
from the database to the API. There were numerous "account number not valid" responses, but
there were also hundreds of responses to queries where valid account numbers were provided.

The CISO is irate. How could this happen? After all, the **d** epartment has a **Web Application**
**Firewall** ( **WAF** ) that is supposed to block such attacks. Plus, that API shouldn't be returning
customer data to that public web page; if the purpose of the query is just to determine whether
the account number is valid, it should just return "account number not valid" or "account
number valid." The development manager explains to the CISO that a developer on their team
used the wrong API for the query on the web page. Instead of the API returning an "account
number valid" response when a valid account number is entered, the API returns several fields

_Chapter 1_ 26

in the database record that contain the customer's personal information. This is the
information that was leaked to the dark web by attackers. The developer had used an API
designed for use on the department's internal network, not for use on a publicly accessible web
page on the internet. They didn't think anyone would see the customer information that the
API returns because it isn't displayed on the web page. It was a simple mistake, but
devastatingly naive.

This issue wasn't caught in testing because the web page wasn't designed to display any of the
data that the API returned—it just indicates whether a valid customer account was found.
However, if the attacker captured the network packets going between their workstations and
the department's website or used free web development tools to debug the department's
customer self-service web page, all the data being returned by the API would be visible to
them. The department's WAF didn't prevent the attack because the web page and API were not
being attacked using **SQL injection**, **Cross-Site Request Forgery**, or any of the typical web
application attacks. The web page and API were operating exactly how they had been designed
to operate.

As the IR investigation progresses, customers begin to hear in the news and from some
industry vendors that the department's network has been compromised. This frustrates the
CISO because the attackers never penetrated their perimeter, never moved laterally on their
network, and never found a way to stay persistent in their IT environment. There was no
network intrusion. The attacker simply sat on the public internet and sent queries to an
insecure API that returned data that it shouldn't have returned.

This type of data breach via an insecure API seems to be a daily occurrence across industries
and around the world. The proliferation of APIs exposed to the internet has outpaced the
adoption of security and privacy standards by developers that would help minimize the
number of vulnerable APIs. Given the rapid and largely ungoverned proliferation of APIs, the
number of APIs with vulnerabilities today is incalculable.

27 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

**Mitigating data breaches via insecure APIs**

Mitigating these types of issues with APIs is very challenging. There are at least two categories
of applications that need attention:

Applications that are currently being developed for release in the future that expose
APIs

Applications that are already in production that expose APIs

A **security development life cycle** that includes security and privacy requirements and
standards for the development of APIs can help in both categories. However, what triggers a
security review for applications already in production? This is the difficult question. Asked
another way, when should developers in your organization stop developing new applications
and spend time reviewing the old ones that were already released? Unfortunately for most
organizations, the answer is when the exploitation of a critical vulnerability in the old
application has been demonstrated either by attackers or in a penetration test. In a world with
limited resources, most organizations simply can't afford to shift resources from work that will
attract more customers, lower costs, and help beat the competition to vulnerabilities they view
as theoretical. Regardless, developers need to be educated on **privacy by design** principles that
help inform the decisions they make when designing and developing applications.

**Threat modeling** can also be an immensely powerful tool. Identifying the things that could go
wrong before developers start writing code means issues can be addressed in the design rather
than after the code is in production. Developers and architects should be trained to perform
threat modeling, and it should be required for new application development.

**Firewalls**, **WAFs**, and **API security platforms** can all play roles in mitigating some issues with
APIs. For example, configuring API query rate limits so that attackers can't drain the database
in a short period of time will give defenders a better opportunity to detect attacks and respond.
In the fictional scenario I described, there was no valid reason for the municipal department to
allow network traffic or API queries from outside their own country; after all, they aren't going
to pick up garbage for customers in other countries. They could not have saved any money by
allowing their customers to adjust the number of garbage cans they have at their home in the
US from Russia or China. There is much more risk than reward in such cases. Restricting
inbound and outbound internet traffic on firewalls to the bare minimum will make it harder
for attackers. By themselves, none of these are silver bullet solutions, but together, they make it
harder for attackers to be successful. Every enterprise and CISO shares the challenge of API
security. So, I have dedicated _Chapter 7_, _Application Programming Interface Security_, to API
security.

The next section discusses the conclusions we can draw from comparing and contrasting the
three types of attacks described in this section.

_Chapter 1_ 28

**Lessons learned: Real-world attack scenarios – conclusions**

The reason I wanted to show you three different types of attacks was to illustrate that not all
data breaches are the same. When you hear about a data breach in the news or your
organization experiences one, don't assume the worst-case scenario. The difference between a
traditional network intrusion and the other two real-world attack scenarios can be
pronounced for victims.

A **traditional network intrusion** can be an extinction event for victims, depending on the
attacker's motivations and whether the attack goes undetected. While a **data breach via an**
**API** can expose sensitive information, victims' infrastructures aren't typically impacted in this
case, and the business can typically continue unabated. Both types of attacks can potentially
have bad legal, regulatory, and reputational outcomes, but extinction for the organization is
unlikely when an attacker simply repeatedly queries an insecure API from the internet.

The potential impact of worms is typically more random. Once a worm is released into the
wild, where it ends up is largely uncontrolled. Even when a worm's developer has a specific
target in mind, they can rarely control the unintended consequences once the worm is
released.

Take the _Stuxnet worm_ as an example, which was developed to target **Programmable Logic**
**Controllers** ( **PLCs** ) leveraging **f** our vulnerabilities. The purported and specific goal of the
attack was to disrupt centrifuges used to enrich uranium at a nuclear facility in Iran. However,
since three of the vulnerabilities that the worm leveraged were in Microsoft Windows, once the
worm was released at the nuclear facility, it found ways to escape onto the public internet,
where it continued to infect systems for years after the initial attack. Other purveyors of
malware began using the same vulnerabilities Stuxnet used in their own malware and
continued to compromise unpatched systems for years (Kaspersky, 2014).

Organizations might or might not be impacted by worms released to the internet. The impacts
on affected organizations might be terrible or limited. There are a number of factors that
influence such outcomes.

You might still be wondering, how do attackers continue to be successful despite
organizations' substantial investments in cybersecurity? Is there a secret to their success? To
answer this question, let's examine how enterprise IT environments get compromised in the
first place, that is, so-called initial access. This is key to understanding, developing, and
evaluating the effectiveness of cybersecurity strategies for enterprise IT environments.
###### **How organizations get initially compromised**

The foundation of an effective cybersecurity strategy is what I call the **cybersecurity**
**fundamentals** . The cybersecurity fundamentals are based on decades of threat intelligence

29 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

that I discuss in detail later in this book. After performing hundreds of IR investigations and
studying Microsoft's and other vendors' threat intelligence for over a decade, I can tell you
with confidence that there are only five ways that organizations initially get compromised. I
call them the "Cybersecurity Usual Suspects":

Unpatched vulnerabilities

Security misconfigurations

Weak, leaked, and stolen credentials

Social engineering

Insider threats

After the initial compromise, there are many, many **Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures**
( **TTPs** ) that attackers can use to move laterally, steal credentials, compromise infrastructure,
remain persistent, gain illicit access to information, destroy data and infrastructure, and so on.
Some of these have been around for decades, and some are newer and novel.

Let's look at each one of these usual suspects in more detail, starting with the exploitation of
unpatched vulnerabilities.

**Unpatched vulnerabilities**

A vulnerability is a flaw in software or hardware design and/or the underlying programming
code that allows an attacker to make the affected system do something unintended. The most
severe vulnerabilities allow attackers to take complete control of the affected system, running
arbitrary code of their choice. Less severe vulnerabilities lead to systems disclosing data in
unintended ways or denying service to legitimate users.

Attackers have been using vulnerabilities to compromise systems at scale since at least the
days of Code Red and Nimda in 2001. In 2003, SQL Slammer and Blaster successfully disrupted
the internet and compromised hundreds of thousands of systems worldwide by exploiting
unpatched vulnerabilities in Microsoft SQL Server and Microsoft Windows operating systems.
In the years following these attacks, a cottage industry developed an ongoing effort to help
enterprise organizations—those with the most complex environments—inventory their IT
systems, identify vulnerabilities in them, deploy mitigations for vulnerabilities, and patch
them. At the end of January 2026, over 241,000 vulnerabilities had been disclosed in software

_Chapter 1_ 30

and hardware products from across the industry in the National Vulnerability Database
(National Vulnerability Database, n.d.). As you'll read in _Chapter 3_, the number of
vulnerabilities disclosed across the industry surged by 128% between 2016 and 2017, reaching
levels never seen before. The number of vulnerability disclosures has increased year over year
every year since, exceeding 48,400 disclosures in 2025.

An economy has evolved around the supply and demand for vulnerabilities and exploits, with a
varied list of participants, including vendors, attackers, defenders, various commercial entities,
and governments. The number of participants in this economy and their relative sophistication
make it harder for organizations to protect themselves from the exploitation of vulnerabilities
in their IT environments. Therefore, using unpatched vulnerabilities becomes a mainstay of
attackers' toolkits.

Organizations that are highly competent at vulnerability management make it much harder for
attackers to successfully attack them. A well-run vulnerability management program is a
fundamental component and a critical requirement of an effective cybersecurity strategy.
Without it, organizations' cybersecurity efforts will fail regardless of their other investments.
Unpatched vulnerabilities in operating systems and the underlying platform components that
even advanced cybersecurity capabilities rely on enable attackers to completely undermine the
effectiveness of these investments. Failing to efficiently address ongoing vulnerability
disclosures in the "trusted computing base" that your hardware and software rely on renders
your hardware and software untrustworthy.

**The importance of asset inventories**

An accurate inventory of **a** ll IT assets is critical for a vulnerability management program.
Organizations that can't perform accurate and timely inventories of all their IT assets, scan all
IT assets for vulnerabilities, and efficiently mitigate and/or patch those vulnerabilities end up
accepting a lot of risk. The following is some advice about asset management inventories.

**The risk of incomplete asset inventories**

Assets that don't show up in inventories won't get scanned or patched and will become the
weak link in your security chain. Therefore, if the CISO and vulnerability management program
managers rely on their organization's IT group or other internal partners to provide IT asset
inventories, those inventories need to be complete and not just include systems that they are
willing to patch. I've seen asset owners and operators willfully conceal IT assets from their
vulnerability management teams because they didn't want those assets to be enrolled in the
regular vulnerability scanning process and subject to the SLAs specified in their organization's
vulnerability management policy. I've seen a range of reasons stated for this behavior,
including the belief that security updates would destabilize critical systems, or that the
systems were just test systems on the production network that the policy didn't apply to.

31 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

However, more commonly, the asset owners simply can't keep up with the pace of new
vulnerability disclosures because they haven't increased resource levels over the years to do so.

**The tension with uptime goals**

Another reason asset owners and operators choose to conceal assets or consistently ask for
vulnerability management policy exceptions to delay patching assets is the _reboots associated_
_with patching_ . Rebooting systems after they have been patched is at odds with the uptime
objectives that IT organizations are measured against, because patching vulnerabilities
increases the number of system reboots and, subsequently, decreases uptime even if
everything goes smoothly.

Rebooting a healthy but very busy database server, for example, can take more time than the
