annual downtime budget permits for a server. Organizations that view the time it takes to
install security updates as a blight on their uptime objectives need to reconsider their
objectives. Organizations require systems to be online to serve their stakeholders' interests.
However, if those servers are taken offline, temporarily or indefinitely, by an avoidable
cybersecurity attack, those objectives clearly aren't met. Only by realizing that IT asset owners,
operators, and their cybersecurity teams all have a shared destiny can they be successful. They
need to adopt SLAs that help them keep fully patched systems continuously meeting
stakeholder requirements, not just running in production. Renegotiating SLA uptime goals
with provisions for regular and emergency security updates is one potential way to accomplish
this.

**The importance of independent verification**

My advice in scenarios where asset inventories are provided by parties other than the
vulnerability management program itself is to _trust but verify_ . Spend the extra effort and budget
to continually check asset inventories against reality. This includes those official and unofficial
development and test environments that have been responsible for so many breaches in the
industry over the years. Shadow IT and unofficial cloud accounts also fall into this category.
Customers, partners, and employees won't care any less if their data was stolen from a test

account instead of a production account.

If the sources of asset inventories resist this requirement or fail to provide accurate, timely
inventories, this represents a risk that the organization's senior leadership and the board of
directors should be aware of. Providing senior leadership with a view of the estimated
percentage of the total asset inventory currently not managed by your vulnerability

_Chapter 1_ 32

management program should result in the sources of asset inventories reprioritizing their
work—a disruption of a dangerous status quo.

Some of the CISOs I have talked to have taken ownership of the IT asset management
programs for their organizations. This can be a significant amount of work in large IT
environments. However, they do this because asset management is critical to operating a
successful vulnerability management program.

I'll discuss traditional vulnerability management in greater detail in _Chapter 3_, and _Chapter 4_ .
I'll also discuss modern approaches to vulnerability management in _Chapter 13_, _Modern_
_Approaches to Security and Compliance_ . The cloud can render the old-fashioned methods of
inventorying, scanning, and patching security vulnerabilities obsolete.

**Bring your own device**

Of course, one challenge with the approach I just described is environments that have
embraced **Bring-Your-Own-Device** ( **BYOD** ) policies that allow employees to use their
personal mobile devices to access and process enterprise data. The underlying question is
whether enterprise vulnerability management teams should inventory and manage personal
devices. This debate is one reason why many security professionals originally dubbed BYOD as
"bring your own disaster."

Different organizations take different approaches when answering this question. Here are
some of the approaches I've seen:

**Corporate-owned devices** : Some organizations decide to solve their mobile
computing requirements by procuring mobile devices for their workers and fully
managing them. This gives them full control of these devices, but it is typically an
expensive option considering the costs of buying the hardware and actively managing
it over time.

**Personal devices** : Many cost-conscious organizations simply allow their workers to
use their own devices for business purposes. This is typically the least expensive option
but provides the least amount of control and visibility. These organizations rely on
their workers to patch their mobile devices and report any misplacements. Hope plays
a big part in the security strategy for organizations that employ this approach. They

33 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

hope nothing bad will happen to these devices because some of their data is accessible
from these devices or might even be stored on these devices. However, they likely won't
know if something bad does happen as these devices are completely unmanaged.

**Hybrid or passive management approach** : A popular approach is a passive
management model, where users are required to have an access PIN on their personal
devices. This provides at least one layer of protection for the device contents if the
device is lost or stolen.
Additionally, these devices aren't allowed to connect to their employers' networks if
the latest mobile operating system version isn't installed. Some organizations take
device health verification one step further by employing **Network Access Control**
( **NAC** ) or **Network Access Protection** ( **NAP** ) technologies to help enforce policies
related to the health of systems connecting to their network. Microsoft Intune and Jamf
are popular choices for mobile device management, among many others.

These characteristics make endpoints more trustworthy because they meet minimum
security standards, thus reducing the likelihood that they are compromised and could
provide attackers with entry into the corporate network. If an endpoint doesn't meet
these minimum standards, remote connection requests from it are refused until it
complies with the policy and has a "clean bill of health."

Regardless of the approach adopted, minimizing the number of unpatched systems allowed to
connect to enterprise networks is a best practice.

Next, we'll consider security misconfigurations. Like unpatched vulnerabilities, security
misconfigurations can potentially enable attackers to take a range of actions on a system,
including disrupting its operation, stealing information, lowering security settings, disabling
security features, seizing control of it, and using it to attack other systems.

**Security misconfigurations**

Security misconfigurations can be present in a system as a default setting, such as a preset key
or password that is the same on every system manufactured by a vendor. Security

_Chapter 1_ 34

misconfigurations can also be introduced gradually as a system's configuration changes
incrementally as it gets managed over time.

This is especially true of internet-facing systems such as **web servers**, **firewalls**, and other
systems found in enterprise **Demilitarized Zones** ( **DMZs** ). If a misconfiguration lets an
attacker take control of a system in the DMZ—or use it to issue authenticated requests on their
behalf, such as through a server‑side request forgery—they will try to use that foothold to
access other systems in the DMZ and eventually pivot into the organization's internal network.
This has been a common pattern in attackers' playbooks for more than 20 years.

Security misconfigurations have also plagued endpoint devices, such as PCs, smartphones, and
**Internet of Things** ( **IoT** ) devices. The infrastructure that these endpoints connect to, such as
wireless access points, is also frequently probed by attackers for common misconfigurations.
Security misconfigurations have also been an issue in **Industrial Control Systems** ( **ICSs** ) for
many years. For example, one scenario involving ICSs that has burned security teams in the
past is "fall back to last known status," which can override more recent security configuration
changes in favor of former, less secure settings. Hardcoded credentials, which are the same on
every device that a manufacturer sells, and vulnerable default configurations have longhaunted manufacturers of all sorts of software and hardware across the industry. Once
attackers learn that specific devices from specific manufacturers all have the same default
password or unchangeable backdoor for their developers, they quickly become perennial
targets.

A well-run vulnerability management program typically includes identifying security
misconfigurations as part of its scope. Many of the same vulnerability scanners and tools that
are used to identify and patch security vulnerabilities are also capable of identifying security
misconfigurations and providing guidance on how to address them. Some vulnerability
scanners can assess whether system configurations align with widely adopted security
baselines, such as the **Center for Internet Security (CIS)** Benchmarks (Center for Internet
Security, n.d.) or an organization's own internal configuration standards.

Again, organizations should forego big investments in advanced cybersecurity capabilities if
they aren't already very proficient at identifying and mitigating security misconfigurations in
their environment. For instance, there's no point in spending a lot of money and effort looking
for **Advanced Persistent Threats** ( **APTs** ) in an environment if attackers can use decades-old

35 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

lists of hardcoded passwords available on the internet to successfully compromise and move
around the environment. Even if CISOs found such attackers in their IT environment, they
would be powerless to exorcise them with common security misconfigurations present.

Some of the biggest breaches in history were a result of an initial compromise through a
combination of unpatched vulnerabilities and security misconfigurations. Both can be
managed through a well-run vulnerability management program. Some CISOs rely on their
offensive security teams to ferret out misconfigurations during **red team operations**, **attack**
**simulations**, or **cybersecurity control testing** . In some cases, these will be more effective
approaches than leveraging vulnerability management tools.

Security misconfigurations can be present by default in new hardware and software or may
creep in over time. Another ongoing threat that requires constant attention is that of
compromised credentials, discussed next.

**Weak, leaked, and stolen credentials**

There's an old saying in the cybersecurity industry: "attackers don't break in, they log in." You
might have also heard, "identity is the new firewall." These reflect the fact that compromised
IT environments due to weak, leaked, or stolen credentials are common. In 2024, Microsoft
reported, "Microsoft Entra data shows that of more than 600 million identity attacks per day,
more than 99% are password-based" (Microsoft, 2024). That's 7,000 password attacks blocked
per second, on average, for the entire year!

There are several ways that credentials get leaked and stolen: **social engineering**, such as
**phishing**, malware that does **keystroke logging** or steals credentials from operating systems
and browsers, and **compromised systems** that **c** ache, store, and/or process credentials.
Sometimes, developers accidentally expose secrets by uploading projects to code-sharing sites
and forgetting to remove any keys or passwords that were embedded in their code. When those
code-sharing sites get compromised, all those secrets are exposed. Similarly, old development
and test environments that are abandoned but left running ultimately yield credentials to
attackers after not being patched over time. Further, some attackers pay insiders to provide

_Chapter 1_ 36

stolen credentials to them. And, of course, as you read in the traditional network intrusion
scenario earlier in the chapter, if attackers successfully exfiltrate an organization's `ntds.dit` (a
copy of their Active Directory), all their credentials are now potentially exposed and can be
sold by access brokers or might simply start to show up in lists of compromised credentials on
the dark web. In fact, many organizations struggle to rotate all their passwords after such an
intrusion because non-human accounts, such as service accounts, likely have never been
rotated before. It can take months to rotate all passwords, while in the meantime, attackers can
continue to use credentials that haven't been rotated.

Massive lists of stolen and leaked credentials have been discovered on the internet over the
years. In addition to these lists, the availability of **High-Performance Computing Clusters**
( **HPCs** ) and GPU-based password-cracking tools has rendered passwords, by themselves,
ineffective in protecting resources and accounts.

The following describes in detail how attackers might use stolen credentials:

1.

2.

3.

4.

When an on-premises enterprise environment is initially compromised, attackers use
leaked or stolen credentials for reconnaissance and look for other credentials that are
cached or stored in the environment. They especially look for administrator credentials
that could give them unlimited access to resources in the compromised environment.

Typically, within seconds of the initial compromise, attackers try to access the victim
organization's user account directory service, such as Microsoft Active Directory, to
dump all the credentials in the directory (the aforementioned `ntds.dit` file). The more
credentials they have at their disposal to move and stay persistent, the harder it is to
expel them from the environment—they can persist indefinitely.

Attackers will also try to steal user account databases. If attackers successfully get all
the credentials from their victim's directory service, then recovery really is aspirational.

Once attackers have stolen hashed credentials, traditionally the weakest of these
credentials can be cracked in offline attacks in under an hour (Kaspersky, 2024).

Longer, uncommon, and truly complex passwords will get cracked last. There have been raging
debates for decades about the efficacy of passwords versus passphrases, as well as appropriate
character lengths, character sets, password lockout policies, password expiration policies, and
the like. Guidance for passwords has changed over the years as threats and risks have changed
and new data has become available. Microsoft has published guidance for Microsoft 365
password policies that is definitely worth a read (Microsoft 2025).

When credentials are leaked or stolen from an organization, it doesn't take attackers long to
run them through scripts that try to log in to financial institutions, e-commerce sites, social
networking sites, and other sites in the hopes that the credentials were reused somewhere.
Reusing passwords across accounts is a terrible practice. Simply put, credentials that provide

37 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

access to more than one account have a higher ROI for attackers than those that don't. Sets of
compromised credentials that can provide access to corporate resources and information, as
well as social networks, which can also serve as a rich source of information and potential
victims, are valuable.

The usefulness of passwords by themselves to protect enterprise resources has long passed.
Consequently, using MFA is a requirement for enterprises and consumers alike. MFA can
mitigate stolen and leaked credentials in many, but not all, scenarios. When MFA is used, even
if attackers possess a valid username and password for an account, they won't get access to the
account unless they also possess the other authentication factor required. These other factors
include digital certificates, one-time passwords, and PINs generated on dedicated hardware or
smartphone apps; a call to a preregistered landline or mobile phone; fingerprints; and facial
recognition.

However, there have been some successful attacks on some MFA methods as well, for example,
**SIM-swapping attacks** to intercept PIN codes sent to preregistered mobile phones via SMS.
Another limitation of MFA is that it isn't ubiquitous in enterprise IT environments.
Organizations with decades-old legacy applications using old-fashioned authentication and
authorization methods are less likely to fully mitigate the risk with MFA. Even if the latest
systems and cloud-based services require MFA, chances are there are more legacy applications
that cannot utilize it easily.

Several CISOs that I've talked to have experienced this limitation firsthand during penetration
tests that exposed the limitations of MFA in their environments. Some vendors specialize in
mitigating such MFA-related risks; one such vendor is called Silverfort (Silverfort, n.d.).

The following are some best practices to follow to protect your organization against credential
leaks or theft:

Using unique passwords for every account can help mitigate this risk. If a password is
unique and it is leaked or stolen, its potential usefulness to attackers will be limited. If
you have too many accounts to assign and track unique passwords for, then use a
password vault to make life easier. There are numerous commercially available
products for consumers and enterprises.

MFA can be very effective; use it everywhere that usernames and passwords are in use.
Microsoft has published a great blog post about the effectiveness of MFA called _Your_
_Pa$$word Doesn't Matter_ (Weinert, 2019), which is recommended reading.

Leveraging passkeys can also be very helpful. Passkeys are a passwordless
authentication method that uses cryptographic key pairs stored on a user's device to
verify identity without ever transmitting a secret that can be phished or stolen. They
replace passwords by relying on biometrics or device-level unlock mechanisms. This

_Chapter 1_ 38

makes them resistant to credential theft and replay attacks. More information is
available on the FIDO Alliance website at `[https://fidoalliance.org/passkeys/](https://fidoalliance.org/passkeys/)` .

Plan for failure; that is, plan for when your organization's `ntds.dit` file gets stolen.
Relatively long passwords or passphrases will make offline cracking of stolen
passwords harder and slower for attackers, which in turn will give your organization
more time to rotate all their passwords before attackers can harvest and use them.
Passwords or passphrases that are 15 characters or longer pose a significant hurdle for
offline cracking tools. Where possible, prevent users from using variations of their old
passwords. Attackers have developed novel methods of using old leaked and stolen
passwords to derive uncreative users' likely new passwords. Use a password manager
solution if these requirements are too hard for users to manage.

You should know whether your organization is leaking credentials and how old those
leaked credentials are. Using a service that collects leaked and stolen credentials and
looks for your organization's credentials being sold and traded online can give you a
little peace of mind that you aren't missing something obvious. Getting some idea of
the age of these credentials can help you decide whether password resets are necessary
and the number of people potentially impacted.

Privileged access management solutions can detect credential theft and credential
misuse attacks (such as pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, and golden ticket attacks), as
well as attackers' lateral movement and reconnaissance in your infrastructure:

Many of these solutions also offer password vaulting, credential brokering, and
specialized analytics. Some of these solutions can be noisy and prone to false
positives, but still, they can help you to manage and detect weak, leaked, and
stolen credentials.

In cloud-based environments, IAM controls are the most powerful controls you have.
Taking advantage of all the power that IAM controls offer can help you to protect and
detect threats to resources in the cloud. But this is one control set area that can
proliferate into an unmanageable mess quickly. Extra thoughtful planning around your
organization's IAM strategy will pay huge security dividends.

I will discuss identity a little more in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_ .

An important aspect of protecting credentials involves educating information workers to be
aware of social engineering attacks in which attackers may attempt to steal credentials
through methods such as phishing. This is not the only way in which social engineering is used
to compromise systems, however. I'll cover social engineering in a little more detail next.

39 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

**Social engineering**

Of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, social engineering **i** s the most widely used method.
Simply put, social engineering involves tricking users into making poor trust decisions.
Examples of poor trust decisions include lowering the security posture of a system by changing
its settings without understanding the possible outcomes of doing so or unknowingly
installing malware on a system. Attackers rely on the naivety of their victims in social
engineering attacks.

The volume of social engineering attacks is orders of magnitude larger than other types of
attacks. For example, the volume of email phishing attacks Microsoft reported for July 2019
was 0.85% of the more than 470 billion email messages that flowed through Office 365 that
month (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). That's 4 billion phishing emails that all relied on social
engineering detected in a single month. Microsoft reported that the domains used in phishing
attacks grew consistently between July 2022 and June 2023, with the period ending with four
times more domains used for phishing (Microsoft, 2023). Attackers continue to use phishing
because it continues to be successful for them. Microsoft reported that between April and June
2023, they alerted users about roughly 10,000 instances per month in which passwords were
entered into malicious websites (Microsoft, 2023). Although it doesn't appear that Microsoft
has published updated phishing volume data for more recent time periods, they have shared
how they have observed attackers leveraging AI to improve phishing attacks:

_"AI-automated phishing emails achieved 54% click-through rates compared to 12%_
_for standard attempts—a 4.5x increase. AI enables more targeted phishing and_
_better phishing lures. More concerning, AI automation has the potential to increase_
_phishing profitability by up to 50 times by scaling highly targeted attacks to_
_thousands of targets at minimal cost." (Microsoft, 2025)_

I discuss phishing in greater detail in _Chapter 6_, _Internet-Based Threats_ .

Trojan, a category of malware that relies on social engineering to be successful, has been the
most prevalent category of malware for many years. In a recent Microsoft Digital Defense
Report, data from Microsoft Defender for Office 365 indicates that 775 million email messages
contained malware between July 2023 and June 2024 (Microsoft Corporation, 2024). I'll
discuss this category of malware and many others in detail in _Chapter 5_ .

Given the massive volume of social engineering attacks and their historical record of success,
mitigating these attacks really isn't optional for enterprises. A fundamental component of an
enterprise cybersecurity strategy is a mitigation strategy for social engineering attacks. Put
another way, not including social engineering attacks in your cybersecurity strategy would
mean ignoring the most common way that organizations initially get compromised.

_Chapter 1_ 40

Social engineering attacks are typically perpetrated by attackers external to organizations, so
users must be prepared through appropriate education and training.

Another challenging threat to defend against is one from within. The final potential route of
initial compromise, which we'll discuss next, is that of the insider threat.

**Insider threats**

When discussing insider threats with CISOs and security teams, I find it useful to break them
down into two different categories, listed here from most likely to least likely:

1.

2.

**Non-malicious intent** : This includes mistakes or poor trust decisions that lead to bad
security outcomes. Unfortunately, I've seen too many incidents start with this
subcategory of insider threats. Some of the worst outcomes include administrators
making high-risk configuration changes without going through their organization's
governance or change control approval processes because they were in a hurry or were
troubleshooting something. Further, poorly thought-through changes to internetfacing firewalls and WAFs that have very bad outcomes seem to be two perennial
examples of such mistakes.

**Malicious intent** : This includes insiders, such as employees or contractors who use
their privileged access to steal information or otherwise negatively impact the
confidentiality, integrity, or availability of the organization's IT and/or data. Malicious
insiders can be motivated by many different things, including their compensation or
title not progressing relative to their expectations, or if they get enticed by financial
incentives offered by attackers. I discuss a broader range of motivations later in this
chapter. Most CISOs I've talked to have three subcategories of malicious insiders in
mind:
The **lone wolf insider** who works by themselves, abusing the privileged access they
have to their organization's infrastructure and data for their own benefit.

A **small group** of individuals who work together to accomplish unauthorized activities
that none of the group members could achieve alone.

A **mass conspiracy**, where multiple insiders work together to overcome the separation
of duties that distributes the span of security control. I've found that CISOs typically
bring this subcategory up in discussions about risks in managed service provider
environments and the cloud, asserting that the entirety of US cloud service providers
are corrupt. I discuss this in more detail in _Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe? The Roles_
_Governments Play in Cybersecurity_ .

41 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

Mitigating insider threats should be fundamental to enterprise-wide cybersecurity strategies.
Enforcing _meaningful separation of duties_ and embracing _the principle of least privilege_ are helpful,
as are _automation_, _monitoring_, and _auditing_ .

From a tools perspective, it has been interesting to watch different approaches emerge in this
space. Some vendors offer products that are grounded in **endpoint forensics** that enable
investigators to get visibility into every keystroke and mouse click users make. Other vendors
have developed products where DLP is central, tracking how users access data and how and
where data moves. Some others offer **deception technology** that helps identify insiders who
poke around network resources without any business cause to do so.

I became a big fan of deception technology after seeing how it can be used to detect insider
threats. There are a few different approaches to deception technology, but the basic concept is
to present attackers with a system, potentially with publicly known vulnerabilities or common
security misconfigurations, that alerts defenders to the presence of attackers when attackers
interact with the system. I've heard some security professionals refer to this as a "canary in the
coal mine" for IT environments.

Something to consider as part of the insider threat tool selection process is to develop some
**insider threat risk indicators** . These indicators can help predict whether an insider might
turn malicious. Some common indicators include declining performance, declining interest in
the goals of the organization, spending less time at work, suddenly printing lots of documents,
or exfiltrating files from work to their personal cloud storage service. Other effective indicators
might be associated with the type of organization, the organization's culture, the country
where they work, and their customs and culture. Some insiders turn malicious after they have

_Chapter 1_ 42

tendered their resignations. This is a key time to watch for and detect malicious activities such
as data exfiltration. Developing a list of the indicators that you think will be effective can help
with choosing the right insider threat tool for your program and give you a better chance at
detecting insider threats.

You are now well versed in the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, that is, the five ways
organizations are initially compromised. Defending against these five vectors of attack is
fundamental to effective cybersecurity.
###### **Focusing on the cybersecurity fundamentals**

In order to achieve a successful cybersecurity program, organizations need to get very good at
continuously mitigating all five of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects. This competency forms
the foundation of a sound cybersecurity strategy. Other cybersecurity-related investments will
potentially have diminishing returns if the foundation of the strategy is not solid.

After an attacker uses one or more of these five ways to initially compromise an organization,
they might employ a plethora of novel and advanced TTPs. Organizations that focus on the
cybersecurity fundamentals make it much harder for attackers to be successful; that is, by
focusing on the inside 85% of the bell curve shown in _Figure 1.4_, in which the cybersecurity
fundamentals sit, instead of the activities in the outlying 7.5% on either end of the curve,
security teams will have a better chance at success.

_Figure 1.4 – A bell curve illustrating that most security teams should spend their time on the_

_cybersecurity fundamentals_

Unfortunately, the allure of hunting APTs can take resources away from the less sexy but
critical work in the middle of the curve.

If there really are only five ways that organizations get initially compromised, why does there
seem to be so much confusion in the industry on proper priorities for cybersecurity programs? I
think there are a bunch of factors contributing to this confusion. One reason is that the way
attacks, security incidents, and data breaches are reported in popular media outlets sometimes
confuses attackers' tactics with their motivations.

43 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

This lack of clarity can lead organizations to make wrong security prioritization decisions. The
next section explains the differences between attackers' motivations and tactics.
###### **Understanding the differences between attackers'** **motivations and tactics**

One of the reasons I've found that so many organizations lack focus and competency around
the cybersecurity fundamentals is confusion surrounding how attacks are perpetrated. There
are a lot of different ways organizations get attacked, as I illustrated with the three real-world
attack examples earlier in this chapter. However, when you take a closer look at these attacks,
the victim organization was _always initially_ compromised by attackers using one or more of the
Cybersecurity Usual Suspects.

**Why the volume of attacks has increased**

There are more attackers operating out in the open than ever before, because they don't believe
there are consequences for their illicit activities, based on their location, legal jurisdiction, or
who sponsors their work. It used to be the exception to the rule that they wouldn't obfuscate
their true affiliations and identities. However, there has been a proliferation of nation-state
threat groups, and some threat intelligence providers are now tracking many such groups that
they identify as _bona fide nation states_ . For example, a recent Microsoft Digital Defense Report
shares that "Microsoft Threat Intelligence now tracks more than 1,500 unique threat groups—
including more than 600 nation-state threat actor groups, 300 cybercrime groups, 200
influence operations groups, and hundreds of others" (Microsoft Corporation, 2024).

The world has changed over the past several years in ways that enable more cyberattacks than
in the past. The poor international relations between Western nations and Russia, China, Iran,
and North Korea enable criminal groups in those countries to attack non-military targets in the
US, Canada, the UK, and other Western nations without consequences. Law enforcement in
those countries has demonstrated their unwillingness to stop attacks against industries in the
Western world. This has emboldened attackers in these locations with literally no downside to
attacking commercial sector organizations. When these attackers' TTPs are discovered and
publicized, it lowers the barrier for entry to lower-skilled criminals in other parts of the world.

**The evolving challenge of attribution**

Attributing an attack to an **i** ndividual or group used to be very aspirational because the
internet is based on a suite of protocols that were developed over 40 years ago. The engineers
who developed these immensely scalable and sophisticated protocols never envisioned a
future world where an entire $271 billion+-dollar-a-year industry (Grand View Research, 2025)
would be based on the discoveries of new security vulnerabilities, malware research, social
engineering protection, and the proliferation of sophisticated criminal organizations and

_Chapter 1_ 44

nation-state actors. The **TCP/IP (version 4) protocol** suite, the basis of the internet, was never
designed to help investigators perform attribution for cyberattacks that leverage vast networks
of compromised distributed systems around the world. Finding "patient zero," where the
compromise started, in large environments that have been compromised for months or years,
using evidence collected from compromised systems, can rarely be done with complete
confidence.

However, attackers that have embraced the modern ransomware business model have made it
easier to do attribution with much more confidence. They essentially identify themselves, or at
least their ransomware gang affiliation, when they demand a ransom from their victims.
Having a known ransomware gang designation can help strike fear in the minds of victims,
especially when the gang has a history of successful attacks. Victims take them seriously when
they have a record of keeping their promises—both good and bad.

Attribution is relatively easy when a known ransomware gang posts a dark web blog post in
the same way they have in the past, publishing some of their latest victim's data. It proves they
have possession of stolen data and are demanding one or more ransoms from the victim. I
examine some of the ways that ransomware has evolved in _Chapter 5_ .

When security teams find IOCs that precisely match the "rat droppings" of a known threat
actor, it's hard _not to_ conclude that the associated threat actor is involved in an attack.

**Attackers' motivations**

In the case of ransomware, it would seem like the motivation is quite straightforward—profit.
However, some Microsoft threat research suggested that attackers used "fake" ransomware
against Ukrainian government targets during the Russian invasion in 2022. The motivation of
these "fake" ransomware attacks wasn't profit; it was really the destruction of Ukrainian
assets. At the time, Microsoft reported, "MSTIC assesses that the malware, which is designed
to look like ransomware but lacking a ransom recovery mechanism, is intended to be
destructive and designed to render targeted devices inoperable rather than to obtain a
ransom" (Microsoft Corporation, January 15, 2022). Apparently, wiper malware was disguised

45 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

as ransomware. The difference is that this wiper malware wasn't designed to encrypt data in a
way that is reversible using a decryption key; the data was instead destroyed ("crypto
deleted"). This wasn't the first time, nor will it be the last, that attackers try to make their
motivations opaque.

Still, many cybersecurity professionals use this type of evidence to surmise the attackers'
motivations, affiliations, and identities. Attacker motivations can include the following:

**Notoriety** : The attacker wants to prove that they are smarter than the big high-tech
companies and their victims.

**Profit** : As I discuss in _Chapter 4_, after the successful global worm attacks in 2003,
malware began to evolve to support a profit motive that continues to the present day.

**Economic espionage** : For example, alleged activities by groups in China to steal
valuable intellectual property from Western nations to give their own industries a
competitive and economic advantage.

**Military espionage** : A motivation as old as governments themselves, where
governments want to understand the military capabilities of their adversaries and
allies.

**Hacktivism** : Attacks against organizations and institutions based on disagreements on
political or philosophical issues.

**Foreign policy objectives** : Governments run sophisticated cyber-influence operations
using cultural manipulation and information warfare tactics, amplifying false
narratives to influence and manipulate target populations. Examples include
influencing elections and lowering the morale of enemy civilian populations during
wartime.

**Many others** : Watch any James Bond movie where the **Special Executive for**
**Counterintelligence, Terrorism, Revenge, and Extortion** ( **SPECTRE** ) is part of the
plot, and you'll see some creative motivations.

Here are some examples of things I see get confused with motivations all the time:

**Cryptocurrency theft** : This isn't a motivation; it's an _action_ attackers take based on
their motivation. Based on the preceding list, obvious motivations for cryptocurrency
theft could be notoriety, revenge, and/or profit. _Theft itself is not a motivation_ .

**Data destruction** : Again, this is an action attackers take in pursuit of their objectives,
which follows one of the motivations on the previously discussed list.

**Ransomware** : This is a family of malware and a _type of attack_, but not a motivation. As
mentioned earlier, profit, revenge, and pursuing foreign policy objectives are three
examples of possible motivations for leveraging ransomware.

_Chapter 1_ 46

This is a subtle but important nuance that CISOs should keep in mind when developing their
cybersecurity strategies, communicating with their stakeholders, and talking with
cybersecurity vendors, especially during IR investigations when it's easy to get distracted.
Focusing on _how_ organizations get attacked instead of _why_ they get attacked will help you
develop a more holistic cybersecurity strategy with measurable efficacy.

**Attribution is not a prerequisite to success**

You might wonder, if attackers' motivations are unclear, how are CISOs supposed to know
what a proportional response is? Who should help the victim organization with the response
to the attack—local authorities, national law enforcement such as the FBI, the military, or an
international coalition?

Security teams armed with the knowledge of attackers' TTPs, catalogs of IOCs, and improved
detection and response automation can definitely defend against known threat actors much
more effectively and efficiently than ever before. However, as successful and promising as new
threat intelligence capabilities are, and even when attackers identify their affiliations with
ransom demands and data leak blog posts, attacks continue unabated, and arguably, attackers
have never been more successful than they are today.

Fortunately, understanding who the attackers are is not a prerequisite for a successful
cybersecurity strategy. Regardless of who sponsors their work or how sophisticated attackers
are, they all use the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects to achieve initial compromise: "the tools
used by nation states to compromise victim networks are most frequently the same tools used
by other malicious actors" (Microsoft Corporation, October 2021). I believe we can, with 99.9%
certainty, predict the tactics that attackers will use when they try to initially compromise an
enterprise IT environment. This is what organizations should invest in first—the cybersecurity
fundamentals to mitigate the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects.

Given everything I've discussed in this chapter, you might be wondering who would be crazy
enough to take a CISO job! In my experience, CISOs can have different motivations, which are
typically based on their experience and backgrounds. I mentioned that I wrote this book for

47 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

CISOs, aspiring CISOs, and other professionals who work with CISOs. Did you know that there
are different types of CISOs? Whether you are a CISO yourself, a security team member of a
vendor account team supporting a CISO, a salesperson trying to sell to a CISO, or a member of
a board of directors that a CISO reports to, understanding the type of CISO you are working
with can help make communicating with them a lot more predictable, efficient, and perhaps
even enjoyable.
###### **Different types of CISOs: "The CISO spectrum"**

Different types of CISOs can have different approaches to cybersecurity that dictate, or at least
strongly influence, the focus of their security programs. I call this list of types of CISOs the
_CISO spectrum_ . This list isn't exhaustive; it simply contains the types of CISOs I encountered
over the past couple of decades of my career:

**Type 1 – the IT director with cybersecurity responsibility** : They were perhaps the
most technical of all the types of CISOs I encountered, typically having had more IT
expertise than cybersecurity expertise. They knew all about the IT infrastructure that
they supported and were trusted members of the IT leadership team. They were
assigned cybersecurity as part of their job function. They had the aptitude and the
desire to learn about security and compliance, sometimes purely out of a sense of selfpreservation. Their comfort zone was IT systems, and when they met with me, they
were typically keen for insights and help with cybersecurity.

**Type 2 – the incident responder** : Some of the CISOs I met became CISOs because they
were the go-to person for responding to incidents for their organization. They were IR
and remediation experts. Their organizations trusted them during crises and looked to
them to help the organization avoid crisis situations in the future. They tended to be
threat intelligence geeks and focused on making it harder for attackers to succeed,
using their technical knowledge. They had deep knowledge of IT systems as they were
typically involved in building and administrating these systems earlier in their career.

**Type 3 – the compliance or audit expert** : These folks tended to focus on control sets
that helped meet regulations and industry standards. Their experience in managing
compliance or audit programs gave them deep expertise in managing large control sets
in large complex IT environments that were required to comply with multiple
standards, such as PCI DSS, CMMC, the NIST **Risk Management Framework** ( **RMF** )
that uses NIST SP 800-53, ISO 27000, and so on. They'd typically rather discuss control
sets and compliance challenges than threats or threat actors. For this type of CISO,
"good" cybersecurity is strict compliance with standards.

_Chapter 1_ 48

**Type 4 – the policy wonk** : I met two different types of CISOs who rely on their strong
policy backgrounds:

**Type 5 – the strategist** : These CISOs tended to focus on aligning resources around
frameworks. To do this, they required some cybersecurity expertise along with some
business acumen. Many of these folks had experience in at least a couple of different
cybersecurity domains, such as IR and risk management. They were always on the
lookout for technologies or processes that would help them address known gaps in
their capabilities and improve the effectiveness of their strategies.

**Type 6 – the risk expert** : In my experience, this type of CISO was rarer than the rest.
Their area of expertise was risk management. They approached cybersecurity like an
actuary, using quantitative risk calculations to determine the potential cost range of
different types of exposures, which helped inform areas of investment for their
cybersecurity program. I met this type of CISO typically when I was advising insurance
companies. They tended to report to the **Chief Risk Officer** ( **CRO** ).

**Type 7 – the cybersecurity advisor** : These CISOs saw themselves as advisors to the
businesses they supported. Typically, their position was that they didn't actually
"own" anything—the business did. They advised the business to make cybersecurity
investments but didn't necessarily design and operate cybersecurity capabilities
themselves—the IT team would instead. This type of CISO was typically able to avoid
the conflict that naturally occurs when there is tension between the autonomy the
business wants and the control necessary to defend the business' assets. Many CISOs of
this ilk didn't believe their role was to provide oversight, just advice.

**Type 8 – the trusted business executive** : These CISOs weren't cybersecurity experts
and sometimes weren't IT experts either. They were executives who had proven
themselves to senior leadership by managing different parts of the business or
particularly difficult or important projects or initiatives. The leadership trusted them
because of their track record of success at the company. Since they had proven that they

**Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) policy experts** : These CISOs
typically had lots of experience writing and **e** nforcing GRC-related policies. To
get things done, they relied on policies the same way police rely on laws.

**Cybersecurity public policy experts** : These CISOs typically weren't IT experts
or enterprise cybersecurity experts. Rather, they tended to be attorneys with
deep public policy and privacy expertise. They had experience with national
cybersecurity policies, that is, cybersecurity policies that national or federal
governments implement to protect citizens, as well as private sector and public
sector organizations within their borders.

49 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

could manage challenging assignments, they were given cybersecurity to manage.
These organizations believed that these CISOs would succeed given their ability to lead
and manage, and that cybersecurity expertise was not a prerequisite for success. Many
of the CISOs that I met in this category were attorneys.

That is the CISO spectrum. The types of CISOs discussed probably describe 90% of the
thousands of CISOs I have met. I don't view any of them as better than the others; they simply
have different backgrounds and approaches to cybersecurity. However, frequently, factors
within the organizations dictate the approach to cybersecurity that their CISOs take, regardless
of their backgrounds or personal preferences.

I learned to identify the type of CISO I was advising as quickly as possible in order to make the
conversation more meaningful for us both. For example, if a CISO was really interested in
discussing how a new exploit worked, it would be a short and annoying conversation trying to
discuss risk management with them. For this reason, many of the sales teams that I supported
at Microsoft and AWS were intimidated by the CISOs of their accounts. Once they learned
about the CISO spectrum, it made it easier for them to understand the CISOs they supported
and connect them with the people and resources that could really address the things they were
most interested in.

In most cases, this would earn some trust with CISOs because the salespeople were perceived
as helpful and not just interested in sales transactions.

On occasion, I've been asked about the type of CISO I am. After working in IT roles for many
years, I started my cybersecurity career in IR. I worked as a cybersecurity advisor for many
years and spent a lot of time working on threat intelligence. However, believe it or not, as hard
as IR jobs tend to be, my "happy place" is IR. For me, understanding how threat actors _really_
operate gives me the confidence to develop and execute on cybersecurity strategies as a CISO.
But, as I'll discuss in _Chapter 9_, _Ingredients for a Successful Strategy_, the challenge CISOs and

_Chapter 1_ 50

security teams face can't be met with confidence alone; managing cybersecurity for large
enterprises is a much harder job than that.
###### **Summary**

In this chapter, I shared examples of different types of cyberattacks and introduced some key
concepts that I will refer to throughout the rest of this book.

First, I introduced the _IR investigation knowledge trend_ to illustrate how IR investigators develop
hypotheses during an investigation and collect evidence to test their hypotheses. Tenacity
fuels good IR teams to make progress and uncover as much about an incident as possible.

I also described three different types of cyberattacks to provide insight into how such attacks
are perpetrated and to illustrate that not all "data breaches" are the same in terms of damage,
remediation efforts, and costs. The three types of attacks I described were as follows:

Global malware attack

Traditional network intrusion

Data breaches via insecure APIs

It can be very difficult to contain and eradicate attackers that successfully perpetrate
traditional network intrusions; for example, data published by Okta suggests that the average
time to detect and contain a breach is 290 days (Okta, n.d.). Although a data breach via
insecure APIs can also negatively impact an organization's employees, customers, and
reputation and have costly legal and regulatory outcomes, attackers aren't typically inside the
victims' networks. Subsequently, the effort and costs to contain attackers in this scenario are
typically a small fraction of what it takes to do so in a traditional network intrusion.

Next, I introduced the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, which covers the five ways enterprises
initially get compromised by attackers and the cybersecurity fundamentals. They include the
following:

Unpatched vulnerabilities

Security misconfigurations

Weak, leaked, and stolen credentials

Social engineering

Insider threats

Organizations that are very proficient at managing the cybersecurity fundamentals and seek to
mitigate the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects make it much harder for attackers to be successful. A
solid foundation, focused on the fundamentals, is required for a successful strategy.

51 _How Enterprises Get Hacked_

I hope the combination of the real-world attack types I described, the Cybersecurity Usual
Suspects, and the difference between attackers' tactics and motivations helps you understand
how enterprises get hacked. Ensuring your organization's cybersecurity team has enough
consistent investment in the cybersecurity fundamentals can make initial compromise much
harder for threat actors. I'll discuss post-compromise tactics that attackers use in detail in
other chapters of this book—they need attention and investment as well.

Finally, I introduced the _CISO spectrum_, which covers the eight types of CISOs I've encountered
in my career. Understanding the type of CISO you are working with or selling to can make
things easier for everyone.

The next chapter dives into one of my favorite topics—threat intelligence. Threat intelligence
can inform your cybersecurity strategy in some key ways that will be discussed in detail.
