# 2
##### What to Know About Threat Intelligence

I admit it, I'm a threat intelligence data geek. I really enjoy studying threat intelligence. It helps
me understand the tactics and techniques that are in vogue with attackers and how the threat
landscape is evolving. One of the best jobs I had at Microsoft was working as a Director of
Trustworthy Computing. In this role, I was the executive editor and a contributor to the
**Microsoft Security Intelligence Report**, which we called " **the SIR** ." During the 8 or 9 years I
helped produce the SIR, we published more than 20 volumes and special editions of this
report, spanning thousands of pages. I gave literally thousands of threat intelligence briefings
for customers around the world, as well as press and analyst interviews. I can tell you from
experience, interviews on live television in front of millions of people, discussing threat
intelligence, are nerve-racking! (BBC News, 2013).

Building **a** nd publishing the SIR was a _lot_ of work, but very rewarding. In this role, I had the
opportunity to work with so many smart people in the **Microsoft Security Response Center**
( **MSRC** ), the **Microsoft Malware Protection Center** ( **MMPC** ), the Microsoft **Digital Crimes**
**Unit** ( **DCU** ), the **Security Development Lifecycle** ( **SDL** ) team, Microsoft IT, and many others.
Doing this work gave me a deep appreciation for the value of good threat intelligence and some
of the ways it is produced. Microsoft has continued to invest in threat intelligence, and they
have a center dedicated to it called the **Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center** ( **MSTIC** ), in
which a few of my former colleagues still work. I provide some data and insights from the SIR
in _Chapter 5_, _The Evolution of Malware_ . I also provide a deep dive into security vulnerabilities in
_Chapter 3_, _Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_ .

Since those days, I have been a consumer of threat intelligence in all the jobs I've had, both in
vendor roles and as an operational cybersecurity team leader. Perhaps, because I spent so
much time in my career developing threat intelligence, I have high expectations about the

_Chapter 2_ 56

intelligence I spend my time studying. Spending time consuming vendors' marketing content
—instead of real threat intelligence that can help operational cybersecurity teams—is
something I avoid like the plague. I'll describe the difference between helpful threat
intelligence and the noise that echoes across the industry as vendors and industry
professionals try to draw attention to themselves, later in this chapter.

In this chapter, I'll provide you with some context that will help you understand the analysis of
various threats that I'll discuss in the rest of this book. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able
to recognize the difference between credible threat intelligence and questionable threat
intelligence.

In this chapter, we'll cover the following topics:

What is threat intelligence

Using CTI

Sharing CTI

How to identify credible CTI

Let's get started!
###### **What is threat intelligence?**

**Threat intelligence** ( **TI** ) is sometimes referred to as **cyber threat intelligence** ( **CTI** ) to clarify
that the intelligence focuses on cybersecurity threats as opposed to other types of threats. The
concept is ancient: the more you know about your enemies and how they plan and execute
their attacks, the more prepared you can be for those attacks.

Simply put, CTI provides organizations with data and information on how attackers have been
leveraging the _Cybersecurity Usual Suspects_ we discussed in _Chapter 1, How Enterprises Get Hacked_
to gain initial access to their victims' environments, what they have been doing in their
victims' environments post initial compromise, and sometimes attribution for attacks to
specific threat actors. Threats can also include various categories of malware, tools,
exploitation of vulnerabilities, web-based attacks, **distributed denial of service** ( **DDoS** )
attacks, social engineering attacks, and others. Of course, as I wrote in _Chapter 1_ there is also
high interest in information about the attackers themselves—who they are, where they are
located, whether they are state-sponsored or an independent criminal organization, and
details on their modus operandi from their past attacks. An entire industry has grown around
the demand for attribution and information on threat actors. Over time, as the world changed
in ways that allowed many attackers to work in the open without concealing their existence,
performing attribution for their attacks became easier.

57 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

**Where does CTI come from?**

Purveyors of CTI collect and analyze data from data sources. Understanding where your CTI
comes from is very important. How CTI is collected, and the way it should be interpreted, are
typically defined by its source. Without knowledge of the source, there's a good chance that
CTI will be misinterpreted.

There are many potential sources of data that CTI providers can use. Here are some examples:

Data on malware threats can come from anti-malware products and services running
on endpoints, networks, email servers, web browsers, cloud services, honeypots, and so
on.

Data on weak, leaked, and stolen credentials can come not only from identity providers
such as Microsoft Entra ID (formerly called Azure Active Directory), Google's identity
offerings, and Okta, but also from monitoring illicit forums where such credentials are
bought, sold, and leaked.

Data on social engineering attacks can come from phishing and spam filtering services,
as well as social networking services.

There is also **open source intelligence** ( **OSINT** ), which leverages publicly available data
sources such as social media, news feeds, court filings, public records such as arrest records,
information attackers disclose about their victims, activity in illicit forums, and many others.
OSINT can help defenders in at least a couple of ways. First, it can help notify you that your IT
environment has been compromised. Observing attackers offering your data for sale or
chattering about illicit access to your network can be leading indicators of a breach that has
gone undetected. Another way many organizations use OSINT is for researching attackers and
the tactics they use.

Of course, attackers can use OSINT to research and perform reconnaissance on their potential
targets as well. We'll discuss some of the ways attackers perform reconnaissance in _Chapter 10,_
_Cybersecurity Strategies_ and _11, Cybersecurity Strategy Implementation_ . There is a plethora of tools
to help find OSINT, including **Maltego**, **Shodan**, **theHarvester**, and many others. A more
comprehensive list of OSINT tools can be found at the OSINT Framework website (OSINT
Framework, n.d.). There are also hundreds of public repositories on GitHub offering OSINT
tools (GitHub, n.d.).

Purveyors of CTI can use data sources that they own and operate, CTI data procured from third
parties, and OSINT data sources. For example, anti-malware vendors that operate their own
research and response labs collect malware for analysis and operate various anti-malware
offerings. They can get malware samples from their customers, partners, and competitors. The
more customers they have running their anti-malware offerings, the more samples they can
collect and the more telemetry they can receive on malware and the systems attacked.

_Chapter 2_ 58

Anti-malware vendors have their customers agree to submit malware samples that they
encounter, and the vendors' products and services generate data from detections, installation
blocking, and disinfections in the course of operating. All this data can be collected,
aggregated, and analyzed to provide the vendor with insight into how their products and
services are operating and steer future research, response activities, and investments.

Many vendors also publish TI reports and provide CTI to their customers via web portals and
emails, but also integrate it into APIs, products, and services. Examples of vendors that do this
include CrowdStrike, Google, Kaspersky Lab, Mandiant, McAfee, Microsoft, Palo Alto
Networks, Recorded Future, Sophos, Symantec, and many others. They primarily do this to
share their CTI and help organizations understand what is happening in the threat landscape.
However, they also integrate reports to generate new business by demonstrating the breadth
and depth of their CTI. Many vendors like to claim they provide better visibility than their
competitors, and thus better protection from threats. This is where scale can be a
differentiator.

Some CTI vendors differentiate themselves not necessarily by scale, but by the quality of their
data and analysis. They can correlate data they have to specific industries and to specific
customers within those industries and provide more actionable insights than high-level,
anonymized, global trends will typically enable.

For example, if I'm the CISO of an organization in the healthcare industry, I am likely interested
in CTI from a vendor that really understands my industry and its unique challenges and has
data on attackers that target this industry, and in the geographic locations my organization
does business. This combination will help me understand the threats specifically impacting my
industry and better prepare for them in a healthcare context that potentially includes heavy

59 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

regulation, a big focus on patient privacy, expensive equipment certification requirements, and
risk to human life. Further, I'm always looking for insights into what other organizations
similar to mine are doing to protect, detect, and respond to these threats. This information will
inform some of my efforts and make it easier to convince the business I support to provide the
budget and resources I need.

Some CTI vendors tout their abilities to perform attribution and their knowledge of nationstate attackers. They have coined sometimes fun, but always intriguing names for such attack
groups. Examples **i** nclude **Lazarus Group**, **Sandworm Team**, **PHOSPHORUS**, and many
others. Each CTI vendor gave their own name to each threat actor group, just as each antimalware lab gave their own names to malware they discovered. Different vendors using
different names for the same threat actor group made it confusing for their customers and the
industry. In June 2025, CrowdStrike and Microsoft announced plans to harmonize
cybersecurity threat attribution:

_"AUSTIN, TX — June 2, 2025 —CrowdStrike[https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-_
_us/](NASDAQ: CRWD) and Microsoft today announced a collaboration to bring_
_clarity and coordination to how cyber threat actors are identified and tracked across_
_security vendors. By mapping threat actor aliases and aligning adversary_
_attribution across platforms, the collaboration minimizes confusion caused by_
_different naming systems and accelerates cyber defenders' response against today's_
_and tomorrow's most sophisticated adversaries."_

_(CrowdStrike, June 2025)_

It can be very interesting to get some insight into how well-funded attackers operate. It doesn't
take long for other attackers to try to mimic the tactics and techniques that the professionals
use once they are revealed via CTI. In this way, nation-state threat actors have been lowering
the barrier to entry for criminals for decades.

However, no matter how well-funded attackers are, they will use one or more of the
Cybersecurity Usual Suspects to initially compromise their targets' IT environment, just like
common criminals will.

_Chapter 2_ 60

After all, becoming excellent at the cybersecurity fundamentals will drive down the ROI
for all potential threat actors that target your organization.

I have talked with plenty of security teams at public sector and private sector
organizations where paying attention to nation-state threat actors is not optional due
to their organizations' own charters or the intellectual property they possess. But even
in these cases, focusing on the cybersecurity fundamentals can pay big dividends.

###### **Using CTI**

Cybersecurity programs can make use of CTI in several ways. Here are some examples (this list
is not exhaustive):

CTI is essential to the effective operation of **security operations centers** ( **SOCs** ); they
are only as good as the CTI they have

CTI can help inform **cybersecurity incident response teams** ' ( **CIRT** ) investigations

CTI can inform threat hunting, red, blue, and purple teams' efforts, and cybersecurity
control testing

CTI can help defenders profile attackers in order to be better prepared for them

CTI can inform executive protection programs designed to protect executives and their
families

CTI is an important input for risk management programs

Let's dig into that last example a bit more: inform risk management. CTI can highlight the risks
that organizations pay attention to. Recall that risk is composed of probability and impact. CTI
can help quantify both the probability and the impact of risk calculations. For example, let's
say you are a CISO and the business leaders you support are very concerned about ransomware
because they keep seeing news stories about attacks. CTI can provide some idea of the
probability of encountering ransomware.

I'll discuss ransomware in detail in _Chapter 5_ but for now, note that ransomware (the category
of malware) is typically one of the least prevalent categories of malware. There are some logical
reasons why this is the case that I'll cover in _Chapter 5_ . Generally, if you were to stack-rank risks
by priority based on probability alone, ransomware would likely show up near the bottom of
the list. However, once we quantify the potential impact of ransomware to reflect that
encountering it could be an extinction event for your business, it likely bumps it way up in the
ranking in the list of risks.

61 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

**Using TTPs**

Another use for CTI is to help security teams mitigate risks by providing details about specific
threats and how they operate. Understanding the **tactics, techniques, and procedures**
( **TTPs** ) that attackers employ can provide some concrete ideas on how they can be mitigated.
NIST defines TTPs as, " _The behavior of an actor. A tactic is the highest-level description of this_
_behavior, while techniques give a more detailed description of behavior in the context of a tactic, and_
_procedures an even lower-level, highly detailed description in the context of a technique._ " (Badger et
al, 2016).

A tactic is the reason the attacker performs a particular action. Why do they decide to take
specific action? It is because it was a tactical goal. For example, once an attacker is inside their
victim's network, they typically need to move laterally to explore the network and find
sensitive data. The tactic in this example is lateral movement. Other examples of tactics
include reconnaissance, persistence, and exfiltration.

Techniques are how the attacker tries to accomplish the tactic—the specific actions they take.
For example, suppose an attacker needed to move laterally (the tactic) on the victim's network,
so they used _pass the hash_ and stolen web authentication cookies (the techniques) to do this.

Using this combination of tactics and techniques enables security teams to take a structured
approach to planning attacks. Knowing the tactics and techniques that attackers use allows
defenders to put people, processes, and technologies in place that will detect or mitigate the
techniques when they are employed. In our example, where _pass the hash_ was employed, we
could plan to mitigate this technique using some guidance from Microsoft or by procuring a
security product designed to detect it.

Using TTPs this way might seem like a daunting task because there can be many combinations
and permutations of attacker tactics and techniques. A great resource to help security teams is
the MITRE ATT&CK® knowledge base (found at `[https://attack.mitre.org/](https://attack.mitre.org/)` ). This
knowledge base contains tactics and techniques that have been seen in use during attacks. It
maps techniques to tactics and provides ways that each technique can potentially be mitigated
and detected. Many cybersecurity teams have standardized their approach to cybersecurity

**b** ased on this model. Further, many cybersecurity products have this same model baked into
them to make it easy for cybersecurity teams to use them.

**Using IOCs**

Many security teams also use **indicators of compromise** ( **IOCs** ) to help determine whether
their enterprise IT environments have been compromised. IOCs can help in post-compromise
situations when response teams are trying to determine when and how the initial compromise
happened, and what the attackers did with their illicit access afterward. IOCs are described in
_NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5_ :

_Chapter 2_ 62

_"Indicators of compromise (IOC) are forensic artifacts from intrusions that are_
_identified on organizational systems at the host or network level. IOCs provide_
_valuable information on systems that have been compromised. IOCs can include the_
_creation of registry key values. IOCs for network traffic include Universal Resource_
_Locator or protocol elements that indicate malicious code command and control_
_servers. The rapid distribution and adoption of IOCs can improve information_
_security by reducing the time that systems and organizations are vulnerable to the_
_same exploit or attack. Threat indicators, signatures, tactics, techniques, procedures,_
_and other indicators of compromise may be available via government and non-_
_government cooperatives, including the Forum of Incident Response and Security_
_Teams, the United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team, the Defense_
_Industrial Base Cybersecurity Information Sharing Program, and the CERT_
_Coordination Center."_

_(NIST Special Publication 800-53 Revision 5, September 2020)_

Examples of IOCs **i** nclude unusual network traffic (destination, origin, or volume), network
traffic to or from known malicious domain names or IP addresses, unusual volumes of
authentication failures, the presence of specific tools, files, or registry entries, recently added
unrecognized accounts, and many others. Incident response and forensics teams can use IOCs
to help them identify compromised systems. To do this, they typically need **SHA-256** hashes
for files, scripts, and tools that attackers leave behind. File hashes can help identify the
presence of files that were potentially used during attacks among the mountains of legitimate
files on systems.

IP addresses for command-and-control servers, data exfiltration locations, and other attackercontrolled resources can also be helpful to investigators as they comb through network flow
data logs on firewalls, proxy servers, and other devices on a network.

_Figure 2.1_ provides some fictional examples of IOCs, including example file hashes for different
types of scripts as well as IP addresses for command-and-control servers. IOCs can be shared in
a few different formats, such as CSV, JSON, or STIX format. I'll discuss sharing CTI in more
detail later in this chapter.

63 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

_Figure 2.1 – An example of IOCs with fictional filenames, hashes, and IP addresses_

I learned so much about the tricks that attackers like to use when I worked on Microsoft's
customer-facing incident response team. We built tools to collect system data on live-running
Windows systems that were suspected of being compromised. We'd compare the data on
system configurations and running states with known good and known bad datasets—
essentially looking for IOCs. This was as much art as it was science because attackers were
using all sorts of creative tricks to try to avoid detection, stay persistent, and perform data
exfiltration.

Some memorable tricks include attackers using IP addresses in Base-8 instead of Base-10
format to bypass proxy server rules, taking advantage of bugs in browsers and proxy servers
when domain names in Cyrillic were used, running processes using the same name as wellknown legitimate Windows system processes, but from slightly different directories to avoid
detection, and so many more. Interesting stuff!

_Chapter 2_ 64

Since then, intrusions have become more science than art, in that many attackers are much
more organized, and their attacks are methodical and leverage automation. After they use one
or more of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects to gain initial access to a victim's environment,
they can execute their attack and accomplish their objectives before the victim's cybersecurity
detection capabilities even flag their potential presence. This sophisticated approach to attacks
has decreased the dwell time that many attackers require after they gain initial access, thus
putting more pressure on security teams to detect attackers as quickly and efficiently as
possible. Recall the traditional network intrusion I described in _Chapter 1_ . In my experience
responding to and investigating these types of attacks, after gaining initial access, most
attackers go straight for their victims' Active Directory so that they can harvest credentials that
will enable them to stay persistent longer, move laterally, access more systems and data,
exfiltrate data, deploy command-and-control tools and other malware, and so on. They
automate the steps needed to **d** - this using batch files, PowerShell scripts, **Windows**
**Management Instrumentation** ( **WMI** ), the victims' own development tools, and so on.
Attackers leverage this type of automation frequently because it reduces their level of effort
and costs associated with their attacks. It can also be very challenging to defend against these
attacks because attackers are using many of the same system commands and legitimate tools
that their victims' IT departments use. Because this is so common, I have dedicated _Chapter 14_
to mitigating _living off the land_ tactics in this book.

This is one reason threat hunting has become such a powerful cybersecurity discipline; instead
of waiting for the bad guys to make a mistake or announce they are in your environment at the
end of their attack, find them and disrupt their attack before they can finish what they plan to
do.

Security teams can leverage TTPs and IOCs with a variety of security tools, products, and
services. Examples include **security information and event management** ( **SIEM** ) systems,
behavioral analytics tools, data visualization tools, email filtering services, web browsing
filtering services, endpoint protection products, **extended detection and response** ( **XDR** )
products, **security orchestration, automation, and response** ( **SOAR** ) products, and many
others. There are a vast number of ways to leverage CTI to protect, detect, and respond to
modern threats.

Different roles in security teams can leverage CTI in slightly different ways. For example, as I
mentioned earlier, CIRTs use IOCs when performing intrusion investigations. Meanwhile, IT
analysts use CTI to ensure that protection and detection capabilities are optimized. Analysts in
SOCs monitor and triage alerts based on data enriched with CTI. Threat hunters use CTI to
inform their hunts. CISOs use CTI to understand whether their cybersecurity strategy is
effective and identify areas that require change or further investment. CTI has the potential to
inform the efforts of many different roles and stakeholders.

65 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

**The key to using threat intelligence**

It's important to recognize that **a** lthough CTI is a product offered by many vendors and
organizations, it's also a process – a process used to collect data, process that data, analyze the
processed data, and then share the results with stakeholders who need them. This typically
takes time, budget, and resources to accomplish. I haven't met a security team yet that has
unlimited resources and does not need to make trade-offs.

The combination of so many potential sources and uses of CTI and limited resources can lead
to security teams drowning in CTI that might not be helpful to them. This is why it is very
important for teams to take the time to develop a set of requirements for their CTI program. In
this context, "requirements" are statements about the specific problems the CTI program is
trying to solve. These requirements tie the specific CTI collected and analyzed to the specific
needs of the program's stakeholders, thus rationalizing its use. If some CTI source has
interesting data, but the data it provides doesn't help fulfill a requirement defined by a
program stakeholder, then that source likely should not be leveraged.

This approach helps the CTI program optimize its resources and prevents it from drowning in
CTI. I've seen a few different approaches to documenting requirements. _Figure 2.2_ provides an
example.

_Figure 2.2 – An example of CTI requirements_

There is no single right way for a CTI team to operate. CTI teams have operated in very
different ways over the years based on the requirements of the organizations they support and
the people managing the teams. For example, some CTI teams support fraud investigations,

_Chapter 2_ 66

and some don't, because some cybersecurity teams have fraud included in their charters, while
others do not.

As a CISO, I always had three functions in mind for my CTI teams:

1.

2.

**Maximize the value of IOCs and TTPs** : In addition to all the sources of OSINT I
mentioned earlier, more and more cybersecurity vendors are now including CTI with
their product and service offerings. A large enterprise that leverages many vendors
typically has some CTI sources it is unaware of or does not leverage. Maintaining an
accurate inventory of CTI sources can be very helpful for CTI teams and their
stakeholders. Many cybersecurity products and tools are capable of consuming CTI by
integrating feeds from CTI sources. In order to maximize the CTI benefits that
enterprises have, I recommend that CTI teams track the following information:

**Validate your cybersecurity strategy** : For CISOs, it is important for them to
understand what threats made their way onto their networks each day or week. Some
CISOs do this by attending daily SOC stand-up meetings where the staff in the SOC
brief each other on the alerts they have been triaging and any other noteworthy work
items. However, I always found this to be a little disruptive to the SOC meetings, and it
didn't help me understand what trends might be emerging in our environment. As a
workaround, I typically ask my CTI team to pull together a snapshot of what happened
each week, from a cybersecurity perspective. Try to provide a 360-degree view by
aggregating threat detection data from the various tools and products that generate it.
This includes detections such as the following:

All the CTI sources and feeds that their organization is entitled to

The type of CTI each source and feed provides

Information that is available on automated CTI feeds/APIs

Each source's funding renewal date (typically part of the product or service
licensing annual renewal)

**_Email threats identified by Microsoft 365, and other filters_** : I like to understand
the volume of attacks and what kinds of attacks are trying to make their way into
our users' inboxes. Also, I like to get an idea of whether the filters are being
effective by understanding how many threats made it through the filters into
users' inboxes and how many were reported by users. This tells me whether my
team's approach to mitigating email-based threats is being effective or if changes
should be considered. Potential changes could include changes to configurations
of the email protections used and changes to the vendors and products used for
email protection.

67 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

**_External attack surface detections_** : These include meaningful alerts from attack
surface management tools and firewalls, brute-force attacks on VPN servers, and
issues identified by third-party risk management platforms such as BitSight,
Security ScoreCard, UpGuard, and so on. This also includes data from **web**
**application firewalls** ( **WAFs** ) that protect applications. Were there any

application attacks, such as password spray or SQL injection attacks, and did the
WAF blunt them successfully?

**_Detections from endpoint products_** : These include anti-malware and XDR/EDR. I
am always interested in understanding what families of malware made their way
into our environment, how, the method of propagation, and what the intended
payload was. Further, understanding which of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects
the malware used to gain initial access is also significant. This information points
to the weakness in our approach that needs to be addressed.

**_Network detections_** from IDS/IPS, firewalls, network traffic analysis, and **cloud**
**access security broker** ( **CASB** ) data on websites that users are accessing. This
helps security teams understand whether network detection tools identified
potential threats that endpoint detection products didn't identify. For example,
attackers were able to execute a file transfer tool from a compromised endpoint.
The endpoint protection suite (EDR/XDR or anti-malware software) didn't detect
that the endpoint was compromised. However, network detection tools
identified suspicious outbound network connection attempts to a known bad
destination on the internet.

**_Application programming interfaces_** ( **_APIs_** ): These are alerts from any APIs
abused over the past week, whether there were alerts that API rate limits were
hit, or whether the request volume for APIs looks normal. Remember the data
breach via insecure APIs attack that I described in _Chapter 1_ - this data can help
us understand what is happening on the "API front of the cyber-war."

**_Data and database-related detections_** : These include details such as whether
there were anomalous database access requests and whether query volume had
unexpected spikes. **Data loss prevention** ( **DLP** ) detections also fall into this
category, such as whether someone tried to use mass storage devices or move a
large amount of data unexpectedly.

_Chapter 2_ 68

**_Identity and access management detections_** : These include repeated login
failures, especially for highly privileged accounts, MFA failures, failed VPN login
attempts, and so on.

**_Meaningful alerts from assets in the cloud and cloud services_** : These include
alerts from any of the built-in security features/functionality in the cloud services
used. Examples include any alerts from Amazon GuardDuty in AWS or Microsoft
Defender for Cloud in Azure.
If security teams can get this type of aggregate visibility once every week or two,
it gives them the opportunity to identify areas that need improvement in the
short term rather than waiting until attackers point those out through a
successful attack. Automating as much of the data collection and aggregation as
possible ensures that gaining this visibility doesn't become a burdensome, timeconsuming chore. This is one area where AI tools such as Microsoft Security
Copilot, Google Gemini, Bricklayer AI, and many others can help by summarizing
such data in seconds.

3.

**Synthesize industry CTI reports and news** : The third function I typically ask my CTI
teams to fulfill is to monitor and analyze cybersecurity industry news to help us
understand how it might apply to our organization – for example, news about zero-day
vulnerabilities or vulnerabilities added to CISA's **Known Exploited Vulnerabilities**
( **KEV** ) catalog. These are topics I will discuss in _Chapter 3_ . This is an area where CTI
teams and vulnerability management teams can collaborate. CTI teams can inform
vulnerability management teams of breaking news that potentially represents high risk
to the organization. As a CISO, it helps me sleep better at night knowing that my CTI
team is paying attention to the daily deluge of cybersecurity industry news and trends,
and flagging potentially important news for other parts of the organization as needed.
This also includes the annual and semi-annual threat reports that major vendors
publish, such as the Verizon **Data Breach Investigations Report** ( **DBIR** ), the Microsoft
Digital Defense Report, CrowdStrike's Global Threat Report, the Palo Alto Networks
Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report, and Mandiant's various reports as examples.

It's also worth mentioning that **artificial intelligence** ( **AI** ) and machine learning capabilities
have matured dramatically in the last few years. Services that leverage these capabilities can
churn through massive amounts of CTI very quickly compared to human analysts. This can
help your organization manage large volumes of CTI on an ongoing basis. Of course, like many
aspects of computer science and cybersecurity, the value derived here is a function of the effort
that is put into it. Using AI to get more value out of CTI seems like a great use case, and I know
every purveyor of CTI is looking at how they can leverage AI.

69 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

Sometimes organizations want to share the CTI they possess with other organizations, such as
partners, vendors, or their industry at large. This turns out to be more complicated than it
sounds. Let's explore this aspect of TI next.
###### **Threat intelligence sharing**

Security teams can find themselves in situations where they want to share the CTI they possess
with security teams at other organizations. There are lots of different scenarios where this
happens. For example, a parent company might want all the security teams at its subsidiaries
to share CTI with each other. Another example is an industry-specific **information sharing**
**and analysis center** ( **ISAC** ) that facilitates CTI sharing among its member organizations.
When the **Financial Services ISAC** ( **FS-ISAC** ) shares CTI on a specific threat actor that has
been actively attacking financial services firms, it helps all the firms in the industry better
protect themselves from the threat actor. Sharing CTI across organizations in the same
industry potentially makes it more challenging for attackers to victimize individual members
because they all have the TTPs that threat actors use when targeting the industry. For this
reason, the financial services industry, the retail industry, and the healthcare industry all have
ISACs, as examples.

However, sharing CTI can be more complicated than it sounds. It is not without risk. Sensitive
information, such as **personally identifiable information** ( **PII** ), can be swept up as part of an
investigation into an intrusion. If its context and sensitivity are lost and the CTI is shared
without the proper safeguards, it could be used as an example of how the organization failed to
keep its regulatory compliance obligations to standards such as PCI DSS, SOX, GDPR, and a
host of others. This could lead to large fines, unwanted scrutiny from regulators, and
reputational damage.

For public sector organizations with classified information that requires security clearance,
information-sharing programs can be fraught with challenges. In many cases, CTI would need
to be declassified before it could be shared, and the inappropriate sharing of that CTI could
have drastic consequences, such as criminal prosecution. Because of all the sensitivities and

_Chapter 2_ 70

potential land mines, many organizations share CTI anonymously. However, CTI that isn't
attributed to a credible source might not inspire the requisite confidence in its quality among
the security teams that receive it and go unused.

**CTI-sharing protocols**

I can't discuss sharing CTI without at least mentioning some of the protocols for doing so.
Recall that protocols are used to set rules for effective communication. Some protocols are
optimized for human-to-human communication, while others are optimized for machine-tomachine (automated) communication, machine-to-human communication, and so on. The
three protocols I'll discuss in this section include **Traffic Light Protocol** ( **TLP** ), **Structured**
**Threat Information eXpression** ( **STIX** ), and **Trusted Automated eXchange of Indicator**
**Information** ( **TAXII** ).

**Traffic Light Protocol**

TLP has become a popular protocol for sharing CTI and other types of information. TLP can
help **c** ommunicate the expected treatment of CTI shared between people. I don't think it is
especially optimized for automated CTI sharing between systems – it's really a protocol for
humans to use when sharing potentially sensitive information with each other. For example, if
a CTI team decides to share some CTI with another CTI team or a CIRT via email or in a
document, they could use TLP.

As its name suggests, TLP uses a traffic light analogy to make it easy for people to understand
information senders' expectations and their intended information sharing boundaries. The
"traffic light" analogy in this case has four colors: red, amber, green, and clear ( _FIRST_, n.d.).
The colors are used to communicate different information-sharing boundaries, as specified by
the sender.

The rule the protocol sets is that the color be specified as follows, when the CTI is being
communicated in writing (in an email or document): _TLP:COLOR_ . " _TLP:_ " is followed by one of
the color names in caps – for example, _TLP:AMBER_ .

**TLP:RED** specifies that the shared information is " _not for disclosure, restricted to participants_
_only_ " ( _FIRST_, n.d.). Therefore, the information is limited to only the people the sender shared it
with directly and is typically communicated verbally as a further step to limit how the
information can be shared, and to make it harder to attribute the information to a particular
sender, thus protecting their privacy. Senders use this color when they want to limit the

71 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

potential impact on their reputation or privacy, and when other parties cannot effectively act
on the information shared.

**TLP:AMBER** specifies " _limited disclosure, restricted to participants' organizations_ " ( _FIRST_, n.d.).
Receivers are only permitted to share _TLP:AMBER_ information within their own organization
and with customers with a need to know. The sender can also specify more restrictions and
limitations that it expects the receivers to honor.

**TLP:GREEN** permits " _limited disclosure, restricted to the community_ " ( _FIRST_, n.d.). Senders that
specify _TLP:GREEN_ are allowing receivers to share the information with organizations within
their community or industry, but not by using channels that are open to the general public.
Senders do not want the information shared outside of the receiver's industry or community.
This is used when information can be used to protect the broader community or industry.

Lastly, using **TLP:CLEAR** means the " _disclosure is not limited_ " ( _FIRST_, n.d.). In other words,
there are no sharing restrictions on information that is disclosed using _TLP:CLEAR_ . Receivers
are free to share this information as broadly as they like. This is meant to be used when sharing
information has minimal risk.

The TLP convention dictates that emails should have the TLP designation in the subject line
and at the top of the email, while the designation should appear in the page headers and
footers in documents (CISA, n.d.). This makes it clear to the receiver what the sender's
expectations are before they read the CTI. Again, the sender trusts the receiver to honor the
TLP designation and any sharing boundaries they have specified.

If you are doing research on the internet on threats, you'll likely come across documents
marked with _TLP:CLEAR_ . For example, both the **Federal Bureau of Investigation** ( **FBI** ) and
**Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency** ( **CISA** ) publish threat reports for public
consumption labeled _TLP:CLEAR_ . If you weren't aware of TLP before, these markings will make
more sense to you now.

_Chapter 2_ 72

**STIX and TAXII**

Now that we've covered a protocol for use among humans, let's look at two complementary
protocols that enable automated CTI sharing: STIX and TAXII. Employing protocols that are
optimized to be processed by machines can dramatically accelerate the dissemination of CTI to
organizations that can benefit from it and operationalize it, as well as across different types of
technologies that know how to consume it.

STIX is a structured language or schema that describes threats in a standard way. The STIX
schema includes core objects and meta-objects used to describe threats. The specification for
STIX version 2.1 is 313 pages (STIX Version 2.1, June 2021). Needless to say, it's very
comprehensive and can be used to describe a broad range of threats.

To give you an idea of what STIX looks like, next, you'll find an example of a campaign
described using STIX. All the data in this example is random and fictional – it's provided so you
can see an example of the format:

```
  {

  "type": "campaign",

  "spec_version": "2.1",

  "id": "campaign—3a3b4a4b-16a3-0fea-543e-10fa55c3cc2c",

  "created_by_ref": "identity—e552e362-722c-33f1-bb4a-7c4455ace3ef",

  "created": "2022-07-09T15:02:00.000Z",

  "modified": "2022-07-09T15:02:00.000Z",

  "name": "Attacker1 Attacks on Retail Industry",

  "description": "Campaign by Attacker1 on the retail industry."

  }

```

While STIX is used to describe threats in a standard way, TAXII is an application-layer protocol
used to communicate that information between systems that can consume it. TAXII
standardizes how computers share CTI with each other. Stated another way, TAXII is a protocol

73 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

designed to exchange CTI between the sender and receiver(s) and enables automated
machine-to-machine sharing of CTI over HTTPS. TAXII supports various sharing models,
including hub and spoke, source and subscriber, and peer-to-peer. To do this, TAXII specifies
two mechanisms: **_collections_** and **_channels_** .

These enable CTI producers to support both push and pull communications models.
Collections are sets of CTI data that CTI producers can provide to their customers when
requested to do so. Channels enable CTI producers to push data to their customers – whether
it's a single customer or many customers. This same mechanism also enables customers to
receive data from many producers (STIX Version 2.1, June 2021). The TAXII version 2.1
specification is 79 pages and contains all the details needed to implement client and server
participants in the CTI-sharing models I mentioned earlier.

A key benefit of using STIX and TAXII is standardization. When CTI producers publish CTI
using a standardized schema such as STIX, it makes it easier for organizations to consume it,
even when they are using technologies from different vendors. If everyone uses the same
standard way to describe threats versus proprietary protocols, CTI consumers get the benefit
regardless of the vendors they procure their cybersecurity capabilities from. In other words,
cybersecurity vendors and teams can focus on innovation using CTI, instead of spending time
devising ways to model and share it. In this manner, these protocols help scale CTI sharing to
organizations and technologies around the world.

**Reasons not to share CTI**

Many of the security teams I have talked to opt not to share CTI with other organizations, even
when they have good relationships with them. This might seem counterintuitive. Why
wouldn't a security team want to help other organizations detect threats they have already
discovered in their own IT environment?

There are at least a couple of good reasons for this behavior. First, depending on the exposure,
disclosing CTI could be interpreted as an admission or even an announcement that the
organization has suffered a data breach. If the organization has suffered a breach, they'll want
to manage it on their own terms and on their own timeline if possible. Keeping such matters
close to the chest minimizes potential legal risks and PR risks, or at least gives the organization
some time to complete its investigation if one is ongoing. Further, many organizations simply

_Chapter 2_ 74

won't share CTI because it could end up disrupting their incident response processes and crisis
communication plans, potentially leading to litigation and class action lawsuits.

A second reason some security teams opt not to share CTI is that they don't want to signal to
the attackers that they know that their IT environment is compromised. For example, when
they'd find a file suspected of being malware on one of their systems, instead of uploading a
copy of it to VirusTotal or their anti-malware vendor for analysis, they'd prefer to do their own
analysis behind closed doors so as not to tip off the attackers.

A _best practice_ that many malware purveyors use is to scan the malware they develop offline
with multiple anti-malware products to ensure that their new malware is not detected by any
of them. This gives them a measure of confidence that they are still undetected in their victims'
IT environments. So, once a security team uploads the malware sample to an anti-malware
vendor, that vendor will develop signatures to detect, block, and clean that malware. They will
also distribute those signatures to their customers and samples of the malware to other antimalware vendors and add the malware to their online threat encyclopedias.

This will let the attacker know that one or more of their victims has found their malware,
submitted it to an anti-malware vendor, and is likely investigating further to determine the
extent of the intrusion. This could accelerate the attackers' timeline with a severe impact on
their victims. For example, knowing that their presence has been detected, attackers might
deploy ransomware and demand a ransom before their victims' incident response teams can
take action.

Subsequently, many security teams do their own in-house malware reverse engineering and do
not share CTI with other organizations or even their security vendors, until they believe there
is no opportunity cost in doing so. They do not want to give attackers any advantage and do
not want to deal with potential negative legal, regulatory, or reputational outcomes that could
arise. This approach gives them the best chance to find and exorcize the attackers before they
decide to perform actions on objectives, such as deploying ransomware or destructive wiper
malware.

Now that we've discussed what CTI is and how it is shared between organizations, let's explore
the characteristics of _credible CTI_ . Knowing how to tell the difference between credible CTI and
not-so-credible CTI can help CISOs and security teams consume and operationalize CTI more
efficiently.
###### **How to identify credible CTI**

In this section, I'm going to give you some guidance on how to identify good CTI versus the
questionable TI I see so often in the industry today. After publishing one of the industry's best

75 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

TI reports for the better part of a decade (OK, I admit I'm biased), I learned a few things along
the way that I'll share with you here.

The only way you'll be able to truly understand whether or how specific threat intelligence can
help your organization is to understand its data sources, as well as the methodology that the
vendor used to collect and report the data; without this context, TI can be distracting and the
opposite of helpful.

There are two challenges security teams must overcome with respect to CTI:

First, they only have so much time to consume and potentially operationalize CTI.
Every minute they spend consuming CTI that won't help them is a minute lost during
the constant deluge of attacks on their organization. Frankly, most security teams are
not resourced well enough that they can spend time consuming CTI that isn't helpful
to them.

The second related challenge they need to overcome is operationalizing the wrong CTI.
In other words, they spend the time, effort, and budget to develop capabilities that
defend against low probability or low impact threats instead of the threats with the
highest probability and potential impact on them. There are a lot of threats that
security teams can spend their time and resources on, but most teams need to be very
good at choosing the most important areas to invest in.

Keep in mind that many cybersecurity vendors, including those that publish CTI, leverage
modern marketing techniques to drive demand for their products and services and build their
brands. Focusing your precious attention on CTI that is designed to help operational
cybersecurity teams instead of marketing vehicles that leverage CTI will help your security
teams stay sane in this noisy industry.

As I previously mentioned, understanding the source of the CTI you consume is very
important. Let's explore this aspect next.

**Data sources**

First and perhaps most importantly, always review the sources of CTI data that you are using
and how the vendors involved are interpreting the data. If the data source is unknown or the
vendors won't share the source of the data, then you simply cannot trust it and the
interpretations based on it.

_Chapter 2_ 76

For example, suppose a vendor claims that 85% of all systems have been successfully infected
by a particular family of malware. But when you dig into the data source used to make this
claim, you find that _85% of systems that used the vendor's online malware cleaner website_ were
infected with the malware referenced. Note that "85% of all systems" is a dramatic
extrapolation from "85% of all systems that used their online tool."

Additionally, you also find that the online tool is only offered in US English, meaning it's less
likely that consumers who don't speak English will use it even if they know it exists, which
further skews the data. For example, if you work at a public sector organization in Japan, how
valuable is CTI to you that focuses on a specific industry vertical in the private sector in the US?
The answer is you don't know until you understand the sources of data and what they might
mean to your organization.

Finally, you discover that the vendor's desktop antivirus detection tool refers users to the
online tool to get disinfected when it finds systems to be infected with the threat. The vendor
does this to drive awareness that their super-great online tool is available to their customers.
This skews the data, as 100% of users referred to the online tool from the desktop antivirus tool
were already known to be infected with that threat. I can't count how many times I've seen
stunts like this over the years.

Examples such as these illustrate why it's always important to dive deep into the data sources
to understand what the data actually means to you.

**Specificity** is your friend in this context. Understanding where the data was collected from and
how, the limitations of the data sources, and the underlying assumptions and biases present
while processing the data are all key to understanding how the resulting CTI might help your
organization. Purveyors of credible CTI are happy to provide this context to you. However, they
might not volunteer this information, and you might need to request it. Providing such
information tends to highlight the limitations of the CTI and the CTI provider's capabilities.
Also, I've found that not everyone is a connoisseur of the finer points of CTI; being prepared to
ask your own questions is typically the best way to get the context you need to truly
understand CTI.

Regarding marketing communications from vendors that leverage CTI, marketing
professionals do this for at least a couple of good reasons. First, if they lead their

77 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

communications with new CTI data, they can potentially drive a news cycle that amplifies
their message and helps drive demand for whatever they are selling. Secondly, including real
CTI in their marketing message gives the message some semblance of credibility. Your job as a
CTI consumer is to recognize the difference between marketing messages that leverage CTI
and CTI that will help your operational security team. Although these aren't mutually
exclusive, recognizing the difference will help avoid randomizing your operational security
team with CTI that is relatively low value for them.

**Time periods**

When consuming TI, understanding the time scale and time periods of the data is super
important. Are the data and insights provided from a period of days, weeks, months, quarters,
or years? The answer to this question will help provide the context required to understand the
intelligence.

The events of a few days will potentially have a much different meaning to your organization
than a long-term trend over a period of months or years. Anomalies will typically warrant a
different risk treatment than established patterns. Additionally, the conclusions that can be
made from CTI data can be dramatically altered based on the time periods the vendor uses in
their report.

Let me provide you with an example scenario. Let's say a vendor is reporting on how many
vulnerabilities were exploited in their products for a given period. If the data is reported in
regular sequential periods of time, such as quarterly, the trend looks really bad, as large
increases are evident. But instead of reporting the trend using sequential quarterly periods, the
trend looks much better when comparing the current quarter to the same quarter last year;
there could actually be a decrease in the exploitation of vulnerabilities in the current quarter
versus the same quarter last year. This puts a positive light on the vendor and obscures the
increase in the exploitation of vulnerabilities in their products quarter over quarter.

Another potential red flag is when you see a vendor report data that isn't for a normal period of
time, such as monthly, quarterly, or annually. Instead, they use a period of months that seems
a little random. If the time period is irregular and the reason it's used isn't obvious, the
rationale should be documented with the CTI. If it's not, ask the vendor why they selected the
time periods they used. In some cases, the timeframe changes for valid reasons, such as
updates to a product or methodology, or the adoption of a new reporting cadence. However,
sometimes, you'll find some vendors use a specific time period because it makes their story
more dramatic, garnering more attention, if that's their agenda. Alternatively, the period
selected might help downplay bad news by minimizing changes in the data.

_Chapter 2_ 78

Understanding why the data is being reported in specific time scales and periods will give you
some idea about the credibility of the data, as well as the agenda of the vendor providing it to
you.

**Recognizing hype**

One of the biggest mistakes I've seen organizations make when consuming CTI is accepting
their vendor's claims about the scope, applicability, and relevance of their data. For example,
suppose a CTI vendor publishes data that claims 100% of attacks in a specific time period
involved social engineering or exploited a specific vulnerability. The problem with such claims
is that no one in the world can see 100% of all attacks, period.

They'd have to be omniscient to see all attacks occurring everywhere in the world
simultaneously, on all operating systems and cloud platforms, in all browsers and applications.
Similarly, claims such as 60% of all attacks were perpetrated by a specific **Advanced Persistent**
**Threat** (APT) group are not helpful. Unless the vendor making this claim has knowledge of
100% of attacks, they can't credibly make claims about the characteristics of 60% of them. A
claim about the characteristics of all attacks or a subset that requires knowledge of all attacks,
even when referencing specific time periods, specific locations, and specific attack vectors,
simply isn't possible or credible. I call these types of claims _claims of omniscience_ .

A good litmus test for CTI is to ask yourself, does the vendor have to be omniscient to make this
claim? This is where understanding the data sources and the time periods will help you cut
through the hype and derive any value the intelligence might have. Purveyors of CTI that
openly state the limitations of their data and properly qualify the conclusions they make earn
trust with me because they are more credible. Outlandish conclusions-based questionable CTI
claims don't impress me, even if they are highly entertaining.

Many times, the vendor publishing the data doesn't make such claims directly in their TI
reports, but the way new intelligence is reported in the headlines is generalized or made more
dramatic in order to draw attention to it. Don't blame CTI vendors for the way the news is
reported, as this is typically beyond their control. But if they make such claims directly,
recognize them and adjust the context in your mind appropriately. For many years, I made
headlines around the world regularly speaking and writing about threats using threat
detection data from a billion Windows systems, but we were always very careful not to
overstep the mark from conclusions supported by the data. Making bolder claims would have
required omniscience and omnipotence.

**Predictions about the future**

I'm sure you've seen some vendors make predictions about what's going to happen in the
threat landscape in the future, and they might even provide data that leads you to believe that
their predictions are accurate.

79 _What to Know About Threat Intelligence_

For this purpose, some CTI vendors use a trick that is again related to time periods. Let's say
I'm publishing a TI report about the last 6-month period covering January through June. By the
time the data for this period is collected and the report is written and published, a month or
two might have gone by. Now it is September. If I make a prediction about the future in this
report, I have two months of data from July and August that tell me what's been happening
since the end of the reporting period.

If my prediction is based on what the data tells us already happened in July and August,
readers of the report will be led to believe that I actually predicted the future accurately, thus
reinforcing the idea that my firm knows more about the threat landscape than anyone else.
Understanding when the prediction was made relative to the time period it was focused on
will help you decide how credible the prediction and results are, and how trustworthy the
vendor making the prediction is. Remember, predictions about the future are guesses —what
happened in the past does not define what can happen in the future.

**Vendors' motives**

Trust is earned with people by behaving with a combination of credibility and character that
they appreciate. You can use both to decide how trustworthy your vendors are. Transparency
around CTI data sources, time scales, time periods, and predictions about the future can help
vendors prove they are credible. Their motives communicate something about their character.
Do they want to build a relationship with your organization as a trusted advisor, or is their
interest limited to a financial transaction? There's a place for both types of vendors when
building a cybersecurity program, but knowing which vendors fall into each category can be
helpful, especially during incident response-related activities, when the pressure is on.

Those are some of the insights I can offer you from a decade of experience publishing TI
reports. Again, the big takeaway here is understanding the methodology and data sources of
the CTI you consume— _this context is not optional_ . One final word of advice: do not consume TI
that doesn't meet this criterion. There is too much fear, uncertainty, doubt, and complexity in
the IT industry. You need to be selective about who you take advice from.
###### **Summary**

I hope you enjoyed this chapter. Over the last 10 years, the CTI industry has exploded. Finding
credible sources of CTI shouldn't be a challenge for well-funded cybersecurity programs. CTI is
being integrated into cybersecurity products and services more and more, which means

_Chapter 2_ 80

protecting, detecting, and responding to threats should be easier and faster than ever.
However, I have to wonder, if this is true, how are attackers being more successful now than
ever before? There are many historical examples that teach us that TI isn't sufficient by itself to
mitigate attacks; defenders need to be willing to act on the intelligence they have and need the
capabilities to do so effectively. Despite the proliferation of CTI, organizations need effective
cybersecurity strategies to be successful. In order to develop an effective strategy for your
organization, it is helpful to first understand the types of threats you face and how they
operate. This is the theme of the next six chapters of this book.

In this chapter, you learned about different aspects of CTI. CTI provides organizations with
data and information on potential cyber threats. Those threats can include various categories
of malware, exploitation of vulnerabilities, web-based attacks, DDoS attacks, social
engineering attacks, and others. OSINT leverages publicly available data sources such as social
media, news feeds, court filings, and arrest records, as well as information attackers disclosed
on their victims, activity in illicit forums, and many others.

I also described how cybersecurity programs can make use of CTI, including in SOCs, to inform
CIRT investigations, to inform threat hunting, red, blue, and purple teams' efforts, and many
others. I discussed how cybersecurity teams use TTPs and IOCs.

I introduced the TLP, which has become a popular protocol for sharing CTI and other types of
information. Finally, we explored how to recognize credible CTI versus noise. To do this, you
need to dive deep into data sources, understand how time periods are being used, learn to
recognize hype, and seek to understand your vendors' motives.

This chapter provided some context to help you understand the analysis of various threats in
the next six chapters: _Chapter 3_, _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_ ; _Chapter 4_, _Product_
_Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_ ; _Chapter 5_, _The Evolution of Malware_ ; _Chapter 6, Internet-Based_
_Threats_ ; _Chapter 7_, _Application Programming Interface (API) Security_ ; and _Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe?_
_The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_ .

## Part 2
### Evolution of the threat landscape

In this section, you'll gain a deeper understanding of how the modern threat landscape has
evolved and what that evolution means for your security strategy. You'll learn from long-term
trends in both industry-wide and product-specific vulnerability disclosures, including a
detailed look at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited
Vulnerabilities catalog and what it reveals about real-world attacker behavior. You'll explore
how malware, especially ransomware, has transformed into one of the most disruptive and
financially damaging tools in an attacker's arsenal.

You'll examine the shifting nature of internet-based threats, from phishing and drive-by
downloads to large-scale distributed denial-of-service attacks, and understand how these
techniques continue to adapt to modern environments. You'll also see why **Application**
**Programming Interfaces (APIs)** have become one of the most consequential enterprise attack
surfaces and learn how to evaluate and secure them effectively.

Finally, you'll unpack the complex and sometimes contradictory roles governments play in
cybersecurity as market participants, standards bodies, regulators, defenders, and at times
adversaries, so you can navigate policy, compliance, and geopolitical risk with clarity and

# 3
##### Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends

Vulnerabilities represent risk and expense to all organizations that use technology. Technology
vendors who are serious about reducing both risk and costs for their customers focus on
reducing the number of vulnerabilities in their products and work on ways to make it hard and
expensive for attackers to exploit their customers, thereby driving down attackers' return on
investment. Identifying the vendors and the products that have been successful in doing this
can be time-consuming and difficult.

Organizations that develop and operate their own software and hardware share this challenge.
It is their responsibility to take commercially reasonable steps to protect their customers' and
employees' data, their intellectual property, and other confidential business data. Failure to
take this responsibility seriously can lead to expensive incident response events, expensive
product rework or canceled products, a diminished brand, expensive lawsuits, fines, and poor
regulatory outcomes. Vulnerability management is a cornerstone of most successful
cybersecurity programs because it is fundamental to cybersecurity.

In this chapter, I will provide you with valuable background information and an in-depth
analysis of how some of the industry's leaders have managed vulnerabilities in their products
over the last several years. I will introduce a vulnerability improvement framework that can
help you identify vendors and products that have been reducing risks and costs for their
customers. This data and analysis can inform your organization's vulnerability management
strategy.

In this chapter, we'll cover the following topics:

From worms to resilience: the evolution of vulnerability management

Vulnerability management primer
