Let's begin by looking at what vulnerability management is.
###### **From worms to resilience: the evolution of** **vulnerability management**

Over the past 25 years, organizations have been challenged to manage a continual volume of
new vulnerabilities in software and hardware. Attackers and malware constantly attempt to
exploit unpatched vulnerabilities on systems in every industry and every part of the world.
Vulnerabilities are a currency for many interested groups, including security researchers, the
vulnerability management industry, governments, various commercial organizations, and, of
course, attackers and purveyors of malware. These groups have different motivations and
goals, but they all value new vulnerabilities, with some willing to pay handsomely for them.

I had a front-row seat at ground zero for the tumultuous period where worms and other
malware first started exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft software at scale. After working on
the Enterprise Network Support team at Microsoft for a few years, I was asked to help build a
new customer-facing security incident response team. I accepted that job on Thursday,
January 23, 2003. Two days later, on Saturday, January 25th, _SQL Slammer_ hit the internet,
disrupting networks worldwide. That Saturday morning, I got into my car to drive to the office
but had to stop for gas. Both the cash machine and the pumps at the gas station were offline
due to "network issues." At that point, I realized just how widespread and serious that attack
was. Then, one day in August 2003, _Blaster_ disrupted the internet to an even greater extent
than SQL Slammer had. Over the course of the following year, Blaster variants followed, as well
as _MyDoom_, _Sasser_, and other widespread malware attacks. It turns out that millions of people
were willing to double-click on an email attachment labeled _MyDoom_ . Most of these attacks
used unpatched vulnerabilities in Microsoft products to infect systems and propagate. This all

happened before Windows Update or any of the tools that are available today for servicing
software existed. Because Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address the
underlying vulnerabilities in the components that Blaster used, many IT departments began a
long-term pattern of behavior, delaying patching systems to avoid patching the same
components repeatedly and rebooting systems repeatedly. Most internet-connected Windowsbased systems were not running antivirus software in those days either, and many of those
that were didn't have the latest signatures installed. Working on a customer-facing security
incident response team, supporting security updates, and helping enterprise customers with
malware infections and hackers was a very tough job in those days—you needed thick skin.
Subsequently, I had the opportunity to learn a lot about malware, vulnerabilities, and exploits
in this role.

87 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Later in my career at Microsoft, I managed marketing communications for the **Microsoft**
**Security Response Center** ( **MSRC** ), the Microsoft **Security Development Lifecycle** ( **SDL** ),
and the **Microsoft Malware Protection Center** ( **MMPC** ). The MSRC is the group at Microsoft
that manages the incoming vulnerability and attack reports. The MMPC was Microsoft's
antivirus research and response lab back then. The SDL is a software development
methodology that was instituted at Microsoft in the years that followed these devastating
worm attacks. I learned a lot about vulnerabilities, exploits, malware, and attackers in the 8 or
9 years I worked in this organization, called _Trustworthy Computing_ . I often get asked whether
things are better today than they were 10 or 15 years ago. _Chapters 3_ and _4_ in this book are
dedicated to answering this question and providing some insights into how things have
changed from a vulnerability management perspective. These chapters also provide you with a
way to identify vendors and products that have been reducing risk and costs for their
customers.
###### **Vulnerability management primer**

Before we dive into the vulnerability disclosure trends for the past 25 years, let me provide you
with a quick primer on vulnerability management so that it's easier to understand the data and
analysis I provide in this chapter, and how some vulnerability management teams use such
data.

There are many different definitions of what a vulnerability is. Let's use the definition provided
by the **National Institute of Standards and Technology** ( **NIST** ):

_"A weakness in the computational logic (e.g., code) found in software and hardware_
_components that, when exploited, results in a negative impact to confidentiality,_
_integrity, or availability. Mitigation of the vulnerabilities in this context typically_
_involves coding changes, but could also include specification changes or even_
_specification deprecations (e.g., removal of affected protocols or functionality in their_
_entirety)."_

_NIST, August 2023_

If you are wondering what a vulnerability actually looks like, this little C code snippet is a good
example, as its author explains in the following quote:

```
  void func(int index, int value)

  {

    char buf[4];

  buf[index] = value;

  }

```

_Chapter 3_ 88

_"Let's assume the arguments index and value come from a call to recv() which reads_
_a packet from the Internet. Is this a security bug? Heck yeah. The attacker controls_
_everything about that poor old buffer. Even with /GS and ASLR in place, this would_
_be a serious bug and would be fixed at the earliest."_

_Howard, May 9, 2021_

In this example, the author is alluding to the developer's failure to validate the input before
processing it. The developer appears to be making the assumption that `index` and `value`
passed into the function will always be valid numbers that can be used to set the value of each
character in the character array buffer allocated (called `buf` ). Since the values of `index` and

`value` are set by the contents of a network packet from the internet, what if attackers set those
values to something the developer didn't expect? Could an attacker corrupt some memory by
passing an `index` value to the function that is beyond the end of the defined buffer? Without
including input validation and error handling in this function, this developer has developed a
potentially exploitable bug. As the author of the code mentions, even enabling compiler
options such as /GS and ASLR, which are designed to make exploitation of vulnerabilities
harder, can't always compensate when developers make mistakes.

Remember the real-world example of the incident I described in _Chapter 1_, _How Enterprises Get_
_Hacked,_ called _Data breaches via insecure APIs_ ? The root cause in both these cases is the same;
developers make mistakes that tools and automation can't always discover. To be fair to
developers, many security class bugs that are exploitable are far more nuanced and harder to
identify than this simple example; modern compilers would likely flag this bug for the
developer. Still, **memory corruption** vulnerabilities constitute the second largest category of
vulnerability type behind **cross-site scripting**, causing 20,789 vulnerabilities between 2016
and the end of 2025 (CVE Details, n.d.). These _weaknesses_ in hardware and software that could
lead to bad security outcomes are tracked and shared.

This vulnerability management primer provides some background and context that will help
you digest all the vulnerability data I share in this chapter as well as the next chapter.

89 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Understanding how vulnerabilities are tracked, scored, and their impact on front-line
enterprise vulnerability management teams will help you interpret the data. Let's start with
Common Weakness Enumeration.

**Common Weakness Enumeration**

The MITRE Corporation is a not-for-profit organization that manages federally funded
research centers for, among other things, cybersecurity. MITRE supports the NIST in a mission
to build trustworthy information systems for US government agencies. These two
organizations are central to how vulnerability management operates across industries around
the world. When a vulnerability in a commercial software or hardware product is discovered,
MITRE and NIST record and track the vulnerability so that anyone using the product can
understand the risk of doing so and what mitigations for the vulnerability exist. As part of this,
MITRE manages a list of common software and hardware weakness types to which
vulnerabilities discovered are mapped. This list is called **Common Weakness Enumeration**
( **CWE™** ). MITRE offers the CWE for free for public sector and commercial sector
organizations, as well as individuals, at `[https://cwe.mitre.org/index.html](https://cwe.mitre.org/index.html)` . MITRE
describes why they offer the CWE this way:

_"Knowing the weaknesses that result in vulnerabilities means software developers,_
_hardware designers, and security architects can eliminate them before deployment,_
_when it is much easier and cheaper to do so."_

_MITRE, n.d._

At the time of writing, version 4.19.1 of the CWE list had 944 weaknesses listed in it. The list
can be navigated based on the area of research you are interested in, such as software,
hardware, or more specific areas, such as **OWASP Top 10**, software written in C++, software
written in Java, and so on. Regardless of the programming language used or the type of product
developed, common weaknesses can be introduced in the development process that can be
identified and fixed before they become vulnerabilities that technology operators must manage
downstream. I mentioned two types of weaknesses earlier, memory corruption and cross-site
scripting. Other examples include exposure of sensitive information to an unauthorized actor,
deserialization of untrusted data, and use of hardcoded credentials.

**The CVE Program and NIST**

When a vulnerability is discovered in a released software or hardware product and reported to
the vendor that owns the vulnerable product or service, the vulnerability will ultimately be
assigned a **Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures** ( **CVE** ) identifier, referred to as a **CVE ID**,
at some point. CVE IDs are alphanumeric strings used to identify publicly disclosed
vulnerabilities. The format of CVE IDs is **CVE-YYYY-NNNN**, where _YYYY_ is the year the CVE ID

_Chapter 3_ 90

was assigned, and _NNNN_ is a unique identifier. _CVE-2018-8653_ is an example of a CVE ID that
was assigned in 2018.

MITRE Corporation started a catalog of all CVEs, called the CVE list, in 1999. There were 321
CVE records in the list at that time. Twenty-five years later, at the time I wrote this, there were
over 332,000 records, representing an increase of about 103,327%. The CVE list can be accessed
at `[https://www.cve.org/](https://www.cve.org/)`, and the history of the CVE list can be found at `[https://](https://www.cve.org/About/History)`

`[www.cve.org/About/History](https://www.cve.org/About/History)` .

The exact date when a CVE ID is assigned to a vulnerability is a function of many different
factors, to which an entire chapter in this book could be dedicated. In fact, I co-wrote a
Microsoft white paper on this topic called _Software Vulnerability Management at Microsoft_,
which described why it could take a relatively long time to release security updates for
Microsoft products. It appears that this paper has disappeared from the Microsoft Download
Center with the sands of time. However, the following are some of the factors explaining why it
can be a long time between a vendor receiving a report of a vulnerability and releasing a
security update for it:

**Identifying the bug** : Some bugs only show up under special conditions or in the
largest IT environments. It can take time for the vendor to reproduce the bug and triage
it. Additionally, the reported vulnerability might exist in other products and services
that use the same or similar components. All of these products and services need to be
fixed simultaneously so that the vendor doesn't inadvertently produce a zero-day
vulnerability in its own product line. I'll discuss zero-day vulnerabilities later in this
chapter.

**Identifying all variants** : Fixing the reported bug might be straightforward. However,
finding all the variations of the issue and fixing them too is important, as it will prevent
the need to re-release security updates or release multiple updates to address
vulnerabilities in the same component. This can be the activity that takes the most
time when fixing vulnerabilities.

**Code reviews and testing** : Ensuring that the updated code actually fixes the
vulnerability and doesn't introduce more bugs and vulnerabilities is important and
sometimes time-consuming.

**Functional testing** : This ensures that the fix doesn't impact the functionality of the
product—customers don't appreciate it when this happens.

**Application compatibility testing** : In the case of an operating system or web browser,
vendors might need to test thousands of applications, drivers, and other components
to ensure that they don't break their ecosystem when they release the security update.

91 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

For example, the integration testing matrix for Windows is huge, including thousands
of the most common applications that run on the platform.

**Release testing** : Ensuring that the distribution and installation of the security update
works as expected and doesn't make systems unbootable or unstable is vital. The last
thing software vendors want to do is push an update to all of their customers that
makes operating systems unbootable. The latest high-impact example of this is
" _KB5042421: CrowdStrike issue impacting Windows endpoints causing an 0x50 or 0x7E_
_error message on a blue screen_ " (Microsoft, n.d.).

The allure of notoriety that comes with announcing the discovery of a new major vulnerability
leads some security researchers to release details publicly before vendors can fix the flaws. The
typical best-case scenario is when the public disclosure of a vulnerability occurs on the same
date that the vendor releases a security update for the vulnerability. This reduces the window
of opportunity for attackers to exploit the vulnerability to the time it takes for each
organization to test and deploy the update in their IT environments.

Let's take a closer look at the details for that example CVE ID I introduced earlier,
_CVE-2018-8653_ . This will help you understand some of the aspects of vulnerabilities that are
tracked and how that **i** nformation is used by vulnerability management teams. As you can tell
from the CVE ID, the number _8653_ was assigned to the vulnerability it was associated with in
2018. When we look up this CVE identifier in the CVE list, we can get access to some basic
information including a short description, the vendor whose code has the vulnerability in it
along with the known affected products and their versions, the CVE Numbering Authority that
assigned the vulnerability, its CVE ID, references to more information, the date the CVE ID was
added to the list, and other information. Here is the description of that CVE ID:

_"A remote code execution vulnerability exists in the way that the scripting engine_
_handles objects in memory in Internet Explorer, aka "Scripting Engine Memory_
_Corruption Vulnerability." This affects Internet Explorer 9, Internet Explorer 11,_
_Internet Explorer 10. This CVE ID is unique from CVE-2018-8643."_

_CVE, 2018_
