**National Vulnerability Database and CVSS**

The **Internet Category of Attack Toolkit** ( **ICAT** ) was started in 1999. It was rebranded as the
**National Vulnerability Database** ( **NVD** ) in 2005 by NIST. The NVD imports data from the
CVE list and adds metadata to it, including metrics and scoring information, in a process
referred to as " _enrichment_ " (CVE, n.d.). The NVD can be used to track publicly disclosed
vulnerabilities in all sorts of software and hardware products across the entire industry. The
NVD is a publicly available database that can be accessed at `[https://nvd.nist.gov](https://nvd.nist.gov)` .

When we look up the CVE ID mentioned earlier, _CVE-2018-8653_, in the NVD, we can get even
more details about it that weren't available in the CVE ID's record in the CVE list. Examples of
these extra details include the severity scores for the vulnerability, potentially from multiple
different sources, whether the vulnerability can be accessed remotely, whether user interaction
is required to exploit the vulnerability, its potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and
availability, and its exploitability score. Enriching the CVE can also include assigning a CWE ID
and **a** dding **Common Platform Enumeration** ( **CPE** ) applicability statements (NIST, 2022).

The CPE provides a standard naming convention for software and hardware affected by
vulnerabilities. This is helpful, as in the past, different names for the same product appeared in
the NVD. For example, "Internet Explorer" and "IE" would both appear as affected products in
different CVE ID records referring to the same product. This made it hard to get an accurate
inventory of CVE IDs for a specific product that suffered from this problem. The CPE addresses
this problem and provides a format that makes CPE applicability statements more machinereadable so that vulnerability management tools and products can consume them more easily.
Here is an example of a CPE applicability statement: `"cpe:`

`2.3:a:microsoft:internet_explorer:8.0.6001:beta:*:*:*:*:*:*"` . If you are interested in
learning more about the CPE and its format, check out the CPE specifications on NIST's website
at `[https://nvd.nist.gov/products/cpe](https://nvd.nist.gov/products/cpe)` .

You might wonder what all the other additional information the NVD provides is used for. A
score is assigned to each CVE ID in the NVD that represents a risk calculation for each
vulnerability. Risk is the combination of probability and impact. In the context of
vulnerabilities, risk is the combination of the probability that a vulnerability can be
successfully exploited and the impact on the system if it is exploited. The **Common**
**Vulnerability Scoring System** ( **CVSS** ) is used to estimate the risk for each vulnerability in the
NVD. The **Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams** ( **FIRST** ) CVSS **Special Interest**
**Group** ( **SIG** ) is the custodian of the CVSS with the goal of improving it over time. You can find
more information on this SIG at `[https://www.first.org/cvss/](https://www.first.org/cvss/)` .

Before getting into the details on the latest version of the CVSS, it is important to know that the
CVSS has evolved over time. Subsequently, there have been different versions released over

93 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

time, such as v1, v2, v3, v3.1, and v4.0. Each newer version incorporated feedback from the CVSS
stakeholder community and improved the industry's ability to manage vulnerabilities in
technologies, and enabled security measurement and compliance objectives.

As the CVSS evolved and different versions were published, a natural question arose. Assuming
organizations will strive to use the latest CVSS version to get its advantages, will all the CVE
IDs that were published in the past get updated with scores using the newest CVSS version?
For example, when we look up the example CVE ID we've been discussing, _CVE-2018-8653_, in
the NVD, it currently has CVSS scores using CVSS versions 2.0 and 3.x, but not 4.0 (the latest
version). If we look up a newer CVE ID, _CVE-2024-24747_, for example, it has a CVSS v3.x score,
but not a CVSS 2.0 or CVSS 4.0 score assigned to it. This is the case despite more than 18
months having passed since _CVE-2024-24747_ was published and CVSS version 4.0 became
available months before the CVE ID was published. The answer to this question can be found
in the NVD's FAQ on CVEs:

_"Q. Have all older CVEs been updated to CVSSv3?_

_A. The NVD is [sic] prioritizes the enrichment of new vulnerabilities or_
_vulnerabilities that have changed since their last enrichment. At this time, there are_
_no plans to retroactively assess vulnerabilities published before Dec 20, 2015 with_
_CVSS v3.0 scores._

_A similar approach is planned for after the release of CVSSv4."_

_NIST, 2022_

While the lack of CVSS version continuity amid the ever-growing population of CVE IDs
introduces a few challenges, the fact that newer versions of the CVSS continue to improve the
industry's ability to manage risks associated with vulnerabilities is very positive. However, in
2024, a variety of factors impacted NIST's ability to keep pace with the volume of CVE IDs
being published by CVE Numbering Authorities. This led to a large backlog of CVE IDs that
were published but had not gone through NIST's NVD enrichment process. NIST published the
following statement about the situation on their website in February 2024 and later updated it
in April of the same year:

_"NVD Program Announcement UPDATED - April, 25th 2024_

_NIST maintains the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), a repository of_
_information on software and hardware flaws that can compromise computer_
_security. This is a key piece of the nation's cybersecurity infrastructure._

_Chapter 3_ 94

_There is a growing backlog of vulnerabilities submitted to the NVD and requiring_
_analysis. This is based on a variety of factors, including an increase in software and,_
_therefore, vulnerabilities, as well as a change in interagency support._

_Currently, we are prioritizing analysis of the most significant vulnerabilities. In_
_addition, we are working with our agency partners to bring on more support for_
_analyzing vulnerabilities and have reassigned additional NIST staff to this task as_
_well._

_We are also looking into longer-term solutions to this challenge, including the_
_establishment of a consortium of industry, government, and other stakeholder_
_organizations that can collaborate on research to improve the NVD._

_NIST is committed to its continued support and management of the NVD._
_Currently, we are focused on our immediate plans to address the CVE backlog, but_
_plan to keep the community posted on potential plans for the consortium as they_
_develop."_

_NIST, 2024_

Some industry estimates put the backlog of new CVE IDs that needed enrichment at over
16,000 by July of 2024 (Phoenix Security, 2024). At the time of writing (February 2026), CVE
IDs in the NVD that have not gone through the enrichment process can still be found. A note in
the details of such CVE IDs in the NVD states: " _AWAITING ANALYSIS. This CVE record has been_
_marked for NVD enrichment efforts_ ." Apparently, the backlog for enriching CVE IDs has not been
cleared yet. The NVD plays a critical role for governments and industry worldwide, and such a
backlog hinders its reliable operation. To reduce reliance on the US NVD, the European Union
created its own equivalent—the **European Union Vulnerability Database** ( **EUVD** )—which
released its first public vulnerability data in April 2025. The EUVD can be accessed at `[https://](https://euvd.enisa.europa.eu/)`

`[euvd.enisa.europa.eu/](https://euvd.enisa.europa.eu/)` .

Now that you've gained some insight into the importance and drama surrounding CVE IDs,
let's look at the latest version of the CVSS more closely. CVSS version 4 was published on

November 1 <sup>st</sup>, 2023 (FIRST, 2023). To calculate a CVSS score, this version of the CVSS uses four
metric groups, including **Base**, **Threat**, **Environmental**, and **Supplemental** .

95 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

The _Base_ metric group leverages two sets of metrics: **exploitability metrics** and **impact**
**metrics** . Notice how these sets of metrics map to probability and impact, respectively.
Exploitability metrics include metrics such as the following:

**Attack vector** : How exploitation is made possible

**Attack complexity** : How hard it is to exploit the vulnerability

**Attack requirements** : Conditions that must be true for an attack to succeed

**Privileges required** : The level of privileges the attacker must have

**User interaction** : Whether a user needs to take action to exploit the vulnerability
(FIRST, 2023)

To calculate an estimate of the impact on a system if a vulnerability is successfully exploited,
the CVSS uses impact metrics, such as the expected impact on confidentiality, integrity, and
availability (FIRST, 2023).

The exploitability metrics and impact metrics are provided in the NVD's details on each CVE
ID. The CVSS uses these details in some mathematical calculations to produce a base score for
each vulnerability (NIST, n.d.). The NVD provides CVSS calculators to help organizations
calculate vulnerability scores. NVD calculators are available on NIST's website for CVSS v2.0,
v3.0, v3.1, and v4.0. CVSS scores can range from 0.0 to 10.0. The scores can be mapped into
qualitative ratings such as _low_, _medium_, _high_, and _critical_ to make it easier to manage than
using granular numeric scores (FIRST, 2023). _Table 3.1_ summarizes the CVSS scoring ranges for
each rating:

|Rating|CVSS Score|
|---|---|
|None|0.0|
|Low|0.1–3.9|
|Medium|4.0–6.9|
|High|7.0–8.9|
|Critical|9.0–10.0|

_Table 3.1 – Rating descriptions for ranges of CVSS version 4.0 scores_

Vulnerabilities with higher scores have higher probabilities of exploitation and/or greater
impacts on systems when exploited. Put another way, the higher the score, the higher the risk.
This is why many vulnerability management teams use these scores and ratings to determine

_Chapter 3_ 96

how quickly to test and deploy security updates and/or mitigations for vulnerabilities in their
environments, once the vulnerabilities have been publicly disclosed.

Vulnerability management professionals can further refine the base scores for vulnerabilities
by using the other aforementioned metric groups, including _Threat_, _Environmental_, and
_Supplemental_ .

_Threat_ metrics are meant to provide insight into the current state of exploit techniques or the
availability of exploit code for each CVE ID scored. The intent of the _exploit maturity_ metric is to
provide some insight into the likelihood that a particular vulnerability will be exploited. The

source for such a metric is **Cybersecurity Threat Intelligence** ( **CTI** ), as we discussed in
_Chapter 2, What to Know About Threat Intelligence_ . The possible values for this metric are as
follows:

**Not Defined** : No reliable CTI is available

**Attacked** : The vulnerability has been used in attacks, or attacks seem imminent

**Proof-of-Concept** : Proof-of-concept code publicly available, no knowledge of actual
attacks

**Unreported** : Based on CTI, no knowledge of proof-of-concept code or attacks

This can be very helpful information if your vulnerability management team is trying to
prioritize which vulnerabilities to address; for instance, vulnerabilities that are categorized as
"attacked" are no longer only theoretically exploitable. Because of this, many CISOs and
vulnerability management policy **service level agreements** ( **SLAs** ) expedite patching for
vulnerabilities with known exploitation.

The _Environmental_ metric group provides another way to tailor CVSS scores. Rather than
measuring the likelihood of exploitation, these metrics reflect how critical the affected systems
are to a specific organization, based on their potential impact on **confidentiality, integrity,**
**and availability** —the classic **CIA** triad. Vulnerability management analysts can assign greater
importance or less importance to each member of the CIA triad. For example, a system that
absolutely must be online always could have a high impact on an organization if availability is
impacted by the exploitation of the vulnerability. At the same time, the confidentiality of the
same system may not represent as big an impact if it is compromised, because that system is
only processing non-confidential, publicly available information.

97 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

The _Environmental_ metric group also contains modified _Base_ metrics, which can be used to
customize CVSS scores based on specific circumstances of an organization's environment, such
as the existence of mitigating factors or controls in a specific IT environment. For example, the
impact of a particular vulnerability might be blunted because a mitigation for the vulnerability
had already been deployed by an organization in their previous efforts to harden their IT

**e** nvironment. While the CVSS base score for the vulnerability might be deemed high severity (a
CVSS score between 7.0 and 8.9), in this organization's environment, the threat of exploitation
has been blunted by system hardening and represents a medium severity vulnerability (a CVSS
score between 4.0 and 6.9) to the organization.

Finally, the _Supplemental_ metric group can also be leveraged to customize the CVSS score for
CVE IDs. Metrics in this group include the following:

**Safety** : Is the safety of humans at risk?

**Automatable** : Can exploitation be automated across targets?

**Value Density** : Can the attacker gain control over diffuse or concentrated systems
using the vulnerability?

**Vulnerability Response Effort** : How difficult or easy is it to mitigate the vulnerability/

All the gory details on the metric groups I discussed are available in the _CVSS version 4.0:_
_Specification Document_, available on `www.first.org` .

Now, let's examine how actively exploited vulnerabilities are tracked, since this information is
crucial for prioritizing remediation.

**CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog**

Once a vulnerability has been successfully exploited in the wild, that is someone has developed
exploit code or tooling and used it against real systems, the risk profile changes dramatically.
As a result, many vulnerability management and remediation teams prioritize patching known
exploited vulnerabilities before all others. This approach provides remediation teams more
time to address vulnerabilities when there is no CTI indicating active exploitation.

The **Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency** ( **CISA** ) maintains a list of
vulnerabilities that are known to have been exploited, called the **Known Exploited**
**Vulnerabilities** ( **KEV** ) catalog. All US federal civilian executive branch agencies are required by
a _Binding Operational Directive_ to remediate the vulnerabilities added to the KEV catalog. Given
this, along with the aggressively growing number of vulnerability disclosures across the
industry, some vulnerability management teams I've talked to have decided to prioritize
remediation of only the vulnerabilities found in the KEV catalog. Other vulnerabilities, such as
critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, get addressed with much less urgency, as they are
viewed by these teams as merely _theoretically exploitable_ . Until proof that they have been

_Chapter 3_ 98

exploited surfaces, they view CVE IDs, even critical-severity CVE IDs, as lower risk and address
them with a slower cadence. I examine the efficacy of this approach later in this chapter in the
section called _Analysis of CISA's KEV catalog_ .

**The risk trade-offs of CTI-driven prioritization**

Arguably, organizations that use this approach accept more risk, at least until all critical and
high-severity vulnerabilities in their IT estates have been addressed. Essentially, they are
gambling on the quality and timeliness of the CTI they use to inform their vulnerability
remediation priorities. However, for organizations that struggle with vulnerability
management and remediation, this approach helps them maintain a manageable scope for
their remediation efforts while genuinely reducing risk. The key, though, is to address the
other critical and high-severity vulnerabilities that weren't being actively exploited when they
were initially evaluated, in a reasonable period of time. Allowing these vulnerabilities to sit in
inventory and accumulate over time is foolhardy. Remember what I wrote in _Chapter 2_ —no
one is omniscient, and subsequently, no one can see 100% of all attacks. Understanding the
sources of data and the limitations of the CTI used to inform vulnerability management is
critical when using this approach.

Leveraging CTI to prioritize vulnerability remediation has become so popular that major
vulnerability scanner vendors offer CTI integrations into their vulnerability scanner products,
and the NVD integrates exploitation information into the details of each CVE ID.

_"The NVD has added information to its CVE detail pages to identify vulnerabilities_
_appearing in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog. CVE [sic]_
_appearing in the catalog will now contain a text reference and a hyperlink to the_
_catalog. CVE not appearing in the catalog will not see any change. Information on_
_exploited vulnerabilities and the affected products will also become available to_
_developers when the NVD releases new APIs in late 2022."_

_NIST, n.d._

To the uninitiated, these approaches and the trade-offs might not make much sense.

The primary pain point that deploying security updates for vulnerabilities creates, besides the
expense, is disruption to the business. For example, historically, most updates for Windows
operating systems required reboots. When systems get rebooted, the downtime incurred is
counted against the uptime goals that most IT organizations are committed to. Rebooting a
single server might not seem material, but the time it takes to reboot hundreds or thousands of
servers starts to add up. Keep in mind that organizations trying to maintain 99.999% (5 "9s")
uptime can only afford to have 5 minutes and 15 seconds of downtime per year. That's 26.3
seconds of downtime per month. Servers in enterprise data centers, especially database and

99 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

storage servers, can easily take more than 5 minutes to reboot when they are healthy.
Additionally, when a server is rebooted, this is a prime time for issues to surface that require
troubleshooting, thereby exacerbating downtime. The worst-case scenario is when a security
update itself causes a problem. The time it takes to uninstall the update, to remediate the
problem it's causing, and reboot yet again, on hundreds or thousands of systems, leaving them
in a vulnerable state, also negatively impacts uptime.

Additionally, patching **a** nd rebooting systems can be expensive, especially for organizations
that perform supervised patching in off-hours, which can require overtime and weekend
wages. The concept of the conventional maintenance window is no longer valid, as many
businesses are global and operate across borders, 24 hours per day, 7 days per week. A
thoughtful approach to scheduled and layered patching, keeping the majority of infrastructure
available while patching and rebooting a minority, has become common.

Reboots are the top reason that many organizations decide to accept some risk by patching
quarterly or semi-annually, so much so that the MSRC that I worked closely with for over a
decade used to try to minimize the number of security updates that required system reboots to
every second month. To do this, when possible, they would try to release all the updates that
required a reboot in one month, and then release updates that didn't require reboots the next
month. When this plan worked, organizations that were patching systems every month could
at least avoid rebooting systems every second month. But the "out of band" updates, which
were unplanned updates necessitated by rapidly changing assumptions about the
exploitability of vulnerabilities, seemed to spoil these plans frequently.

Rebooting servers has traditionally created tension between IT operations teams focused on
uptime as an indicator of success and cybersecurity teams focused on preventing long-running
unpatched systems from being the Achilles heel in their security postures. So much so that in
2025, Microsoft announced " _hotpatching_ " [sic] for security updates for select versions of
Windows Server and Windows 11 Enterprise (Microsoft, April 24, 2025). Windows
" _hotpatch_ " [sic] packages install without the need to schedule a reboot. Other update packages
for Windows that install features are released quarterly and likely will require a reboot after
installation. The net is that using hotpatching enables rapid installation of security updates
while reducing the requirement to reboot to quarterly for select Windows Server and client
versions. For organizations that run the latest versions of Windows, this new capability is sure
to reduce the tension between IT operations teams and cybersecurity teams by allowing
security updates to be deployed faster.

When you see how vulnerability disclosures have trended over time, the trade-offs that
organizations make between the risk of exploitation and uptime might make more sense.
Running servers in the cloud can dramatically change this equation—I'll cover this in more
detail in _Chapter 13_, _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_ . There are many other

_Chapter 3_ 100

aspects and details of the NVD, CVE, and CVSS that I didn't cover here, but I've provided
enough of a primer that you'll be able to appreciate the vulnerability disclosure trends that we
dive into next. I'll introduce a few more CVE ID-related concepts as we make our way through
the data.

**Zero-day vulnerabilities**

Another important term to understand is **zero-day vulnerability** . A zero-day vulnerability is a
vulnerability that has been publicly disclosed before the vendor responsible for it has released
a security update to address it. These vulnerabilities are the most valuable of all vulnerabilities,
with attackers and governments willing to pay relatively large sums for them.

A scenario that vulnerability management teams dread is when a critical-rated zero-day
vulnerability in their software or hardware has been publicly disclosed. This means the risk of
exploitation could be significantly high, and that a security update to prevent exploitation of
the vulnerability is not publicly available. Sometimes in these scenarios, there are _workarounds_
that can be implemented to help make exploitation of the vulnerability harder or impossible.
Workarounds, such as specific system configurations that prevent exploitation, are typically
meant to be temporary. After all, if the only thing preventing exploitation is a configuration
setting, what happens if that setting gets changed inadvertently or by an attacker who already
has initial access? Often, changing a configuration setting as a workaround also disables
functionality that was previously available. The one way to address vulnerabilities with the
highest confidence and least impact is to install an update that fixes them.

An even worse scenario is when a vendor releases a security update for an exploitable, criticalrated vulnerability, but the update doesn't fix the vulnerability completely. In this scenario, the
existence of the vulnerability is public knowledge, and the publicly available security update
that isn't 100% effective essentially draws a map to the vulnerability for attackers to use.
Typically, in such scenarios, the exploit code for such a vulnerability becomes publicly
available and widely circulated on the internet very quickly.

This scenario might sound theoretical, but unfortunately, it has occurred numerous times over
the past two decades. Perhaps the best examples are the dreaded _Log4j_ vulnerabilities
( _CVE-2021-44228_ and _CVE-2021-45046_ ). These vulnerabilities were in the ubiquitous Java
logging library Apache Log4j2. _CVE-2021-44228_ has a "perfect" 10 CVSS v3.x score (9.3 CVSS
2.0 score, no CVSS 4.0 score published), meaning it is easy to exploit and can result in attackers
taking complete control of impacted systems. It is so easy to exploit that some cybersecurity
professionals nicknamed it _Log4Shell_ —a tongue-in-cheek reference to the ability to remotely
run any **c** ommand on systems compromised using this vulnerability. The Software Engineering
Institute CERT Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon University described it this way:

101 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_"Apache Log4j allows insecure JNDI lookups that could allow an unauthenticated,_
_remote attacker to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the vulnerable Java_
_application using Log4j."_

_Software Engineering Institute CERT Coordination Center, Carnegie Mellon_
_University 2021-12-15_

Because this vulnerability was in a very popular software library, it impacted literally
thousands of products that leveraged that library across operating systems such as Windows,
Linux, and macOS. Recall that I mentioned that NIST adds CPE applicability statements to CVE
IDs as part of its enrichment process. The " _known affected software configurations_ " section of
_CVE-2021-44228_ has pages of CPE applicability statements listing impacted products,
including everything from firmware to Linux operating systems, to email platforms, to identity
services, and so on.

For many security teams, the ubiquity of Log4j and the wide variety of places it could be
present in enterprise IT environments made it challenging to find and remediate.
Organizations that had immature asset management practices or imperfect asset inventories
(almost everyone) were left with a ticking time bomb on their hands. Subsequently, many of
the customers I advised managed the remediation of this vulnerability the same way they
would manage an active cybersecurity incident. Using incident response processes instead of
their vulnerability management processes enabled these teams to deem remediation as a top
priority for their organizations and get access to resources commensurate with this
declaration.

However, to make matters worse, more than one security update had to be released to fully
address this critical-rated vulnerability, which was already in active use by attackers at the
time. _CVE-2021-45046_ stated, " _It was found that the fix to address CVE-2021-44228 in Apache_
_Log4j 2.15.0 was incomplete in certain non-default configurations_ " (CVE, December 14, 2021).

These factors resulted in much more work for cybersecurity and IT teams than remediating a
typical critical-rated vulnerability. This scenario occurred at Christmas time in 2021 and spilled
over into the new year, forcing many security teams to work through the holiday season on
remediation. All these factors conspired to exhaust many cybersecurity and IT professionals.
Months later, vulnerable versions of Log4j continued to endear themselves to cybersecurity
and IT teams around the world, by continuing to "pop up" unexpectedly in many enterprise IT
environments, seeping back in from a variety of sources such as vulnerable systems restored
from backups, spinning up virtual machines from unpatched images, vendors continuing to
deploy unpatched applications and appliances, continuing to operate systems past the end of
their supportability dates, and many others. This fun and the associated risks will be around
for years to come.

_Chapter 3_ 102

If you are interested in reading all the details about how the Log4j vulnerabilities were
reported and the crisis unfolded, the US Cyber Safety Review Board investigated and published
a report on their findings. I saw the board's chair from the Department of Homeland Security
and the deputy chair from Google discuss the report and their findings at the Black Hat 2022
conference. It was interesting to hear about the **People's Republic of China** ( **PRC** )
government's reaction to the security researcher from Alibaba who found the vulnerability and
initially reported it to the Apache Software Foundation, instead of to the PRC's **Ministry of**
**Industry and Information Technology** ( **MIIT** ).

_"Independent of a possible sanction against Alibaba, the Board noted troubling_
_elements of MIIT's regulations governing disclosure of security vulnerabilities. The_
_requirement for network product providers to report vulnerabilities in their products_
_to MIIT within two days of discovery could give the PRC government early_
_knowledge of vulnerabilities before vendor fixes are made available to the_
_community. The Board is concerned this will afford the PRC government a window_
_in which to exploit vulnerabilities before network defenders can patch them. This is a_
_disturbing prospect given the PRC government's known track record of intellectual_
_property theft, intelligence collection, surveillance of human rights activists and_
_dissidents, and military cyber operations."_

_Cyber Safety Review Board. July 11, 2022_

This quote lays bare how globally important and politically charged vulnerability disclosures
can get! I'll discuss this tension in _Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in_
_Cybersecurity_ . If you are interested in reading the report, it can be downloaded from `[https://](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/CSRB-Report-on-Log4-July-11-2022_508.pdf)`

```
www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/CSRB-Report-on-Log4```

`[July-11-2022_508.pdf](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/CSRB-Report-on-Log4-July-11-2022_508.pdf)` .

Zero-day vulnerabilities aren't as rare as you might think. Data published by Microsoft
indicates that, of the CVEs that were known to be exploited in Microsoft products in 2017, the
first time they were exploited, 100% were zero-day vulnerabilities, and, in 2018, 83% were
zero-day vulnerabilities (Miller, Matt, 2019).

Since then, data published by Google indicates there were a total of 490 zero-day
vulnerabilities exploited in the wild between 2019 and 2025. That's an average of 70 zero-day
vulnerabilities disclosed across the industry per year (an average of 6 per month) over a sevenyear period. _Figure 3.1_ illustrates the number of zero-day vulnerabilities that were confirmed to
have been exploited in the wild between 2019 and 2025, published by Google.

103 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_Figure 3.1 – Number of zero-day vulnerabilities disclosed across the industry per year between 2019 and 2025_

_Chapter 3_ 104

Over the years, I have talked to thousands of CISOs and vulnerability program managers about
the practices they use to manage vulnerabilities for their organizations. These teams' time is
typically consumed with ensuring that their asset management inventories are as accurate as
possible, triaging incoming volumes of CVE IDs, ensuring that the design and operation of
their vulnerability scanning infrastructure is sufficient, scanning for vulnerabilities and
misconfigurations, communicating scan results and SLA compliance status, patching systems,
and/or working with asset operators to patch systems, ideally within SLAs. Ideally, this work is
like a well-oiled machine, but all too often, it is stressful and frustrating because of the tension
between the goals of asset operators and their cybersecurity teams' desire to constantly reduce
the risk for their organizations. If the goals and resources are not aligned between these two
teams, they both struggle to meet expectations while the risks increase. This can lead CISOs
and vulnerability management team managers to adopt different processes to manage
vulnerabilities and misconfigurations based on the different philosophies and risk appetites
their leadership expresses. Historically, the four most common groups of thought on the best
way to manage vulnerabilities in large, complex enterprise environments are as follows:

**Prioritize critical-rated vulnerabilities** : When updates or mitigations for criticalrated vulnerabilities become available, they are tested and deployed immediately.
Lower-rated vulnerabilities are tested and deployed during regularly scheduled IT
maintenance in order to minimize system reboots and disruption to business. These
organizations are mitigating the highest-risk vulnerabilities as quickly as possible and
are willing to accept significant risk in order to avoid constantly disrupting their
environments with security update deployments.

These organizations are gambling that high-severity vulnerabilities won't be exploited
as quickly as critical-severity vulnerabilities. This reduces the number of CVE IDs they
need to patch quickly, as the number of critical-rated vulnerabilities is typically a
fraction of high-severity vulnerabilities. For example, in 2024, the number of highseverity vulnerabilities was 2.6 times that of **c** ritical-severity vulnerabilities (CVE
Details, n.d.).

**30/60/90-day policy approach** : This approach addresses critical and high-risk
vulnerabilities within 30 days, medium-risk vulnerabilities within 60 days, and lowrisk vulnerabilities within 90 days. Alternatively, I've seen 30-day SLAs assigned to

105 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

critical-severity CVE IDs, 60 days to high-severity CVE IDs, and 90 days for mediumand low-severity CVE IDs. When high- and critical-rated vulnerabilities are publicly
disclosed and are being actively exploited on the internet, these organizations'
vulnerability management policies dictate that they will patch critical vulnerabilities
or deploy available mitigations within 24 hours and high-rated vulnerabilities within a
month. This approach aims to strike a balance between the number of CVE IDs that
need to be addressed immediately, those that can wait a month, and those that can
wait much longer. It is noteworthy that the number of medium-severity CVE IDs is
typically comparable or even higher than the number of high-severity vulnerabilities in
any given year.

**No prioritization—just patch everything** : Some organizations have concluded that,
given the continuous and growing volume of vulnerability disclosures that they are
forced to manage, the effort they put into analyzing CVSS scores and prioritizing

updates isn't worthwhile. Instead, they simply test and deploy all updates on
essentially the same schedule. This schedule might be monthly, quarterly, or, for
organizations with inflated risk appetites, semi-annually. These organizations focus on
being really efficient at deploying security updates regardless of their severity ratings.
Believe it or not, these vulnerability management teams tend to be the happiest of
those I've met over the years. Expectations are set across the entire organization that
this is simply the way IT is done, which dramatically reduces all the analysis paralysis,
arguing, and negotiating timelines and scope that typically accompany processes that
rely on CVSS scores for prioritization.

**Delay deployment** : For organizations that are acutely sensitive to IT disruptions and
have been disrupted by poor-quality security updates in the past, delaying the
deployment of security updates has become an unfortunate practice. In other words,
these organizations accept the risk related to all publicly known, unpatched
vulnerabilities in the products they use for a period of months to ensure that security
updates from their vendors aren't re-released due to quality issues. These
organizations have decided that the cure is potentially worse than the disease; that is,
disruption from poor-quality security updates poses the same or higher risk to them
than all potential attackers in the world. The organizations that subscribe to this
school of thought tend to bundle and deploy months' worth of updates. The appetite
for risk among these organizations is high, to say the least.

A newer approach to managing vulnerabilities in large enterprise IT environments focuses
even further on prioritizing specific vulnerabilities for remediation. It has become very popular
among security teams. As I wrote in _Chapter 2_, **CTI** has many uses. One of those uses is to
inform the priority of vulnerability remediation. Most of the organizations I have advised now

_Chapter 3_ 106

use CTI to identify the vulnerabilities that are being used in active attacks on the internet. They
view these vulnerabilities as the highest risk because their exploitation isn't just theoretical,
which is what a CVSS score represents to many people. CVSS v4.0 does have an _exploit maturity_
metric that can influence the CVSS scores for vulnerabilities with active exploits. Also, in an
effort to help organizations prioritize remediation of CVE IDs, FIRST offers the **Exploit**
**Prediction Scoring System** ( **EPSS** ). It provides the probability of exploitation in the wild for
each CVE ID during the 30 days following its publication. FIRST describes the EPSS this way:

_"The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) is a data-driven effort for estimating_
_the likelihood (probability) that a software vulnerability will be exploited in the_
_wild. Our goal is to assist network defenders to better prioritize vulnerability_
_remediation efforts. While other industry standards have been useful for capturing_
_innate characteristics of a vulnerability and provide measures of severity, they are_
_limited in their ability to assess threat. EPSS fills that gap because it uses current_
_threat information from CVE and real-world exploit data. The EPSS model produces_
_a probability score between 0 and 1 (0 and 100%). The higher the score, the greater_
_the probability that a vulnerability will be exploited."_

_FIRST, n.d._

You can get all the details on this model at `[https://www.first.org/epss/model](https://www.first.org/epss/model)` .

The bulk of the rest of this chapter is devoted to data and analysis with many graphs and
tables. If you aren't interested in seeing the data and analysis, you can skip it and go right to
the summary called _Vulnerability improvement framework summary_ .
###### **Industry vulnerability disclosure trends**

Before we dig into the vulnerability disclosure data, let me tell you where the data comes from
and provide some caveats regarding the validity and reliability of the data. There are three
primary sources of data that I used for _Chapters 3_ and _4_ :

The CVE list: `[https://www.cve.org/](https://www.cve.org/)`

The NVD: `[https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/search](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/search)`

CVE Details: `[https://www.cvedetails.com/](https://www.cvedetails.com/)`

The CVE list is the _de facto_ authoritative source of vulnerability disclosures for the industry. The
NVD imports data from the CVE list and adds metadata to it (including metrics and scoring
information) (CVE, 2020). Finally, the CVSS is used to calculate severity scores for each CVE ID
imported into the NVD.

107 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

However, this doesn't mean the data in the CVE list or the NVD is perfect, nor is the CVSS. I
attended a session at the Black Hat USA conference in 2013 called _Buying into the Bias: Why_
_Vulnerability Statistics Suck_ (Martin, Brian, 2013). This session covered numerous biases in CVE
data. You might be able to find this talk or the associated paper online, and I recommend
watching the video or reading the paper so that you understand some of the limitations of the
CVE data that I discuss in this chapter.

_CVE Details_ is a great website that saved me a lot of time collecting and analyzing CVE data.
CVE Details inherits the limitations of the NVD because it uses data from the NVD. It's worth
reading how CVE Details works and its limitations (CVE Details, n.d.). Since the data and
analysis that I provide in this chapter are based on the NVD and CVE Details, they inherit these
limitations and biases. As I discussed earlier in this chapter, the CVSS versions were updated
over time, and older CVE IDs were not going to be re-scored using the latest CVSS version.
Subsequently, my analysis of CVSS scores mostly uses CVSS v3 as it was consistently the
newest version of the CVSS that was used to score most of the CVE IDs I examined. For really
long timelines, I was forced to use a mix of CVSS v3 and v2. The lack of CVSS version continuity
across CVE IDs is not ideal for such an analysis.

Given that the two primary sources of data that I used for the analysis in this chapter have
stated limitations and the CVSS has changed dramatically over the years, I can state with
confidence that my analysis is not entirely accurate or complete. Also, vulnerability data
changes over time as the NVD is updated constantly. My analysis is based on a snapshot of the
CVE data taken months ago that is no longer up to date or accurate. I'm providing this analysis
to illustrate how vulnerability disclosures were trending over time, but I make no warranty
about this data—use it at your own risk.

**Vulnerability disclosures 1999 to now**

First, let's look at the vulnerability disclosures each year since the CVE list was started in 1999.
It is interesting to note that I can find vulnerabilities with publication dates going back to
January 1989 ( _CVE-1999-1471_ ) in the NVD. Vulnerabilities published prior to 1999 appear to
have been assigned CVE IDs starting with "1999" because that's when the first CVE list was
collected and published by MITRE. An archived bulletin published by the **Computer Security**
**Division Information Technology Laboratory** ( **ITL** ) at NIST in July 2000 provides some
historical insight into the early days of the NVD. NIST's original CVE search service was called
ICAT, as described here:

_"The Computer Security Division at NIST's Information Technology Laboratory has_
_created a searchable index containing 700 of the most important publicly known_
_computer security vulnerabilities. This index, called ICAT (pronounced eye-cat),_
_helps the user to search for specific vulnerabilities and identify those vulnerabilities_
_that are applicable to their organizations… The vulnerability information indexed_

_Chapter 3_ 108

_by ICAT pertains to those vulnerabilities included in a standard vulnerability_
_naming scheme called CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)… Since the_
_current list of 700 vulnerabilities is too large for system administrators to manually_
_review, we created ICAT to allow one to search for vulnerabilities applicable to a_
_particular organization's hosts."_

_Mell, Peter. NIST. 2000_

The reviewer for the second and third editions of this book, Karen Kent, worked closely with
Peter Mell and others at NIST to develop the NVD as the successor to ICAT. The NVD was
launched in mid-2005. Analysts at NIST performed CVSS v1 scoring for all the existing ICAT
vulnerabilities. They then used that body of scoring data to inform improvements for CVSS v2
(Kent, Karen, personal communication, September 4, 2022).

The total number of vulnerabilities assigned a CVE ID between 1999 and the end of 2025 was
over 309,000 (CVE Details, n.d.). As _Figure 3.2_ illustrates, there was a large increase in
disclosures in 2017 that has not receded to historically typical volumes since; a new era in
vulnerability disclosures started in 2017.

_Figure 3.2 – Vulnerabilities disclosed across the industry per year (1999–2025)_

There was a 128% increase in disclosures between 2016 and 2017, and a 157% increase between
2016 and 2018. Put another way, in 2016, vulnerability management teams were managing 18
new vulnerabilities per day on average. That number increased to 40 vulnerabilities per day in
2017 and 45 per day in 2018, on average. As _Figure 3.3_ illustrates, vulnerability management
teams were managing 55 new vulnerabilities per day on average in 2021, a 206% increase from
2016 levels:

109 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_Figure 3.3 – Average number of vulnerabilities disclosed per day between 1999 and 2025_

If things couldn't be more challenging for vulnerability management teams, the number of
disclosures continued to increase rapidly during the next three years. Average daily
vulnerability **d** isclosures increased 25% in 2022, another 16% in 2023, another 39% in 2024,
and 20% in 2025. That's a 651% increase in the average number of daily disclosures between
2016 and 2025, with vulnerability management teams facing 110 disclosures per day on
average in 2024 and 133 disclosures per day in 2025.

Vulnerability management teams review new disclosures to determine which ones affect the
software and hardware in their asset inventories. No organization—unless it's a technology
museum—runs every affected product, but most will have a subset of disclosures that apply to
them each week or month. Larger and older organizations typically face a broader impact
because they carry decades of legacy technology alongside modern systems.

_Chapter 3_ 110

Once affected technologies are identified, vulnerability teams work with asset owners to
remediate them. The workload scales with both the number of new vulnerabilities and the
number of systems, devices, or instances they impact. Organizations that can't keep pace
quickly accumulate a backlog while still facing a constant stream of new CVE disclosures,
dramatically increasing their risk exposure. In large enterprises without mature vulnerability
management capabilities, this can balloon into hundreds of thousands or even millions of
unpatched vulnerabilities. At that scale, the problem becomes overwhelming, and teams
struggle to see a viable path to reducing the inventory of unpatched vulnerabilities.

Remember that a single unpatched vulnerability can be all the opportunity attackers need to
initially compromise an enterprise IT environment. There are many examples of a single
unpatched vulnerability leading to data breaches of major corporations that made headlines.
Attackers can take advantage of unpatched vulnerabilities in many different ways, including
using purpose-built tools, malware, email attachments, and drive-by download attacks,
among other methods. Unpatched vulnerabilities are also used by attackers to move laterally,
persist, and get access to systems post-compromise. Unpatched vulnerabilities are also used in
dreaded mass ransomware attacks—remember the WannaCry "crypto-worm" ransomware
attack that impacted hundreds of thousands of systems around the world?

Subsequently, carrying massive inventories of unpatched vulnerabilities is like setting sail in a
submarine that you know has holes in the hull. I'd often ask executives that I advised, who
were a little cavalier about the state of vulnerability management in their IT environments,
whether they would put their families and retirement savings in such a submarine and set sail,
knowing the state of the condition of the hull. To date, I haven't found one executive who said
they would do such a thing.

A risk-based approach, informed by the **CTI** that I discussed in _Chapter 2_, that makes heavy use
of automation can help manage this new normal. Alternatively, as I have pleaded with so many
enterprises to do, moving to modern compute environments such as the cloud can
dramatically change this calculus. I'll share more on this approach in _Chapter 13_ .

**CVE Numbering Authorities**

You might be wondering what factors contributed to such a large increase in vulnerability
disclosures since 2016. The primary initial factor was likely a change made to how CVE
identifiers are assigned to vulnerabilities in the CVE list. During this time, the CVE anointed
and authorized what they call **CVE Numbering Authorities** ( **CNAs** ) to assign CVE identifiers
to new vulnerabilities (CVE, n.d.). According to MITRE, the organization that manages the CVE
process that populates the NVD with data,

111 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_CNAs are vendor, researcher, open source, CERT, hosted service, bug bounty_
_provider, and consortium organizations authorized by the CVE Program to assign_
_CVE IDs to vulnerabilities and publish CVE Records within their own specific scopes_
_of coverage._

_CVE (n.d.)_

The advent of CNAs means that there are now many more organizations assigning CVE
identifiers since 2016. On January 1, 2020, there were 110 organizations in 21 countries
participating as CNAs. By July 2022, the number of CNAs had grown to 232 organizations in 35
countries, and by July 2025, there were 458 CNAs in 39 countries (CVE, n.d.). That's a 316%
increase in the number of organizations entering CVEs into the NVD, in less than 6 years! The
names, locations, and program roles of the CNAs are available at `[https://www.cve.org/](https://www.cve.org/PartnerInformation/ListofPartners)`

`[PartnerInformation/ListofPartners](https://www.cve.org/PartnerInformation/ListofPartners)` .

CNAs using automation to rapidly find and document more CVEs have also been credited, or
blamed (depending on your point of view), for the exponential increases in CVE IDs over the
past few years. The quality and efficacy of such CVE IDs have been questioned. Clearly,
allowing CNAs to assign CVE IDs has made the process of assigning CVE identifiers more
efficient, thus leading to a large increase in vulnerability disclosures in 2017 and every year
since.

There are several other factors that have contributed to the higher volumes of vulnerability
disclosures since 2017. First, the software industry has expanded dramatically with more
people and machines churning out code than ever before. AI coding assistant tools have
enabled developers to churn out more code than ever before. There have been studies that
detract from such tools, claiming they actually make developers slower. However, the
developers I work with indicate that these tools that write, fix, and improve code have
definitely helped them write code faster. More code means more vulnerabilities in the code.

_Chapter 3_ 112

There are more people and organizations doing vulnerability research than ever before, and
they have better tools than in the past. Finding new vulnerabilities is big business, and a lot of
people are eager to get a piece of that pie. However, most of the focus has been on critical and
high-severity vulnerabilities. This is where the money is, and many security researchers are
only interested in finding the most valuable vulnerabilities to maximize the return on their
investments in time, expertise, and expenses. This leaves reporting of lower severity
vulnerabilities largely to the vendors themselves. Stated another way, vendors largely engage
in the honor system to self-report low-rated vulnerabilities. This has likely led to the underreporting of low-rated vulnerabilities. After all, it is easier to simply fix low-risk bugs that
aren't exploitable, for the next product update, than go through the vulnerability-reporting
process and patch them individually.

The distribution of the severity of the CVE IDs assigned between 1999 and 2025 is illustrated in
_Figure 3.4_ (CVE Details, n.d.):

_Figure 3.4 – CVSS scores by severity (1999–2025)_

There are almost three times more CVEs rated medium severity (136,450 CVEs with CVSS
scores between 4 and 6.9) than critical severity (52,865 CVEs with CVSS scores between 9.0
and 10.0). The number of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities combined constitutes a little
more than half (53%) of all the vulnerabilities disclosed in this 26-year period. The weighted
average CVSS score over this period is 7.6.

113 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

For organizations that have vulnerability management policies dictating the emergency
deployment of all critical-rated vulnerabilities, that's potentially almost 53,000 emergency
deployments over this 26-year period. For most organizations, it will be a fraction of this
number, but this is still likely to represent hundreds or thousands of emergency deployments
over the years. This is one reason why some organizations decide not to prioritize security
updates based on severity—there are too many high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities to
make managing them differently from lower-rated vulnerabilities an effective use of time.

Many of the best vulnerability management teams I've advised over the years focused on
becoming really efficient at testing and deploying security updates in their environment so
that they could deploy all updates as quickly as possible without disrupting the business,
regardless of their severity. This represents real risk reduction for their organizations and,
frankly, they were among the most satisfied vulnerability management teams I met.

It is easy for vulnerability management teams to feel overwhelmed and underappreciated.
Many of them focus on crunching numbers and over-analyzing data to justify testing and
patching fewer security updates, reducing their workloads, and asking the organization to
accept more risk. These teams tend to spend more time analyzing and arguing about asset
inventories, asset ownership, the efficacy of workarounds, and modified CVSS base scores than
turning the crank and just patching. I have a high level of empathy and a lot of respect for all
vulnerability management teams, regardless of the approach they adopt—these are among the
hardest jobs in cybersecurity and tend to be under-resourced.

Let's dive a little deeper into the long-term trends of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities
that have CVSS scores of 7 and higher. As I mentioned previously, most security teams focus on
remediating these vulnerabilities first because they are the highest risk. As _Figure 3.5_
illustrates, the number of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities jumped dramatically
between 2016 and 2017, moving from 3,879 in 2016 to 8,994 CVE IDs disclosed in 2017.

_Chapter 3_ 114

_Figure 3.5 – Total number of CVEs by year and the total number of critical- and high-severity CVEs by year (1999–_

_2025)_

This represents a 132% increase in disclosures of the most severe vulnerabilities in a single year.
The figure also shows us that although the number of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities
was relatively flat between 2018 and 2020, as the total number of vulnerabilities continued to
increase, there has been a dramatic upward trend since (CVE Details, n.d.). The advent of the
CNAs assigning CVE IDs and publishing CVE records has essentially supercharged
vulnerability disclosures compared to the prior 17 years of the NVD. Clearly, the CNAs are not
just filing low- and medium-severity vulnerabilities, when more critical and high-severity
vulnerabilities were filed in 2017 than vulnerabilities of all severities in 2016.

_Figure 3.6_ reveals that 2018 was the year that the industry hit an all-time high of 62.8% of total
vulnerability disclosures rated critical and high severity:

115 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_Figure 3.6 – CVEs rated critical or high severity as a percentage of the total of all CVEs, by year (1999–2025)_

The figure also shows us that in 2021, critical and high vulnerabilities represented 59% of all
vulnerability disclosures that year, and 60% in 2022. These recent highs receded to 58%, 50%,
and 49.6% in 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively.

However, don't open the champagne just yet. The aforementioned 132% increase between 2016
and 2017 is plain as day in _Figure 3.7_ . When translated into potential work for vulnerability
management teams and remediation teams, _Figure 3.7_ reveals that the average number of
vulnerability disclosures per day that have CVSS scores of 7 or higher has never been higher:

_Chapter 3_ 116

_Figure 3.7 – Average number of vulnerabilities disclosed per day that are rated critical or high severity, by year_

_(1999–2025)_

With an average of 66 new critical or high-rated CVEs disclosed every day in 2025,
vulnerability management teams and remediation teams need highly efficient people,
processes, and technologies to keep up with the volume. Left untended, that volume is
potentially 461 CVEs per week, 1,975 CVEs per month, and over 24,000 CVEs per year, all of
which have the highest probability of exploitation. The number of vulnerabilities multiplied by
the number of instances, systems, and IoT devices that these vulnerabilities impact means the
inventory of unpatched vulnerabilities can get very large, very fast.

Remember my story about all the successful worm attacks in 2003? The daily average volume
of critical- and high-severity vulnerability disclosures back then was 30 times less than it was
in 2024. How times have changed. Fortunately, the volume of vulnerability disclosures isn't the
only thing that has changed; capabilities to detect, block, contain, and respond to exploitation
have as well.

For example, security teams would have been able to reduce the potential maximum average
number of new vulnerabilities to investigate every day from 110 to 55 in 2024 by using
vulnerability severity to prioritize near-term remediation. Focusing on the most severe
vulnerabilities helps reduce the number of vulnerabilities to triage every day and reduces risk.

After 8 years of significantly increased volumes of vulnerability disclosures, which continue to
grow every year, this appears to be the new normal for the industry, leading to much more risk
and more work to manage. And with the specter of ransomware, which could be an extinction
event for a business, the pressure on security teams has never been higher. I attended multiple
briefings at the Black Hat conference in 2025, where the topics discussed included how to use

117 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

AI (large language models specifically) to find, exploit, and fix vulnerabilities. This area of
security research is nascent and promises to help identify vulnerabilities faster and more
efficiently than ever. Given this, CVE ID volumes are likely to continue increasing.

**Analysis of CISA's KEV catalog**

Security teams that use CTI on active exploitation can potentially reduce the number of CVE
IDs to triage every day, even further. As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, CISA provides an
authoritative list of CVE IDs that **a** re known to have been exploited in the wild, called the KEV
catalog. Although I use the KEV catalog frequently in my job as a CISO, since I'm not intimately
familiar with this source of CTI, my observations here are more speculative and limited to
comments about the data itself. At the time of writing, I counted 1,483 CVE IDs in the KEV
catalog entered in the 5 years between 2021 and 2025. I counted 185 CVE IDs that were added
to the KEV catalog in 2024 and 245 added in 2025 (a 32% increase from 2024). This means
CISA identified 185 CVE IDs that were being actively exploited in the wild in 2024 and 245 in
2025, which were previously not known to be exploited by CISA. _Figure 3.8_ shows the volume
of CVE IDs published in the KEV catalog each year since 2021.

_Figure 3.8 – Number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog each year between 2021 and 2025_

CISA started publishing the KEV catalog in November 2021. This means they only had 2
months of operating time in 2021, in which they managed to add 311 vulnerabilities that they
had confirmed were exploited in the wild. 2022 was the first full year of the KEV catalog's
operation, in which CISA added 555 CVE IDs to the catalog of known exploited CVE IDs. They

_Chapter 3_ 118

had public exploitation of CVE IDs from the prior 20 years to potentially enter into the KEV
catalog, which might explain why so many were entered in 2022 compared to other years. In
2023 and 2024, the volume of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog was 187 and 187 CVE IDs,
respectively, as _Figure 3.8_ illustrates. My uninformed interpretation of these five years of data is
that 2022 was an outlier, as they likely had a large backlog of known exploited vulnerabilities
that they processed that year. I surmise that after the backlog was processed, 2023 and 2024
represented more typical years in terms of the volume of new CVE IDs added to the KEV
catalog. To test this hypothesis, I analyzed which year each CVE ID was published in and the
year it was added to the KEV catalog. I wanted to see which year each CVE ID was added to the
catalog to get a view into how old each CVE ID was when it was added to the catalog. _Figure 3.9_
provides the results of this analysis:

_Figure 3.9 – Number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog each year between 2021 and 2025 by the date when the_

_CVE ID was first published_

Looking at the CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2022, we can see that CVE IDs that were
published in 19 different years were added to the catalog that year, going as far back as 2004.
There's no other year where CISA added so many CVE IDs published from so many different
years. The data suggests that CISA added 91 CVEs that were published in 2022 to the KEV
catalog that same year. However, the other 464 CVE IDs (84%) were from other years. The
average age of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2022 was 5 years, because of the age of the
CVE IDs in the backlog that were added that year. The average age of CVE IDs added to the KEV
catalog in 2023, 2024, and 2025 was 1.2 years, 1.3 years, and 1.5 years, respectively. However,
note that very old CVE IDs were added to the KEV in all these years, the oldest being 19 years
old in 2023, 12 years old in 2024, and 18 years old in 2025.

Now, let's look at the severity of the CVE IDs added to the KEV during those five years. To do
this, we need to use data from CVE Details because CISA doesn't publish CVSS scores in the

119 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

downloadable version of the KEV catalog. At the time of writing, CVE Details provides a subset
(1,348 CVE IDs) of the 1,483 CVE IDs in the KEV. The average, median, and lowest CVSS scores
of the CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog during this time period are 8.6, 8.8, and 3.3,
respectively. _Figure 3.10_ illustrates the CVSS max base score distribution of the 1,348 CVE IDs
added to the KEV catalog between 2021 and 2025:

_Figure 3.10 – CVSS max base score distribution of the CVE IDs added to the KEV between 2021 and 2025 (CVE_

_Details, n.d.)_

This shows us that 4 CVE IDs (0.15% of the total) were low severity, 151 (11.2% of the total) were
medium severity, 590 (43.8%) were high severity, and 603 (44.7%) were critical severity.
Looking at only the CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2025 (the last full year we have data
for), the average CVSS score of CVE IDs added was 8.3, the median score was 8.8, and the
lowest CVSS score added was 4.

The rate at which CVE IDs were added to the KEV catalog was 0.5 CVE IDs per day, on average,
in both 2023 and 2024. In 2025, this increased to 0.67 CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog per
day. This represents a substantial increase in the number of CVE IDs that CISA saw exploited in
the wild in 2025 compared to the previous two years. One could argue that CISA has just gotten
more **e** fficient at finding evidence of vulnerability exploitation, but this data suggests that
vulnerability management teams will continue to have their hands full managing
vulnerabilities with the highest possible risk.

What other conclusions do I draw from this analysis? First, it is very helpful to have an
authoritative source of exploited vulnerabilities to help drive remediation of vulnerabilities
with the highest probability of exploitation. Every time old, known exploited CVE IDs seep
back into your environment or new ones are added to the KEV catalog, having a list of them at
your fingertips makes it easier to identify them in your asset inventory and track their

_Chapter 3_ 120

remediation. Sometimes, this type of data is necessary to get stubborn stakeholders to approve
near-term action.

My second observation is that 5 years of KEV catalog data is likely not enough data to draw
solid conclusions from, given that the first 2 years of data reported were during the years the
KEV catalog program was bootstrapping and addressing a 20-year backlog. The question is
whether the volume of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2025 is the beginning of a new
normal or an outlier? Only time will tell.

My third observation is that, assuming that the data from 2023 and 2024 describe more
normal volumes of CVE IDs being added to the KEV catalog, vulnerability management teams
will have to triage fewer than 200 CVE IDs per year if all they focused on was CVE IDs that
were added to the KEV catalog. However, in each of those years, about one-third of all CVE IDs
added to the KEV catalog were years old, and in several cases, over a decade old. The
requirement to have evidence of exploitation means that by the time vulnerability
management teams understand the need to triage a given vulnerability, it has already been
used for attacks on the internet. It's hard to believe that CVE IDs that are 5, 10, or 20 years old
haven't been used in attacks until they suddenly show up in the KEV catalog. The time
between a CVE ID's publication and the time it shows up in the KEV catalog represents risk to
those vulnerability management teams that choose to only take action once CVE IDs show up
in the KEV.

There is time between when attackers can start exploiting a vulnerability, when they are
observed doing so, and when up-to-date CTI that reflects this is distributed. Some
exploitations might never be observed. Most vulnerability management teams would be
uncomfortable leaving a 10-year-old critical-rated vulnerability unpatched on internet-facing
assets because it hasn't appeared in the KEV catalog. CISA doesn't advocate such an approach,
but I still run into CISOs that gravitate heavily towards it because it reduces the amount of
work their over-worked vulnerability management and remediation teams must do. Using the
KEV catalog to inform a broader vulnerability prioritization framework seems to be a less risky
approach to vulnerability management than mitigating only those CVE IDs that appear in the
KEV catalog.

Finally, it is likely surprising to some that there are low- and medium-severity CVE IDs in the
KEV catalog. About 11% of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog between 2021 and 2025 weren't
high- or critical-severity CVE IDs. Lower severity CVE IDs generally get forgotten among the

121 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

huge volumes of higher severity vulnerabilities. This raises the question as to whether
deprioritizing medium-severity vulnerabilities is the right approach for more risk-averse
organizations.

In June of 2025, it was reported that CISA faced dramatic budget and staffing cuts of
approximately $495 million and 1,000 staff (Scroxton, June 2, 2025). However, it doesn't
appear that those reductions impacted the operation of the KEV catalog, given there was a 32%
increase in CVEs entered into the KEV catalog in 2025. The future volumes of CVE ID additions
to the KEV catalog can be compared to _Figure 3.8_ to gain insight into volume changes.

Now that we have visibility into the growing volume of vulnerability disclosures across the
industry, it is likely obvious that huge backlogs of unpatched vulnerabilities mount quickly if
teams don't work with enough urgency to address them. Let's discuss how quickly
vulnerability management and remediation teams should work to address vulnerabilities.

**Vulnerability remediation SLAs**

Today, many security teams use CTI to identify and remediate the CVE IDs that are actively
being exploited as quickly as possible. Then, they work to meet the SLAs that their
organization has put in place for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities. Many CISOs and
vulnerability management teams I've met use the 30/60/90-day policy approach; they address
critical and high-risk vulnerabilities within 30 days, medium-risk vulnerabilities within 60
days, and low-risk vulnerabilities within 90 days. Alternatively, I've seen 30-day SLAs assigned
to critical severity CVE IDs, 60 days to high severity CVE IDs, and 90 days for medium and low
severity CVE IDs. I have also seen much more aggressive SLAs and much less aggressive SLAs—
theoretically, these SLAs are a function of the risk appetite of each organization. However, I
have met very few executives who really understand just how much risk their vulnerability
remediation SLAs represent to their organizations; these SLAs and compliance with them are
typically a function of how fast their remediation teams can work based on target resourcing
levels.

As a CISO who has managed several vulnerability management teams in my career, I typically
advocate for aggressive vulnerability remediation SLAs, especially if there is a large backlog of
vulnerabilities. To do this, I have found it helpful to define different SLAs based on asset value
or the probability of unpatched vulnerability exploitation. Using this approach, there are
typically three different categories of assets I employ: internet-facing, crown jewels, and
everything else.

**Internet-facing**

**Internet-facing** IT assets are systems that are not only accessible from inside the
organization's network perimeter, but also from the internet. This includes systems behind
firewalls and inside **demilitarized zones** ( **DMZs** ). For example, an application server that

_Chapter 3_ 122

hosts applications to users on the internet is internet-facing even if it is behind a firewall or
inside a DMZ. Another example is an email server; they typically process inbound and
outbound email using network connections to other email servers on the internet. It doesn't
matter that the email server is behind firewalls because it is receiving packets from the internet
regardless of whether those packets get proxied by firewalls or proxy servers. The increased
risk for these systems is that attackers can interact with them, by design, regardless of how
many firewalls they are behind. Application servers, email servers, and other internet-facing
systems expose network ports and potentially receive input from actors on the internet. These
systems are more accessible to attackers than other systems (insider threat scenarios aside).
The internet-facing category of assets is important to get right because assets in this category
have the highest probability of getting attacked, given their proximity to attackers and their
functions. If a system accepts unsolicited TCP/IP packets from the internet, even if they go
through multiple firewalls or other routing and switching equipment, it's an internet-facing
asset for vulnerability management purposes.

Some vulnerability remediation teams love to get lawyerly in conversations about this asset
category, coming up with imaginative arguments about why assets that receive network traffic
from the internet shouldn't be considered internet-facing. Successfully claiming that an asset
isn't really internet-facing means they'd have to comply with a much less aggressive
remediation SLA. An example is arguing that since an asset has two network interfaces and one
is used for management and only connected to a management network, then the asset isn't
internet-facing, although the other network interface sends and receives network traffic to and
from the internet. They are essentially arguing that the system can only be attacked using the
vulnerability in question via the management interface on an internal network. Sometimes,
the vendor that owns the technology in which the vulnerability is, makes these statements
when they release the update to address it. But I can tell you from my experience working in
the MSRC, attackers live to prove such vendors wrong.

Internet-facing assets need to be patched aggressively, especially critical and high-severity
vulnerabilities, and those CVE IDs in the KEV catalog. If a vulnerability on an internet-facing

123 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

asset is in the KEV catalog, an aggressive SLA is appropriate. I've seen organizations use SLAs
between immediately and 15 days for these types of vulnerabilities. Although I'm sure there are
organizations that don't prioritize this category of vulnerability and patch them with other
CVE IDs 30 days or 60 days after the updates have been published. In my opinion, giving
attackers more than 24 hours to attack unpatched and proven exploitable vulnerabilities on
internet-facing assets is a recipe for failure. It's not the kind of failure you learn from, because
this failure is predictable and not something you have to experience to learn from. It is also the
very type of risk that cybersecurity teams get paid to mitigate.

Critical and high-severity CVE IDs without known exploitation on internet-facing assets get a
bit more lead time, such as 48 or 72 hours. These can be super aggressive and hard to achieve,
depending on the size and complexity of the environment. Often, remediating operating
systems and applications is managed by two different teams. Application owners and
operators tend to have the most challenging job patching because they need to test that their
applications will still work as designed after security updates are deployed. Compressed
timeframes in which to accomplish this add pressure on these teams. This is why so many
organizations opt to patch every quarter or every 6 months.

Finally, it seems like medium- and low-severity vulnerabilities are an afterthought for most
organizations. Most organizations rightfully focus their attention and efforts on the constant
drumbeat of new critical and high-severity CVE IDs. But they rarely get the time to drain the
swamp of the growing number of lower-severity vulnerabilities. Simply failing to patch
medium- and low-severity vulnerabilities is riskier than it seems. Since many security teams
focus on mitigating critical and high-severity vulnerabilities first, attackers have been using
combinations or _chains_ of lower-severity vulnerabilities to compromise systems for many
years. Failing to address such vulnerabilities in a timely fashion and allowing large inventories

_Chapter 3_ 124

to accumulate is not a best practice of a well-run vulnerability management program.
Remember, critical and high-severity vulnerabilities combined only comprise roughly 50–60%
of all CVE IDs in any given year.

**Crown jewels**

The second category of assets that I typically assign a vulnerability remediation SLA to is the
**crown jewels** . Crown jewels are the _highest-value assets_ an organization has. These assets can
be **systems**, **infrastructure**, **processes**, and **data** . Examples of crown jewels include systems
that process, store, or transmit customer data, employee data, intellectual property, and
unreleased financial data. I will discuss the crown jewels in more detail in _Chapter 9_, _Ingredients_
_for a Successful Cybersecurity Strategy_ . Given their value to the organization, if a crown jewel
were compromised, it would be very impactful to the organization, perhaps devastating.
Subsequently, the crown jewels should have aggressive vulnerability remediation SLAs
assigned to them. If a crown jewel is internet-facing, it already should have a super-aggressive
SLA assigned to it, as I previously discussed. Crown jewels that are not internet-facing typically
do not need such an aggressive SLA, but vulnerabilities in them should be remediated faster
than the average IT asset. After all, crown jewels are the highest value assets. If the SLA to
address a critical-rated vulnerability is 30 days for ordinary assets, for example, the SLA for a
crown jewel should be half that: 15 days. Unlike an internet-facing asset's super-aggressive SLA
for critical vulnerabilities in the KEV catalog, crown jewels get more lead time for testing and
deployment, such as 5 days instead of 24 hours. This approach acknowledges the outsized
importance of crown jewels but gives their owners and operators time to test updates before
deploying them, so they don't disrupt regular operations. Again, I've seen a range of SLAs used
for crown jewels among the vulnerability management teams I've advised over the years. Some
teams adopt aggressive SLAs to reduce the risk of a potential extinction event, while others
assign the same SLAs they have on all other assets to their highest value assets. We'll revisit
this topic in _Chapter 9_ .

**Everything else**

These assets aren't internet-facing and aren't crown jewels, so they generally carry lower
inherent risk. They're less likely to be compromised because they sit behind multiple layers of
protection, and a breach typically has a smaller organizational impact. As a result, they often
have longer vulnerability-remediation SLAs.

However, once attackers gain initial access, they readily exploit unpatched vulnerabilities and
misconfigurations on these lower-value systems to move laterally, maintain persistence,
exfiltrate data, or deploy ransomware. An organization may view these assets as low risk, but
attackers do not.

Establishing remediation SLAs that accurately reflect your organization's risk appetite and
regularly reporting SLA performance to senior leadership is strongly recommended.

125 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

So far, we've looked at the growing volume of vulnerability disclosures and discussed how
quickly they need to be remediated based on the relative value of assets and the likelihood of
exploitation. Now, let's dive deeper into the vulnerability disclosure trends for specific popular
vendors. This will give you some idea of the volume of vulnerability disclosures that your
organization faces if it is leveraging these vendors.

This list shouldn't be all that surprising, as some vendors in this list are also the top vendors
