Back in 2003, when the big worm attacks on Microsoft Windows occurred, many of the
organizations I talked to at the time believed that only Microsoft software had vulnerabilities,
and other vendors' software was free from them. This is despite the fact that thousands of CVE
IDs were being assigned each year before and after 2003 to software from many vendors.

More than two decades later, I haven't talked to any security teams recently that still believe
this myth, as they are dealing with vulnerabilities in all software and hardware. This data is not
perfect, and counting the total number of CVE IDs in this manner does not necessarily tell us
which of these vendors and products have improved over the years or whether the industry has
improved its security development practices as a whole. Let's explore these aspects more next.

In the next sections of this chapter, I provide a deep dive analysis of select vendors that have
had the most vulnerability disclosures over the years. All these numbers and graphs will
provide you with insight into how these popular vendors have been trending with regard to
the volume of CVE IDs assigned to them.

**Interpreting vendor and product vulnerability data**

Before we dive into more data, I wanted to offer a few thoughts on the reliability of this data
and how to use it.

First, this data is not perfect. As I mentioned previously, at the time of writing, there is a
backlog of data that has not been through the NVD enrichment process. Since I am counting
and analyzing CVE IDs with specific characteristics, this will undoubtedly have an impact on
the accuracy of the data, especially for more recent years, such as 2023, 2024, and 2025.

129 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Second, this data is only a snapshot of the available data. The data at their sources continued
to change the moment I took each snapshot. The NVD constantly receives new information
and improves the accuracy of the data it has. The world keeps rotating, meaning researchers
and attackers are constantly looking for new discoveries in new and existing CVE IDs. Things
are constantly changing, but the data I provide next is only a snapshot at one point in time. In
the analysis in this section, I used CVSS v3 in most cases because CVSS v3 scores were available
for almost all the CVE IDs I examined in the years between 2017 and 2025. In some cases, when
I examined data from earlier time periods, I used CVSS v1 or v2 scores because CVSS v3 scores
were not available. This isn't ideal, but it helped ensure consistent CVSS scoring for the CVE
IDs in the most recent years. Also note that I used the publication dates of CVE IDs, not the
year when the CVE ID was first assigned. This helps ensure the CVE ID is counted in the year it
was added to the NVD.

One way to interpret this data is through the lens of an SDL. In the wake of the big worm
attacks in 2003, Microsoft started developing the Microsoft SDL (Microsoft, n.d.). Microsoft
continues to use the SDL to this day. I managed marketing communications for the SDL for
several years, so I had the opportunity to learn a lot about this approach to development. The
stated goals of the SDL are to decrease the number and severity of vulnerabilities in Microsoft
software. The SDL also seeks to make vulnerabilities found in software after development
harder or impossible to exploit.

It became clear that even if Microsoft were somehow able to produce vulnerability-free
products, the applications, drivers, and third-party components running on Windows or in
web browsers would still render systems vulnerable. Subsequently, Microsoft shared some
versions of the SDL and some SDL tools with the broader industry for free. It also baked some
aspects of the SDL into some of their publicly available development tools. You can get access
to these resources at `[https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/securityengineering/sdl](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/securityengineering/sdl)` .

We can use the goals of the SDL as an **i** nformal **vulnerability improvement framework** to get
an idea of whether the risk (probability and impact) of using a vendor or a specific product has
increased or decreased over time. This framework has four criteria:

Is the total number of vulnerabilities trending up or down?

Is the severity of those vulnerabilities trending up or down?

Are the EPSS scores trending lower or higher?

Is the number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog trending up or down?

Why does this seemingly simple framework make sense? Let's walk through it.

_Is the total number of vulnerabilities trending up or down?_ Vendors should be working to reduce
the number of vulnerabilities in their products over time. An aspirational goal for all vendors
should be to have zero vulnerabilities in their products. But this isn't realistic, as humans write

_Chapter 3_ 130

code, and they make mistakes that can lead to vulnerabilities. However, over time, vendors
should be able to show their customers that they have found ways to reduce vulnerabilities in
their products to reduce risk and costs for their customers.

_Is the severity of those vulnerabilities trending up or down?_ Given that there will be some security
vulnerabilities in products, vendors should work to reduce the severity of those vulnerabilities.
Reducing the severity of vulnerabilities reduces the number of emergency security update
deployments I mentioned earlier in the chapter. It also gives vulnerability management teams
more time to test and deploy vulnerabilities, which reduces disruptions to the organizations
they support. More specifically, the number of critical and high-severity CVEs should be
minimized as these pose the greatest risk to systems.

_Are the EPSS scores of those vulnerabilities trending up or down?_ Again, if there are vulnerabilities
in products, making those vulnerabilities as hard as possible to exploit should be something
vendors focus on. EPSS is an estimate of the probability of exploitation of a vulnerability for the
first 30 days after it is published.

_Is the number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog trending up or down?_ The number of
vulnerabilities that are added to the CISA KEV catalog is also a good indicator of whether
exploitation is getting harder over time. As we discussed, CISA's KEV catalog is an
authoritative list of CVE IDs that have been exploited in the wild. Vendors that pay attention to
this measure and demonstrate they can effectively reduce the number of their vulnerabilities
that get exploited are vendors who are reducing risk for their customers.

Using these measures, we want to see vendors making the vulnerabilities in their products
consistently hard to exploit. We also want to see fewer vulnerabilities that attackers actually
end up exploiting and that get added to the KEV catalog.

When you interpret CVE ID data for vendors or their products, I suggest you keep these
questions in mind:

Is the CVE ID count increasing or decreasing each year?

Are the numbers of critical-rated and high-rated CVE IDs increasing or decreasing each
year?

Are the EPSS scores advantageous for you or attackers?

Is the number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog increasing or decreasing each year?

One limitation of this approach is that it won't be helpful in cases where vendors and/or their
products are new, and there isn't enough data to evaluate. Another limitation is the _mergers and_
_acquisitions_ scenario, where vendors acquire new companies and their products. For example,
Oracle acquired numerous technology companies and new technologies along with their
vulnerabilities, including MySQL and Sun Microsystems. Acquisition of new technologies can

131 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

lead to significant changes in CVE ID numbers for vendors. It can take time for vendors to
shape the products they obtain to meet or exceed their standards, during which their
customers manage increased volumes of CVE IDs in their products.

Let's start our **d** eep dive by examining some vulnerability disclosure trends for some big
software and cloud vendors, those with the most CVE IDs. Let me make one more important
point before we dive into the data. As I mentioned earlier, I've done thousands of threat
intelligence briefings around the world. I've given enough briefings to enough people to
recognize behavioral curiosities among the audiences I've briefed. There were typically one or
two people in every audience who, upon seeing vulnerability disclosure trends, even for
vendors they said they weren't fans of, suddenly became _vendor apologists_ . The typical refrain
was that we can't really see how vendors are performing by counting CVE IDs unless we
examine specific products, or even a subset of distributions of products. After all, they could be
developed by different development teams, and we really want to measure how those specific
development teams improve over time.

However, after working at two of the world's pre-eminent technology companies for more
than two decades in my career, I have a different view. Every product and every distribution is
the output of the people, processes, and technologies that each vendor uses to develop them.
The vendors we will examine in this chapter are some of the biggest software vendors in the
world. They all have **Software Development Lifecycles** ( **SDLCs** ) and **Security Development**
**Lifecycles** ( **SDLs** ) of some sort to meet their own requirements for minimum viable products,
while improving security and controlling development costs. Some smaller vendors might
suffer from inconsistent quality across the products they develop because they lack these
things, but these big vendors have people, processes, and technologies that help them meet
their minimum requirements to ship their products. If they don't have effective processes and
tools, that's worth knowing. This is what we are measuring in this chapter—the effectiveness
of their people, processes, and technologies, to continuously develop better quality products,
measured by the number of serious vulnerability disclosures they have had. Once a product or
distribution is released to its customers, the customers bear the brunt of the volume of security
updates that follow, in the form of dramatically increased risk, disruptions to their operations,
and associated expenses. Remember, _all_ vulnerability management teams dealt with 133 new
CVE IDs per day on average in 2025, with an average of 55 new critical or high-rated CVEs
disclosed every day. Don't make excuses for the vendors that have the most vulnerabilities—
demand better products instead. All these vendors have the best access to security tools, cloud
services, and AI in the world. If they can't reduce the number and severity of vulnerabilities in
their own products over a period of years, then what chance do smaller, less sophisticated
organizations have?

In this section, I'll focus on three years of data. At the time of writing, CVE data for 2025 is still
being updated frequently, so I'll use data from 2022 to 2024, which is likely more stable at this

_Chapter 3_ 132

point. Three years is sufficient time to make performance course corrections to individual
products, especially in an industry where Agile, continuous integration, continuous
deployment, and AI code assist tools are the mantra. They all take security seriously, so let's
take an objective, quantitative approach to examining their performance. Now let's dive into
the data!

**Microsoft vulnerability trends**

Let's look at how Microsoft has been managing vulnerabilities in its products over the past 26
years. They typically top the list of vendors with the most CVE IDs, with approximately 13,008
between 1999 and the end of 2025 (CVE Details, n.d.). However, in 2025, Linux ascended to the
top of the list of vendors with the most CVE IDs. I will discuss this in more detail in the next
chapter, which focuses on CVE IDs in products. Remember, these numbers are constantly
being updated. Of the aforementioned 13,008 CVE IDs assigned to Microsoft products, 8,450
were rated critical or high. That's 65% of all CVE IDs assigned to Microsoft during this time
that had CVSS scores of 7 or higher. However, note that these CVSS scores were calculated
using a mix of CVSS v1, v2, and v3 base scores because of CVSS version changes during those 26
years. _Figure 3.11_ provides a very long-term view of the volume of vulnerability disclosures, as
well as those CVE IDs with critical or high-severity ratings:

_Figure 3.11 – The number of CVEs and the number of CVEs rated critical or high in Microsoft products per year_

_(1999–2025) (CVE Details, n.d.)_

The products that contributed the most to Microsoft's overall CVE ID count include Windows
Server 2016, Windows Server 2019, Windows Server 2012, Windows Server 2008, and
Windows 10 (CVE Details, n.d.).

Let's focus on the last three years for which we have full-year data: 2022, 2023, and 2024.
_Figure 3.12_ illustrates the key statistics regarding the questions I previously posed.

133 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_Figure 3.12 – Volumes of CVE IDs and CVE IDs with CVSS scores 7 or higher added to NVD assigned to Microsoft_
_products; the percentage of total CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog, including average EPSS scores (2022–2024)_

_(CVE Details, 2025)_

The following is clear from the preceding figure:

First, it shows us that the number of CVE IDs for Microsoft products increased each
year, from 953 in 2022 to 1,030 in 2023, and to 1,125 in 2024. That's a total of 3,108 CVE
IDs assigned to Microsoft products in 3 years, equivalent to 2.8 new CVE IDs per day on
average.

Second, it shows us that the number of critical and high-severity CVE IDs also grew
each year, starting with 683 in 2022, to 754 in 2023, to 850 in 2024, for a total of 2,287
in 3 years. That's an average of two critical or high-severity CVE IDs disclosed per day.
Neither of these measures is moving in the direction we want them to go. Ideally, we
want fewer vulnerabilities for our vulnerability management and remediation teams to
triage, test, and deploy, and especially fewer of the most severe vulnerabilities. There
was a 17% increase in the number of CVE IDs assigned to Microsoft during these years
and a 22% increase in critical and high severity vulnerabilities.

_Figure 3.12_ also shows us that the probability that these CVE IDs would be exploited
during the first 30 days after they were published was, on average, 5.6% in 2022, 5.09%
in 2023, and 4.96% in 2024. This measure did reduce each year, which is positive news
for Microsoft customers.

Finally, _Figure 3.12_ also shows us that the number of CVE IDs assigned to Microsoft
products that CISA put into the KEV catalog was 25 in 2022, 31 in 2023, and 33 in 2024.
A total of 89 CVE IDs assigned to Microsoft products entered the KEV catalog, meaning

_Chapter 3_ 134

they were being exploited in the wild. This is equivalent to 2.5 CVE IDs for Microsoft
products added each month, on average, to the CISA KEV catalog during these years.

The most frequently identified common weaknesses enumerated in Microsoft's vulnerabilities
during these three years included cross-site scripting (37 CVE IDs), memory corruption (23
CVE IDs), and classic buffer overflows (12 CVE IDs).

Now, let's apply the vulnerability improvement framework that I introduced earlier in this
chapter to the Microsoft CVE ID data from 2022 to 2024. The four measures of the framework
are the following:

Did they reduce the number of CVEs during this three-year period? _No_ .

Did they reduce the number of critical and high-severity CVEs? _No_ .

Did they reduce the average EPSS scores, thus reducing the probability of exploitation
after CVE IDs are published? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog? _No_ .

As you can see, Microsoft only accomplished one of the goals defined by the framework. Let's
see how some other vendors performed across these same four measures.

**Google vulnerability trends**

Since Google is #3 in the top 10 list of vendors with the most CVE IDs since the NVD's
inception, let's examine their CVE trends next (CVE Details, n.d.). _Figure 3.13_ shows us that
between 2017 and 2025, there were 10,110 CVE IDs assigned to Google. Of those CVE IDs in
Google products, 5,529 or 55% were rated critical or high severity:

_Figure 3.13 – Number of CVE IDs and critical and high-severity CVE IDs in Google products (2017–2025) (CVE_

_Details, n.d.)_

According to CVE Details, the products contributing the most CVE IDs to Google's totals
included Android, Chrome, and TensorFlow.

135 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Looking at the 3 years between 2022 and the end of 2024, there was a 67% decrease in CVE IDs
assigned to Google products. This dramatic decrease in CVE IDs is further illustrated by _Figure_
_3.14_ .

_Figure 3.14 – Volumes of CVE IDs and CVE IDs with CVSS scores 7 or higher added to NVD assigned to Google_
_products; the percentage of total CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog, including average EPSS scores (2022–2024)_

_(CVE Details, 2025)_

The total number of CVE IDs assigned to their products during these three years was 4,403, of
which 2,032 or 46% were rated critical or high severity. This is equivalent to 4 new CVE IDs
disclosed per day on average and 1.9 critical or high-severity CVE IDs per day on average. As
_Figure 3.14_ illustrates, 2024 was a curious year for Google CVE IDs, as the total number was
dramatically reduced, while the proportion of critical and high-severity CVE IDs increased to
62%, but the number of CVE IDs that were added to the KEV catalog remained the same from
the previous year. The raw number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2024 was the same
as in 2023 (11 CVE IDs added), but the reduction in total CVE IDs in 2024 meant the proportion
of that year's total CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog increased. However, Google did reduce
the total raw number of CVE IDs from 13 in 2022 to 11 in 2024. The same thing happened with
critical and high-severity CVE IDs—the raw total number decreased while the proportion of
the total increased. The average EPSS score was also reduced in 2024 to 0.45%.

The most frequently identified common weaknesses enumerated in Google's vulnerabilities
during these three years included memory corruption (919 CVE IDs), overflow (330 CVE IDs),
and input validation (146 CVE IDs).

_Chapter 3_ 136

Let's apply the vulnerability improvement framework that I introduced earlier in this chapter
to Google's CVE ID data from 2022 to 2024. The four measures of the framework are as follows:

Did they reduce the number of CVEs during this three-year period? _Yes._

Did they reduce the number of critical and high-severity CVEs? _Yes._

Did they reduce the average EPSS scores, thus reducing the probability of exploitation
after CVE IDs are published? _Yes._

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog? _Yes._

Google met the four goals of our vulnerability improvement framework between 2022 and
2024. Congratulations Google! The dramatic reduction in total CVE IDs in 2024, as well as the
reduction in 2024's average EPSS score, fewer critical and high-severity vulnerabilities each
year, and ending the three-year period with fewer CVE IDs added to the KEV are all risk
reductions for Google's enterprise customers.

Google and Microsoft are fierce competitors, both offering consumers and enterprises
operating systems, web browsers, and cloud services, among other products. They are under
similar competitive, legal, and regulatory pressures. They are both based on the West Coast of
the US and have global operations, and they compete for the same pool of technical talent for
their workforces. So, you might wonder how they compare when it comes to vulnerability
disclosures? _Figure 3.15_, _Table 3.4_, and _Table 3.5_ reveal the answer to this question. There are
some differences, but it is interesting how similar these tech titans' CVE data points are at the

###### **Summary**

Vulnerability management is a cornerstone of cybersecurity programs. I started this chapter by
mentioning that I get asked frequently whether cybersecurity is better now than 10 or 15 years
ago. The data we examined in this chapter suggests that things have become much worse, as
evidenced by much higher volumes of severe security vulnerabilities. It is not all bad news,
though, as the data also suggests that some of the vendors we examined have improved in
important ways.

Risk is the combination of probability and impact. The CVSS is used to estimate the risk for
each vulnerability (CVE) in the NVD. This freely available data should be used to inform your
vulnerability management program. Using vendors who have been successful at reducing the
number of vulnerabilities in their products can potentially reduce the time, effort, and costs
related to your vulnerability management program. If you choose vendors who have also
invested in reducing attackers' return on investment by making the exploitation of
vulnerabilities in their products hard or impossible, you'll also be reducing your risk and costs.

Of the three vendors examined in this chapter, Google and Oracle met the criteria of our
vulnerability improvement framework by reducing the number of vulnerabilities in their
products, reducing the severity of vulnerabilities in their products, and reducing the number of
exploited vulnerabilities during the years studied.

Please keep in mind that the data used for these comparisons has many biases and is not
complete or completely accurate. But you can do your own CVE ID research and use the
informal vulnerability improvement framework I've provided in this chapter.

In the next chapter, we are going to dive into the vulnerability disclosure trends for
workstation, server, and mobile operating systems, as well as some popular web browsers. I'll

143 _Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

also provide some guidance on vulnerability management programs based on the lessons I've
learned in the trenches over the years.

# 4
##### Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends

In _Chapter 3_, _Vendor Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_, we took a close look at the three vendors
with the most CVE IDs assigned to them. Now, let's examine vulnerability trends for some
specific popular products. Most enterprises leverage a mix of different hardware and software
products from different vendors. Most of the enterprises I've worked at employ multiple
operating systems and web browsers from different vendors. This adds complexity for the
vulnerability management teams that track vulnerabilities in their technology estates.
Leveraging hardware and software products with consistently elevated levels of vulnerabilities
makes it more expensive and riskier for enterprises. Using vulnerability disclosure trends as an
input to your product selection process can help you understand the relative risks and costs
associated with the products you consider adding to your technology estate. Let's explore some
of the data.

This chapter will cover the following topics:

Product vulnerability trends

Vulnerability management guidance

###### **Product vulnerability trends**

The aggregate vulnerability trend of an individual vendor helps us understand whether and
how that vendor is trying to improve their overall security development processes and drive
costs down for their enterprise customers. However, enterprise customers use products such as
operating systems, web browsers, applications, routing and switching equipment, firewalls,
and so on. Does your organization use vulnerability statistics to inform its IT product
procurement process? Using products that have fewer vulnerabilities, fewer severe

_Chapter 4_ 148

vulnerabilities, and fewer exploitable vulnerabilities can help reduce the total cost of
ownership and the unwanted drama that comes with emergency security patching. Let's start
by examining the vulnerability trends for some popular operating systems.

**Operating system vulnerability trends**

Operating systems have garnered a lot of attention from security researchers over the past 25+
years. A working exploit for a zero-day vulnerability in a popular desktop or mobile operating
system can be potentially worth a lot of money. Let's look at the vulnerability disclosure trends
for operating systems and look closely at a few of the products that have the highest
vulnerability counts. _Figure 4.1_ illustrates the operating systems that had the most unique
vulnerabilities between 1999 and February 2026, according to CVE Details (CVE Details, n.d.):

_Figure 4.1 – Operating systems with the most unique vulnerabilities by total number of CVE counts (1999 to 2026_

_(Jan–Feb) (CVE Details, n.d.))_

The list contains **d** esktop, server, and mobile operating systems from an array of vendors,
including Apple, Google, Linux vendors, Microsoft, and others. Note that _Figure 4.1_ does not
include firmware products, which also have vulnerabilities in them.

In this section, I'll select a few **operating systems** ( **OSes** ) and examine three full years of
vulnerability disclosure measures, as I did with vendors in the last chapter. I'll examine CVE ID
data from 2022, 2023, and 2024, as at the time of writing (January 2026), CVE ID data from
2025 is still being updated frequently. The OSes I select will be based on their popularity with

149 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

the enterprise customers I've advised in the past. Since Debian Linux has one of the highest
CVE ID counts, let's start with it.

As we did in _Chapter 3_, we will use the goals of the **Security Development Lifecycle** ( **SDL** ) as
an informal **vulnerability improvement framework** to get an idea of whether the risk
(probability and impact) of using a specific product has increased or decreased over time. This
framework has four criteria:

1.

2.

3.

4.

Is the total number of vulnerabilities trending up or down?

Is the severity of those vulnerabilities trending up or down?

Are the **Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS)** scores trending lower or higher?

Is the number of CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog trending up or down?

Let's start with a popular Linux distribution – Debian Linux.

**Debian Linux vulnerability trends**

According to CVE Details, Debian Linux **a** ccumulated 9,908 CVE IDs in the NVD between its
inception and February 2026. There are numerous versions of Debian Linux that have CVE IDs
assigned to them, including version 9, version 10, version 11, and others. As _Figure 4.2_
illustrates, between 2017 and 2024, there were 7,341 CVE IDs assigned to Debian Linux, of
which 4,223 or 58% were rated critical or high severity:

_Figure 4.2 – Number of CVE IDs and critical- and high-rated CVE IDs in Debian Linux (2017–2024) (CVE Details, n.d.)_

_Chapter 4_ 150

Focusing on the three years between the beginning of 2022 and the end of 2024, _Figure 4.3_
reveals that Debian was able to reduce the number of CVE IDs, the severity of CVE IDs, and
make them harder to exploit in Debian Linux. There was a 69% decrease in the number of CVE
IDs in Debian Linux by the end of this three-year period, with an 82% decrease in the most
severe CVE IDs. On **a** verage, there were 1.61 new vulnerability disclosures per day in Debian
Linux during these three years and 0.93 new critical or high-severity vulnerabilities per day.
With just three Debian Linux CVE IDs added to the KEV catalog in 2024 and 0.3 critical or
high-severity vulnerability disclosures per day on average, vulnerability management teams
had minimal drama that year.

_Figure 4.3 – Volumes of CVE IDs and CVE IDs with CVSS scores of 7 or higher added to NVD assigned to Debian_
_Linux; the percentage of total CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog, including average EPSS scores 2022-2024 (CVE_

_Details, n.d.)_

Now, let's apply the vulnerability improvement framework to the Debian Linux CVE ID data
from 2022 to 2024. The four measures of the framework are as follows:

1.

2.

3.

4.

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs during this three-year period? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the number of critical- and high-severity CVE IDs? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the average EPSS scores, thus reducing the probability of exploitation
after CVE IDs are published? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog? _Yes_ .

Debian Linux met the criteria of our vulnerability improvement framework because all four
measures were lower at the end of the period than where they started. Well done, Debian! The
data suggests that they did a great job of reducing CVE IDs in Debian Linux in the three years
we examined. This means the people, processes, and technologies they leveraged had a
meaningful security impact and cost reduction for their customers.

151 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Let's examine the vulnerability trends for the Linux kernel next, as it is #1 on the list of
operating systems with the most CVE IDs.

**Linux kernel vulnerability trends**

The Linux kernel isn't a full operating system per se, but it is the kernel that some of the most
popular Linux operating systems are based on. The Linux kernel has a long history of relatively
low volumes of CVE IDs. The first thing you'll likely notice about _Figure 4.4_ is the big spike in
CVE IDs in the Linux kernel in 2024:

_Figure 4.4 – Number of CVE IDs and critical- and high-rated CVE IDs in the Linux kernel (2017–2024) (CVE Details,_

_n.d.)_

For vulnerability data geeks like me, there **i** s an interesting backstory behind this big increase.
It appears that in the community that develops and maintains the Linux kernel, there were
different opinions about whether assigning CVE IDs to vulnerabilities that weren't clearly
exploitable in the Linux kernel was necessary. In February of 2024, MITRE announced that
kernel.org was becoming a **CVE Numbering Authority** ( **CNA** ) (MITRE, 2024). This enabled
kernel.org to assign CVE IDs to Linux kernel vulnerabilities, which then led to a large number
of new CVE IDs being disclosed for the Linux kernel.

Of the 3,782 CVE IDs published in the NVD in 2024 for the Linux kernel, 1,435 (38%) appear to
be CVE IDs from the prior few years, from 2019 to 2023. 1,026 of the 3,782 (27%) CVE IDs were
rated critical or high severity. That's equivalent to 10.4 new CVE IDs per day and 2.8 critical or
high-severity CVE IDs per day.

_Chapter 4_ 152

The following explanation was provided in the official kernel documentation:

_"Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE®) numbers were developed as an_
_unambiguous way to identify, define, and catalog publicly disclosed security_
_vulnerabilities. Over time, their usefulness has declined with regards to the kernel_
_project, and CVE numbers were very often assigned in inappropriate ways and for_
_inappropriate reasons. Because of this, the kernel development community has_
_tended to avoid them. However, the combination of continuing pressure to assign_
_CVEs and other forms of security identifiers, and ongoing abuses by individuals and_
_companies outside of the kernel community has made it clear that the kernel_
_community should have control over those assignments."_

_(The kernel development community. n.d.)_

Another explanation was published on LWN.net, the primary news and information source for
the Linux software community:

_"The kernel project has, for the most part, declined to participate in the CVE game._
_Famously, the project (or, at least, some of the most influential developers within it)_
_has long taken the position that all bugs are potentially security issues, so there is no_
_point in making a fuss over the fixes that have been identified by somebody as having_
_security implications. Still, the kernel has proved fertile ground for those who would_
_pad their resumes with CVE credits, and that grates on both developers and_
_distributors._

_The situation has now changed, and the kernel will be assigning CVE numbers for_
_itself. If that idea brings to mind a group of grumpy, beer-drinking kernel developers_
_reviewing and rejecting CVE-number requests, though, then a closer look is_
_warranted. The key to how this is going to work can be found in this patch to the_
_kernel's documentation:_

_As part of the normal stable release process, kernel changes that are potentially_
_security issues are identified by the developers responsible for CVE number_
_assignments and have CVE numbers automatically assigned to them. These_
_assignments are published on the linux-cve-announce mailing list as_
_announcements on a frequent basis._

_Note, due to the layer at which the Linux kernel is in a system, almost any bug might_
_be exploitable to compromise the security of the kernel, but the possibility of_
_exploitation is often not evident when the bug is fixed. Because of this, the CVE_
_assignment team is overly cautious and assigns CVE numbers to any bugfix that_

153 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

_they identify. This explains the seemingly large number of CVEs that are issued by_
_the Linux kernel team."_

_(Corbet, Jonathan. February 14, 2024)_

It turns out that Red Hat products also saw a marked increase in CVE IDs in 2024. Red Hat
Linux is based on the Linux kernel. Subsequently, the increase in CVE IDs in the Linux kernel
also led to increases in Red Hat Linux in 2024, as described in a Red Hat blog post:

_"The common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) count skyrocketed to 4272, a_
_significant increase from previous years, which were relatively stable. What caused_
_this? The report highlights the Linux Kernel Organization becoming a CVE_
_Numbering Authority (CNA) in February 2024. They began assigning CVEs to_
_numerous kernel issues, many of which wouldn't have received assignments_
_previously. If you filter out those new kernel.org CVEs, the trend line appears more_
_familiar, with a slight increase, likely reflecting Red Hat's growing portfolio but_
_nothing alarming." (Hughes, Maria H. June 6, 2025)_

_Figure 4.5_ dives a little deeper into the Linux kernel's CVE ID data between 2022 and 2024. As
the figure illustrates, despite the high number of CVE IDs in 2024, the average EPSS score was a
tiny 0.08%, and only 7 CVE IDs (0.19% of the total) from that year were added to CISA's KEV
catalog:

_Figure 4.5 – Volumes of CVE IDs and CVE IDs with CVSS scores of 7 or higher added to NVD assigned to Linux_
_Kernel; the percentage of total CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog, including average EPSS scores 2022-2024_

_(CVE Details, n.d.)_

_Chapter 4_ 154

Interestingly, there were many CVE IDs published in 2024 that did not have CVSS v3 scores;
however, they all had CVSS v2 scores. The average CVSS v2 score for the 3,782 CVE IDs in 2024
was 5.6, and the median score was 5.5. The lowest CVSS v2 score was zero, and the highest was
9.8.

Let's apply the vulnerability improvement framework to the Linux kernel CVE ID data from
2022 to 2024. The four measures of the framework are as follows:

1.

2.

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs during this three-year period? _No_ .

Did they reduce the number of critical- and high-severity CVE IDs? _No_ .

Did they reduce the average EPSS scores, thus reducing the probability of exploitation
after CVE IDs are published? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog? _No_ .

Although the Linux kernel does not meet the requirements for our vulnerability improvement
framework because of the CVE ID count spike in 2024, it is sure to earn the respect of many
CISOs, security teams, and other industry stakeholders for trying to be more transparent and
precise about vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel. Typically, it is easier to manage something
that you measure. Although in the short term this has generated more work for the developers
who work on the Linux kernel and more work for enterprise vulnerability and remediation
teams, in the long term, it will be a measurably higher-quality product with higher levels of
security assurance. Besides, would CISOs and other industry stakeholders be satisfied if Apple,
Google, or Microsoft stopped disclosing kernel vulnerabilities because every bug could be a
vulnerability?

Next, let's examine one more flavor of Linux, Ubuntu Linux.

155 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

**Ubuntu Linux vulnerability trends**

Canonical Ubuntu Linux also appears on the list of operating systems with the most CVE IDs
(CVE Details, n.d.), with 4,107 CVE IDs in total in February of 2026. As you can see from _Figure_
_4.6_, there was a dramatic (96%) reduction in CVE IDs in Ubuntu Linux in 2021, which has been
sustained since:

_Figure 4.6 – The number of CVEs, critical- and high-rated severity CVEs, and low-complexity CVEs in Ubuntu Linux_

_per year (2017–2024) (CVE Details, n.d.)_

In my dataset of Ubuntu-related CVE IDs, there were approximately 1.5 CVE IDs per day on
average in 2020. This dropped to 0.069 per day in 2021. However, the proportion of _high_ and
_critical_ severity vulnerabilities increased from 40% in 2020 to 80% in 2021. The proportion
peaked at 83% in 2022 before trending down to 73% in 2023 and 67% in 2024. A sharp
reduction in CVE volume within a single year often occurs when an older Ubuntu LTS release
reaches its end-of-life and is no longer receiving standard security updates. This may be the
case here, as Ubuntu 16.04 LTS (Xenial Xerus) reached its end-of-life in April 2021 and
transitioned into **Expanded Security Maintenance** ( **ESM** ) (Ubuntu, n.d.). Regardless of why
the big reduction in CVE IDs occurred, Canonical was able to sustain the much lower CVE ID
counts for at least four straight years, which is a super achievement.

_Chapter 4_ 156

_Figure 4.7_ reveals fewer CVE IDs each year for Ubuntu Linux between 2022 and 2024, as well as
fewer CVE IDs in CISA's KEV catalog than at the beginning of the period:

_Figure 4.7 – Volumes of CVE IDs and CVE IDs with CVSS scores of 7 or higher added to NVD assigned to Ubuntu_
_Linux; the percentage of total CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog, including average EPSS scores 2022-2024 (CVE_

_Details, n.d.)_

The average EPSS score is higher for Ubuntu Linux during these years than for the other
vendors we've looked at so far. But frankly, once the number of CVE IDs is driven down to very
low levels, as seen here, one or two CVEs with relatively high EPSS scores can impact the
average dramatically.

Let's apply the vulnerability improvement framework to the Ubuntu Linux CVE ID data from
2022 to 2024. The four measures of the framework are as follows:

1.

2.

3.

4.

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs during this three-year period? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the number of critical- and high-severity CVE IDs? _Yes_ .

Did they reduce the average EPSS scores, thus reducing the probability of exploitation
after CVE IDs are published? _No_ .

Did they reduce the number of CVE IDs added to CISA's KEV catalog? _Yes_ .

Canonical has clearly done an outstanding job managing vulnerabilities in Ubuntu Linux over
a period of years. This benefits its enterprise customers' vulnerability management and
remediation teams by keeping associated costs low. Unfortunately, because the average EPSS
score is higher at the end of the period than at the beginning of the period, Ubuntu Linux does
not meet the criteria of our vulnerability improvement framework. It missed by the slimmest
of measures.

Now that we've looked at some popular server operating systems, let's shift our focus to a
couple of popular client operating systems.

**Windows 11**

Microsoft Windows 11 was released in October 2021, giving us three full years of data to
analyze. Evaluating CVE assignments for Windows 11 is more complex than for other operating
systems because Microsoft's annual feature update cadence bundles security fixes into
cumulative releases. These feature updates are labeled 21H2, 22H2, 23H2, and 24H2 to indicate
the year of release (Microsoft, June 2025).

Next, let's look at one final category of popular software, web browsers.

**Web browser vulnerability trends**

Web browsers attract a lot of attention from security researchers and attackers alike. This is
because they are hard to live without. Everyone uses at least one browser on desktops, mobile
devices, and on some types of servers. Operating systems' development teams can bake layers
of security features into their products, but web browsers tend to bring threats right through
all those host-based firewalls and other security layers. Web browsers have been notoriously
difficult to secure, but have improved over the years.

I hope this lengthy analysis in _Chapters 3_ and _4_ has given you some insights into which vendors
and products have been improving recently across some of the key measures that enterprise
vulnerability management and remediation teams can leverage to manage vulnerabilities. Let
me finish this chapter by providing some general guidance on vulnerability management.
###### **Vulnerability management guidance**

A well-run vulnerability management program is critical for all organizations. As you've seen
from the data and analysis in this chapter, there have been lots of vulnerabilities disclosed
across the industry, and the volumes have been increasing, not decreasing. By the end of 2025,
there were over 309,000 CVE IDs in the NVD. Attackers know this and understand how
challenging it is for organizations to keep up with the volume and complexity of patching the
various hardware and software products they have in their environments. Defenders must be
perfect, while attackers just have to be good or lucky once. Let me provide you with some
guidance regarding vulnerability management programs based on my experience managing
some large programs.

**Asset inventories**

First, I cannot overstate the importance of asset management and its role in enabling effective
vulnerability management, incident response, and other key aspects of cybersecurity and IT
management. If an organization doesn't maintain an accurate inventory of IT assets, it is very
difficult, indeed nearly impossible, to effectively manage vulnerabilities and security
misconfigurations. For example, let's say a vulnerability management team scans a system for
unpatched vulnerabilities. They discover numerous unpatched critical and high-severity
vulnerabilities present on the system that exceed remediation time service-level agreements.

171 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

The next step would be to quickly remediate these findings. Who should the vulnerability
management team or remediation team contact to perform application compatibility testing
for the security updates and install the updates on the system? Without an accurate asset
inventory, finding the owner of that system might be a daunting task in a large enterprise
environment. The same problem is pressurized during an active cybersecurity incident when a
system has been compromised, but there isn't an accurate asset inventory to use to find the
owner and get other vital details on the system being investigated or other systems that might
also need to be investigated. One fundamental question in these scenarios is, who has the
administrator credentials?

Organizations that are really good at managing their assets' life cycles and maintaining
accurate, detailed inventories have a much easier time in such scenarios. For example, imagine
if a vulnerability management team didn't have to scan hundreds of thousands of systems
looking for the dreaded Log4j vulnerability during the Christmas holiday period. What if,
instead, they could simply query their asset management database and find a list of assets with
the vulnerable component? What if the asset management database could provide the name
and contact information of the owner of every system where the vulnerable component exists?
Remediation could be a lot faster and with less drama than scanning hundreds of thousands of
systems looking for the vulnerable component, while active attacks are underway on the
internet, and scrambling to try to find system owners to start testing and remediation efforts.
There are some powerful integrations between enterprise asset management products and
many enterprise vulnerability scanners that make vulnerability management and incident
response easier.

Additionally, there are several vendors that make products that help automate asset discovery
on large networks. Some examples **i** nclude **Axonius**, **Lansweeper**, **runZero**, and **Qualys**,
among others. These products can help continuously discover assets on-premises and in the
cloud and feed their details into asset management solutions such as **ServiceNow** .

The key to efficient vulnerability management, including vulnerability reporting, is good asset
management. Investing in asset management will pay dividends in many ways in large
enterprise environments. That said, asset management is neither easy nor inexpensive for
large enterprises that have complex, diverse computing environments. I have talked to some
CISOs who have taken ownership of asset management for their enterprises because it is too
critical for the success of their cybersecurity programs to leave it to other teams to halfheartedly manage. In my experience, this is the exception, not the rule. However, I can see
some wisdom in this approach. Asset management can be an immense amount of work,
especially for organizations that are just starting or resuming that journey after many years
without focusing on it. But since it's on the critical path for some key cybersecurity functions, I
can understand why some CISOs would want to manage it themselves.

_Chapter 4_ 172

**Governance, risk, and compliance**

**Governance, risk, and compliance** ( **GRC** ) are super important for cybersecurity programs,
but are often overlooked or undervalued by CISOs and CIOs of organizations that don't have
mature IT operations or cybersecurity programs. If you don't try to govern things rationally
upfront, you'll have to deal with them later when they are an unwieldy mess, more resourceintensive, and more costly.

In a vulnerability management context, understanding the risk that unpatched vulnerabilities
pose to your organization is a great starting point. The better you are at translating that risk
into a dollar figure range representing the potential cost of an exposure, the easier it will be to
compare it with other cybersecurity and business risks that the organization pays attention to.
For example, if you have credible quantitative risk calculations that show that an unpatched
vulnerability on an internet-facing system would likely cost the organization between
$250,000 and $2,000,000, it makes it easier for business executives to understand the
difference between that risk and other risks they manage, such as legal, human resources, and
financial risks. It also makes it easier for everyone to understand why it would be
advantageous to spend $150,000 to treat that risk, given that it would be potentially much
more expensive to accept the risk.

Once you can articulate the risk, developing a policy that supports managing and minimizing
the risk can be very helpful. Most technical CISOs I've advised don't see the value in writing
corporate policies because no one reads them, and anyone who does complains about them. It
took me a long time in my career to truly appreciate the roles that governance and policies play
in supporting a successful cybersecurity program. I discussed vulnerability management SLAs
in _Chapter 3_, so I won't duplicate that discussion here. Developing a vulnerability management
policy that clearly articulates vulnerability remediation SLAs, as well as other requirements, is
important for a few reasons:

First, it sets expectations among asset owners and operators about how quickly they
need to remediate vulnerabilities in the assets they own. Since policies aren't
discretionary, asset owners and operators are bound to comply with the policy's
requirements or potentially suffer consequences. This tension is helpful to teams as

173 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

they perform resource and budget planning, to ensure they ask for what they need to
meet the requirements of the policy. They aren't "empire building" when asking for
more people for vulnerability remediation; they can use vulnerability program data to
prove they are under-resourced.

Second, a good vulnerability management policy reflects the risk appetite of the
organization. This **i** s helpful to CISOs and other executives as they navigate the riskbased decisions that unfold in front of them. If a CISO knows that the organization has
an enormous risk appetite because it is in a hyper-competitive industry, for example, it
makes it easier for them to accept that they need to manage large inventories of
vulnerabilities, because this is supported by the policy that the organization approved.

A third thing that a clearly articulated vulnerability management policy helps with is
vulnerability management program reporting. Instead of providing elaborate reports
with all sorts of interesting cuts of vulnerability data, simply reporting on whether
each part of the organization is complying with the approved policy and what the
variances are is typically all that is necessary for most executives.

My advice for organizations that are just developing vulnerability management policies for the
first time or trying to mature and operationalize their existing policies is to consider including
the following in their policies:

**Service-level agreements** : Include SLAs based on risk appetite, credible quantified
costs of exposures, and asset values to the organization. As I discussed earlier, I
typically advocate for different SLAs for internet-facing assets, crown jewels, and a
third category for everything else.

**Technology** : The vulnerability management policy should include requirements for
asset owners and operators to install and maintain the specific technologies that the
asset management and vulnerability management programs require to function
effectively. This could include agents that enable the vulnerability management team
to perform authenticated scans of all assets, such as agents from Qualys, Tenable,
Rapid7, or others. If every system doesn't have these installed, then every system can't
be scanned for vulnerabilities effectively. Your asset inventory and overall security
posture depend on ensuring that required technologies are installed on every system in
the environment. Embedding these technology requirements directly into policy
reinforces that unmanaged or isolated "shadow" networks, often maintained to avoid
compliance obligations, are no longer acceptable. All newly provisioned and existing
systems must run the tools that allow the organization to track them, assess the risk
they introduce, and keep them properly updated.

_Chapter 4_ 174

**Scope** : Make the scope of the policy clear so that everyone knows it applies to all
software and hardware, in on-premises environments, containers, virtual machines, in
the cloud, and hosted by third parties. It applies to all software and hardware procured
from third parties and developed by your own development teams (whether they are
FTEs, contractors, or third-party development organizations). This includes operating
systems, web browsers, all applications, appliances such as firewalls and storage
arrays, as well as routing and switching equipment.

**End of Life (EOL)** : EOL software and hardware can pose a grave risk to enterprise
environments. Many non-security managers view decommissioning assets, whose
vendors will no longer release security updates for them, as an expense. They typically
reason, why spend time and effort decommissioning old technology when they could
expend that effort getting new capabilities into the hands of customers and partners?
Just let it decay in place. But letting EOL software and hardware decay on an enterprise
network quickly provides oxygen for attackers. As the inventory of unpatched
vulnerabilities and security misconfigurations mounts, it makes it easier and easier for
attackers to initially compromise an environment, move laterally, stage their attacks,
stay persistent, exfiltrate data, and perform actions on objectives. The inventory of
vulnerabilities on EOL software and hardware represents zero-day vulnerabilities to
organizations foolish enough to let them persist, because the manufacturers of those
technologies will never release security updates for them. Attackers will happily use
that to their advantage over and over. In the meantime, most organizations'
vulnerability management policies have the most aggressive SLAs for active zero-day
exploits. So, then the question becomes _Why perform emergency patch cycles for new zero-_
_day vulnerabilities if you are willing to let them accumulate by running EOL software and_
_hardware on your network perpetually?_ Decommissioning EOL software and hardware is
the same as patching zero-day vulnerabilities. Including language in your vulnerability
management policy that prohibits EOL software and hardware without approved
exception requests is strongly recommended. Exceptions of this nature need to be
recorded in the organization's cybersecurity risk register and periodically reviewed
with senior leadership to ensure the appetite to carry such risk endures.

**Consequences of lack of compliance** : Some of the IT workers I worked with in the
past didn't think the rules applied to them. Some of them spent more time and effort
trying to skirt the rules than it would take to comply with them. Since corporate
policies are non-discretionary, including language that outlines the consequences for
non-compliance gives them gravity they otherwise wouldn't have. It sends the
message that it's not acceptable to ignore the policy. The first person who gets
terminated for non-compliance is typically the last person to get terminated for non

175 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

compliance because everyone else gets the message. If there truly is no consequence for
non-compliance with security policies, then the best effort of some subset of team
members is what you can reasonably expect.

**Policy approvals** : Vulnerability management policies should be signed off by the
largest group of most senior executives that is practical. This is to ensure that asset
owners and operators can't interpret the lack of their leadership's signatures as a sign
that they do not need to comply with the policy. I've literally had senior directors tell
me that the company's vulnerability management policy wasn't signed off by their Vice
President, so it doesn't apply to them. Having a policy that is approved by the largest
group of the most senior leaders sends a message to everyone that security is a priority
at the company, and no one is an exception, based on who they report to. The size of
the organization, how it is organized, and its culture are all factors in how high and
broad security policy approvals need to be. Compliance with vulnerability
management policies is not limited to IT groups, and the policy signatories should
reflect this. Legal, HR, Finance, Marketing, Sales – anywhere IT and OT asset owners
and operators exist – should be covered by the umbrella of the signatories.

**Education and awareness** : Once you have your vulnerability management policy
approved, it's time to drive awareness of the existence of the policy and educate asset
owners, operators, and the stakeholder communities they serve about the details.
Ultimately, you want all the stakeholders to understand that it is their responsibility to
understand and comply with the policy. It's not their vulnerability management team's
responsibility to catch them in the act of non-compliance in order to get them to
comply with the policy. This is why awareness and education are key to the success of
vulnerability management policies. This isn't a one-time activity because every
organization has staff turnover and people who change roles over time. Periodic
refresher awareness and training sessions on vulnerability management policies are
very important to the long-term success of the program. Related to education and
awareness is the topic of reporting, which I'll discuss in depth later in this chapter.

That's my advice for developing vulnerability management policies. Next, let's talk about
another critical factor for a successful vulnerability management program: how often to scan
assets for vulnerabilities.

**Scanning for vulnerabilities**

One objective of a vulnerability management program is to understand the risk that
vulnerabilities present in your IT environment. This understanding is not static or slowmoving. As you saw from the vendor and product CVE ID analysis I provided earlier in this
chapter, vulnerabilities are constantly being disclosed in all hardware and software. Because of

_Chapter 4_ 176

this, data on the vulnerabilities in your environment can get stale quickly. The organizations
that I have met that decided they would deploy security updates once per quarter, or once
every six months, have an unusually high appetite for risk. Although, paradoxically, some of
these same organizations told me they have no appetite for risk. It is always interesting to meet
people who believe their highest priority risks are their vendors, instead of the cadre of
attackers who are actively looking for ways to take advantage of them – attackers who, given
the chance, will gladly encrypt all their data and demand a ransom for the decryption keys.

When I meet an organization with this type of policy, I wonder whether they really do have a
data-driven view of the risk and whether the most senior layer of management really
understands the risk that they are accepting on behalf of the entire organization, the Board of
Directors, and all of their shareholders. Do they know that 110 new CVE IDs per day on average
were published in 2024, with an average of 55 new critical or high-rated CVE IDs disclosed
every day? If they are patching quarterly, that is equivalent to 9,900 vulnerabilities they'll need
to triage to determine whether they impact their organization.

As an example, let's say a large enterprise runs Windows 11 on 10,000 clients and Windows
Server 2022 on 5,000 servers in its data centers. Windows 11 had 1.44 new CVE IDs per day on
average between 2022 and 2024, and 1.09 CVE IDs rated critical or high severity per day on
average during the same period. That means at the end of the quarter, they'd have almost 1.3
million security updates to deploy on their Windows 11 systems, of which 981,000 would be
critical or high severity. Windows Server 2022 had 1.5 vulnerability disclosures per day during
these years, with 1.14 critical or high-severity CVE IDs per day. This would add another
675,000 security updates to deploy, of which 513,000 would be critical or high severity. Then
add security updates for applications running on those systems, along with firewalls and
routing and switching equipment. Double these figures for organizations that patch semiannually. It is very easy for organizations to become overwhelmed with the number of updates
they need to deploy when they have risk appetites this large. One compatibility issue,
deployment issue, recalled security update, or high-severity incident, and they could delay
deploying some security updates until the next patching cycle, 90 or 180 days in the future,
further compounding the numbers.

They also accept the risk associated with large and quickly growing inventories of all those
critical and high-severity vulnerabilities every day for 90 or 180 days. All the while, attackers
only require one exploitable vulnerability in the right system to successfully initially
compromise their environment. Remember the _Cybersecurity Usual Suspects_ ? Attackers can use
any one of them or a combination of them to gain initial access, then use the huge inventory of
unpatched vulnerabilities to move laterally, stay persistent, deploy ransomware, and gain
access to systems that can be used for data exfiltration.

177 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

Instead of avoiding patching and rebooting systems to minimize disruption to their business,
most of these organizations need to focus on building very efficient vulnerability management
programs, with the goal of reducing risk in a more reasonable amount of time. Attackers have a
huge advantage in environments that are both brittle and unpatched for long periods.

For most organizations, my recommendation is that vulnerability management teams _scan_
_everything, every day_ . Read that line again if you have to. Remember the submarine analogy I
used in the _Preface_ section of this book. Your vulnerability management program is one of the
ways in which you look for defects in the hull of your submarine. Scanning every asset you
have in your environment for vulnerabilities every day will help identify cracks and
imperfections in the hull that, if exploited, would sink the submarine. Scanning everything
every day for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations provides the organization with important
data that will inform its risk decisions.

For example, scanning everything every day will help identify when the most severe
vulnerabilities, such as Log4j, show up in an environment months or years after it was thought
to be remediated. Scanning every day provides the organization with the visibility required to
identify and mitigate high- and critical-risk vulnerabilities before they can become
problematic.

Note that I'm not recommending patching every day, just scanning to get a daily snapshot of
the risk. As I discussed earlier in this chapter, remediation-time SLAs should be based on the
risk appetite of the organization. Remember what I recommended earlier: use CTI to inform
remediation priorities. This will help your organization reduce the highest-risk vulnerabilities
first and provide the prescriptive priorities that remediation teams so often want. The
combination of CTI and effective asset management can simplify and reduce costs related to
your vulnerability management and remediation efforts.

For organizations that can accomplish it, using MITRE ATT&CK <sup>®</sup> to also inform vulnerability
remediation priorities can reduce the number of high-priority vulnerabilities while reducing
the risk of exploitation. I discuss this framework in detail in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_ .
Prioritizing patching the vulnerabilities that can support the techniques and procedures that
attackers are known to use makes it harder for them to be successful.

_Chapter 4_ 178

It's important to note that mobile devices, especially of the BYOD variety, pose a significant
challenge to vulnerability management teams. The data on mobile OS vulnerabilities provided
earlier in this chapter indicates that there are hundreds or thousands of CVEs in popular
mobile OSes every year. Most organizations simply can't scan these devices for vulnerabilities
the same way they scan other assets. Instead, limiting mobile devices' access to sensitive
information and high-value assets is more common. Requiring newer operating system
versions and minimum patch levels in order to connect to corporate networks or services is
also common. To this end, most of the enterprises I've met with over the years leverage **Mobile**
**Device Management** ( **MDM** ) or **Mobile Application Management** ( **MAM** ) solutions.

For some organizations, scanning everything every day will require more resources than they
currently have. For example, they might require more vulnerability scanning engines than they
currently have in order to scan 100% of their IT assets every day. They might also want to do
this scanning during off hours to reduce network traffic generated by scanning during regular
work hours. This might mean that they must scan everything, every night, for a defined
number of hours. To accomplish this, they'll need a sufficient number of scanning engines and
staff to manage them. Another issue that plagues organizations that try to scan everything
every day is that their networks were not designed with this requirement in mind. The volume
of traffic generated by all that scanning can impair routing and switching equipment, internal
firewalls, and proxy servers whose capacities have not been scoped to support such a task.
Unfortunately for them, this limitation won't stop attackers. This type of limitation can lead to
a rapid proliferation of scanning engines on network segments if the network capacity issues
cannot be addressed.

Once vulnerability management teams have up-to-date data on the state of the environment,
that data can be used to make risk-based decisions – for example, how quickly newly
discovered vulnerabilities and misconfigurations should be addressed. Without up-to-date
data on the state of the **e** nvironment, hope will play a continual and central role in their
vulnerability management strategy.

Next, let's discuss one final aspect of vulnerability management that I'd like to provide you
with guidance on – reporting.

**Reporting**

The data generated by all this vulnerability scanning is gold dust for CISOs, especially for
security programs that are relatively immature. Providing the C-suite and board of directors
with data from this program can help CISOs get the resources they need and communicate the
progress they are making with their security program. Effective reporting also helps asset
owners and operators understand what their inventory of unpatched security vulnerabilities
looks like and how they are performing in complying with remediation SLAs.

179 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

This list contains some useful example data points:

A breakdown of the number of assets in inventory.

A breakdown of the number of assets in inventory versus the total number of known
assets. This provides visibility into the number of systems that are not in inventory and
therefore not being scanned for vulnerabilities.

The number of assets that are authenticated as scanned for vulnerabilities (the
vulnerability scanner agent is installed and running on the system being scanned).
Authenticated scans provide the maximum visibility to vulnerabilities on a system.
Unauthenticated scans are more like network port scans that provide limited visibility
of the vulnerabilities that might be present on a system. Note that not all systems
support vulnerability scanning agents, so in some cases, unauthenticated scans are as
good as it gets.

The number of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities present.

The average remediation time for vulnerabilities.

This type of data can inform an estimate of how long it will take to address all these
vulnerabilities and can help build an effective business case for more investment in the
vulnerability management program and remediation teams. Providing senior management
with quantitative data like this helps them understand reality versus opinion.

Asset owners and operators tend to request one of two views of their vulnerability inventories,
depending on how efficient they are at remediating them:

Teams that have effective remediation processes typically request the number of
vulnerabilities in inventory, the breakdown by severity, a list of the systems that need
to be patched, and guidance on the most effective way to deploy the updates.

Teams that struggle patching vulnerabilities and meeting SLAs tend not to appreciate
this type of reporting because it lays bare how many unpatched vulnerabilities they
have in inventory, how far behind remediation SLAs they are, and how much risk they
are exposing the organization to. Instead, they typically want reporting to focus on the
number of systems that need to be updated as opposed to the number of security
updates that need to be deployed. This is typically a much smaller number that they
don't feel so embarrassed about. However, the challenge they soon face with this type
of reporting is that the numbers don't improve very quickly because all the
vulnerabilities on each system need to be patched before their status changes in the
reports. Because of this, their progress appears to be super slow, even if they are
deploying a lot of security updates.

_Chapter 4_ 180

Another approach is to simply report average days to remediate for each asset type (internetfacing, crown jewels, etc.). That average is easily compared to the SLA for each asset type to
reveal how well or poorly they are complying with the policy.

I typically provide my stakeholders with both a dashboard that provides near real-time
inventories and weekly roll-up reports. I like the "9-Box" format because it maps to the policy
SLAs I discussed earlier and makes it easy for stakeholders to understand. _Figure 4.16_ is an
example of what it looks like:

_Figure 4.16 – An example of a "9-Box" vulnerability reporting format designed for executives to understand what_

_their vulnerability inventory looks like_

181 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

It is evident that the two left boxes on the top row need to be zero all the time. Non-zero values
in these boxes mean there's work to do immediately in order to comply with the SLAs in the
vulnerability management policy. The 5-week trend sparklines help communicate whether
vulnerabilities have been getting remediated regularly or if they just keep accumulating. It's
normal for these lines to reveal large increases because many vendors, such as Microsoft, for
example, release their security updates once per month. On that day, the number of unpatched
vulnerabilities in inventory typically increases, sometimes dramatically.

This is just a basic example of a dashboard. The data in this dashboard can be supplemented by
other interesting statistics, such as the average number of vulnerabilities per asset in each box,
the average number of days to remediate vulnerabilities in each box, and the variance between
that number and the policy SLAs. Asset operators, those typically responsible for patching,
need much more granular information in order to identify the systems that need to be patched
and the optimal order in which to install the updates. Subsequently, clicking on the boxes in
the dashboard allows them to dive into the data to show them the assets and CVE IDs that
need to be remediated for each asset. These details can be exported from the dashboard so they
can be shared with remediation teams. Of course, the companies that offer vulnerability
management software, such as Rapid7, Qualys, and Tenable, offer their own dashboards that
can be customized.

The vendor and product CVE ID data we looked at earlier revealed that the volume of
vulnerabilities has largely grown unrestrained since 2016. Many cybersecurity and IT
professionals have come to the conclusion that the volumes are now too large for reasonably
sized vulnerability management teams to be successful and have adopted other approaches. I'll
discuss this now to conclude this chapter.

**More modern approaches**

Of course, there are more modern approaches to vulnerability management that can reduce the
number of assets that vulnerability management teams need to scan every day or even
deprioritize the type of scanning we've been discussing altogether. This topic could be a
lengthy chapter in itself, but let's discuss a few of these approaches.

Using more modern "Zero Trust" approaches that verify systems are fully patched before they
are allowed to connect to corporate networks is a popular approach. Requiring systems that are
missing security updates to self-remediate prior to being trusted enough to connect to a
corporate network can dramatically reduce the amount of vulnerability scanning and patching
that vulnerability management and remediation teams must do. Microsoft Defender for
Endpoint is an example of a product that supports this approach. However, most large
organizations have complex IT estates that were built over a period of decades and that
typically rely on significant amounts of legacy technologies. Unfortunately, there's no shortcut
to transforming massive legacy IT environments into modern Zero Trust architectures. Most

_Chapter 4_ 182

organizations modernize parts of their IT estates over a number of years, never able to
modernize everything at once. These environments very often require legacy approaches, such
as scanning everything every day, to truly manage them effectively.

**Virtual machines** ( **VMs** ), containers, and the cloud have enabled an approach to patching that
some IT professionals call "repaving." Instead of scanning every system for vulnerabilities and
security misconfigurations, they scan the images that these transient compute resources are
based on and patch them. Then, when they launch new VMs, they are based on a fully patched
image with a known good configuration state. This approach can reduce costs and effort
related to vulnerability management dramatically. I'll discuss this in _Chapter 13_, _Modern_
_Approaches to Security and Compliance_ .

Finally, there's another approach gaining popularity in the industry that distills much of what
we discussed in _Chapters 3_ and _4_ and marries it with the ability to discover viable attack paths.
Since scanning and remediating every critical and high-severity vulnerability has become too
difficult to achieve in a reasonable amount of time, prioritizing remediation of the specific
vulnerabilities that can be exploited in a non-theoretical attack path helps reduce the risk of
exploitation. Tackling the truly exploitable vulnerabilities first provides remediation teams
with more time to manage the other vulnerabilities in inventory, regardless of their CVSS
scores. If they can't be exploited, they aren't a priority. **Continuous Threat Exposure**
**Management** ( **CTEM** ) and Continuous Red Teaming are two such approaches. They both seek
to identify the ways and vulnerabilities that attackers could actually use in a successful attack
versus prioritizing vulnerability remediations based on the type of CVE ID data we reviewed in
this chapter. A Gartner analyst describes CTEM this way:

_"Continuous threat exposure management is a pragmatic and effective systemic_
_approach to continuously refine priorities and walk the tightrope between two_
_modern security realities. Organizations can't fix everything, nor can they be_
_completely sure what vulnerability remediation they can safely postpone." (Gartner,_
_August, 2023)._

The success of these approaches is highly dependent on their ability to discover all the viable
attack paths. If they fail to discover viable attack paths and the infrastructure remains
unpatched, it could provide attackers with an advantage. Still, if vulnerability management
and remediation teams are faced with ever-growing volumes of severe vulnerabilities, newer,
more efficient approaches will prevail.

This is an area ripe with opportunity for AI. Both defenders and attackers are already
leveraging AI to find exploitable vulnerabilities faster, both in code and in infrastructure. We'll
dive deeper into this in _Chapter 15_, _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for_
_Better Cybersecurity_ .

183 _Product Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_

###### **Summary**

The only operating system of the six that I examined to see whether they achieve the objectives
of our vulnerability improvement framework over a 3-year period was Debian Linux. However,
Ubuntu Linux was very close to satisfying the criteria. Of the three web browsers I examined,
Google Chrome had the best vulnerability management track record between 2022 and 2024,
but also had the highest number of CVE IDs assigned to it. Apple Safari was very close to
satisfying the criteria as well, and it had the lowest number of CVE IDs assigned to it of any of
the browsers I studied. The way vulnerabilities were managed in these browsers during these 3
years reduced the risk to the enterprises that leveraged them.

Please keep in mind that the data used for these comparisons has many biases and is not
complete or completely accurate. But you can do your own CVE ID research and use the
informal vulnerability improvement framework I've provided in this chapter.

Accurate asset inventories are rare, but crucial for vulnerability management, incident
response, and other aspects of operational cybersecurity programs. Don't underestimate the
value of governance, risk, and compliance to your vulnerability management program.
Quantitative risk estimates help stakeholders understand cybersecurity risks in familiar
financial terms, while associated policies should be written to treat these risks with the
stakeholders' risk appetite in mind.

Vulnerability management teams that scan everything, every day, provide the best visibility for
their organizations to manage risk. Data from vulnerability management programs provides
CISOs with some of the data they need to manage the performance of their security programs
and steer future investments into the programs. Reporting scan results to asset owners and
operators helps drive compliance with the vulnerability management policy.

In the next chapter, we are going to dive into the world of malware and examine how the threat
landscape has evolved over the years. Did you know that socioeconomic factors, such as GDP,
are related to regional malware infection rates? We are going to look at this as well.
