# 5
##### The Evolution of Malware

In _Chapters 3, Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_ and _4, Product Vulnerability Disclosure_
_Trends_, I provided a deep dive into vulnerability management, vendor vulnerability trends, and
product vulnerability trends because managing vulnerabilities is a cornerstone of a successful
cybersecurity program. Understanding how enterprise vulnerability management and
remediation teams operate, and the trade-offs they must make, are prerequisites for being a

cybersecurity executive, such as a **chief information security officer** ( **CISO** ).

Another subject that cybersecurity executives need to be well-versed in is malware. One role I
had during my time working at Microsoft was as a product manager in Microsoft's
antimalware lab. In this role, I had the opportunity to work with some seriously talented
malware researchers and analysts. At that time, when Microsoft decided they wanted to enter
the enterprise antimalware business with their Forefront line of products, Microsoft hired
some of the best researchers and analysts from other antimalware labs around the world, such
as Symantec, McAfee, and CA, among others. As I discussed in _Chapter 2_, _What to Know About_
_Threat Intelligence_, I co-authored 20+ volumes of the **Microsoft Security Intelligence Report**
( **SIR** ) with researchers and analysts from the **Microsoft Malware Protection Center** ( **MMPC** ).
Over the years, I learned a lot about malware, malware analysis, and endpoint protection from
these colleagues. What an education! My experience working on Microsoft's customer-facing
incident response team, and then in its antimalware lab, prepared me for the later chapters in
my career as a CISO. I'm happy to share some of what I learned in this chapter.

This chapter will provide a unique, detailed, data-driven historical perspective of how malware
has evolved around the world. There are some very interesting differences in regional malware
encounter rates and infection rates that I'll also dive into in this chapter. This view of the threat
landscape will help CISOs and security teams understand how attackers change their malware
ambitions over time. Not only is this data super interesting, but it can help take some of the

_Chapter 5_ 188

**fear, uncertainty, and doubt** ( **FUD** ) out of conversations about malware and how to manage
the risks it poses.

I'll also provide a deep dive into how ransomware has changed over time to demystify this
term, as it has largely been hijacked and overloaded in recent years. I'll explain how
ransomware has always been one of the least prevalent categories of malware, but continues to
strike fear into CISOs and security teams, and has become a fixture in the news.

The following topics will be covered in this chapter:

The era of advanced threat begins

Why is there so much malware on Windows?

Malware data sources

About malware

Measuring malware prevalence

Global Windows malware infection analysis

Regional Windows malware infection analysis

Global malware evolution

###### **The era of advanced threats begins**

In 2003, when I worked on Microsoft's customer-facing incident response team, we began
finding user-mode rootkits on compromised systems with some regularity, so much so that
one of our best engineers built a tool that could find user-mode rootkits that were hiding from
Windows. A user-mode rootkit runs like any other application that a normal user would run,
but it hides itself. Then, one day, we received a call from a Microsoft support engineer who was
helping troubleshoot an issue that an enterprise customer had on an Exchange email server.
The symptom of the problem was that once every few days, the server would blue-screen. The
support engineer couldn't figure out why and was doing a remote debug session, trying to find
the code that caused the server to blue-screen. It took weeks, but once they found the code
responsible for the blue screen, he couldn't explain what the code was, nor how it got installed
on the server. That's when they called us for help.

When the server blue-screened and rebooted, this enabled us to look at a partial memory
dump from the system. After a few days of analysis, we determined that the server was
compromised in a way we had never seen before. A device driver on the system was hiding
itself and other components. We had found the first _kernel-mode rootkit_ that we had ever seen
in the wild.

189 _The Evolution of Malware_

This was a big deal. Unlike a user-mode rootkit, developing and installing a kernel-mode
rootkit required incredible expertise. This is because this type of rootkit runs in the most
privileged part of the operating system, called the kernel, which few people really understand.
At the time, although the concept of kernel-mode rootkits was discussed among security
experts, finding one installed on a server running in an enterprise's production environment
signaled that attackers were becoming far more sophisticated than ever. Graduating from usermode rootkits to kernel-mode rootkits was a major leap forward in the evolution of malware.

To our incident response team, this was a call to action. We had to let the Windows kernel
developers at Microsoft know that the thing that makes Windows a trusted computing base,
its kernel, was being directly attacked by sophisticated authors of malware.

We scheduled a meeting with the lead developers, testers, and program managers on the
Windows kernel development team. We gathered in a room used for training, with an
overhead projector, so that we could walk the developers through the memory dump we had
from the compromised server to show them how the rootkit worked. We provided them with
some context about the server, such as where it was running, the operating system version, the
service pack level, a list of all the applications running on the server, and so on. We answered
numerous questions about how we debugged the source of the blue screen, found the hidden
driver, and discovered how it worked.

At first, the Windows kernel team was skeptical that we had found a kernel-mode rootkit
running on a Windows server. But after we presented all the evidence and showed them the
debug details, they gradually accepted the fact that it was indeed a kernel-mode rootkit. Our
team expected adulation and respect for all the very technical work we had done, as well as our
expertise on Windows kernel internals that allowed us to make this discovery. Instead, the
kernel developers told us that our tools and our methods were as bad as the malware authors'.
They warned us to stop using our tools to find rootkits, as the tools could make the Windows
systems they ran on unstable unless rebooted. Finally, they offered to do nothing to harden the
kernel to prevent such attacks in the future. It was a disappointing meeting for us, but you
can't win them all!

_Chapter 5_ 190

After the successful large-scale worm attacks of 2003 and 2004, this tune changed. The entire
Windows team stopped the development work they were doing on what would later become
Windows Vista. Instead, they worked on improving the security of Windows XP and Server
2003, releasing Windows XP Service Pack 2 and Windows Server 2003 Service Pack 1. There
was even talk of a new version of Windows, code-named Palladium, that had a security kernel
to help mitigate rootkits like the one we discovered, but it never came to pass (Wikipedia, n.d.).
Ultimately, our work on detecting kernel-mode rootkits did help drive positive change, as
future 64-bit versions of Windows would not allow kernel-mode drivers, like the one we
discovered, to be installed unless they had a valid digital signature.

As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, later in my career at Microsoft, I had the chance to work
with world-class malware researchers and analysts in Microsoft's anti-malware research and
response lab, who were protecting a billion systems from millions of new malware threats.
Malware like the kernel-mode rootkit we had discovered 4 or 5 years earlier was now a
commodity. Attackers were using large-scale automation and server-side polymorphism to
create millions of unique malware every week. To win this war, the anti-virus industry needed
to have bigger and better automation than large-scale purveyors of commodity malware,
which has proven to be surprisingly difficult to accomplish. But the industry is now pushing
new boundaries in malware research and response using **artificial intelligence** ( **AI** ) systems.

I have always thought of malware as a synonym for "attackers' automation." Purveyors of
malware seek to compromise systems for a range of motivations, as I described in _Chapter 1,_
_How Enterprises Get Hacked_ . Any system that sends and receives email, is used to surf the
internet, runs applications that connect to a network, or takes other forms of input can be
attacked, regardless of whether it was manufactured in Redmond, Raleigh, Cupertino, Helsinki,
or anywhere else. Simply put, if you don't trust the source of the code, don't run it. That might
sound overly cautious or even pessimistic to some, but once you look at the growth of malware
over the years, you will get a sense of the scope of this threat.

191 _The Evolution of Malware_

###### **The scope of the malware problem**

The AV-TEST Institute, one of the world's premier independent anti-virus testing labs, based in
Germany, has one of the world's largest malware collections (AV-Test Institute, 2025). They
have accumulated this collection for over 20 years. "Every day, the AV-TEST Institute registers
over 450,000 new malicious programs (malware) and potentially unwanted applications
(PUA). These are examined and classified according to their characteristics and saved" (AVTest Institute, n.d.). Based on the data they published for the three years between 2023 and
2025, the rate of new malware is estimated to be 298,733 unique samples per day (AV-Test
Institute, February, 2026). The statistics that they have published indicate that the total
number of malware programs in their collection at the end of 2025 was approximately 1.3
billion (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026). If malware were a country, it would be the thirdmost-populated country in the world behind India and China.

Each year, the rate of growth in total malware is slightly different, with 2021 appearing to be
the peak, with almost 162 million new malware programs detected that year, according to AVTest. 2022 had the lowest growth level of the decade, with only 102 million new malware
samples detected, a 37% decrease from the prior year. In the 11 years between 2015 and 2025,
the average growth in new malware samples was approximately 112.2 million per year (AV-Test
Institute, February, 2026). These growth rates are staggering when you consider that, if
malware were a country, during the year with the lowest malware growth rate (2022), its
population grew 10 times faster than the population of India grew in 2022.

You might wonder what all this malware was designed to attack. According to the data that
AV-Test has published, during those 10 years, the number of malware programs designed to
run on the Windows operating system grew 351% from 221,508,845 unique malware samples
in 2015 to 997,878,296 malware samples in 2025 (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026). Looking
at each individual year during that decade, the proportion of malware developed for Windows
operating systems versus other operating systems targeted by malware ranged from as low as
74% of all malware detected to as high as 83% (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026). In the three
years between 2023 and 2025, on average, 76% of all the malware samples AV-Test collected
were designed for the Windows operating system.

The operating system with the next highest share of malware samples during those years was
Google Android, with 3% of the total malware samples per year reported (AV-Test Institute,

_Chapter 5_ 192

February, 2026). The number of malware samples detected for Android surged in 2016, 2017,
and 2018, with 18.7 million new malware samples collected during those three years,
representing 50% of all the malware samples collected for Android between 2015 and 2025. In
February 2026, AV-Test had 37,322,716 unique malware samples for the Android operating
system (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026).

The total number of malware samples detected for Linux operating systems was 5,061,774 in
February of 2026 (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026). The amount of malware detected for
Linux in 2015 was just 54,827 samples. However, the amount of malware designed for Linux
grew dramatically in 2021 and 2022, adding 1.5 million and 2.0 million new samples,
respectively. The malware collected for Linux in these two years represents 70% of all the
malware collected for Linux in the 11 years between 2015 and 2025. The proportion of malware
designed for Linux operating systems represents a fraction of 1% of all malware detected each
year during this period, ranging from 0.02% to 0.42% of the total.

macOS had the least amount of malware designed for it of any of the operating systems I've
discussed. AV-Test had 998,817 malware samples for macOS as of February 2026 (AV-Test
Institute, February, 2026), starting the 11-year period in 2015 with just 41,527 malware samples
and ending it in 2025 with 997,932, a 2,303% increase. 2020 stands out as the single largest
year of growth in malware for macOS, with 656,597 samples detected that year, 66% of all the
malware collected for macOS between 2015 and 2025. Malware for macOS represented
between 0.0034% and 0.08% of all malware AV-Test collected each year during those 11 years
(AV-Test Institute, February, 2026).

_Figure 5.1_ is a pie chart that illustrates the relative proportions of AV-Test's malware sample
collection for each operating system at the end of 2025:

193 _The Evolution of Malware_

_Figure 5.1 – Unique malware sample distribution by operating system (AV-Test Institute, February, 2026)_

This data clearly suggests that the platform of choice for malware authors is the Windows
operating system. That is, more unique malware is developed to attack Windows-based

_Chapter 5_ 194

systems than any other platform. Once Windows systems are compromised, attackers will
typically harvest software and game keys, financial information such as credit card numbers,
and other confidential information they can use to steal identities, sometimes taking control of
the system and its data for ransom. Many attackers will use compromised systems as platforms
to perpetrate attacks from, using the anonymity that such systems provide.

Given that attackers have been targeting and leveraging Windows-based systems more than
any other platform, and given the ubiquity of Windows, security experts need to understand
how and where attackers have been using these systems. CISOs, aspiring CISOs, security
teams, and cybersecurity experts can benefit from understanding how Windows-based
systems are attacked in at least a few ways. The following are some advantages of this:

Knowledge of malware and how it attacks systems can be useful to help recognize the
fear, uncertainty, and doubt that some security vendors use to sell their products and
services.

Understanding how attackers have been using malware will help CISOs make better
security-related investments and decisions and will help security teams do their jobs
better.

CISOs and security teams can take lessons from the Windows ecosystem and apply
them to Linux-based systems and other platforms. Very often, the methods that
malware authors use on the Windows platform will be adapted to attack other
platforms, albeit usually on a smaller scale.

Finally, in my opinion, it will be **d** ifficult for cybersecurity _subject matter experts_ to use this
moniker if they are blissfully unaware of malware trends in an online ecosystem consisting of
over a billion systems that support, at times, more than three-quarters of all the new malware
in the world. It doesn't matter if there are more mobile devices, more IoT devices, or more
secure operating systems. It is undeniable that Windows is everywhere. Subsequently, all
cybersecurity experts should know a little about the largest participant in the global threat
landscape.

Next, let's examine why there's so much malware designed to attack Windows-based systems.

195 _The Evolution of Malware_

###### **Why is there so much malware on Windows?**

The data we just looked at suggests that 76% of all new malware in 2025 was designed for the
Windows operating system, and that 77% of all malware in AV-Test's malware collection was
coded for Windows. Let's take a moment to consider why this is the case. After all, there are
certainly more mobile internet-connected devices today than there are Windows-based
systems. Mobile device adoption exploded as Apple, Google, Samsung, and others brought very
popular products to the global marketplace. But if there are far more mobile devices, shouldn't
there be far more families of malware developed for those platforms?

The answer to this question lies in how applications get distributed in these ecosystems.
Apple's App Store was a game changer for the industry. Not only did it make it easy for iPhone
users to find and install applications, but it also _almost completely eliminated malware_ for iOSbased devices.

Apple was able to accomplish this by making the App Store the one and only place consumers
could install applications from (jailbreaking aside). **Independent software vendors** ( **ISVs** )
who want to get their apps onto consumers' iOS-based **d** evices, such as iPhones and iPads,
need to get their apps into the App Store. To do this, their apps need to meet Apple's security
requirements, which they verify behind the scenes. This makes the App Store a perfect choke
point that prevents malware from getting onto Apple devices.

In contrast, Microsoft Windows was developed in more naive times, when no one could predict
that, one day, there would be more malicious files in the Windows ecosystem than legitimate
files. One of the big advantages of Windows, for developers, was that they could develop their
software for Windows and sell it directly to consumers and businesses. This model was the
predominant software distribution model for PCs for decades. Since software can be installed
without regard for its provenance and with limited ability to determine its trustworthiness,
malware flourished in this ecosystem and continues to do so. Microsoft has taken numerous
steps over the decades to combat this "side effect" of its software distribution model, with
limited success. It turns out that the flexibility to deploy software without using an App Store
model is coveted by operators of enterprise IT estates.

Some would argue that the Android ecosystem has ended up somewhere in between these two
extremes. Google also has an app store, called the Play Store. Google has also taken steps to
minimize malware in this app store. However, third-party app stores for Android-based
devices didn't all maintain Google's high security standards, subsequently allowing malware
for these devices to get into the ecosystem. Zscaler's ThreatLabz reported that 77 malicious
Android apps with more than 19 million installs were delivering multiple malware families to
Play Store users (Toulas, Bill. August 25, 2025). However, the data from AV-Test suggests that

_Chapter 5_ 196

the number of malware samples detected for Android-based devices was 27 times smaller than
that of Windows-based devices at the end of 2025 (AV-Test Institute, February, 2025).

These differences in software distribution models, at least partially, help to explain why there
is so much more malware developed for Windows than for other platforms. Cybersecurity
professionals can take some lessons from this into their own IT environments. Controlling how
software is introduced to an enterprise IT environment can help minimize the amount of
malware in it.

Here is some basic advice for CISOs and security teams that manage large IT estates of
Windows-based devices.

**Restrict how many users run in local administrator context** : One mistake I've seen
numerous IT teams make in trying to enable users to perform self-service IT functions,
such as installing software, is giving large swaths of their user bases standing local
administrator privileges or other elevated user contexts. Users with elevated privileges
are targets for attackers, who seek to trick them into installing malware and remotecontrol software, as well as disabling security features. When these accounts get
compromised, they are a gift to attackers, who use their escalated privileges to
accelerate their attacks. Allowing users to run in local administrator context on
systems that they use to surf the internet, send and receive emails, and access
removable mass storage devices on is an attacker's dream come true. It's a bonus to
them if these systems are also used to commit code. What could go wrong? Re-read
that last line with a heavy dose of sarcasm in your mind. This level of naivete is exactly
what attackers hope to find as they use the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects to initially
compromise systems and then take advantage of the user's elevated privileges to steal
more credentials, move laterally, stay persistent, access sensitive data and exfiltrate it,
and deploy ransomware. For example, when attackers have local administrator
privileges, it potentially enables them to "bring their own vulnerable driver" or to
"bring their own **endpoint detection and response** ( **EDR** )" that disables the
legitimate endpoint protection software. Both tactics result in attackers disabling
security software and controls to have complete control of systems. Restricting the
number of user accounts that have standing administrator privileges has been a
Microsoft best practice for more than 20 years.

197 _The Evolution of Malware_

**Leverage Microsoft Software Center to enable users to install software on their**
**own Windows systems** : In large enterprises, the top use case for giving users standing
local administrator privileges is to enable them to install software on their systems
themselves. Users do not require escalated privileges to install software from the
Software Center. The IT team that manages user desktops will need to maintain the
Software Center by ensuring the latest versions of the software their organizations
have procured are published in it and available for users. This includes newer versions
of that software as it becomes available. This centralized approach also ensures users
aren't installing software that didn't go through their organization's legal and
procurement processes, helping to avoid running pirated software. In large enterprise
environments, this isn't a part-time job. It takes resources, time, and dedication to
ensure users have access to the latest versions of the software they need to perform
their roles, published in the Software Center. This is an important function that rarely
gets the credit it deserves.

**Consider whether a local privilege escalation tool will meet their needs instead of**
**giving them persistent administrator privileges** : This applies to users who require
escalated privileges to do their jobs. Examples of vendors that offer these tools include
CyberArk, Delinea, BeyondTrust, and others. Microsoft announced a new Windows 11
platform security feature in 2025 called Administrator Protection with this same goal
in mind (Microsoft, May 2025).

**Leverage Continuous Integration (CI)/Continuous Deployment (CD) pipelines for**
**applications developed in-house** : CI/CD pipelines can help enterprises restrict how
software is introduced into their environments and ensure it meets security and
compliance requirements before deploying it into production.

**Block outbound user access to unneeded internet domains** : It turns out that most, if
not all, the malware trying to get into enterprise IT environments is on the internet
(USB mass storage devices excluded, of course). Do any of your users speak or read
Russian, or a dialect of Chinese, Persian, or Arabic? Does your organization have
customers, partners, or employees who live in foreign countries where these languages
are used? If not, then why would your users need unfettered access to the country code
top-level domains on the internet where these languages are predominant, such
as _.ru_, _.cn_, and _.ir_ ? Blocking outbound user access to unneeded internet domains can
provide high security ROI. Applying the principle of least privilege to internet access
will result in mitigating many internet-based threats, such as phishing attacks and
drive-by download attacks. If your users can't get to the sites hosting malware,
credential theft attacks, and other threats, it makes it harder for malware and attackers
to get into your IT environment. I've used this tactic with great success at very large

_Chapter 5_ 198

organizations. The key is to ensure users have access to the websites they need access
to. I'll discuss this tactic more in _Chapter 14_, _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Tactics_ .

Now that we've briefly discussed how software distribution models can impact the
distribution of malware, let's dive deep into malware. Security teams can learn a lot from
studying malware developed for Windows operating systems, even if they don't use Windows
themselves. The methods that malware authors employ on Windows can be and are used for
malware developed for many different platforms, including Linux and macOS. Studying how
malware works in the largest malware ecosystem can help us defend against it almost
everywhere else. But before I dive right into the historical malware trend data, it's important
for you to understand the sources of the data that I'm going to show you. As I discussed in
_Chapter 2_, to truly understand threat intelligence, also known as **Cyber Threat Intelligence**
( **CTI** ), you need to understand the data sources.
###### **Malware data sources**

The primary source for the historical data in this chapter is the Microsoft **Security**
**Intelligence Report** ( **SIR** ) and newer reports such as the Microsoft Digital Defense Reports
(Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). As I mentioned earlier in the chapter, I worked on 20+ volumes
of the SIR and understood the data sources we used intimately. In each volume of the SIR, we
documented the data sources used in the appendix. Microsoft still uses many of these data
sources to protect its customers today and inform their investments in security.

The **d** ata **i** n these historical reports comes from Microsoft's anti-malware products that
enterprises and consumers used, including the **Malicious Software Removal Tool**, **Microsoft**
**Safety Scanner**, **Microsoft Security Essentials**, **Microsoft System Center Endpoint**
**Protection**, **Windows Defender**, **Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection**,
**Windows Defender Offline**, **Azure Security Center**, and the **SmartScreen** filter built into
Microsoft web browsers. Other non-security products and services that provide valuable data
for volumes of this report include Exchange Online, Office 365, and Bing (Note that some of the
names of these products and tools have changed since these reports were published). Let me
explain in more detail how this eclectic group of data sources helps paint a well-rounded
picture of the threat landscape.

**The Malicious Software Removal Tool**

**The Malicious Software Removal Tool** ( **MSRT** ) is an interesting tool that provides valuable
data. In the wake of the Blaster worm attacks (there were variants) (Microsoft Corporation,
n.d.) in the summer of 2003, Microsoft developed a free **Blaster Removal Tool** that was
designed to help customers detect and remove the Blaster worm and its variants (Leyden, J.,
January 7, 2004). Remember that, at that time, very few systems ran up-to-date, real-time
anti-virus software. The Blaster Removal Tool was free. This tool made a huge difference as

199 _The Evolution of Malware_

tens of millions of systems ran it. Because of the tool's success and the constant barrage of
malware attacks that followed it in history, such as Sasser, MyDoom, and many others, and the
fact that so few systems had anti-virus software running, Microsoft decided to release a
_malicious software removal tool_ every month. The MSRT was born.

It was meant to be a way to detect infected systems and clean the most prevalent or serious
malware threats from the entire Windows ecosystem. Microsoft's anti-malware lab decides
what new detections to add to the MSRT every month. A list of all the malware it detects is
published on Microsoft's website (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). Between January 2005 and
February 2026, 487 malware families were added to the detections for the MSRT. Keep in mind
that there are at least hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of known malware families, so
this is a very small subset of the total that real-time anti-malware software packages detect.
The MSRT is released monthly (more or less) with security updates on "Patch Tuesday," the
second Tuesday of every month. It gets automatically downloaded from Windows Update or
Microsoft Update to every Windows system in the world that has opted to run it. During the
time I was publishing data from the MSRT in the SIR, the MSRT was running on hundreds of
millions of systems per month on average.

Once the MSRT's **End User License Agreement** ( **EULA** ) is agreed to, the MSRT runs silently
without a user interface as it's a command-line tool. If it doesn't find any malware infections, it
stops execution and is unloaded from memory. No data is sent to Microsoft in this case. But if
malware is detected by the MSRT, then it will try to remove the malware from the system and
report the infection to the user and to Microsoft.

Microsoft publishes the specific list of data fields that the MSRT sends back for analysis,
including the version of Windows that the malware was detected on, the operating system
locale, and which malware family was detected, among others (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.).
Administrators can download the MSRT and run it manually; the MSRT can also be configured
not to send data back to Microsoft. Most enterprises that I advised, who executed the MSRT on
their Windows systems, typically blocked data sent to Microsoft at their firewall.
Subsequently, my educated guess is that 95% or more of the hundreds of millions of systems
returning MSRT data to Microsoft are likely consumers' systems.

The MSRT provides a great post-malware exposure snapshot of a small list of known, prevalent
malware that is **i** nfecting consumers' systems around the world. When Microsoft's antimalware lab adds a detection to the MSRT for a threat that's very prevalent, we should expect
to see a spike in detections for that malware family in the data. This happens from time to
time, as you'll see in the data shared later in this chapter. Keep in mind that the infected
systems might have been infected for weeks, months, or years prior to the detection being
added to the MSRT. Since the MSRT runs on systems all over the world and it returns the

_Chapter 5_ 200

Windows locale and country location of infected systems, it provides us with a way to see
regional differences in malware infections. I will discuss this in detail later in this chapter.

**Real-time anti-malware tools**

Unlike the MSRT, which cleans Windows-based systems that have already been successfully

**i** nfected with prevalent malware, the primary purpose of real-time anti-malware software is to
block the installation of malware. It does this by scanning incoming files, monitoring systems
for tell-tale signs of infection, scanning files when they are accessed, and periodically scanning
storage. Real-time anti-malware software can also find pre-existing infections on systems
when the real-time anti-malware package is initially installed. Real-time anti-malware
software typically gets signature and engine updates periodically (daily, weekly, monthly, and
so on). This helps it block new and emerging threats, as well as old threats it wasn't previously
able to detect.

For example, if detection is added for a malware threat, but that malware threat has already
successfully infected systems that are running the real-time anti-malware software, the update
could potentially enable the anti-malware software to detect, and hopefully remove, the
existing infection.

My point is that data from real-time anti-malware software provides us with a different view
of the threat landscape compared to MSRT. Microsoft has offered different solutions for threat
detection and rebranded its Windows anti-malware solution a few times over the years.
Microsoft Defender Antivirus, Microsoft Defender XDR, Windows Defender, Microsoft Security
Essentials, Microsoft System Center Endpoint Protection, and Windows Defender Advanced
Threat Protection are all examples of real-time anti-malware software that are data sources.
Microsoft Defender Antivirus is the default anti-malware package for Windows 11-based
systems. Windows Defender was the default anti-virus solution on Windows 10-based systems
until it was rebranded Microsoft Defender. In a blog post in August of 2025, Microsoft
mentioned that _"Microsoft's Defender platform scans more than one billion monthly active devices_
_through the company's Defender suite of products…"_ (Microsoft Corporation, August 5, 2025).

This massive scale makes Microsoft's Defender-branded products a great source of threat

**i** ntelligence data. Incidentally, Windows Defender was the original name of Microsoft's antispyware solution when personal computers required separate solutions for malware and
spyware. I'll touch on this conundrum later when I discuss "potentially unwanted software."
Also note that some of these real-time anti-malware solutions are for consumers and others
are for enterprise customers. Enterprise customers demand methods to deploy, manage, and
observe data from their anti-malware solutions that protect thousands of systems, as well as
faster research and response. Today, enterprises leverage **Endpoint Detection and Response**
( **EDR** ) or **Extended Detection and Response** ( **XDR** ) that provide real-time antimalware

201 _The Evolution of Malware_

protection as well as a range of other functions that go well beyond malware detection. I'll talk
about these in more depth in _Chapter 14._

During some of the threat **i** ntelligence briefings I've done, some attendees asserted that using
Microsoft data sources for intelligence only provides a view of malware that Microsoft knows
about. But this isn't quite true. The major anti-malware vendors share information with each
other, including malware samples. So, while the first anti-malware lab that discovers a threat
will have detections for that threat before anyone else, over time, all anti-malware vendors will
have detections for it. Microsoft manages several security information-sharing programs, with
the goal of helping all vendors better protect their shared customers (Microsoft Corporation,
2019). Additionally, Microsoft has expanded support for Microsoft Defender to non-Microsoft
operating systems, such as Android, iPhone iOS, and macOS, which will give them even more
data on threats across these platforms (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.).

Microsoft's web browsers have had the SmartScreen filter—think anti-malware software for
the browser—built into them for many years. The SmartScreen filter gives us a view of
phishing sites and malware hosted on the web (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). As users browse
the web, SmartScreen will warn them about known malicious websites they try to visit and
scan files that are downloaded in the browser, looking for malware. The data on sites hosting
malicious software, and the malicious files themselves, can give us a view of the most common
threats hosted on the web, as well **a** s where in the world threats are hosted most, and the
regions that the victim populations are in. The current version of this feature is called
Microsoft SmartScreen Defender and is built into Windows 10 (Creators Update and above)
and Windows 11.

**Non-security data sources**

Sources of data, such as email services and internet search services, can provide an additional
dimension to threat intelligence. For example, data from Microsoft 365 (formerly called Office
365) and Outlook.com provides visibility of the threats that flow through email, including the
sources and destinations of those threats and their volumes. The volume of data that Microsoft
has from Microsoft 365 is mind-boggling, with hundreds of millions of users all over the world
and hundreds of billions of email messages flowing through it every month (Microsoft
Corporation, 2018).

Bing, Microsoft's internet search engine service, is also a rich source of threat intelligence data.
As Bing indexes billions of web pages so that its users can get quick, relevant search results, it's
also looking for drive-by download sites, malware-hosting sites, and phishing sites. This data
can help us better understand where in the world malware is being hosted, where it migrates
to over time, and where the victims are.

_Chapter 5_ 202

When data from some select non-security data sources is combined with data from some of the
security sources of data I discussed previously, we can get a more rounded view of the threat
landscape. Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com receive emails sent from all sorts of non-Microsoft
clients and email servers, and Bing indexes content hosted on all types of platforms. Certainly,
the combination of this data does not provide us with perfect visibility, but the scale of these
data sources gives us the potential for good insights.

Now that you know where I retrieved the historical malware-related data from that I'm going
to share with you, let's take a quick look at the different categories of malware that are
included in the data and analysis. These categories of malware have been fixtures in the global
threat landscape for decades, meaning that CISOs and security teams should be very
knowledgeable about these categories. I'm going to show you how attackers change the
malware categories they use over time when those categories become less effective. Some
people call this "evolution," but I call it old wine in new bottles because the data clearly shows
us attackers moving from one known malware category to another known malware category.
It's not very often that a novel **c** ategory of malware is discovered—more often, attackers use
variations on themes invented decades ago. This isn't to say that nothing has changed; as an
example, we will examine the ways that ransomware has changed over time later in this
chapter.
###### **About malware**

Before we dive into the historical threat data, I need to provide you with some definitions for
terms I'll use throughout the rest of this chapter.

**Malicious software**, also known as malware, is software whose author's intent is malicious.
The developers of malware are trying to impede the confidentiality, integrity, and/or
availability of data and/or the systems that process, transmit, and store it.

As I discussed in _Chapter 1_, malware authors can be motivated by many different things,
including hubris, notoriety, military espionage, economic espionage, and hacktivism, among
others.

Most malware families today are blended threats. What I mean by this is that, many years ago,
threats were discrete. That is, they were either a **worm** or a **backdoor**, but not both. Today,
most malware has characteristics of multiple categories of malware. Analysts in anti-malware
labs that reverse-engineer malware samples typically classify malware by the primary or most
prominent way each sample behaves.

For example, a piece of malware might exhibit characteristics of a worm, a Trojan, and
ransomware. An analyst might classify it as ransomware because that's its dominant behavior
or characteristic.

203 _The Evolution of Malware_

Generally speaking, malware research and response is more about automation and science
now than the art it once was. Don't get me wrong; if you can understand how a piece of
malware spreads and what its payload is, then you can effectively mitigate it. But the volume
and complexity of threats seen today will challenge any organization to do this at any scale.
Instead, security teams typically must spend time and resources mitigating as many malware
threats as possible, not just one popular category or family. As you'll see from the historical
data I provide in this chapter, some attackers even use old-school file infectors (viruses).

All that said, AI is playing a bigger role in the categorization of malware in antimalware labs to
help manage the massive volume and complexity. In August of 2025, Microsoft announced
"Project Ire" in a blog post published on the Microsoft Research blog. The team working on this
project described it this way:

_"Today, we are excited to introduce an autonomous AI agent that can analyze and_
_classify software without assistance, a step forward in cybersecurity and malware_
_detection. The prototype, Project Ire, automates what is considered the gold standard_
_in malware classification: fully reverse engineering a software file without any clues_
_about its origin or purpose. It uses decompilers and other tools, reviews their output,_
_and determines whether the software is malicious or benign…_

_Based on these early successes, the Project Ire prototype will be leveraged inside_
_Microsoft's Defender organization as Binary Analyzer for threat detection and_
_software classification._

_Chapter 5_ 204

_Our goal is to scale the system's speed and accuracy so that it can correctly classify_
_files from any source, even on first encounter. Ultimately, our vision is to detect novel_
_malware directly in memory, at scale." (Microsoft Corporation, August 5, 2025)_

**How malware infections spread**

Malware isn't magic. It must get into IT environments somehow. Hopefully, you'll remember
the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, that is, the five ways that organizations are initially
compromised, which I wrote about in detail in _Chapter 1_ . To refresh your memory, the
Cybersecurity Usual Suspects are as follows:

Unpatched vulnerabilities

Security misconfigurations

Weak, leaked, and stolen credentials

Social engineering

Insider threats

Malware threats can use all the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects to compromise systems. Some
malware is used to initially compromise systems so that threat actors achieve their objectives.
Some malware is used in IT environments after the environment has already been
compromised. For example, after attackers use one or more of the Cybersecurity Usual
Suspects to initially compromise a network, they can use malware that will encrypt sensitive
data and/or find cached administrator credentials and upload them to a remote server. Some
malware is sophisticated enough to be used for both initial compromise and post-compromise
objectives. As I mentioned earlier, I have always thought of malware as a synonym for
"attackers' automation." Instead of the attacker manually typing commands or running
scripts, malware is a program that performs illicit activities for the attacker, autonomously or
in a semiautonomous fashion. Malware can help attackers achieve their objectives, whether
their objective is destruction and anarchy or economic espionage.

The categories of malware I'll discuss in this chapter include different types of Trojans, browser
modifiers, exploits, exploit kits, potentially unwanted software, ransomware, viruses, and
worms. Microsoft provides definitions for these categories of malware and others (Microsoft
Corporation, March 13, 2025). Your favorite anti-malware provider or threat intelligence
provider might have different definitions than these. That's perfectly okay, but just keep in
mind that there might be some minor, nuanced differences between definitions. I'll provide
you with my own, less formal definitions to make this chapter easier to read and understand.

205 _The Evolution of Malware_

**Trojans**

I'll start with Trojans since, worldwide, they have been the most prevalent category of malware
for the last 15 years or more. A **Trojan** is **a** program or file that represents itself as one thing
when really it is another, just like the Trojan horse story that it's based on. The user is tricked
into downloading it and opening or running it.

**Backdoor Trojans** and **remote access Trojans** are variations of this. Once the user is tricked
into running the malicious program (scripts and macros can be malicious too), a backdoor
Trojan gives attackers remote access to the infected system. Once they have remote access, they
can potentially steal identities and data, software and game keys, install software and more
malware of their choice, enlist the infected system into botnets so that they can do "project
work" for attackers, and so on. Project work can include extortion, **Distributed Denial of**
**Service** ( **DDoS** ) attacks, storing and distributing illicit and questionable content, or anything
else the attackers are willing to trade or sell access to their network of compromised systems
for.

**Trojan downloaders** and **droppers** are yet **a** nother variation on this theme. Once the user is
tricked into running the malicious program, the Trojan then unpacks more malware from itself
or downloads more malicious software from remote servers. The result is typically the same—
malicious servitude and harvesting the system for all that it is worth. Trojan downloaders and
droppers were all the rage among attackers in 2006 and 2007 and have made dramatic
appearances in limited time periods since then.

A great example of a Trojan downloader and dropper is the notorious threat called **Zlob** . Users
were tricked into installing it on their systems when visiting malicious websites that had video
content they wanted to view. When they clicked on the video file to watch it, the website told
them they didn't have the correct video codec installed to watch the video. Helpfully, the
website offered the video codec for download so that the user could watch the video. The user
was really downloading and installing Zlob (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.). Once installed, it
would then expose the user to pop-up advertisements for free "security software" that would
help them secure their system. Users who clicked on the ads to download and install the
security software were giving the attackers more and more control over their systems. More
recent examples of prevalent Trojans include _Agent Tesla_ and _AsyncRAT_, which **b** oth rely on
users being tricked into taking some action to **i** nfect their systems. Trojans remain popular
with attackers and purveyors of malware because they are flexible weapons and can be

_Chapter 5_ 206

distributed in many different ways, including email, drive-by **d** ownload **a** ttacks, and watering
hole attacks, among others.

Let's look at another type of threat that relies on social engineering, potentially unwanted
software.

**Potentially unwanted software**

While I am discussing threats that use social engineering, another near-ubiquitous threat
category is called **potentially unwanted software**, also known as potentially unwanted

applications, potentially unwanted programs, and a few other names. Why does this category
have so many seemingly unassuming names? This is a category of threats that lawyers
invented. That's not necessarily a bad thing—it really is an interesting threat category. There
are some shades of gray in malware research, and this category exposes those.

Let me give you a hypothetical example of potentially unwanted software that isn't based on
any real-world company or organization. What would happen if a legitimate company offered
consumers a free game in exchange for monitoring their internet browsing habits, all so that
they could be targeted more accurately with online advertising? I think most people I know
would think that's creepy and not give up their privacy in exchange for access to a free game.
But if this privacy trade-off was only listed in the free game's **end user license agreement**
( **EULA** ), where very few people would read it, how many people would simply download the
free game and play it? In this case, let's say the free game ended up as a malware sample in an
anti-malware company's threat collection. The analysts in the anti-malware lab could decide
that the game company wasn't being transparent enough with the game's users and categorize
the game as a Trojan. The anti-malware company would then update the signatures for its
anti-malware products to detect this new threat. The anti-malware company's anti-malware
solution would then detect and remove the game from every system where it was running. Did
the anti-malware company help its customers by removing the game and its ability to track
their internet browsing habits? Or, did it damage a legitimate company's business by deeming
its product as malware and removing it from its customers' systems without permission?

The answer that the anti-malware industry came up with was to call it "potentially unwanted
software" (or a similar name), flag it for users when it's detected, and ask the users to explicitly
approve or disapprove its removal. This way, the game company's customer decides whether
they want to remove the game company's product, not the anti-malware company. This helps
mitigate the predictable damage claims and litigation that the anti-malware industry faces
with potentially unwanted software.

Many, many variations of the example I described have been offered on the internet and are
installed on systems all over the world. Some of them are legitimate companies with legitimate
businesses, while others are threat actors pretending to be legitimate companies. Some

207 _The Evolution of Malware_

families of this threat category start off as legitimate programs but later turn malicious when
their supply chain is compromised, or their operators turn malevolent. Other examples of this
category include fake anti-virus software, fake browser protector software, software bundles
that contain a bunch of different software offerings and components, and so on. This is the
most common "threat" found in the curated app stores and the mobile devices they support.
My advice and mantra for many years has been don't trust the software if you don't trust the
people who wrote it.

**Viruses**

**Viruses** have been around for decades. They are typically self-replicating file infectors. Viruses
can spread when they are inadvertently copied between systems. Because they infect files and/
or the **master boot record** ( **MBR** ) on systems, sometimes indiscriminately, they can be very
"noisy" threats that are easy to detect, but hard to disinfect. Viruses are another malware
category that seems to have periodic resurgences in popularity among some attackers. Modern
attackers who develop viruses typically don't just infect files like their predecessors did
decades ago; they can be more imaginative and malicious.

In modern times, viruses have not been anywhere near as prevalent as Trojans or potentially
unwanted software, but there always seems to be some volume of detections. A great example
of a family of viruses that has been around for many years is **Sality** (Microsoft Corporation,
n.d.).

**Browser modifiers**

Browser modifiers are designed to modify browser settings without users' permission. Some
browser modifiers also install malicious browser add-ons/extensions without permission,
change the default search provider, modify search results, inject ads, and change the home
page and pop-up blocker settings.

Browser modifiers typically rely on social engineering for installation. The motivation for
browser modifiers is typically profit; attackers use them to perpetrate click fraud. But like all
threats, they can be blended with other categories and provide backdoor access and download
command and control capabilities for attackers. Next, let's look at exploits and exploit kits.

_Chapter 5_ 208

**Exploits and exploit kits**

_Chapters 3_ and _4_ were dedicated to vulnerabilities. Remember that a vulnerability can allow an

attacker to compromise the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of hardware or software.
An exploit is a technique or piece of code that leverages a vulnerability in hardware or software
to bypass security controls and execute malicious actions. You might also remember from my
discussion of vulnerabilities in _Chapter 3_ that not all vulnerabilities are the same. Some
vulnerabilities, if exploited, have a higher potential impact on the system than others. Exploits
for critical-rated vulnerabilities are highly sought after by attackers. This is because they give
attackers the best chance to take full control of the vulnerable system and run arbitrary code of
their choice. That arbitrary code can do anything that the user context it is running in can do.
For example, it can download more malware from servers on the internet that will enable
attackers to remotely control the system, steal identities and data, enlist the system into a
botnet, and so on.

Exploits must be delivered to their target. They can be delivered in several different ways, some
of which rely on social engineering to succeed. For example, an attacker might deliver an
exploit by developing a malformed `.pdf` file designed to exploit a specific unpatched
vulnerability in a parser such as Adobe Acrobat Reader or Microsoft Word.

When a victim opens the `.pdf` file with a parser that isn't patched for the vulnerability that the
attacker is using, and if no other mitigations are in place, then the vulnerability is exploited on
the system, potentially running arbitrary code of the attacker's choice. But how does the
attacker get the victim to run the exploit? One way is social engineering. The malformed `.pdf`
file can be sent to the victim via email, with the sender masquerading as a co-worker or friend
of the victim. Since the victim trusts their co-worker or friend, they open the email attachment,
and the exploit is executed. Exploits can also be hosted on web pages as downloads for victims,
sent via social networks, and distributed on USB drives and other removable media.

An exploit kit is a library of exploits with some management software. A kit's exploit library
can contain any number of exploits for any number of products. An exploit kit might also
provide attackers with web pages that make it easy to deliver the exploits. The management

209 _The Evolution of Malware_

software built into the kit helps attackers understand which exploits are successful and which
are not. This helps attackers make better decisions about which exploits to use and where to
maximize their return on investment. This management software might also help attackers
identify and replace exploits on their web pages that are no longer effective with new ones.
Examples of exploit kits include **Angler** (also known as **Axpergle** ), **Neutrino**, and the
notorious **Blackhole** exploit kit. Examples of newer exploit kits include **Rig EK**, **Magnitude**
**EK**, and **Fallout EK** . This approach underpins a **b** usiness model and has led to the coining of a
new phrase, **Malware as a Service** ( **MaaS** ). Exploit kits fall in and out of favor with attackers,
but exploits don't.

**Worms**

A **worm** provides its own **d** elivery mechanism so that it can automatically spread from system
to system. Worms can use unpatched vulnerabilities, security misconfigurations, weak
passwords, and social engineering to propagate themselves from system to system. A great
example of a worm is **Conficker** . There were at least a few variants of this worm. It used
unpatched vulnerabilities, such as MS08-067, a hardcoded list of weak passwords, and
Autorun feature abuse (a feature in Windows) to spread from Windows system to Windows
system (Microsoft, 2017). It could spread via removable drives, such as USB drives, as well as
across networks. Successful worms can be very difficult to remove from an IT environment
once they get into the environment. This is because they can _hide_ in online and offline storage
media and operating system images.

Other examples of successful worms include SQL Slammer and Microsoft Blaster, which both
spread like wildfire around the world using unpatched vulnerabilities. There are also worms,
such as MyDoom, that spread via email. It's interesting that millions of people were willing to
double-click on an email attachment called MyDoom when it arrived in their inbox. Opening
this attachment ran the worm that then sent a copy of itself to all the email addresses in the
user's contact list. Worms are not a threat from the distant past. Since the days of Conficker
(2007), there have been a few wormable vulnerabilities in Windows that were accessible
through default exceptions in the Windows Firewall. In all of these cases, Microsoft was able to
patch hundreds of millions of systems on the internet quickly enough so that large-scale worm
attacks were avoided. But this is as dangerous a scenario as it can get for a world that relies so
heavily on technology.

Recall the global malware attack scenario that I described in _Chapter 1_ . I painted a picture of a
worst-case worm scenario, based on my personal experience leading Microsoft's response to
Blaster and Conficker.

Once a worm successfully spreads on the internet, it will continue until there's no fuel left for
it. No more systems left unpatched with the vulnerabilities it knows how to exploit, no more
weak passwords it attempts to use, no more users plugging USB drives into vulnerable

_Chapter 5_ 210

systems, and so on. In other words, these worms continue to lurk on the internet and private
networks for many years after the initial worm attack event. When governments use worms in
cyber-attacks, as they did with Stuxnet, for example, they accept that there will be unintended
consequences and collateral damage for years after the attacks. Worms combined with a
ransomware payload can be devastating for their victims—WannaCry being the best example
of this type of threat (Fruhlinger, Josh. August 24, 2022). Speaking of ransomware, let's discuss
that next.

**Ransomware**

None of the other categories of malware strike fear into the hearts of CISOs and other
executives like ransomware does. However, part of the reason for this is the litany of threats
that this label is applied to by the industry and the media. For example, ransomware is used to
describe all of these:

A category of malware with many families

Any attack where attackers deny the victim access to data and/or systems by leveraging
encryption or any other method

Any attack where attackers demand a ransom to stop the attack, including DDoS
attacks

Any attack where attackers steal data and demand a ransom not to publish it

Any attack that involves extortion

Any attack where the attackers' goal is destruction, not profit

The meaning of the term _ransomware_ has become overloaded over time and is now a source of
confusion among cybersecurity practitioners, business and government leaders, and public
policy influencers. Labeling all these different types of attacks as _ransomware_ isn't helpful in my
view. I've seen confusing conversations among CISOs, security teams, their stakeholders,
cybersecurity vendors, and even government agencies that provide cybersecurity guidance. I've
been in so many meetings where one person is talking about the classic malware category that
employs file encryption, while the others are discussing targeted attacks where sensitive data
is stolen and attackers threaten to release it publicly (also known as **Doxware** ). The ways they
need to protect, detect, respond, and recover can be quite different depending on which of
these threats they really intend to focus on. In such meetings, I found it helpful to provide a
definition of ransomware to the participants so that everyone in the meeting was referring to
the same thing. Then the group could have a productive, single-threaded conversation about
the specific mitigations they had in mind. Being explicit about the type of threat helps scope
the conversation, reduce confusion among its participants, and usually results in better
outcomes. The use of "ransomware" has evolved so much over the past 40 years. Let's look at
some of the ways this term and the threats associated with it have evolved.

211 _The Evolution of Malware_

**Ransomware: the classic malware category**

Ransomware still does refer to the classic category of malware first seen in the 1980s. Besides **a**
couple of malware categories that are capable of self-propagating, such as worms and viruses,
other malware categories generally must rely on humans and other malware to spread.
Ransomware is no exception. Once ransomware malware gets onto a system via a human or
other malware using one or more of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, it will then encrypt data
(crypto ransomware) and/or lock the users out of the desktop of the system (locker
ransomware). The locked desktop typically displays a message that demands a ransom to be
paid and instructions on how to pay it. Successful ransomware attacks have made headlines

around the world. Good **e** xamples of ransomware families include **Reveton** (Krebs, Brian.,
August 13, 2012) and **Petya** (Microsoft Corporation, February 5, 2018). In the case of Reveton, it
was a blended threat that was primarily a Trojan married with a ransomware payload. Petya
initially compromised its victims via the installation of a compromised legitimate application,
after which it used an unpatched vulnerability and stolen credentials to further spread.
Attackers who use ransomware are brazen in their attempts to extort all sorts of organizations,
including hospitals and all levels of government.

Although ransomware gets headlines, it is actually one of the least prevalent malware
categories, from a global perspective. Even old-fashioned viruses are typically more prevalent
than ransomware malware. Many of the executives I briefed were skeptical when I told them
this. After all, how could one of the least prevalent categories of malware garner so much
attention and drive so much investment in cybersecurity programs? Remember that risk is
composed of probability and impact. The thing that makes ransomware a high-risk threat isn't
the probability of encountering it; it's the impact when it's encountered. Data that has been
encrypted by ransomware that utilizes properly implemented strong encryption is gone
forever without the decryption keys. Subsequently, many organizations decide to pay the
ransom without any guarantee that they will be able to recover all of their data. Spending time
and resources to implement a ransomware mitigation strategy is a good investment. Making
offline backups of all datasets that are high-value assets is a good starting point. Backups are
targets for attackers who use ransomware so keeping backups offline is an effective and
necessary practice. I'll discuss this in more depth in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_ .

Also, keep in mind that nothing stays the same for long, and ransomware is constantly

evolving. There is nothing preventing authors of more prevalent and successful threats from
incorporating ransomware tactics as the payloads in their malware. Ransomware has been
used in targeted attacks for years. One thing that likely governs the use of ransomware tactics
is just how criminal the attackers are; it's one thing to develop and anonymously release
malware on the internet that disrupts people and organizations, but holding the assets of big
corporations and government departments for a ransom and collecting that ransom is a

_Chapter 5_ 212

different proposition, usually perpetrated by a different kind of criminal altogether. The world
has changed in dramatic ways, enabling some attackers to work in the open without threat of
consequence to them by local or international authorities. Attackers based in Russia, China,
the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), and Iran have little to fear when
attacking targets in Western countries.

We will examine some data that helps us understand the prevalence of ransomware malware
relative to other prevalent categories of malware. I'll explain the concept of prevalence in a
little more detail later in the chapter. But before I show you prevalence data on ransomware
from Microsoft, I must first explain one of the ways Microsoft measured the prevalence of
malware over the years, called the malware **encounter rate** ( **ER** ). Microsoft defines ER as the
following:

_"The percentage of computers running Microsoft real-time security software that_
_report detecting malware or potentially unwanted software, or report detecting a_
_specific threat or family, during a period." (Microsoft Corporation, 2016)_

Put another way, of the systems running one of the real-time anti-malware software options
from Microsoft (that I described earlier in this chapter), the ER represents the percentage of
those systems where malware was blocked from being installed or where a malware infection

was cleaned. The ER provides us with a good idea of how many Windows systems encountered
ransomware out of the sheer number of Windows systems running Microsoft's real-time antimalware software. Let's compare the ER for ransomware to the ER of other categories of
malware. _Figure 5.2_ illustrates the ER for Trojans and worms compared to that of ransomware
over eight quarters between 2013 and 2016.

213 _The Evolution of Malware_

_Figure 5.2 – ER for ransomware, worms, and Trojans between the third quarter of 2014 and the fourth quarter of_

_2017 (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.)_

In the second quarter of 2016 (2Q16), ransomware was encountered on 0.30% of systems
running Microsoft real-time anti-malware software, while worms were encountered on 3.7% of
systems and Trojans on 11.30% of systems. During this quarter, Trojans were encountered
almost 38 times more frequently than ransomware was. During the quarter where
ransomware had its highest ER during this period, the fourth quarter of 2014 (4Q14), the ER of
Trojans and worms were 18 times and 17 times that of ransomware, respectively.

Let's look at some slightly newer data that AV-Test published. _Table 5.1_ contains data from the
AV-Test Security Report 2018/19 (AV-Test Institute, April 2019) comparing the percentage of
new Trojans developed for Windows to the percentage of new ransomware developed for
Windows based on the samples that AV-Test collects.

|Period|Development of New Trojans % of<br>Total|Development of New Ransomware % of<br>Total|
|---|---|---|
|Jan-18|69.46|0.26|
|Aug-18|71.12|0.54|

_Chapter 5_ 214

|Period|Development of New Trojans % of<br>Total|Development of New Ransomware % of<br>Total|
|---|---|---|
|Mar-19|55.25|0.39|

_Table 5.1 – New Trojans and new ransomware developed for Windows as a percentage of all new malware_

_developed for Windows in January 2018, August 2018, and March 2019 (AV-Test Institute, April 2019)_

This data indicates that new ransomware collected in January 2018, August 2018, and March
2019 was a fraction of a percent, while new Trojans constituted the majority of new malware.

The next year, the AV-Test Security Report 2019/2020 reported that new unique ransomware
samples had tripled in 2019, reaching their highest level to date, with almost 910,000 samples
(AV-Test Institute, April 2019). However, even after tripling the number of unique ransomware
malware samples in 2019, the data AV-Test published reveals that ransomware comprised just
0.78% of overall malware distribution that year. Meanwhile, Trojans constituted 58.29% with
68,048,576 unique samples during the same period, 75 times the number of samples as
ransomware (AV-Test Institute, April 2019). Just focusing on Windows in 2019, ransomware
made up under 1% of the total distribution of malware.

Let's look at AV-Test's latest data from 2025 to see if the mix of malware threats has changed.
In the two-week period between August 17, 2025, and August 31, 2025, the development of new
Trojans trended between 66% and 80% of all new malware developed for Windows-based
systems, totaling 1,712,160 samples. During the same period, just 1,674 new ransomware
samples were collected, representing just 0.07% of all the malware developed and collected for
Windows.

We've now looked at data from two credible sources across a 10-year period, and ransomware,
the classic category of malware, didn't even reach 1% of encounters on hundreds of millions of
systems running Microsoft real-time software, nor 1% of collected malware samples, among
the millions of samples collected by one of the top independent anti-virus testing
organizations in the world. This is also consistent with my experience publishing thousands of
pages of CTI in the SIR during my time at Microsoft. Ransomware, the category of malware,
simply isn't as prevalent as most other categories of malware. We could examine even more
data from other credible sources that support the notion that the classic malware category
called ransomware isn't anywhere near as prevalent as other malware categories. However, I
think the explanation as to why this is the case is straightforward, and more data won't be
necessary once that becomes clear.

Remember that _ransomware can't spread by itself_, as a worm or virus can. Like other malware,
ransomware must rely on humans and other malware to spread. As I mentioned earlier,
Trojans have been the highest-volume malware category for a very long time. Once attackers

215 _The Evolution of Malware_

have initially compromised a system using a Trojan, they typically unpack or download more
malware to the system that enables them to move forward with their objectives. If their
objective is profit, destruction, or anarchy, deploying ransomware could be the second stage or
payload of their attack.

What happens when the initial compromise attempt is unsuccessful? That is, when the Trojan
isn't successful because it's **d** etected and blocked by anti-malware software, the second stage
of the attack involving ransomware doesn't have a chance to execute. When we use CTI data
sources such as anti-malware software, the data will typically show the malware encounters
for the Trojans, but not for the ransomware, because the ransomware was never encountered.
The attack was stopped before the ransomware was unpacked or downloaded to the system by
the Trojan. This is another reason why first-stage malware, such as Trojans, is so much more
prevalent than second-stage malware, such as ransomware.

If ransomware really is far less prevalent than other malware categories, why, then, is it viewed
as such a severe threat? Recall that risk is the combination of probability and impact. I don't
think I have seen extinction events announced for organizations after they've encountered
Trojans, despite how prevalent they have been. On the other hand, the probability of
encountering ransomware might be low, but the impact could be super high. High-risk threats
such as ransomware typically warrant some extra attention from security teams because their
strategies to mitigate threats like this shouldn't be hope—playing the odds that their
organizations simply won't encounter it. If the threat of ransomware really were limited to
malware, then offline backups of critical data and pervasive endpoint protection would likely
mitigate it sufficiently for most enterprises.

However, during the past **d** ecade, the threat of ransomware has grown dramatically, as
evidenced by the proliferation of ransomware gangs and their victims. This growth isn't
because the classic category of malware suddenly became more prevalent. The taxonomy
changed. That is, the way the industry started using the term "ransomware" has evolved. Let's
look at some of the key ways ransomware has evolved in order to understand what this threat
really looks like.

**The evolution of ransomware**

Over the past few years, "ransomware" has been routinely used to describe any attack where
extortion is involved. This includes the same types of targeted attacks we've seen over the past
two and a half decades, even when ransomware (the classic category of malware) isn't used at
all. Ransomware is now the label used for DDoS attacks where attackers demand a ransom to
prevent or stop an attack. There's no ransomware malware involved in these DDoS attacks. The
current trend is for attackers to simply steal sensitive data and demand a ransom not to
publish it. There's no malware, no encryption, or DDoS attacks involved—just old-fashioned
extortion.

_Chapter 5_ 216

How did the concept behind a single relatively unpopular malware category evolve to become
so muddy and so pervasive at the same time? At least part of the answer to this question lies in
the ways ransomware malware evolved. There are at least five different ways ransomware has
evolved over time. Let's look at each one briefly.

**Delivery mechanisms**

For decades, the classic category of malware was largely spread by humans and other malware.
Prior to the advent of the internet, floppy disks and local area networks were really the only
ways to spread this type of malware. Luck played a role in which systems would get victimized
and which would not, because there wasn't really a targeted delivery system for malware. In
the past 15 years, as ransomware became more popular with attackers, more blended malware
was developed that enabled ransomware to spread more easily, such as worms that also
encrypted data as they self-replicated from system to system. Today, ransomware is routinely
leveraged in targeted attacks where humans, on their keyboards, are initially compromising
their victims' IT environments (or buying access from an access broker), moving laterally,
discovering valuable data and systems, and then using ransomware or other tools to deny
access to the legitimate owners.

Some vendors have called this type of attack "human-operated ransomware." Targeted attacks
have been commonplace for at least 20 years, but instead of trying to stay persistent and
exfiltrating data to sell or trade, many attackers simply go for their victims' jugulars as quickly
as possible by encrypting and/or exfiltrating data as soon as they can. This has resulted in a
shift in some attackers' dwell times from several months to just a few hours; as soon as they
find valuable enough data to extort their victims, they exfiltrate it, encrypt it, delete it, and so
on, after which they aren't concerned whether their presence is detected. To facilitate this
compressed "smash and grab" attack pattern, attackers have been using **commercial threat**
**emulation tools** that **a** ccelerate their attacks, lower the barrier to entry for less technically
sophisticated attackers, and act as a delivery mechanism for ransomware. These tools are
designed to simulate real-world attacks. Attackers misuse these tools because they provide
several advantages to them, including the following:

Prebuilt attack chains (automated playbooks) they can leverage

217 _The Evolution of Malware_

Automated exploitation workflows

Continuous reconnaissance and lateral-movement logic

Their operation can blend into legitimate red team activities

This is how a Sophos report puts it:

_"Hacked Cobalt Strike suites have become the Saturday Night Specials of_
_cybercrime: they are widely available on underground marketplaces and can be_
_easily customized…As a result, most of the ransomware cases we've seen over the last_
_year have involved the use of Cobalt Strike Beacons. While many malware operators_
_use backdoors associated with the open source Metasploit framework, Cobalt Strike_
_Beacons have become the favored tool of ransomware affiliates and access brokers_
_who sell compromises to ransomware gangs and are often seen tied to ransomware_
_execution." Sophos 2022 Threat Report_

Of course, there are those who aspire to collect rich ransom demands and do not have the
requisite technical skills to develop sophisticated ransomware tools and attack patterns. For
these people, access brokers and **Ransomware-as-a-Service** ( **RaaS** ) are available. Access
brokers are people who sell the details of compromised networks to other criminals. In other
words, they have knowledge of organizations that have been compromised and are willing to
sell the _keys_ to attackers who will use them to pursue their own motivations.

Attributing ransomware attacks to specific ransomware gangs and nation states started as a
boutique cottage industry and has evolved into big business. All the big cybersecurity vendors
tout their attribution capabilities to generate interest and sales of their products and services,
and to help their customers defend themselves. These include Check Point, CrowdStrike,
Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, RecordedFuture, and Sophos, to name just a few. Examining the
various security intelligence reports that these vendors published in the recent past reveals
that most of these vendors have identified and tracked many of the same ransomware groups
and associated families of malware. The ransomware gangs most often cited in these reports in

**2** 024 included **3AM**, **Akira**, **Fog**, **LockBit**, **Medusa**, **Play**, **Qilin**, and **RansomHub**, among

many others. The Check Point security vendor describes the scope of the gangs they track this
way in their Check Point Cyber Security Report, 2025:

_"This section presents data and insights drawn from over 140 ransomware Data_
_Leak Sites (DLS) operated by more than 90 double-extortion ransomware groups._
_The details of more [sic] 5,200 companies have been published on data leak sites by_
_cyber criminals who use these platforms to increase pressure on organizations that_
_refuse to comply with ransom demands." (Check Point Cyber Security Report, 2025)_

_Chapter 5_ 218

Microsoft described the scope of ransomware gangs this way in the Microsoft Digital Defense
Report 2023:

_"Approximately 40 percent of the ransomware encounters we detected in June were_
_human driven. Most of these attacks can be attributed to 123 tracked ransomware-_
_as-a-service affiliates. The number of affiliates grew by 12 percent in the last year,_
_setting up conditions for human-operated ransomware attacks to continue to grow_
_in 2024." (Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2023)_

Of course, ransomware gangs aren't the only organizations that leverage ransomware and
extortion as part of their attacks. Some nation-state-backed groups do as well. According to the
Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024, several nation-state threat **a** ctors Microsoft tracks
leverage ransomware tactics and are motivated by extortion and/or profit; these threat actors
include **Seashell Blizzard**, **Moonstone Sleet**, **Cotton Sandstorm**, **Mint Sandstorm**, **Octo**
**Tempest**, **Storm-0501**, **Storm-0784**, and **Storm-0842** .

One of the reasons that cybersecurity teams generally like it when specific attacks can be
attributed to specific groups is that it helps them understand the **tactics, techniques, and**
**procedures** ( **TTPs** ) that attackers have used in the past. This gives them more confidence that
