Beyond the notable volume of phishing emails, here are some recent interesting data points
that help us understand other characteristics of phishing emails, as published in the _KnowBe4_
_Phishing Trends Report_ that focused on the period between September 15, 2024, and February
14th, 2025 (KnowBe4, March 2025):

They saw a 57% increase in phishing attacks sent from compromised accounts during
the period, with 11.4% sent from trusted senders in victims' supply chains

The most impersonated brands they identified during the period were Microsoft,
DocuSign, Adobe, PayPal, and LinkedIn

The top five legitimate platforms used to send phishing emails during the period were
DocuSign, PayPal, Microsoft, Google Drive, and Salesforce

81.9% of victims' email addresses were previously leaked in data breaches

According to data published in the _Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024_, phishing emails
leveraged URLs/links 56% of the time, QR codes 25% of the time, and attachments 19% of the
time during the second half of 2024 (Microsoft Corporation, October 2023). Microsoft
published an earlier _Microsoft Digital Defense Report_ that revealed attackers were increasing
their usage of URLs with open redirectors and open shorteners. Phishing emails with URL
redirects were counted in the millions each month of the first half of 2023, and the count of
URL shorteners used in phishing emails numbered hundreds of thousands per month during
the same period.

_"URL open redirectors are vulnerabilities found in web applications that enable_
_attackers to manipulate URLs to redirect unsuspecting users to malicious websites._
_Here, they may be victim to phishing attacks, data breaches, account takeovers, or_
_malware infections." Microsoft Corporation, October 2023_

Given the huge volume of phishing emails and all the tactics these attackers employ, you might
wonder how many people get tricked into disclosing their credentials. Using data from
Microsoft Defender SmartScreen that was published in the _Microsoft Digital Defense Report_
_2023_, Microsoft revealed that " _in April-June 2023 we alerted users of approximately 10,000_
_password entries per month into malicious sites_ " (Microsoft Corporation, October 2023). This gives
us some insight into the number of people running Windows 11 who were warned about
phishing sites. However, according to StatCounter, in April to June 2023, Windows 11 was
running on 24% of personal computers, while Windows 10 was running on 71% (StatCounter,
n.d.). So, this particular Windows 11 SmartScreen data point gives us insight into only part of
the total picture. And, of course, there are many other systems running on non-Windows
platforms, including mobile platforms, that this data doesn't provide visibility into. Based on
this, we can assume that the number of people tricked into entering their credentials into
phishing sites is much larger than 10,000 per month.

261 _Internet-Based Threats_

Another source of data that can help us gain insight into the scale of the success of phishing is
the number of victims who filed complaints with law enforcement. According to the US Federal
Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center's _Internet Crime Report 2024_, of the
859,532 total complaints filed with them in 2024, "phishing/spoofing" was the top crime type,
with 193,407 complaints (Internet Crime Complaint Center, n.d.). Extortion was a distant
second with 86,415 complaints. The losses associated with the phishing/spoofing complaints
were $70,013,036. Typically, English-speaking countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom,
and the United States endure more phishing attacks than non-English-speaking countries, but
phishing is a global challenge. The number of victims is undoubtedly much higher than the
numbers I discussed here.

Allow me to paint a picture of phishing using the 2023–2025 phishing data that I discussed:

There were hundreds of thousands of phishing sites on the internet at any given time.

There was an average of 2.5 billion phishing emails sent per month, trying to lure
victims to those sites.

There were 10,000 attempts from systems running Windows 11 to enter credentials
into those phishing sites per month.

Of the people who were victimized by phishing, fewer than 200,000 filed a complaint
with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2024.
The financial losses associated with these complaints were about $70 million.

82% of victims' email addresses were previously leaked in data breaches.

Vishing, smishing, and **quishing** ( **QR code phishing** ) are rapidly growing in popularity
among attackers.

The number of victims seems surprisingly small given the massive number of lures that
phishers are constantly deploying. However, remember that it takes just one compromised
account to provide attackers with initial access to an enterprise IT or OT environment. Given
this, the proportion of lures deployed to the number of people who click on them and enter
their credentials isn't something security teams can really take comfort in.

It's not all bad news, though. Microsoft, Google, and other organizations take a range of
actions to disrupt and take down phishing sites. For example, in September 2025, Microsoft
announced that it had seized 338 websites to disrupt the RaccoonO365 phishing service.
Microsoft described the operation this way:

Regardless of where **a** ttackers host their phishing operations, organizations need to mitigate

**Mitigating phishing**

Phishing websites used to be easier for users to identify than they are today. If a web page was
asking you for credentials or confidential information, but was not protecting that data in
transit using HTTPS (the lack of the legitimate lock icon in the web browser indicates this),
then why would you type anything into that page? But this is no longer an effective way to
identify phishing sites, as they leverage TLS certificates routinely now.

In this section, I'll give you some advice on how to mitigate phishing, informed by my
experience managing cybersecurity programs for large enterprises. As you can see from the
data I provided in this chapter, phishing is a constant threat that never really recedes – at any
moment, someone in your organization can fall victim to a phishing attack, providing attackers
with initial access to your organization's network. There are several things you can do to
protect people from these attacks and minimize the impact that a successful phishing attack
has on your organization. Some of my favorite mitigations are somewhat unconventional;
however, I hope you'll see the wisdom in them.

_Chapter 6_ 264

**Multi-factor authentication**

Mitigating phishing attacks that are focused on credential theft is both easy and difficult at the
same time. For example, phishing attacks that seek to steal credentials can largely be mitigated
by enforcing the requirement to use **multi-factor authentication** ( **MFA** ). NIST defines MFA
this way:

_"An authentication system that requires more than one distinct type of_
_authentication factor for successful authentication. MFA can be performed using a_
_multi-factor authenticator or by combining single-factor authenticators that_
_provide different types of factors." (NIST, July 2025)_

Some examples of vendors and commercial products that enterprises use for MFA include
Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, RSA SecurID, Cisco Duo, Auth0, PingID, Okta,
and many others.

How effective is MFA at mitigating phishing? According to studies conducted by Microsoft:

_"Your password doesn't matter, but MFA does! Based on our studies, your account is_
_more than 99.9% less likely to be compromised if you use MFA." (Weinert, 2019)_

Requiring a second factor for authentication largely mitigates the risks associated with weak,
leaked, and stolen passwords. If an attacker successfully tricks a user into disclosing their
credentials in a phishing attack, but access to the account requires another factor, such as
physical access to a token, access to the victim's mobile phone, or their authenticator
application then the credentials by themselves won't give attackers access to the account. Of
course, that doesn't stop attackers from trying to use those stolen credentials on hundreds of
online financial and e-commerce sites, betting on the chance that the user used the same
credentials multiple times; their scripts do this within seconds of obtaining leaked and stolen
credentials. Reusing the same password across accounts is still too common but can be largely
mitigated by leveraging MFA everywhere.

Unfortunately, this is more challenging to accomplish than it sounds. MFA isn't available
everywhere, especially in enterprise environments with decades of legacy applications. In
every operational cybersecurity program I managed, I started an "MFA Everywhere" initiative.
The objective of these initiatives was to enforce MFA everywhere a username and password are
used in enterprise IT environments. This includes device access (desktop computers, laptops,
and mobile devices), VPN access, **Virtual Desktop Infrastructure** ( **VDI** ) access, and
application access. Literally everywhere a password is used to authenticate for access to
resources, MFA should be enforced. There are some exceptions where MFA can't easily be
leveraged, but everywhere it can be leveraged, it should be enforced.

265 _Internet-Based Threats_

This starts by writing or updating an existing network access policy that requires MFA to be
used everywhere passwords are used for access, unless an explicit exception is granted. Let's
use VPN access as an example. Attackers commonly leverage VPNs to access their victims'
networks. A very common scenario is for attackers to trick a user into disclosing their
credentials in a phishing attack and then use their credentials to access their organizations
network using the stolen credentials. If phishing-resistant MFA is enforced on every VPN
connection, attackers will not be able to access the victim's network via VPN because they
don't have access to the second authentication factor. In the case of VPN, examples of second
authentication factors include a digital certificate installed on the organization's systems or
having the user approve an MFA prompt in an authenticator application on their mobile
phone.

Here are some useful recommendations for MFA:

The organization's network access policy should require that MFA be enforced on every
VPN connection to the organization's network. Be explicit and highlight that this
includes user account access as well as point-to-point VPN connections that connect
entire offices of users, and any other scenario where VPN is used.

The policy should also specify that the MFA control implementations be audited
periodically to ensure that MFA doesn't get disabled in the future, unbeknownst to the
security team.

Security teams should configure monitoring and alertingon VPN MFA configuration
changes so that their security operations centers are alerted quickly when
configuration changes are made to these critical settings.

If someone decides to disable the MFA requirement or give specific users or systems
exceptions without going through proper governance channels, this should garner
scrutiny very quickly. Without MFA, it's only a matter of time before the constant
brute-force and password spray attacks that plague internet-facing VPN services
succeed.

_Chapter 6_ 266

You need to know with certainty that VPN access to your network can only succeed
with MFA.

Even when MFA is available, it is typically viewed by consumers and enterprise information
workers alike as a hassle, regardless of how effective it is. Many information workers and
executives love to complain about the necessity of using a second authentication factor, even if
it is as easy as pressing a button on their mobile device. To counter this perception, I happily
share how many attacks MFA blocks each week or month with my stakeholder communities.
Once they see the large volume and constant barrage of attacks on internet-facing VPN servers,
for example, complaints tend to simmer down.

One effective tool I've seen used in cases where executives demand exceptions for security
policies is risk acceptance letters. A **risk acceptance letter** or risk acknowledgment letter
documents that the risks associated with the security policy exception have been explained to
the executive, they understand these risks, and accept them on behalf of their entire
organization. If accepted, that risk is entered into the cybersecurity risk register. Periodically,
these risks in the cybersecurity risk register should be reviewed by the CISO, senior executives,
and potentially the Board of Directors, to ensure that systemic, long-term risk has not been
inappropriately accepted. When confronted with one of these risk acceptance letters,
executives who want security policy exceptions typically pause at the last minute once they
have time to reflect on the potential consequences to their organizations and their own careers.
In the end, many such executives prudently decide not to demand security policy exceptions.

267 _Internet-Based Threats_

**Phishing training and simulations**

Of course, phishing isn't limited to credential theft. Attackers use phishing in their attempts to
trick people into disclosing information that they otherwise would not share. MFA doesn't
mitigate these types of attacks. In these cases, the best mitigation is _education_ . Training
information workers to recognize potential phishing attacks and other social engineering
tactics isn't foolproof, but it can be very effective. Some organizations simply refuse to approve
phishing exercises designed to train their information workers to recognize phishing attacks.
In many cases, the justification is that they don't want to embarrass anyone. The management
of these organizations does their employees a disservice with such decisions, in my opinion.

One of the tools that CISOs have, when faced with management teams that do not support this
type of training, is _risk management_ . Simplify the decision by using math. In my experience,
CISOs who quantify risk for their management teams have a better chance of success; it helps
put their efforts into context, even when nothing bad happens. Remember that _risk_ is the
combination of _probability_ and _impact_ . The fact that most of the largest and highest-profile data
breaches in history started with a phishing email can help communicate the risk. So can the
volume of phishing emails and the number of phishing sites that I provided in this chapter.
Recall that Microsoft's data from 2024 revealed that 2.5 billion phishing emails are sent every
month on average. Additionally, at least a few hundred thousand active phishing websites are
online at any given time. Combine this with phishing data from your own organization to
quantify the probability that information workers will receive phishing emails and visit
compromised websites, how many, and how often.

Then, develop some quantitative impact estimates, ranging from no impact because phishing
emails were filtered before they made it to information workers, to a successful compromise
that involved data exfiltration and subsequent reputational damage and legal liability for the
organization. Such figures can help make the decision to train people to recognize social
engineering attacks that are less abstract and easier to compare to the other risks that
management teams already manage.

In 2023, Microsoft published data related to phishing simulations. They examined Microsoft
Defender for Office 365 attack simulation training data from tens of millions of users to better
understand the impact of phishing training. Their data revealed that 45% of users who
received phishing emails read them, 11% reported them, 8% clicked on the link in the phishing
email, while 0.8% opened malicious attachments, and 2.3% supplied their credentials to
attackers (Microsoft, October 2023). 2.3% might not sound like a big number, but again,
remember that it only takes one user to get phished successfully to give attackers the initial
access they need.

Not everyone agrees that phishing awareness training and simulations are effective. After
studying 19,789 personnel for 8 months in 2023, a team of researchers from the University of

_Chapter 6_ 268

Chicago, the **University of California, San Diego** ( **UCSD** ), and UCSD Health concluded that
the typical type of industry phishing training wasn't effective in preventing users from getting
tricked by phishing emails:

_"The big finding is that these standard, out-of-the-box industry trainings are not_
_efficacious in preventing users from clicking on emails in the future," says Ariana_
_Mirian, one of the co-authors and senior security researcher at Censys. She adds,_
_though, that "there's a lot of nuance there." (Nelson, Nate, July 1, 2025)_

My own experience with phishing training and awareness is that there always seems to be 1–
2% of email users who are willing to click the malicious links in emails and enter their
credentials into phishing sites. Identifying those email users who consistently behave this way
and targeting them with extra training and attention can make a difference. But frankly, the
days when enterprises could simply trust their employees to make the right choices 100% of
the time are long over. The stakes are too high with pervasive ransomware gangs seemingly
always at the door. This is why the next two mitigations that I'm going to discuss are so
important and actually a little less common than MFA and training.

**Restricting inbound network traffic**

Recall that when a user is tricked into entering their credentials into a phishing site, the very
next thing to happen is that attackers attempt to use those credentials to gain initial access to
the victim's network and internet-facing applications. Restricting the places from which
authentication traffic can originate can make it harder for attackers. For example, it's common
for attackers to attempt to use stolen credentials to access their victim's network by logging in
via the victim's VPN service. Why allow attackers to even get to the VPN login portal to enter
the credentials if they are doing so from a location that has no value to the victim? If the victim
organization does not have any employees, supply chain partners, or customers in Russia, for
example, why allow network traffic from Russia to get to the VPN login portal? Geo-blocking
network traffic from entire countries and restricting inbound network traffic selectively will
make it a little harder for some attackers to use the credentials they have stolen.

Many security experts and networking subject matter experts will be quick to point out that
attackers will just stage their attacks from a location that does have access. That's correct, but
security teams should make each step in attackers' kill chains as difficult as possible.

269 _Internet-Based Threats_

This will enable your organization to continue to function normally while reducing the
number of places you can be attacked from. If your organization isn't doing business in Russia,
the People's Republic of China, Iran, or the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North
Korea), why would you allow network traffic from these locations to your VPN service, your
online email service, or other internet-facing applications?

Adding inbound network restrictions also makes it easier to detect unexpected changes in your
organization's external attack surface. If network traffic from Spain is blocked because your
organization has no business interests there, it makes it easy to spot login attempts from Spain
to your internet-facing applications and VPN login portals. Simply stated, there should be zero
login attempts from Spain because network traffic from Spain can't make it to the network port
that the login services are listening on.

If you don't believe there's value in implementing these types of restrictions, go check out all
the brute-force attacks and password spray attacks on your organization's VPN service and
Microsoft 365 portal from locations where your organization has no business interests. You
might be surprised to see a constant barrage of attacks from all over the world. There are 195–
200 countries in the world, depending on how you count them (US Department of State,
March 12, 2025). If your organization doesn't have business interests in all these places, why
allow attackers to use them to stage their attacks against you? Of course, for global
organizations that do business in nearly all these countries, the value of geo-blocking won't be
as great. But even those organizations are likely to have countries they can't do business in
because of international sanctions or other restrictions, such as the Democratic People's
Republic of Korea (North Korea), for example. Blocking network traffic from such locations has
security value.

For countries where your organization does have business interests, such as customers and
supply chain partners, a blunt tool such as geo-blocking won't be useful. However, that doesn't
mean you can't use inbound network restrictions to your advantage. To complement geoblocking, use automation to temporarily block the IP addresses used in attacks. For example,
let's say you are a US-based company with millions of customers in the US. You can't geo-block
network traffic from the US, as it would negatively impact your organization. However,
leveraging automation that blocks US-based IP addresses that are used for brute-force and
password spray attacks against your VPN portal at the network level for a random period of
time (1–4 hours) will blunt such attacks and frustrate attackers by forcing them to change IP
addresses constantly. It should become clear to the attacker that this tactic increases the
amount of time they need for their attack dramatically. Combined with lengthy passwords (15
characters) and MFA, their chances of success with brute-force and password spray attacks are
very low. In my experience, these attackers move on to other targets. It's no fun for them if they
can't even get through their big list of passwords for months or years.

_Chapter 6_ 270

You might wonder why I recommend using inbound network blocking if MFA has been
implemented. The concept of "defense in depth" has fallen out of favor with many
cybersecurity professionals. However, as I mentioned earlier, MFA is extremely effective – until
it isn't. I've been burned more than once by unapproved changes to MFA settings, made by
administrators and attackers alike. Some administrators can't help themselves but turn off
security mitigations during troubleshooting exercises to simplify the variables they are dealing
with. But often, these administrators fail to turn the security mitigations back on, either
unintentionally or purposely. One of the first things many attackers do after initial access is
identify the "MFA exception" group in Active Directory and add the accounts they are using to
it. Alternatively, they simply add their own MFA second factors to the accounts they use so that
they have both the credentials and the second factors to enable them to log in like any other
user. During the subsequent intrusion reconstruction that the **i** ncident response team does,
one of the findings is that the initial access would have been prevented had inbound
connections to VPN been restricted.

**Restricting outbound network traffic**

Earlier, I mentioned that some mitigations that I was going to recommend were somewhat
unconventional. This is one of them. Not only is it unconventional, but it's also unpopular
among almost everyone, including users, executives, IT operators, cybersecurity practitioners,
and, most importantly, attackers. But for CISOs who can manage skeptical stakeholder
communities, this mitigation pays high dividends because it adds friction to so many attacker
activities.

This mitigation involves embracing the principle of least privilege for outbound network
access to the internet – that is, giving users on your network access to only the internet sites
they actually need access to. This can involve a combination of technical controls, such as DNS
sinkholing and egress firewall filters that block users' attempts to get to sites on the internet
that aren't authorized to visit. DNS sinkholing redirects or blocks DNS name resolution
requests for malicious or unwanted domain requests, while egress filtering on firewalls
restricts outbound traffic to permitted sites. Let me provide a concrete example of how such
restrictions can be helpful.

Recall how a phishing attack works. Let's use a phishing email example because it's the most
popular lure based on the data we examined. The attacker sends an email to the intended
victim with a link to a website that the attacker controls. On that website, the attacker has
crafted a web page that looks just like a legitimate login portal that the victim uses, such as
Microsoft 365, for example. The victim believes it's the legitimate login portal and enters their
credentials. The attacker immediately starts using those stolen credentials for illicit purposes.

What if, when the user clicked the link in the phishing email, it was simply broken? That is,
their browser opened and gave them an error message telling them the remote server didn't

271 _Internet-Based Threats_

respond: `This site can't be reached. Try checking the connection. Try checking`

`the proxy, firewall, and DNS configuration. (ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED)` . Alternatively,
the browser could display a custom error message telling the user that access to the website
was restricted and point them to an internal internet access policy exception intake form to fill
out if they really need access to the website.

Notice that, in this case, our phishing and awareness training failed, our email phishing filters
failed, the rewritten URL provided by the phishing filters failed, and the web browser's built-in
phishing protection didn't help, but we still prevented the user from getting to a malicious site
and prevented attackers from stealing their credentials. Simply preventing the user from
getting to the phishing site compensated for the failure or lack of other security controls. Some
cybersecurity professionals are bound to ask: why not just remove URLs from email before they
get to inboxes or just rewrite URLs so they can be checked when the user clicks on them? These
mitigations have real efficacy, but they don't provide the "bonus" that outbound internet
restrictions provide.

The bonus is that outbound restrictions can also make it harder for attackers to download their
tools to the victim's network. They can also make it harder for attackers to remotely control
compromised systems on their victim's network from the internet. It can also make it harder
for attackers to perform data exfiltration from their victim's network to systems or sites they
control on the internet. It turns out that many attackers rely heavily on broad outbound access
to the internet for their attacks to succeed. When outbound access is materially restricted,
attackers' scripts break, and they are potentially forced to spend significantly more time and
effort on critical parts of their kill chain. More time and effort mean lower ROI for attackers. If
the time and effort become practically insurmountable, they will move on to other easier
targets.

Many of the detractors of this tactic are quick to point out that users won't like being
restricted. This is certainly true. But if you do your job with a high level of competence, they
should rarely even notice. I've implemented draconian outbound internet restrictions at a few
companies during my career with great results. Some of these companies were quite large
(200,000+ employees in 30 countries) and some smaller (15,000 employees). In every case,
successful phishing attacks were virtually eliminated, the leakage/theft of credentials stopped,
and incident response volumes dropped. It gave these organizations the time and space they
needed to get other **i** mportant mitigations in place, such as TLS inspection and **secure access**
**service edge** ( **SASE** ).

Consider whether your organization's information workers really require unfettered access to
the internet. Do they really need to visit websites with content in languages that they do not
know how to read? I've had plenty of executives assert that their teams need unfettered access
to the internet. I typically ask them how many people on their team can read Russian, or a

_Chapter 6_ 272

dialect of Chinese, Persian, or Korean. That's when the look on their faces typically changes
because they've never considered the non-English-speaking parts of the internet before. Is
there really a legitimate business need to allow everyone in an organization to go everywhere
on the internet? They typically quickly backtrack their demands for unfettered access and
begin to consider the things their teams really need access to. Of course, global organizations
will need access to huge swaths of the internet, but even they don't have a need for everyone to
access everything on the internet.

If you decide to go down this path, you don't have to start from a place where no one has access
to anything. Use DNS logs and firewall logs to identify the most popular sites for your user
population. When you start restricting access to the internet, most of these sites should be on
your allowlist and accessible. Everything listed on internal human resources websites should
also be accessible. You'll need a process that enables users to request access to URLs that get
added to the allow list over time – for example, a ServiceNow form that intakes requests and
enables the firewall team to process them. Allow users to submit multiple URLs (hundreds) in
each request to make it less frustrating for them. In my experience, once the allow list gets to
about 70,000 sites, the complaints and volume of allow list requests drop significantly. Given
that there are hundreds of millions of websites on the internet, access to only 70,000 or even
100,000 sites dramatically reduces the number of sites that can be used for phishing, malicious
downloads, remote-controlling compromised systems, data exfiltration, and other parts of
attackers' kill chains.

The objective is to give users and executives access to all the resources they need to do their
work and to support a positive culture within the organization. I recommend allowing access
to popular news sites, social media sites, and financial sites to support these objectives. The
more sensitive sites that you want to limit access to, or block altogether, are those that enable
data exfiltration, such as internet storage services, unapproved email services, unapproved
instant messaging, and even legitimate businesses that enable their customers to upload files.
I'll discuss outbound internet restrictions in more detail in _Chapter 14_, _Mitigating "Living Off the_
_Land" Tactics._

The combination of MFA, commercial phishing filters, URL rewriting, and outbound internet
blocking will make successful phishing attacks much harder to accomplish and add friction
into other parts of attackers' kill chains. If they are going to accomplish **i** nitial access,
download their tools, remote-control systems, and exfiltrate data, they are going to have to
find and compromise the accounts that enable all these activities.

Now, let's look at the second tactic the attackers used in our example of a typical attack, a
drive-by download attack.

273 _Internet-Based Threats_

###### **Drive-by download attacks**

While phishing attacks are at the intersection of social engineering and weak, leaked, and
stolen passwords, drive-by download attacks are at the intersection of social engineering and
unpatched vulnerabilities. Drive-by attacks are typically performed by attackers using social
engineering to trick users into visiting a malicious website. They can do this in several ways,
including via email, online ads, putting links to malicious sites in the comments sections of
web pages and social network posts, and many other tactics. Sometimes, attackers
compromise a legitimate website and use it to host drive-by download attacks; the more
popular the website, the better for the attackers, as it increases their chances of successfully
compromising as many systems as possible.

Getting potential victims to malicious websites under the control of attackers is the first step in
the attack. The next step is to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities on the victims' systems. To do
this, attackers will attempt to run scripts that have embedded URLs, or they will use an **inline**
**frame** ( **IFrame** ) to load another HTML document page unbeknownst to the user. IFrames have
legitimate uses, making it complicated to distinguish between good ones and malicious ones.
Attackers will place IFrames the size of a pixel on their malicious web pages so that users
cannot see them. When these HTML documents load, they can, among other things, run
scripts that detect the victim's operating system and browser versions, select and download
corresponding exploits for common vulnerabilities for these versions, and, ultimately,
download and install other malware that gives attackers illicit control of the compromised
system. Such malicious IFrames can be placed on web pages of legitimate websites that have
been compromised. This means that visiting a trusted website with a system that is not fully
patched can result in a compromised system that attackers can control remotely, cripple with
ransomware, and so on.

MITRE lists "drive-by compromise" as a known technique that attackers use in their enterprise
ATT&CK framework, along with 43 "procedure examples" that illustrate how real-world
attackers are known to have leveraged them (MITRE, April 15, 2025). However, drive-by
download attacks have become less common over time. Let's look at some historical data from
Microsoft.

_Figure 6.5_ reveals that, for the period between July 2012 and January 2020, the highest number
of drive-by download pages discovered on the internet was in 2013, where more than one
drive-by download page was found per thousand URLs indexed by Microsoft's Bing search
engine.

_Chapter 6_ 274

_Figure 6.5 – Drive-by download pages per 1,000 URLs indexed by Microsoft's Bing search engine between 2012–_
_2020 as published in the Microsoft Security Intelligence Report Volumes 14–21 (Microsoft Corporation, 2012–2017)_
_and Interactive Microsoft Security Intelligence Reports (Microsoft Corporation, May 2020)_

However, more recently, the worldwide average was 0.09 and 0.08 of these malicious sites per
1,000 URLs indexed in 2018 and 2019, respectively. That means the number of drive-by
download sites per thousand URLs in 2013 was 14 times higher than the number in 2019.

The components used in **d** rive-by download attacks can be distributed, with several different
remote systems hosting them. The scripts that run can be hosted on different "redirector"
servers, the exploits used to exploit unpatched vulnerabilities can be hosted on separate
exploit servers, and the malware that ultimately gets downloaded to the victims' systems can
be hosted on separate malware-hosting servers. Distributing components of drive-by
download attacks this way provides several advantages to attackers. It allows attackers to be
more agile, enabling them to adjust their attacks quickly. This helps them optimize their
attacks and makes it harder to find and dismantle all the components attackers use.

Subsequently, the infrastructure used to host the components of drive-by download attacks is
distributed all over the world. _Table 6.1_ provides the locations with the highest number of
drive-by download URLs per 1,000 URLs indexed by Microsoft's Bing search engine in 2019
(Microsoft Corporation, 2020). I'm sharing data from this specific time period with you
because it is especially interesting – note the top entry in the table:

The number of drive-by download pages per 1,000 URLs in Oman in 2019 isn't a typo.
According to data published by Microsoft, there were 687.3 drive-by download URLs for every
1,000 URLs in Oman, averaged across the 12 months of 2019 (Microsoft Corporation, 2020).
That's 8,591.25 times higher than the worldwide average. In November 2019, Microsoft
reported that there were 1,251.94 drive-by download URLs for every 1,000 URLs found by Bing
in Oman (Microsoft Corporation, 2020). This means that on average, each URL Bing indexed in
Oman triggered more than one drive-by download attempt. That suggests a very high
concentration of drive-by download URLs in this ccTLD at the time. It might also be the case
that a small set of URLs generated a disproportionately large number of malicious events.

Although this could be a simple error in the data, there could be another, less banal
explanation. The ccTLD for Oman is `.om` . Attackers could have registered and used domain
names in this ccTLD to catch web browser users who type `.om` instead of `.com` . This hypothesis
seems plausible given how often people could make the trivial mistake of typing `google.om`
instead of `google.com`, `apple.om` instead of `apple.com`, and so on. How many people would

_Chapter 6_ 276

make mistakes like this every day? It seems it was enough to get the attention of attackers
leveraging drive-by download sites. This is what some cybersecurity researchers were
reporting back in 2016. It seems that this tactic was still in widespread use almost three years
later in the last quarter of 2019:

_"According to Endgame security researchers, the top level domain for Middle_
_Eastern country Oman (.om) is being exploited by typosquatters who have registered_
_more than 300 domain names with the .om suffix for U.S. companies and services_
_such as Citibank, Dell, Macys, and Gmail. Endgame made the discovery last week_
_and reports that several groups are behind the typosquatter campaigns." —(Spring,_
_2016)_

In more recent periods, drive-by attacks appear to have become less popular with attackers, so
much so that it is hard to find credible sources of data to help quantify the likelihood that you'll
encounter one.

_"Although drive-by download attacks don't appear to be as popular with attackers_
_as they used to be, that doesn't mean modern attackers don't leverage them. Every_
_once in a while, the methods of a named attacker come to light, and drive-by_

**Mitigating drive-by download attacks**

These attacks tend to rely on unpatched vulnerabilities to be successful. Attackers have exploit
libraries that they leverage for their drive-by download attacks. Studies have shown that
attackers have used between one and over 20 exploits on a single drive-by URL. If the
underlying vulnerabilities that these exploits try to take advantage of are patched, these
attacks won't be successful. Therefore, a well-run vulnerability management program will
mitigate drive-by download attacks. Keeping systems that are used to access content on the
internet up to date with security updates is a very effective mitigation.

277 _Internet-Based Threats_

Additionally, preventing exposure to malicious websites such as drive-by download sites can
be helpful. Consider whether allowing information workers and system administrators
unfettered access to the internet is required and worth the risk. Why do they need access to
the `.om` ccTLD, for example, or any of the other ccTLD domains where there likely aren't
legitimate business reasons to visit? Leveraging actively managed web filtering services can be
helpful; blocking access to parts of the internet from corporate assets that don't have a clear
business purpose can also be helpful.

Don't allow system administrators to visit the internet using web browsers from servers that
process anything, or from systems that are important. Secure access workstations or privileged
access workstations should be used for server administration to limit risk to important
systems. Browsing sites on the public internet should be strictly forbidden on such systems
and prevented with technical controls. In environments where this simply isn't possible,
restrictive outbound internet access should be enforced to enable access to approved websites
while preventing unfettered access to the internet.

Running up-to-date anti-malware software from a trusted anti-malware vendor can also be an
effective mitigation. Drive-by download attacks typically result in malware being downloaded
to the victim's system. If anti-malware software detects the exploit attempt and blocks the
download and **i** nstallation of such malware, a potential disaster is averted.

Next, let's discuss a couple of threats that compromised systems are used for after they are
compromised – botnets and DDoS attacks.
###### **Botnets and DDoS attacks**

Once systems have been initially compromised via one or more of the Cybersecurity Usual
Suspects, such as unpatched vulnerabilities and/or social engineering, as we discussed in this
chapter, any information of value is siphoned from victims' systems to be sold or traded. At this
point, attackers have full control of the systems they have compromised. Many times, victims'
systems are enlisted into botnets and used to perform whatever illicit projects their operators
desire, including DDoS attacks.

There's a lot that can be written about botnets, how they operate, and the projects they are
typically employed on. In fact, entire books have been dedicated to botnets. I won't try to
duplicate those here. But I do want to briefly mention a few things on this topic.

It goes without saying that botnets have garnered a lot of attention over the years. When I
worked at Microsoft, the Microsoft **Digital Crimes Unit** ( **DCU** ) worked with law enforcement
and industry experts to disrupt some of the largest botnets in operation. This work helped to
dramatically reduce spam on the internet and degrade the attack power these botnets
provided to their operators. Some of these botnets were composed of hundreds of thousands or

_Chapter 6_ 278

millions of compromised systems and were capable of sending tens of billions of spam and
phishing email messages per day. Rustock and Waledac are two examples of such botnets. To
do this, the DCU had to approach the problem as a novel legal challenge in which they sought
and were given legal control over the domains and physical infrastructure these botnets used
(Microsoft Corporation, 2011).

In 2024, the top botnets identified by Recorded Future included Mozi Botnet, 7777-Botnet,
Mirai, Hajime, and Moobot:

_"In 2024, the top five botnets based on Insikt Group Botnet Validation data are_
_Mozi Botnet, 7777-Botnet (also known as Quad7), Mirai, Hajime, and Moobot…_
_Mozi Botnet and Hajime operate on a peer-to-peer model, offering greater resilience_
_to takedowns but with increased complexity in implementation and_
_management...In contrast, 7777-Botnet, Mirai, and Moobot use a client-server_
_model with centralized control, simplifying management for their operators. While_
_all botnets except the 7777-Botnet are primarily used for DDoS and occasionally_
_spamming attacks, the 7777-Botnet has been observed for password spraying_
_attacks…" (Recorded Future, February 28, 2025)._

The Mirai botnet gained notoriety back in 2016 when it was discovered that it was composed of
online cameras, routers, and other IoT devices that leveraged ARC processors and a Linuxbased operating system. The attackers behind the Mirai botnet leveraged an unchanged
default username and password (a security misconfiguration) to grow it (CloudFlare, n.d.).
Variants have flourished since then.

The Mozi botnet was the largest botnet, by number of identified bots tracked in 2024 by
Recorded Future (Recorded Future, February 28, 2025). Like the Mirai botnet, the Mozi botnet
targets IoT devices. Microsoft describes it this way:

_"Mozi is a peer-to-peer (P2P) botnet that uses a BitTorrent-like network to infect_
_IoT devices such as network gateways and digital video records (DVRs). It works by_
_exploiting weak telnet passwords and nearly a dozen unpatched IoT vulnerabilities_
_and it's been used to conduct distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, data_
_exfiltration, and command or payload execution." (Microsoft Corporation, August_
_19, 2021)_

Attackers will drain anything of value from the systems they have complete control over,
including cached credentials. Massive lists of leaked and stolen credentials have been found on
the internet over the years, including a list with 16 billion passwords that had been amassed
over the years that was discovered in June of 2025 (Sayegh, June 30, 2025). If the compromised
systems or accounts have authenticated and authorized access to other systems in the

279 _Internet-Based Threats_

environment, attackers will potentially have access and control over them as well,
exacerbating the damage to organizations.

Accelerating detection and recovery activities can reduce the amount of time attackers control
these assets, thus potentially reducing the damage they do to other victims and the costs
associated with the recovery and restoration of normal operations. Threat intelligence can help
organizations identify systems communicating with known botnet command-and-control
infrastructures. Attackers know this and have been hosting some of their infrastructures in
public web hosting and cloud environments in an effort to hide their operations among
legitimate network traffic.

If you are interested in the granular details of attackers' internet-based infrastructures, I
recommend reading the _Malicious Infrastructure Reports_ published by Recorded Future's Insikt
Group. They describe these reports this way:

_"Building on Insikt Group's annual adversary infrastructure reports from 2022 and_
_2023, the 2024 Malicious Infrastructure Report provides a concise, data-based_
_overview of malicious infrastructure observed throughout 2024. This year, it_
_specifically emphasizes the synergy among passive infrastructure detection, higher-_
_tier infrastructure insights powered by Recorded Future Network Intelligence, and_
_victim identification. Overall, this report is for anyone interested in malicious_
_infrastructure, offering a high-level overview of its current state as well as_
_summaries of key findings to inform decision-making and provide a broad_
_perspective in this highly dynamic environment." (Recorded Future, February 28,_
_2025)_

Their _2024 Malicious Infrastructure Report_ can be downloaded from `[https://](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/2024-malicious-infrastructure-report)`

`[www.recordedfuture.com/research/2024-malicious-infrastructure-report](https://www.recordedfuture.com/research/2024-malicious-infrastructure-report)` .

One of the illicit purposes that botnets have been employed to perform over the years has been
DDoS. Modern DDoS attacks use sophisticated techniques to overwhelm their targets with
network traffic, thus depriving legitimate users of the services hosted by the victim.

**Types of DDoS attacks**

The three most common types of DDoS attacks include volumetric attacks, protocol attacks,
and application attacks (Kesavan, November 15, 2016). There are many variations of attacks in
these categories. Here is a non-exhaustive list of some examples:

**Volumetric attack** : The attacker attempts to exhaust all available bandwidth to/from
their victim's server by sending large volumes of requests to the server. Examples of
types of volumetric attacks include UDP flood, reflection amplification attacks, and
many others.

_Chapter 6_ 280

**Hyper-volumetric** : L3/4 DDoS attacks that muster at least 1 **billion packets per**
**second** ( **Bpps** ) or **terabits per second** ( **Tbps** ). Also included in this category are HTTP
DDoS attacks that exceed 1 million requests per second (Cloudflare, July 15, 2025).

**Protocol attacks** : These attempt to exploit weaknesses in TCP/IP and related protocols
and their implementations. Examples include `SYN` flood and `RST` flood attacks
(Kesavan, November 15, 2016).

**Application attacks** : These attempt to exploit weaknesses at the **a** pplication layer
(layer 7) of the protocol stack. Examples include HTTP flood attacks and attacks that
target DNS servers (Kesavan, November 15, 2016).

**DNS flood attack** : These hammer DNS servers with high volumes of DNS queries to
disrupt regular DNS service.

**SYN flood attack** : Every TCP session starts with a three-way handshake ( `SYN`, `SYN-ACK`,
and `ACK` ). This attack floods a server with `SYN` requests, but doesn't complete the threeway handshake, in an attempt to exhaust the server's memory and resources.

**UDP flood attack** : Attackers send a high volume of UDP packets at the victim's server
in an attempt to exhaust the server's resources and/or the network connection to the
server.

**RST flood attack** : The TCP protocol uses "reset" packets when a server needs to close a
TCP session unexpectedly (when the connection can't close gracefully). Attackers flood
the victim's server with TCP reset packets using spoofed sender IP addresses in an
attempt to disrupt legitimate TCP sessions.

**A ping or ICMP flood attack** : TCP/IP uses the **Internet Control Message Protocol**
( **ICMP** ) to test and manage connectivity to networking devices. Attackers flood the
victim's server with ICMP requests in an attempt to disrupt connectivity to the server.

How large can DDoS attacks get? In February 2018, attackers launched an attack on GitHub.
This DDoS attack is said to have peaked at 1.35 Tbps, which is the equivalent of more than 126
million packets per second (Kottler, 2018). This attack used a novel approach by abusing
memcached instances that were not secured. This approach enabled attackers to amplify their
attack by a factor of 51,000; put another way, for every 1 byte of network traffic that attackers
sent, up to 51,000 bytes (51 KB) were sent to their target. This allowed attackers to overwhelm
GitHub's network capacity with a massive amount of UDP traffic that interrupted network
connectivity to the site for almost 10 minutes.

In January of 2022, Microsoft mitigated another record-breaking volumetric DDoS attack that
threw 3.47 Tbps at their network, sending approximately 340 million packets per second.

281 _Internet-Based Threats_

_"The attack Microsoft mitigated came from about 10,000 sources and from_
_countries that include the United States, China, South Korea, Russia, Thailand,_
_India, Vietnam, Iran, Indonesia, and Taiwan. Attack vectors were floods of User_
_Datagram Protocol packets reflected over port 80 using SSDP, CLDAP, NTP, and_
_Domain Name System servers." – (Goodin, Dan., January 2022)_

On June 1st, 2022, Google reportedly prevented the largest HTTPS DDoS attack ever recorded at
the time, from denying service to one of their customer's internet services hosted in Google's
cloud. This 69-minute attack peaked at 46 million requests per second using HTTPS-based
requests. According to the Google product manager who was interviewed after the attack, it
was like " _receiving all the daily requests to Wikipedia (one of the top 10 trafficked websites in the_
_world) in just 10 seconds_ " (Kan, August 18, 2022). A botnet was suspected of generating this
attack.

Since that time, DDoS attacks have continued to get larger. On September 2 <sup>nd</sup>, 2025, Cloudflare
reported that they had blocked the largest volumetric DDOS attack in history. They reported
that the attack originated from several cloud and IoT providers.

_"Cloudflare's defenses have been working overtime. Over the past few weeks, we've_
_autonomously blocked hundreds of hyper-volumetric DDoS attacks, with the largest_
_reaching peaks of 5.1 Bpps and 11.5 Tbps," the company said in a Tuesday_
_tweet." (Sergiu, Gatlan., September 2, 2025)_

Then, just three weeks later, Cloudflare reported blocking another record-setting DDoS attack
that peaked at 22.2 Tbps and 10.6 Bpps (Toulas, September 23, 2025). This is a 1,544% increase
in Tbps since that quaint 1.35 Tbps DDoS attack that I mentioned occurred in 2018. Recall that
the attack generated 126 million packets per second compared to the attack in 2025, which
generated 10.6 Bpps. 10.6 billion is 84 times more packets per second than 126 million.

Of course, not all DDoS attacks need to be that large or innovative to be disruptive. Cloudflare
published some statistics, presented here, that reveal DDoS attack sizes and durations in the
second quarter of 2025 (Cloudflare, July 15, 2025):

6 out of every 100 HTTP DDoS attacks exceed 1 million HTTP requests per second

5 out of every 10,000 Layer 3/Layer 4 DDoS attacks exceed 1 Tbps

92% of Layer 3/Layer 4 DDoS attacks and 75% of HTTP DDoS attacks end within 10
minutes

_Chapter 6_ 282

Cloudflare blocked over 6,500 hyper-volumetric attacks in the quarter, which is an
average of 71 per day

The majority of DDoS attacks each year are Layer 3/Layer 4 DDoS attacks as opposed to
HTTP DDoS attacks

Perhaps a less sophisticated but more interesting DDoS attack from the history books was the
attack on critical infrastructure in Estonia in 2007. Some attributed this attack to Russia
(Anderson, 2007). The reason this is interesting is that it perhaps gave us a preview of what to
expect in future cyberwar conflicts – simultaneous kinetic and online attacks that overwhelm
the defending state's ability to wage warfare physically and logistically. A modern version of
this playbook was reportedly used just prior to Russia's military invasion of Ukraine, 15 years
later in 2022. In mid-February of that year, DDoS attacks targeted military and financial
institutions in Ukraine (Antoniuk, February 14, 2022). Eight days later, Russia crossed the
border and started its invasion of Ukraine. These DDoS attacks were not record-setting but
could have been much more disruptive had they not been effectively mitigated. The attack
playbook used against Ukraine before and during the invasion is of high interest to many
people, including other governments and DDoS mitigation vendors themselves.

Organizations have options to help them mitigate such attacks. There are many vendors that
offer DDoS protection services, some of which include AWS Shield, Amazon CloudFront,
Google Cloud Armor, Microsoft Azure DDoS Protection, Cloudflare, Akamai, and many others.
In addition to protection services, the cloud offers techniques that can be used to scale
infrastructure automatically as needed during DDoS attacks (Amazon Web Services, August 9,
2023).

To summarize, the key is to focus on the cybersecurity fundamentals, so your systems do not
end up being part of a botnet and used to attack countless other organizations and consumers.
As I will discuss in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_, investing in detection and response
capabilities will help organizations minimize the damage and costs associated with botnets
and the grief they bring with them to the internet.
###### **Summary**

This chapter focused on internet-based threats. We examined phishing attacks and drive-by
download attacks. So many attacks leverage social engineering that CISOs and security teams
must spend time and resources to mitigate it. For example, every week, tens of thousands of
new phishing sites are connected to the internet, and every month, billions of phishing emails
are sent to prospective victims.

Most phishing emails include a link to a phishing site, and most phishing sites leverage HTTPS
(TLS certificates). Accounts are nearly 100% less likely to be compromised when MFA is

283 _Internet-Based Threats_

enabled. Anti-social engineering training for information workers can also help organizations
avoid falling victim to phishing attacks.

Drive-by download attacks leverage unpatched vulnerabilities to install malware
unbeknownst to the user. According to data released by Microsoft, Oman's ccTLD hosted 8,591
times more drive-by download sites than the worldwide average in 2019 (Microsoft
Corporation, 2020). This could indicate that attackers are using the `.om` domain to attack users
who mistype URLs in the `.com` domain.

The number of drive-by download sites and phishing sites changes over time, sometimes
dramatically. Subsequently, a cybersecurity strategy that doesn't include mitigations for these
types of internet-based threats could have high-risk gaps.

A well-run vulnerability management program and running up-to-date anti-malware from a
trusted vendor can be effective mitigations for drive-by downloads. Aggressive inbound and
outbound internet access restrictions can help security teams mitigate phishing attacks, driveby download attacks, complicate attackers' ability to command and control compromised
systems, and their data exfiltration efforts. We'll discuss this in more detail in _Chapter 14_ .

Systems compromised by phishing attacks, drive-by downloads, and other malicious websites
can end up being enlisted into botnets and used to attack other organizations and consumers,
including participating in DDoS attacks. There are different types of DDoS attacks, including
volumetric and hyper-volumetric attacks, protocol attacks, and application layer attacks. DDoS
attacks have been getting more intense and increasing in frequency over the years. DDoS
mitigation is no longer optional for enterprise organizations. Many vendors offer DDoS
protection services that enterprises can employ to mitigate even the largest DDoS attacks.

That wraps up our look at internet-based threats. I've exposed you to a lot of data, graphs, and
tables in the last four chapters in an effort to provide a data-driven view of some of the threats
that CISOs and security teams face every day. Another threat that CISOs and security teams
need to be prepared for is attacks on **application programming interfaces** ( **APIs** ). Let's
examine API security in the next chapter.

# 7
##### Application Programming Interface Security

We live in an **application programming interface** ( **API** )-driven world. Whether you are
banking, making travel arrangements, listening to music or watching a show or movie on a
streaming service, checking the weather, counting steps with a fitness tracker, or using almost
any application in any scenario, it is likely APIs are involved. Most modern applications use
APIs to interact with other software systems. APIs have become ubiquitous as developers have
put them everywhere to enable data exchanges and functionality sharing across digital
platforms.

Of course, this involves considerable complexity. Although APIs simplify the knowledge of
software systems that developers require to leverage them, there are a myriad of details that
developers must tend to to protect the software they develop and the systems their software
runs on from exploitation.

As the number of APIs that enterprises develop and rely on continues to proliferate, few
organizations have paused to ask their CISOs about the resources needed to identify, protect,
detect, and respond to threats against their APIs. These conversations typically happen only
after an organization runs out of luck and gets burned by poor choices made during
application development or vulnerabilities in their APIs. But by then, the challenge of securing
APIs that are already in production is typically compounded by their numbers and their
complexity. They also need to secure the APIs they are currently developing for release into
production in the future. These are not insurmountable tasks, but they do need to be taken
seriously if organizations want to avoid potentially expensive and embarrassing data breaches
via insecure APIs.

It is important that CISOs and security teams understand the security and privacy challenges
that developers have when developing and working with APIs. The choices that developers

_Chapter 7_ 292

make turn out to be critical to the security of their software and the data it processes.
Unfortunately, network and security infrastructure cannot compensate for many of the poor
choices developers can make using APIs. A combination of security and privacy requirements
during the development process, along with processes and technologies that identify, protect,
detect, and respond to threats against APIs, is necessary.

In this chapter, we'll examine the most common vulnerabilities in APIs through a CISO lens. By
the end of this chapter, you'll understand some of the most important aspects of API security
and be able to discuss them with developers, vendors, and other stakeholders.

The following topics will be covered in this chapter:

An API primer

The web application and API threat landscape

The security development lifecycle

OWASP API Security Top 10

Let's start with a quick primer on APIs.
###### **An API primer**

The **National Institute of Standards and Technology** ( **NIST** ) defines **a** n API as " _a system access_
_point or library function that has a well-defined syntax and is accessible from application programs or_
_user code to provide well-defined functionality_ " (NIST, n.d.). As this relatively broad definition
suggests, there are many different types of APIs. For example, when I worked at Microsoft in
the Core Operating System Division, I worked with APIs for operating systems, programming
languages, and software libraries. This chapter will focus on web APIs that enable applications
running on internet-connected systems to communicate with each other.

As the web came to support different types of media over the decades, APIs evolved and
became more sophisticated. Web APIs rely on a combination of data formats, protocols, and
architectural styles, such as the following:

**Extensible Markup Language** ( **XML** )

**Hypertext Transfer Protocol** ( **HTTP** )

**Representational State Transfer** ( **REST** )

**Simple Object Access Protocol** ( **SOAP** )

**JavaScript Object Notation** ( **JSON** )

Basic system interaction involves four main components: clients, requests, servers, and
responses. Software running on a client (such as a workstation, laptop, device, virtual machine,
agent, etc.) sends a request over a network to an API running on a server. The server hosts the

293 _Application Programming Interface Security_

API and receives the client's request. The server then processes the request according to how
the developer of the API designed it. For example, it might include performing calculations,
retrieving data from a database, or executing automation functions. Once the server processing
is complete, the server sends a response back to the client. This could contain the data it
requested, a status message, or an error code. The developer of the API determines what the
API will return to the client and how it behaves. _Figure 7.1_ illustrates a simplified example of
how a web API works. In this example, the user uses a weather application on their mobile
device to get the current weather forecast for their location. The application makes an API call
to a weather service on the internet, which returns the weather forecast to the application for
the user.

_Figure 7.1 – An example of how a web API works_

Let's take an example of a client running a web browser. The client sends an HTTP request to a
web server requesting access to a specific web page specified by a **Uniform Resource Locator**
( **URL** ). If the web page exists and the user is authorized, the server returns the web page to the
client in a format that it expects, and the browser reads and renders the web page for the user.
If the web server doesn't have the requested web page, it returns an HTTP 404 (Not Found)
error to the client, and the user's browser displays the error to them.

In this case, both the developers of the web server and the web browser needed to understand
how the APIs they used were implemented. By using existing APIs, they saved on the time and
effort it would have taken to implement their own TCP/IP stack, HTTP protocol, and so on.
When a user enters a URL, developers use APIs to send that request to the server. The operating
system and network manage most of the underlying details for the developer. Because of this,
developers don't need deep expertise in the HTTP protocol, TCP/IP, authentication and
authorization methods, web browsers, or web servers. This model simplifies and accelerates
web development.

_Chapter 7_ 294

Developers can work with an API only when they understand how it's built, which means they
rely on the API's specification to see how its endpoints, inputs, and behaviors are defined. API
specifications are written in a standard, structured way. This helps developers understand and
use APIs and makes testing easier.

Let's look at an example where a developer is developing an application that requests data
from a web server that returns the requested data in JSON format. In this example, the client
application asks the API on the remote server where a picture is and uses the response to
display the picture.

First, the client sends a request to the API on the remote server using an `HTTPS GET` method.
This request looks like a standard URL:

```
  GET https://api.packt.com/picture

```

The URL is the API's endpoint for the resource requested – in this case, the picture. The `GET`
requests a representation of the specified resource. In this example, the API does not require
authentication.

The server processes the request and returns the requested data as a JSON object. The client
application uses the returned data to locate and display the picture for the user:

```
  {

   "date": "2025-10-31",

   "explanation": "This is the picture you requested...",

   "hdurl": "https://api.packt.com/images/610/picture_610.jpg",

   "media_type": "image",

   "title": "Your Picture",

   "url": "https://api.packt.com/images/610/picture_610.jpg"

  }

```

In today's API-driven world, APIs have been built into everything to make leveraging services
and accessing data over networks easy. Payment services offer payment APIs, map services
offer mapping APIs, e-commerce platforms provide APIs that support shopping and inventory
management, and social media platforms offer APIs that enable developers to interact with
them.

Because APIs are so ubiquitous and play critical roles in modern applications, many threat
actors focus on attacking APIs. The categories of attacks include the following:

   - **Exploiting vulnerabilities** : We **d** iscussed vulnerabilities and their exploitation in
detail in _Chapters 3, Industry Vulnerability Disclosure Trends_ and _4, Product Vulnerability_

295 _Application Programming Interface Security_

_Disclosure Trends_ . In 2025, there were more than 48,500 vulnerability disclosures across
the entire industry, equivalent to 133 new vulnerability disclosures per day on average.
Many of these vulnerabilities were in APIs. We'll spend some time later in the chapter
looking at the most common types of vulnerabilities in APIs.

**Abuse of functionality** : This **i** nvolves threat actors manipulating an API to perform an
action or return data it was never intended to provide. Attackers probe APIs to learn
about the business logic they support and then devise ways of abusing the APIs. Recall
the "data breach via an insecure API" example attack we discussed in _Chapter 1, How_
_Enterprises Get Hacked_ . In this example, the attacker queried an API repeatedly,
increasing the customer ID by 1 each time. This allowed them to get unauthorized
access to customer account data. To do this, the attacker had to figure out the length
and format of customer account numbers and study how the API worked. The attacker
also took advantage of the lack of query rate limiting on the API, which allowed
thousands of queries for different accounts from the same small group of systems –
unlikely behavior of legitimate customers.

**Access violations** : Managing authentication and authorization for APIs from so many
possible devices and types of identities is a challenge many developers struggle with.
Threat actors will take advantage of weaknesses in APIs' authentication and
authorization controls if given the opportunity. Properly implemented authentication
and authorization mechanisms are critical for API designs and implementations. I'll
discuss authentication and authorization in detail later in this chapter.

**Denial of service (DoS)** : If threat actors can consume all the resources on the server
hosting an API or all the network bandwidth of the connection to the server, legitimate
API transactions will fail. If attackers can deny service to legitimate API transactions for
long enough, they can force the service offline and even demand a ransom from the
victim to restore service.

**Operational threats** : For years, the IT environments of many big enterprises have
deployed large numbers of APIs ungoverned. Large enterprises rarely have full and
accurate inventories of all the APIs they use. This makes it much harder to understand
where sensitive data flows are occurring or to properly manage vulnerabilities in APIs.
Over time, some APIs are abandoned as their owners change roles or when teams are
reorganized. Documentation is lost; inventories begin to allow technical debt and risk
to accumulate. Forgotten APIs can sit exposed on the external internet-facing attack
surfaces of enterprises for years before anyone notices and decommissions them.
Additionally, shadow IT plagues big enterprises, which leads to shadow APIs. These are
undocumented APIs created and used without IT's knowledge. All these issues give an

_Chapter 7_ 296

advantage to attackers who are not encumbered by their victims' lack of management
discipline.

We'll take a deeper look at each of these categories of threats and how they can be mitigated in
the remainder of this chapter. If you don't recall the "data breach via an insecure API" example
attack I provided in _Chapter 1_, I suggest that you review it now as I'll be referencing it in this
chapter.

First, let's look at the web application and API threat landscape to understand how often
attacks on APIs happen and what some of their impacts are. This will give you an idea of both
the probability and impact sides of the risk equation regarding API threats. When your
stakeholders ask why they should care about API security, you should be able to give them an
answer based on data instead of just opinion.
###### **The web application and API threat landscape**

Let's get a sense of how often APIs are attacked. Akamai's _State of Web and API Security 2025_
report gives us several insights. One insight is that attacks are happening at a massive scale
and increasing:

_applications — Akamai observed more than 311 billion web application and API_
_attacks in 2024 alone, representing a 33% year-over-year increase. This surge_
_correlates directly with the accelerated adoption of cloud services, microservices_
_architectures, and artificial intelligence (AI)–powered applications." (Akamai, State_
_of Apps and API Security 2025, Vol. 11, Issue 02, 2025)_

These are a few other insights from Akamai's _State of Web and API Security 2025_ report (Akamai,
State of Apps and API Security 2025, Vol. 11, Issue 02, 2025):

33% increase in global web attacks year over year

The most impacted industry, based on Akamai's data, was commerce organizations,
with more than 230 billion attacks in 2025

The number of Layer 7 DDoS attacks that targeted organizations in North America was
11.9 trillion between Q1 2023 and Q4 2024

Cloudflare's 2024 _API Security & Management Report_ also contains data that helps us
understand the nature of attacks on APIs. Here are some key findings from their report
(Cloudflare, 2024):

Successful API requests accounted for over half (57%) of dynamic HTTP traffic on the
