There are some conclusions that I think we can draw from these insights. First, APIs are critical
to web applications, given that more than half of the dynamic HTTP traffic on the internet is
API traffic. One major cloud provider observed more than 311 billion attacks on web
applications and APIs in 2024. That's an average of more than 850,000,000 attacks per day. If
we extrapolate this data by assuming that the number of attacks observed by other major
cloud providers is similar, the number of attacks each year on web applications and APIs is
certainly several hundred billion, if not more.

These numbers could grow even more as generative AI services continue to expand the use and
creation of APIs. Almost all of these attacks are from authenticated sources, and most of them
are on internet-facing APIs. Attackers have been primarily using techniques reflected in the
OWASP API Security Project, which we will examine in this chapter. This means that although
the number of attacks is huge, the majority of them should be mitigatable.

However, this isn't as easy as putting your web applications behind a firewall or **web**
**application firewall** ( **WAF** ). The data suggests that 20% of attacks are not reflected in
OWASP's current list of top API vulnerabilities. 20% of such a huge number of attacks must
also be mitigated. Identifying, protecting, detecting, and responding to threats against your
organization's APIs will require the same effort it takes to do so for web applications.
Application security starts with the development process, so let's discuss that next.

_Chapter 7_ 298

###### **The security development lifecycle**

I had the opportunity to work closely with the **Security Development Lifecycle** ( **SDL** ) team at
Microsoft for several years, where I learned a lot about this approach to development. The SDL
was mandated at Microsoft after devastating worm attacks in 2003 and 2004, including SQL
Slammer and MSBlaster. Teams that develop code at Microsoft for enterprise customers are
required to meet the requirements of the SDL. This includes web applications and APIs.

The objectives of the SDL are straightforward:

Reduce the number of vulnerabilities in Microsoft products

Reduce the severity of vulnerabilities in Microsoft products

Make vulnerabilities in Microsoft products difficult or impossible to exploit

The SDL is a set of practices and supporting tools designed to achieve these objectives. The SDL
can be applied regardless of whether you are developing software using a traditional waterfall
approach or a more modern DevOps methodology. It can also help with developing more
secure applications and APIs across platforms such as on-premises IT environments, cloud,
hybrid infrastructures, and mobile platforms.

The example Microsoft provides has a four-stage development process underpinned by Zero
Trust architecture and governance principles. The four stages illustrated in _Figure 7.2_ are as
follows (Microsoft, n.d.):

1.

2.

3.

4.

**Design** : The design should prevent attackers from easily getting unauthorized access

**Code** : Develop code in a way that prevents attackers from taking unauthorized actions
or accessing data

**Build and deploy** : Secure **continuous integration and continuous deployment** ( **CI/**
**CD** ) processes to prevent unauthorized changes to the code

**Run** : Security best practices should be adopted across the platforms where the code
runs, including on-premises IT environments, cloud, hybrid, and mobile

_Figure 7.2 – Microsoft's four-stage development process (Microsoft, n.d.)_

299 _Application Programming Interface Security_

These stages of development should follow Zero Trust principles, including the following
(Microsoft, n.d.):

**Assume breach** : The system will be compromised at some point, so plan for that
eventuality.

**Explicitly verify trust** : Don't assume trusted relationships. Reauthenticate parties for
every action and verify authorization.

**Embrace the principle of least privilege** : Assign only the minimum privileges to
identities required for any operation.

There are 10 key practices that integrate security into the development process (Microsoft,
n.d.):

Establish security standards, metrics, and governance

Require the use of proven security features, languages, and frameworks

Perform security design review and threat modeling

Define and use cryptography standards

Secure the software supply chain

Secure the engineering environment

Perform security testing

Ensure operational platform security

Implement security monitoring and response

Provide security training

Microsoft provides details on each of these practices at `[https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/securityengineering/sdl/practices)`

`[securityengineering/sdl/practices](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/securityengineering/sdl/practices)` . I recommend that you take the time to review each
practice in detail. Next, I'll highlight a few of these practices that I think have particularly high
security return on investment for web applications and APIs.

**Privacy by design**

Some development teams spend time thoroughly thinking about security **f** or their applications
and APIs. But privacy is often overlooked, as it was in the "data breach via an insecure API"
example attack I discussed in _Chapter 1_ . In my experience, the lack of understanding and focus
on privacy considerations during development projects is widespread, and as data breaches
around the world have illustrated, it's a challenge for development teams everywhere. I
examine privacy in more detail in _Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in_
_Cybersecurity_ . Let's discuss privacy by design here, in the context of API development, because
it could help many developers avoid self-inflicted data breaches that can't be mitigated using
traditional IT infrastructure, such as firewalls or WAFs.

_Chapter 7_ 300

One of the organizations that helped formalize this approach describes privacy by design this
way:

_"Privacy by Design is a methodology for proactively embedding privacy into_
_information technology, business practices, and networked infrastructures. The_
_Privacy by Design measures are designed to anticipate and prevent privacy invasive_
_events before they occur." (Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario,_
_January 2018)_

Privacy by design espouses seven principles (Information and Privacy Commissioner of
Ontario, January 2018). Let's look at what these principles are:

**Proactive not reactive** : Prevent problems before they occur. Don't wait for attackers to
point issues out to you. Proactively anticipate data breaches involving sensitive data
and try to prevent them.

**Privacy as the default setting** : System users shouldn't have to take any actions, such
as opting in, for their privacy to be protected. Privacy controls should be turned on by
default.

**Privacy embedded into design** : Design and configure systems with privacy in mind
from the outset. Avoid designing systems and then attempting to add privacy controls
and related configurations after the fact.

**Full functionality** : It's not about privacy versus security. Instead of focusing on
privacy and security trade-offs, look for ways that users can get both.

**End-to-end security** : Data should be protected during its entire life cycle, so plan
accordingly and embed the appropriate security measures to accomplish this.

**Visibility and transparency** : Transparency helps build trust with users and other
stakeholders. Leverage open privacy standards and plan to provide third-party
attestations that the system is designed and operated in accordance with those
standards.

**Respect for user privacy** : Turn privacy controls on by default and provide users with
appropriate notice when privacy-related controls change or other material changes to
the system are implemented that impact users' privacy. In short, keep it user-centric.

As you can see from the principles, embedding privacy considerations into the development
process doesn't necessarily require more resources or longer schedules. Developers need to be
educated on these principles and trained in the development practices that help them to align
with them. A little effort here can result in an outsized return on investment for data
protection.

301 _Application Programming Interface Security_

One of the key practices of Microsoft's SDL is "Establish security standards, metrics, and
governance." Microsoft describes this practice as follows:

_"This practice focuses on continually updating and communicating security_
_requirements to reflect changes in functionality and to the regulatory and threat_
_landscape._

_Clear guidance and rules are required to guide team members (product line leaders,_
_product owners, developers, operations, and other roles) through what they need to_
_do for security, how success is measured, and what resources are available to help_
_them._

_The need to consider security and privacy is a fundamental aspect of developing_
_highly secure applications and systems and regardless of development methodology_
_being used. Security requirements must be continually updated to reflect changes in_
_required functionality and changes to the threat landscape." (Microsoft, n.d.)_

Next, let's look at another practice that typically provides high security return on investment
and helps organizations identify avoidable cybersecurity issues – threat modeling.

**Threat modeling**

Another SDL key practice I want to highlight for you is "Perform security design review and
threat modeling." Microsoft describes this practice as follows:

_"Threat modeling and security design reviews of threat models identify potential_
_security threats so that designers can mitigate them early in the development_
_process, resulting in systems that are Secure by Design. Adding security during the_
_design process is much cheaper and less risky than adding it after the_
_fact." (Microsoft, n.d.)_

Threat models help developers determine which security features and functionality their
specific application requires. Without a threat model, developers are left to arbitrarily decide
where to add appropriate security protection for the data flowing through their systems. For
example, a threat model helps developers determine where they need to implement encryption
for data at rest and data in transit. Without a threat model, developers might implement such
protections at points in their application where they are not necessary or not implement

**a** ppropriate security controls where they are necessary. For example, without a threat model,
developers might decide to forgo authentication for low-value transactions to streamline
users' experiences. This might be an appropriate trade-off when considering the
confidentiality of the data, but they also need to consider potential impacts on the integrity of
the data. Good threat models contemplate different types of threats to the systems they are
associated with.

_Chapter 7_ 302

There are at least a few different threat-modeling frameworks available to leverage, including
PASTA, LINDDUN, OCTAVE, and VAST. The framework I've used the most is **STRIDE**, which
was the framework developed at Microsoft when I worked there. STRIDE stands for the
following:

**Spoofing** : Impersonating someone or pretending to be something to interact with the
system for illegitimate purposes. For example, an attacker sends a login request
impersonating a legitimate user by forging their authentication token.

**Tampering** : Changing the system for illegitimate purposes, typically without
authorization. For example, a threat actor makes a change to a configuration file to
disable logging to avoid detection during an intrusion.

**Repudiation** : Allows an entity, such as a user, to deny that they were responsible for
making a change to the system, a transaction, or an event. For example, a user deletes
audit logs and later plausibly denies it because the system lacks authentication and
non-repudiation controls.

**Information disclosure** : Making the system disclose data that it was not intended to.
For example, an attacker is able to access confidential data by providing non-secret,
easily guessable inputs to the system, such as phone numbers.

**Denial of service** : Abusing system resources to deny legitimate use or operation. For
example, an attacker floods an API endpoint with excessive requests, exhausting
system resources and preventing legitimate users from accessing the service.

**Elevation of privilege** : An unprivileged user gains privileged access to the system that
enables unauthorized actions on the system. For example, a low-privileged user
exploits a flawed access control check to gain administrative rights and performs
actions reserved for administrators.

Developing a threat model generally requires the application to develop data flow diagrams
first. So many development teams I've worked with over the years didn't take the time to
develop detailed data flow diagrams or threat models before they started writing code. Data
flow diagrams are like the blueprints of a system and illustrate how the developers envision
data flowing through the system, including computing resources, storage, databases, and
networks. A level 1 or level 2 data flow diagram typically has enough detail to develop a threat
model for the system.

With data flow diagrams in hand, a threat model will take a short period of time (hours) to
develop if the right people with knowledge of the system's design participate. System
architects who have knowledge of the system's design, including storage, databases, network,
and computing resources, working with developers and cybersecurity subject matter experts,
can typically develop a threat model efficiently.

303 _Application Programming Interface Security_

With a data flow diagram, the threat-modeling process involves identifying the trust
boundaries between processes in the diagram. _Figure 7.3_ illustrates how authentication
boundaries are added to a simple data flow diagram. Then, the STRIDE framework is applied to
each of those boundaries to identify potential threats to the system. Context is important as
not every threat will be relevant to every part of the system.

_Figure 7.3 – An example of a threat model developed from a simple data flow diagram_

For each threat **i** dentified, a corresponding mitigation or a list of potential mitigations should
be developed. A list of potential mitigations gives the development team options on how to
mitigate the threats identified and informs the design choices they make and the code they
write.

Without a threat model, development teams tend to develop systems that meet functional
specifications but are largely uninformed by threats to the system. Traditionally, if a postdevelopment penetration test uncovered unmitigated threats, development teams would
either go back and fix them or seek policy exceptions that preserved these risks to the system,
usually until they were exploited. This is the most expensive and highest-risk approach to
development, but also the most popular in my experience. Spending the few hours it typically
takes to develop a threat model almost always has a high security return on investment.

_Chapter 7_ 304

Microsoft offers a free Threat Modeling Tool to make threat modeling even easier; the
tool is available at `[https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool)`

`[develop/threat-modeling-tool](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool)` .

Even with a threat model, typically not all threats identified get mitigated during the
development of large complex systems. Real trade-offs between risks, schedules, budgets,
customer expectations, the competitive nature of organizations' industries, and other factors
exist. If development teams are making risk-based decisions, they ultimately decide whether
to mitigate each identified risk, transfer it to another party, such as a cyber-insurance
company, or accept it. This is where a cybersecurity risk register can be important for CISOs
and security teams. Let's discuss this next.

**Cybersecurity risk register**

A cybersecurity risk register **i** s a tool that security teams can use to track **c** ybersecurity risks,
their severity, who owns each risk, and dates for any planned threat mitigations. Recording the
risk acceptance and risk transfer decisions in the cybersecurity risk register (a document, a
spreadsheet, or a risk register tool) provides formal documentation of what each risk is, who
accepted or transferred the risk, and any future mitigation plans.

If the risk is realized in the future, the cybersecurity risk register keeps the organization honest
with itself and prevents stakeholders from pretending that the organization didn't know about
the risks before they were exploited. It also helps CISOs avoid becoming scapegoats for risks
that development teams and other executives had knowingly accepted on behalf of the entire
organization, its boards of directors, and its shareholders. CISOs who review their
cybersecurity risk register with their senior stakeholders periodically can insulate themselves
from the "blame game" that ensues at many organizations when their stakeholders' risk
choices are realized. For some organizations, leveraging a formal risk acceptance form that
explains the risk and is signed by the risk owner is necessary to ensure everyone has the same
understanding of the risk and its potential impact on the organization. Later, if the risk is
realized, signed risk acceptance forms ensure everyone remembers the risk the same way.

A cybersecurity risk register also provides helpful context on each risk treatment decision,
which can otherwise be lost as personnel changes over time. CISOs shouldn't rely on tribal
knowledge for risk management. Recording the risks in a cybersecurity register, sharing it, and
reviewing it with senior stakeholders periodically is strongly recommended. Share these risks
often enough that the most severe risks in the register aren't surprises to senior stakeholders
when they see them.

305 _Application Programming Interface Security_

Some organizations have an enterprise risk register that captures risks to the entire enterprise.
These risks include economic, financial, and legal risks, among others. Cybersecurity is likely in
this register too. However, the altitude of enterprise risks tends to be much higher level than
the granular security risks, such as risks to specific IT systems. For this reason, I recommend
using a separate risk register to track the treatment of more granular security-related risks.

**Security training**

The final SDL practice I'll highlight is training. Organizations can't expect developers and
architects to simply possess innate knowledge of cybersecurity threats and mitigations or risk
management. They don't all need to be subject matter experts, but they do all need to
understand the basics, as well as how the organization's SDL process works. Developing a
repeatable process that improves itself over time and training development teams to use this
process is key.

For organizations that are in hyper-competitive industries that need to move as fast as
possible, such as high tech or finance, the key is to train as many people as possible. The
traditional friction in the development process isn't security professionals pointing out
security threats or design deficiencies that need attention; it's untrained developers and
architects constantly pushing back on the notion that security threats exist. These threats
exist, clearly. We have decades of data on cyber-attacks that is undeniable. As entertaining as it
is to see smart developers assert that they are omniscient, this is what slows development
teams down.

Training as many people as possible on your organization's SDL will minimize the friction and
allow them to embed security into every phase of development. When organizations do this
successfully, they can develop software as quickly as their resources allow them to. Securityrelated processes won't slow them down because they are baked into the software
development process. Program managers and project managers will be able to more accurately
plan the time it takes for software to make it through the entire development process. Security
will be integrated into the schedule because it is built into the process, not added at the end.
The key is to train people to stop objecting to doing basic security-related work and simply
follow the organization's SDL process as the only way to release software. The more people
who understand the process for releasing software, the more efficient it becomes. Greater
awareness and adherence to the process reduces the likelihood of expensive, untreated security
vulnerabilities and issues making their way into production.

Unfortunately, training isn't a one-time activity. As development tools and threats evolve,
development teams must evolve with them. Training during onboarding and conducting
annual refreshers are common practices I've seen in the industry.

_Chapter 7_ 306

There are numerous options for security training for development teams, including training
from Avatao, Black Duck, Immersive, SANS Institute, Secure Code Warrior, SecureFlag,
Microsoft, and Google.

I've only scratched the surface here.

Now that I've addressed how important the SDL, privacy concerns, threat modeling, a risk
register, and training are to API security, let's shift focus and talk about the specific
vulnerabilities that APIs suffer from and how to mitigate them.
###### **OWASP API Security Top 10**

OWASP is an international non-profit foundation that focuses on software security. OWASP
projects are open source and managed by communities of volunteer members. There are many
OWASP projects, including OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks, OWASP GenAI
Security Project, OWASP Mobile Application Security, and OWASP Software Assurance
Maturity Model, to name a few. The OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks has become
an invaluable resource to application security teams and cybersecurity teams around the world
who use it to identify and remediate code-level security issues, as well as monitoring and
blocking related attacks on web applications.

The OWASP project most relevant to our discussion in this chapter is the **OWASP API Security**
**Project** . OWASP typically publishes updated Top 10 lists every two or three years. OWASP
published the second edition of the OWASP API Security Top 10 in mid-2023, called OWASP
API Security Project 2023. It describes the top 10 list as follows:

_"API Specific Risks_

_The list is built to address security risks that are more specific to APIs._

_It does not imply that other generic application security risks don't exist in API based_
_applications. For example, we didn't include risks such as "Vulnerable and Outdated_
_Components" or "Injection", even though you might find them in API based_
_applications. These risks are generic, they don't behave differently in APIs, nor [sic]_
_their exploitation is different._

307 _Application Programming Interface Security_

_Our goal is to increase the awareness of security risks that deserve special attention_
_in APIs." (OWASP, 2023)_

This Top 10 list is comprised of the following risks (OWASP, 2023):

API1:2023 – Broken Object Level Authorization

API2:2023 – Broken Authentication

API3:2023 – Broken Object Property Level Authorization

API4:2023 – Unrestricted Resource Consumption

API5:2023 – Broken Function Level Authorization

API6:2023 – Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows

API7:2023 – Server Side Request Forgery

API8:2023 – Security Misconfiguration

API9:2023 – Improper Inventory Management

API10:2023 – Unsafe Consumption of APIs

Development teams can use this Top 10 list to learn about the common mistakes that
developers make that create security risks and avoid them. Cybersecurity teams can use this
Top 10 list to inform the types of web application and API attacks to monitor and block. Entire
books have been written on OWASP Top 10 lists, and OWASP provides a lot of guidance on
their website, so I won't try to duplicate that work in this chapter. But let's look at the top two
risks in detail to give you insight into what they are and how to mitigate them.

**Broken object-level authorization**

According to OWASP, this API vulnerability is "extremely" common, thus it sits in the top spot
on the Top 10 list.

Let's start with an example. An employee wants to check their work schedule for the week
using their employer's web application. The employee installs their employer's app on their
mobile device so they can check their work schedule from any place, at any time. The
application also stores users' personal information, such as their full name, address, phone
number, Social Security number, and banking information. Employees can use the application
to change this information when they need to and make scheduling requests. When the
employee starts the app on their mobile device, it prompts them for a username and password
to log in. The app then sends an API request to the scheduling web application running on
their employer's web server. The request contains the employee's employee ID so that the
application can look up their schedule and share it with them.

_Chapter 7_ 308

This application seems simple enough, but let's see how attackers can use broken object-level
authorization to get unauthorized access to data.

**How do attackers use this type of vulnerability?**

In this example, the web application running on the employer's web server accepts a request
via an API from the employee's mobile device, with the "object ID" set to the employee's
employee ID in the request. The web application uses that object ID to query a backend
database for the schedule associated with that employee ID and then returns the schedule to
the user's mobile app that requested it.

The issue here is that the application didn't first check whether the user using the mobile app
was authorized to access the schedule for that particular employee. That is, the application
didn't perform object-level authorization – the developers assumed that since the user had a
valid username and password, any API request from their mobile app would be valid and
authorized. In other words, the web application running on the employer's web server would
happily process any API request for any employee's schedule, as long as the user was
authenticated and the API request had a properly formatted object ID.

The risk is that an attacker who has access to one compromised user account for the
application can manipulate the object IDs in API requests to get access to all employees'
schedules. This type of attack is typically easy to perpetrate, especially when object IDs sent in
API requests, in this case, employee IDs, are predictable. It wouldn't be difficult to predict
employee IDs if they were all six digits long and issued in sequential order. An attacker with
access to a compromised account could send a series of API requests incrementing the object
ID by 1. Every time the object ID turns out to be a valid employee ID, the API will return the
schedule for that employee to the **a** ttacker. Recall that this is exactly how the data breach via
the insecure API happened in the scenario I described in _Chapter 1_ .

Once attackers have fine-tuned the API request for their attack, they can choose to exfiltrate
data from the insecure API very quickly or take a "low-and-slow" approach to minimize the
chances of their illicit activity being detected and shut down. In such attacks, attackers might
choose to exfiltrate data, or they could alter or delete it if the API allows it. Attacks on the
integrity of data can be challenging to detect and recover from. This type of vulnerability could
also enable the full takeover of impacted accounts, depending on the application.

You might wonder how the attacker got access to a compromised account in the first place.
Remember, attackers typically gain initial access via the cybersecurity usual suspects. In this
case, the attacker could have used social engineering, such as a smishing text message, to trick
the user into disclosing their username and password. Or the user could have used the same
password as they do for all their online accounts, and it has ended up on the large lists of
compromised credentials from past breaches that attackers have accumulated. This

309 _Application Programming Interface Security_

dramatically increases the odds that attackers' password-spray attacks on the employer's web
server will be successful. The attacker could be a disgruntled employee who has turned into an
insider threat and sold their credentials to attackers or is perpetrating attacks themselves.

In my experience, when security teams flag this type of vulnerability for development teams
before it is exploited, developers typically have two naive retorts as they resist the
recommendation to fix their code:

" _No one would do that type of attack_ "

" _Attackers wouldn't have the expertise to do that_ "

However, there are reasons this type of vulnerability tops OWASP's Top 10 list – it's common
and easy to exploit, making it popular with attackers. Next, I'll provide some guidance on how
to prevent a broken object-level authorization vulnerability.

**Mitigation**

The following non-exhaustive list contains some of the ways that broken object-level
authorization vulnerabilities and related attacks can be mitigated:

**Implement proper authorization** : Applications should have authorization
mechanisms that enable the application to check whether users are authorized to
perform actions.

**Authorization checks** : Every time an authenticated user attempts to perform some
action in the application, the authorization mechanism should be used to check
whether the user has permission to do so. Don't simply assume that since the user was
authenticated or authorization was previously checked, the user is authorized to
perform the action they are attempting, for example.

**Least privilege** : Ruthlessly apply the principle of least privilege by ensuring every user
has only the privileges to perform the functions required. To do this, every new user
account should have the absolute least privileges in the application, and more
privileges should be granted to those accounts as needed. This means the so-called
"birthrights" of applications' users are designed with security in mind, not to minimize
work for application administrators. **Role-based access control** ( **RBAC** ) is a
mechanism that makes this easy for application administrators.

**Avoid predictable values** : Don't use easy-to-predict or incremental values such as
employee IDs or phone numbers in API requests; use **globally unique identifiers**
( **GUIDs** ) instead.

**Constantly test security assumptions** : Don't "set and forget" this control. If your
development teams are constantly updating their applications, test to ensure that the
authorization mechanisms in applications are working as expected in production. This

_Chapter 7_ 310

minimizes the time between an update that inadvertently breaks the authorization and
its detection and remediation. Don't wait until there's a security incident to discover
the issue.

**Enforce multi-factor authentication** ( **MFA** ): The key to this attack was that the
attacker was able to use a compromised account to send API requests. Enforcing
phishing-resistant MFA on all user accounts makes this harder. It also provides
mathematically provable non-repudiation for insiders who perpetrate this type of
attack.

**API motherhood and apple pie** : Always have API request monitoring and rate limiting
configured. This won't stop this type of attack, but it will potentially slow it down and
help operations and security teams detect it early. API management platforms offer

rich sets of such capabilities.

Next, let's look at broken authentication vulnerabilities.

**Broken authentication**

This is #2 on the OWASP API Security Top 10 list. Like broken object-level authentication,
which we discussed earlier, this type of vulnerability is common and relatively easy to exploit.
Broken **a** uthentication is a vulnerability category that includes several different vulnerabilities,
any of which can help attackers gain complete control of users' accounts, exfiltrate their
account information, and perform actions while impersonating them. The key is for developers
and operations staff to implement controls that make it harder for attackers to attack the
authentication mechanisms their applications rely on.

**How do attackers use this type of vulnerability?**

Attackers leverage a range of tactics to attack the authentication mechanisms that applications
rely on, including the following:

**Guess weak passwords** : Applications that allow users to set easily guessed passwords
make it easy for attackers to compromise accounts.

311 _Application Programming Interface Security_

**Use default credentials** : Attackers compromise administrator accounts using default
credentials that vendors release with their applications, and their customers don't
change in production – for example, username "admin" and password "admin."

**Brute-force attacks** : The application allows attackers to continually guess the
password for a single account until a valid password is discovered. This type of attack is
typically automated.

**Credential-stuffing attacks** : The application allows attackers to use username and
password pairs in continual login attempts until a valid username and password are
found. This type of attack is typically automated. Massive lists of vulnerabilities, such
as valid usernames and passwords from past breaches, are available on the internet for
this purpose. This attack can be especially effective when users use the same
passwords across multiple applications and internet services because attackers get
valid passwords to all of them when one of them is breached.

**Attack password reset mechanism** : The application doesn't confirm the current
password before allowing users to change the current password, email addresses, and
other mechanisms used to reset account passwords.

**Exposed sensitive authentication details** : Applications that send user authentication
details (tokens and passwords) in URLs make it easy for attackers to find and leverage
this information to take over accounts.

**Weak protection for authentication secrets** : Applications that leverage unencrypted,
plaintext passwords or weak encryption keys can enable unauthorized access to
applications.

**Token validation issues** : Attackers take advantage of applications that don't validate
the authenticity of tokens or their expiration dates or accept unsigned tokens.

This list is not exhaustive. There are many other tactics that attackers can use to overcome
poorly implemented authentication mechanisms. These are likely the most common attacks
on applications and systems. Remember the old saying: " _attackers don't break in, they log in_ ."
This is why broken authentication is #2 on OWASP's Top 10 list. Given this, let's discuss some
of the ways to mitigate this type of vulnerability and some of the associated attacks.

**Mitigation**

The following non-exhaustive list provides several ways to mitigate broken authentication
vulnerabilities and attacks that use them:

Start by cataloging the authentication flows for your APIs. You have a better chance of
success if you know all the ways API authentications happen, including web and
mobile. Catalog the mechanisms each API leverages for authentication.

_Chapter 7_ 312

Developers shouldn't develop their own authentication mechanisms – use industrystandard mechanisms. This practice prevents well-intentioned developers from
unwittingly introducing new vulnerabilities into their authentication processes and
allows them to invest their time in other areas that have not already benefited from
decades of industry rigor.

User accounts should be protected by MFA so that even if their passwords are known
by attackers, they can't access user accounts without also possessing the other factors.

Always have API query monitoring and rate limiting configured. This won't stop these
types of attacks, but it will potentially slow them down and help operations teams and
security teams detect them early. API management platforms offer rich sets of such
capabilities.

Consider using "advanced bot" protection offered by WAF vendors to detect and blunt
password-spraying and brute-force attacks. These services typically leverage
algorithms that detect and blunt automated attacks from botnets and attackers'
malicious infrastructures.

Passwords cannot be relied on to protect enterprises' data and systems by themselves,
but if your application uses them, ensure it enforces long (15 characters), complex
passwords, and does not allow the use of known compromised passwords or variants
of old passwords.

I used to believe that account lockout mechanisms to slow down brute-force and passwordspray attacks weren't needed if 15-character passwords were enforced. Mathematics tells us
that attackers shouldn't be able to guess a password that long in any useful period of time. But
it turns out that attackers have all sorts of shortcuts to dramatically reduce the amount of time
required to derive users' passwords. Attackers have access to huge networks of systems with
GPUs optimized for password-cracking calculations in the cloud. This enables them to crack
the weakest passwords in stolen Active Directories ( `ntds.dit` files) within minutes.

Predictable human behavior that leads some users to use the same passwords across internet
services, reuse old passwords, or use simple variants of old passwords gives attackers a big
head start in guessing their current passwords. Those huge lists of compromised passwords
available on the internet, combined with other tools, such as _cracklib_ and _passwdqc_, will likely
enable attackers to overcome traditional assumptions about password strength for some
subset of user accounts. Subsequently, I recommend enforcing account lockouts for a short
duration after a small number of failed login attempts, as this will introduce friction into these
attacks.

313 _Application Programming Interface Security_

I hope this dive into broken authentication and broken object-level authorization gave you a
taste for the types of vulnerabilities APIs commonly have and the attacks that target them. Visit
OWASP's website to learn more about the OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks and access more
resources: `[https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/)` .
###### **Summary**

This chapter examined API security through a CISO and enterprise risk lens, emphasizing why
APIs have become one of the most critical, and most targeted, components of modern digital
systems. It introduced APIs, explained how web APIs function, and highlighted how their
ubiquity, scale, and complexity make them a prime attack surface for threat actors.

A central theme of this chapter was that you cannot bolt on API security after deployment.
Instead, it must be embedded throughout the SDL, with strong alignment to Zero Trust
principles, including assume breach, explicit verification, and least privilege. Key development
practices such as privacy by design, threat modeling, security training, and the use of a
cybersecurity risk register were presented as high-return investments that help organizations
prevent self-inflicted vulnerabilities and manage unavoidable risks transparently.

We explored the API threat landscape, using recent industry data to show the scale, frequency,
and nature of attacks against web applications and APIs. A key takeaway is that most API
attacks exploit well-known weaknesses, not novel techniques, making them largely
preventable with disciplined engineering and governance.

Finally, the chapter introduced the OWASP API Security Top 10, with a deeper dive into broken
object-level authorization and broken authentication, the two most common and impactful
API vulnerabilities. Through concrete examples, the chapter illustrated how these flaws are
exploited and provided practical mitigation guidance that development, security, and
operations teams can apply immediately.

In the next chapter, we'll examine what some CISOs and cybersecurity teams consider a
cybersecurity threat – governments.
