# 8
##### Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity

I spent most of the preceding chapters of this book examining different types of cybersecurity
threats in detail. These threats include vulnerabilities in software and hardware, malware such
as Trojans and worms, various types of ransomware extortion schemes, internet-based threats
such as phishing **a** nd **Distributed-Denial-of-Service** ( **DDoS** ) attacks, and attacks on
**Application Programming Interfaces** ( **APIs** ) and web applications. CISOs and security teams
manage their cybersecurity programs to measure and mitigate all of these threats. However,
many CISOs and security teams also focus on one other type of cybersecurity threat—
governments.

In this context, in the US, CISOs and security teams tend to focus on nation-state threat actors,
sponsored by governments such as the **People's Republic of China** ( **PRC** ), the Russian

_Chapter 8_ 318

Federation, the Islamic Republic of Iran, and the **Democratic People's Republic of Korea**
( **DPRK** ).

However, outside the US, some organizations view certain US government legal and
intelligence authorities as presenting cybersecurity-related risks. CISOs of these organizations
aren't typically worried about the risk of US government-sponsored threat actors attacking
them the way they are with the PRC or DPRK. However, many organizations outside the US
perceive US legal authorities—such as warrants, subpoenas, **National Security Letters**
( **NSLs** ), **Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act** ( **FISA** ) court orders, and the **Clarifying Lawful**
**Overseas Use of Data** ( **CLOUD** ) Act—as mechanisms that can compel access to sensitive data
under certain circumstances. This has led to a proliferation of regulations in the **European**
**Union** ( **EU** ) and other countries that seek to control the flow of their data outside their
borders, including to and from the US. This has also led to US-based companies being fined
billions of dollars for insufficient compliance with EU regulations.

In this chapter, I'll explain the roles that governments play in cybersecurity and why they are
viewed as threats by many organizations. I'll describe the cybersecurity tension that exists
between the US and the EU, drawing on my experience working as a cybersecurity advisor at
both Microsoft **a** nd **Amazon Web Services** ( **AWS** ). During the years that I lived in Europe, I
had thousands of conversations with representatives of governments and European-based
firms about cybersecurity, regulatory compliance, data residency, data sovereignty, the
PATRIOT Act, the CLOUD Act, and other related topics. From these conversations, I learned a
lot about the European perspective on privacy. This is central to understanding why the US
government's legal and intelligence authorities are considered to present cybersecurity-related
risks by so many organizations outside the US. I'll also offer some guidance to CISOs who seek
to protect their organization's data from the threat that governments pose.

Before we dig into these super interesting topics, let me provide a little background on my
exposure to them.

**Background information**

In my career, among other experiences, I have been fortunate enough to work as one of the
most senior cybersecurity advisors at both Microsoft and AWS. I led teams of cybersecurity
advisors at both of these companies. In these roles, I met with literally thousands of
organizations all over the world. I learned so much through these discussions.

When I worked as Microsoft's global chief security advisor, I traveled the world meeting with
CISOs and security teams to give threat intelligence briefings and discuss how we could help
their cybersecurity programs. I would spend weeks at a time in Europe, Africa, Asia, and South
America. I also hosted the CISOs of Microsoft's biggest accounts at Microsoft headquarters in
Redmond, Washington. I learned so much from spending time with these people and listening

319 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

to how they thought about threats, risk, mitigations, and cybersecurity. Many of the things I
learned from them have informed my own thinking about cybersecurity. The collective
wisdom of these CISOs has been incredible.

Initially, I spent most of my time with private sector customers who were focused on
protecting company data, assets, and, ultimately, their shareholders' value. Then I started
meeting more and more public sector organizations and learned that their challenges were a
lot more complex and arguably more important than developing products and services for
markets, creating meaningful brands, maximizing profit, and driving growth. Some examples
of public sector challenges include issues related to elections, taxation, education, food supply
chain safety, and national defense.

When I joined AWS as their worldwide public sector security and compliance leader for
**Europe, the Middle East, and Africa** ( **EMEA** ), my family and I moved to London, UK. In this
role, my full-time job was advising federal and provincial/state governments, pan-European
institutions, national security agencies, healthcare and educational institutions, non-profit
organizations, federal banks, and other public sector verticals across EMEA. Over the next two
and a half years, I traveled to two or three cities a week in EMEA to meet with public sector
organizations to discuss cybersecurity. I spent a lot of time in cities that were the centers of
government for their countries or regions, such as London, Paris, Brussels, The Hague, Berlin,
Stockholm, Helsinki, and Bern. Later, I relocated back to AWS headquarters in Seattle,
Washington, where I worked as AWS' worldwide public sector security and compliance leader.
I led a geographically dispersed team that worked with governments in Asia, Oceania, South
America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Canada, and the US.

In the next role I had in my career, as vice president of trust and cyber risk at T-Mobile, I had
the opportunity to serve as a member of the president of the United States' **National Security**
**Telecommunications Advisory Committee** ( **NSTAC** ). The subcommittee was tasked with
developing recommendations for the president on improving national cybersecurity. We
developed a report for President Biden focused on incentivizing and measuring the adoption of
cybersecurity best practices among critical infrastructure providers. I had the opportunity to
work with luminaries and senior leaders from across the cybersecurity industry, including the
**Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency** ( **CISA** ). It was an amazing experience.

One of the things I learned from all these conversations is that governments play a myriad of
roles in cybersecurity. CISOs and security teams cannot simply treat all governments as threats
because they rely on them for many things.

_Chapter 8_ 320

standards, while others looked to governments as a source of threat intelligence,
guidance, and protection; yet other CISOs viewed governments as threats to their
organizations.

What role do governments really play in cybersecurity? After thousands of conversations with
private and public sector organizations around the world about cybersecurity, I thought I'd
share some insights that might help answer this question.

The following topics will be covered in this chapter:

The roles governments play in cybersecurity

Governments as cybersecurity threats

The threat of lawful government access to data

###### **The roles governments play in cybersecurity**

Most federal, state, provincial, and large municipal governments organize themselves into
departments, divisions, agencies, ministries, and other organizational units. These different
parts of each government help them function by dividing roles and responsibilities among
them.

It is important to be aware that some parts of a government might pursue their agendas in
ways that potentially conflict with other parts of the government. For example, an agency with
some responsibility for public safety might participate in industry efforts to reduce
vulnerabilities in software and drive awareness among consumers to keep their systems up to
date. Driving down the number of vulnerabilities in the products that consumers use and
keeping consumers' systems patched means less criminal exploitation of citizens, less crime
for law enforcement to manage, fewer criminal cases in the courts, less associated costs to
society, and so on. But in another part of the same government that has some responsibility for
national security, they are proactively trying to discover new vulnerabilities and buy new
vulnerabilities from other security researchers. Instead of reporting vulnerabilities to the
vendors that can fix them, like the public safety agency and the industry both recommend,
some government agencies have acknowledged retaining undisclosed software vulnerabilities
for intelligence or national security purposes, a practice that has generated ongoing public
policy debate. It is important to recognize that both of these contrasting agendas are important
and support citizens' pursuit of happiness.

Although it might seem innocuous, referring to a government as a simple, single entity instead
of a group of individual departments or ministries with different, sometimes conflicting
charters often leads to some overly simplistic conclusions in a cybersecurity context. In my

321 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

experience, this tended to be especially true of statements made about the US government by
security professionals outside the US. Once they deemed "the US government" to be a threat to
their organization, that simplistic thinking meant that every government department and
every private sector firm doing business with the government was suspect at best. It was guilt
by association—software, hardware, cloud services, and encryption technologies—all
suddenly became untrustworthy simply because the entire US government was labeled as
untrustworthy and a threat. I had this conversation with so many CISOs in EMEA. I'll dive into
this topic in more detail later in this chapter.

Let's take a closer look at some of the roles that governments play in cybersecurity.

**Governments as cybersecurity market participants**

The economies of most countries rely on governments as major sources of spending and
employment. Governments require IT and cybersecurity. All government departments and
agencies must have the people, processes, and technologies required to forward their charters
and to protect, detect, respond to, and recover from modern-day threats. To do this, they must
procure a lot of the same technologies as companies operating in the private sector. The
combination of these factors typically gives governments immense purchasing power.

While governments procure lots of technologies and cybersecurity capabilities, they also
require technical expertise to develop, deploy, and operate these capabilities. Governments are
major employers of IT and cybersecurity professionals and compete with the commercial
sector for professional talent.

Since governments' purchasing power is quite significant, they typically require their supply
chain partners to comply with specific standards. Let's examine governments' roles as
standards bodies next.

**Governments as standards bodies**

Because governments procure so many goods and services, it is important that they set and
maintain standards to ensure measurable minimum levels of functionality and quality in their
procurements. Sometimes governments accomplish this through formal standards bodies, and
sometimes formal standards bodies aren't involved. Although governments are not formal
standards development organizations, they often act as _de facto_ standard setters by embedding
technical requirements into procurement contracts and then reinforcing them through
regulation. In cybersecurity, this happens when governments require vendors to meet specific
security baselines, such as standardized incident reporting, supply chain controls, or maturity
certifications, as a condition of selling to the state. In some cases, they use acquisition rules
such as the US **Federal Acquisition Regulation** ( **FAR** ) to make those requirements mandatory
across agencies. Because governments are among the largest buyers of technology, these
procurement requirements effectively set market-wide norms, pushing private companies to

_Chapter 8_ 322

adopt the same cybersecurity practices even outside government contracts. Over time,
regulatory follow-through and enforcement further solidify these requirements into widely
accepted "standards," even when they did not originate in a traditional standards
organization.

Many CISOs and security teams rely on the **National Institute of Standards and Technology**
( **NIST** ) for cybersecurity standards. NIST is a non-regulatory federal science agency within the
US Department of Commerce. NIST operates as a bureau of the Department of Commerce and
is led by a director, who is appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate. It is
primarily funded through congressional appropriations as part of the Department of
Commerce budget.

This is how NIST **d** escribes cybersecurity standards:

_"The goal of cyber security standards is to improve the security of information_
_technology (IT) systems, networks, and critical infrastructures. A cyber security_
_standard defines both functional and assurance requirements within a product,_
_system, process, or technology environment. Well-developed cyber security standards_
_enable consistency among product developers and serve as a reliable metric for_
_purchasing security products." (Scarfone, K., Benigni, D., and Grance, T., 2009)_

Most of the CISOs I advised over the years typically used NIST cybersecurity standards in at
least three ways:

First, if their organization did business with the US federal government or aspired to,
they would select one or more NIST standards that were applicable to the product or
service they wanted to sell, and work to comply with the requirements of those
standards.

Many CISOs leveraged NIST standards to ensure their security control sets were
complete. They would compare the controls implemented in their IT estates and their
settings to NIST standards to ensure that they didn't have obvious gaps. NIST **Special**
**Publication** ( **SP** ) 800-53 is an example of a standard (control catalog) used in this
manner. Security teams take their current control set, which includes technical
controls, policies, procedures, and operational practices, and map them to the relevant
SP 800-53 controls. NIST supports this exercise by publishing the control catalog in
spreadsheet and machine-readable formats, explicitly to enable comparison, mapping,
and analysis. Once this mapping is complete, CISOs review unmapped or weakly
mapped controls to identify obvious gaps in coverage.

323 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

Some organizations take this one step further and use compliance with standards as
their enterprise cybersecurity strategy. I'll discuss this strategy, what I call "compliance
as a security strategy," in detail in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity Strategies_ .

CISOs also use NIST standards to prove that they are managing their security programs
in a way that complies with stringent US government cybersecurity standards, whether
they do business with the US government or not. If these CISOs experienced a data
breach, they could point to their NIST standards compliance as evidence that they
weren't an outlier and that they were managing their cybersecurity program
responsibly and in alignment with others in the industry. This could help blunt the
potential negative reputational and financial damage and regulatory outcomes that
accompany data breaches so often today.

Of course, the US government isn't the only government that publishes cybersecurity
standards. This is a good place to insert a joke for geeks: "The good thing about standards is
that there are so many to choose from" (Tanenbaum, Andrew S. n.d.). Governments in other
countries besides the US also have bodies that publish cybersecurity standards for
organizations in their regions and their supply chain partners. A great example is the **Federal**
**Office of Information Security** (known as the **BSI** ) in Germany. I had the opportunity to meet
with representatives of the BSI a few times over the years. Germany is the single largest market
in the EU. This means that the standards published by the BSI are very influential in Germany
and the EU. Subsequently, big global technology providers such as Microsoft and AWS, among
others, as well as technology providers based in Western Europe, pay close attention to the
guidance and standards that the BSI publishes. The BSI describes their mission this way:

_"We assume responsibility for all issues related to information security. We protect_
_the federal administration from cyber attacks and monitor the current cyber security_
_situation nationally and internationally, investigate and assess existing security_
_risks and anticipate the impact of new developments. Based on this knowledge, we_
_support citizens, companies and authorities at federal, state and municipality level_
_with services in the core areas of information, consulting, operational protection and_
_development, including standardisation [sic] and certification." (BSI, n.d.)_

Most large, developed countries have some office or agency responsible for developing
cybersecurity standards for their national government's use or more broadly across industries
within their borders. However, in many cases, I've found that they are similar to NIST SP
800-53. This is another reason why so many of the CISOs I know adopt NIST SP 800-53 as the
standard they try to conform to.

Next, let's examine governments' role as enforcers.

_Chapter 8_ 324

**Governments as enforcers**

Governments provide at least two different functions in their role as enforcers, in a
cybersecurity context—regulators and law enforcement. Let's briefly look at both functions.

**Regulators**

We just discussed governments as standards bodies. As we discussed, standards are important
not only for government procurement purposes but also for the broader markets. However, just
because a standards body publishes some standards, it doesn't necessarily mean that private
and public sector organizations will spend the time, effort, or budget to conform to those
standards. Typically, there must be some sort of clear benefit or incentive for organizations to
change the way they operate.

Sometimes, despite the right incentives, markets or industries are too slow to change by
themselves, and a "market failure" occurs. In cases such as this, governments use the tools they
have in their toolboxes; in the case of cybersecurity, this includes _regulation_ . Regulations
typically implement restrictions that industries must conform to. Examples of regulated
standards for cybersecurity purposes include the **California Consumer Privacy Act** ( **CCPA** ),
the **Federal Information Security Modernization Act** ( **FISMA** ) in the US, and the **General**
**Data Protection Regulation** ( **GDPR** ) in the EU and the **European Economic Area** ( **EEA** ). To
give you a sense of the teeth that the European Parliament put into GDPR, failure to comply
with it could result in a fine of up to €20 million or up to 4% of annual worldwide revenue,
whichever is larger. More than 2,600 administrative fines related to GDPR non-compliance
have been levied since enforcement started in 2018, the largest of which were given to large
high-tech companies such as Meta (€1.2 billion), Amazon (€746 million), and LinkedIn (€310
million) (GDPR Enforcement Tracker, n.d.). Avoiding these administrative fines is the incentive
for private and public sector organizations to comply with this regulation.

Ransomware is another area where regulation is changing market behavior. In the wake of the
Colonial Pipeline Company ransomware attack that shut down a pipeline system in the
Eastern US for several days in May 2021, calls for new regulation resulted. Here are some
examples of regulatory-related activity resulting from this one cyberattack:

The US **Federal Energy Regulatory Commission** ( **FERC** ) renewed calls for mandatory
cybersecurity standards for the US' pipeline infrastructure (Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission, 2021).

The US **Environmental Protection Agency** ( **EPA** ) issued a second emergency fuel
waiver meant to further alleviate fuel shortages in US states impacted by the pipeline
shutdown (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2021). This waived requirements for
low-volatility conventional gasoline and **Reformulated Gasoline** ( **RFG** ) in a dozen
states.

325 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

The Department of Homeland Security approved a temporary Jones Act waiver to ease
oil supply constraints in targeted parts of the US eastern seaboard (U.S. Department of
Homeland Security, 2021). This waiver enabled the transport of oil products between
the Gulf Coast and the East Coast of the US.

The US **Department of Transportation** ( **DOT** ) allowed states to use Interstate
highways to transport overweight loads of gasoline and other fuels, to help address
shortages (U.S. Department of Transportation, 2021).

The President of the United States signed an _Executive Order on Improving the Nation's_
_Cybersecurity_ (The White House, 2021). This executive order had a profound effect on
how the US federal government was expected to manage cybersecurity moving
forward, including all its suppliers in its supply chain.

Typically, a cyberattack on a US-based company would not result in this significant regulatory
activity. However, in this case, the convergence of a high-profile ransomware attack, a multimillion-dollar ransom demand that was paid potentially in violation of US Department of the
Treasury's **Office of Foreign Assets Control** ( **OFAC** ) regulations, an attack on a company in an
industry that was deemed US critical infrastructure, the interruption of nearly half the gas
supply in the Eastern seaboard of the US, and the attackers' location in Russia contributed to
this crescendo of government activity. At the core of all this activity was the uncertainty
around the attackers' motivation—was it simply profit or was it a state-sponsored attack?
Even after the attack was attributed to attackers in Russia using DarkSide ransomware, their
motivations were still suspect. As I mentioned in _Chapter 5_, _The Evolution of Malware_, the
attackers issued a statement to try to make their motivations clear and de-escalate the
situation.

Notice how some of the regulatory activity that resulted from this ransomware attack were
unintended consequences, easing or waiving regulatory restrictions to blunt the effects of the
attack. What if the opposite was also possible? What if attackers could use regulations to
attack their victims? For example, in a completely hypothetical scenario, suppose a criminal
noticed that a large, multi-national company was recording personal information of their
customers, which included residents of the EU, in an immutable blockchain ledger. Although
the company could have completely legitimate business reasons for doing this, the immutable
property of the database they chose to use makes it impossible for the company to delete
customer information if an EU-based customer requested it. Realizing that this misstep likely
violates GDPR, and it **c** ould cost the company tens of millions of dollars in administrative fines,
the criminal issues a ransom demand to the company in exchange for their promise not to file a
privacy complaint with a data protection authority in the EU. Interesting conundrum!

_Chapter 8_ 326

**Law enforcement**

The other function that governments perform in their role as enforcers is law enforcement.
Law enforcement is intended to deter crime by imposing consequences, such as arrest and
prosecution, that most people seek to avoid. However, just as the internet has leveled the
playing field for individuals and small businesses to compete with large enterprises, it has also
enabled crime at a scale and speed not previously possible. The internet allows individuals or
small groups to simultaneously target vast numbers of people, businesses, and institutions
with relative anonymity and low cost. This creates an unprecedented form of asymmetry,
where small numbers of attackers can impact far larger organizations across jurisdictions.
Traditional law enforcement mechanisms have proven far less effective as a deterrent to
cybercrime under these conditions, and this structural mismatch may be one of the
contributing factors.

AI makes this even easier for the criminally minded by reducing the technical skills they need
to perpetrate such attacks. An individual can perpetrate a large DDoS attack or a drive-by
download attack against very well-resourced organizations and be successful.

There are at least a few reasons why this is the case. First, the internet is a global network that
allows attackers to perpetrate their attacks from almost anywhere in the world against victims
located almost anywhere. Criminals have used borders to evade arrest and prosecution for
centuries, and the internet enables this on a vast scale. For example, given the current situation
with Russia invading Ukraine and all the sanctions placed on it, it is highly unlikely that Russia
will prioritize investigating cybercrimes against organizations in Western countries. The same
can be said for the DPRK (North Korea), Iran, and the PRC (China).

The second reason why traditional law enforcement has been a less effective deterrent to
serious cybercrime is the challenge of strong attribution. If victims don't know who is
attacking them, how can they determine what a proportional response is? Which government
(national, regional, or municipal) should help with the response, and which specific ministry,
department, or agency should lead? Is the attack a matter of national security where
intelligence agencies and the military should be involved or a criminal matter? If it is a criminal
matter, which law enforcement agencies should be involved—national police (such as the FBI
in the US), regional (state/provincial) police, or municipal police? Which jurisdiction should
lead the investigation—where the victims are located, where the attack originated from, or
where it is suspected that the attackers are based?

Still, if law enforcement doesn't make a serious effort to investigate, arrest, and prosecute
cybercriminals, then there really is no deterrent at all. Of course, law enforcement in most
major countries takes cybercrimes very seriously because of the consequences for victims, their
communities, industry, and society.

327 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

In the US, several federal agencies have authority to bring cybercrime-related law enforcement
actions, including the **Federal Bureau of Investigation** ( **FBI** ), the **Securities and Exchange**
**Commission** ( **SEC** ), the Secret Service, the US Attorney's Office, the **Internal Revenue Service**
( **IRS** ), the **Federal Trade Commission** ( **FTC** ), and US **Immigration and Customs**
**Enforcement** ( **ICE** ). Because of the scale of the problem, none of these organizations can
investigate all cybercrimes where US citizens are victimized. The FBI has published some
guidelines for the voluntary sharing of cyber-incident information between **State, Local,**
**Tribal, and Territorial** ( **SLTT** ) law enforcement organizations and the US federal
government; these guidelines provide insight into the types of incidents that the FBI is willing
to engage in:

_"In particular, a cyber incident should be reported if it:_

_May impact national security, economic security, or public health and safety._

_Affects core government or critical infrastructure functions._

_Results in a significant loss of data, system availability, or control of systems._

_Involves a large number of victims._

_Indicates unauthorized access to, or malicious software present on, critical_
_information technology systems._

_Violates federal or SLTT law." (US Federal Bureau of Investigation, n.d.)_

The FBI's guidelines further note that "no matter which 'door' SLTT law enforcement uses,
information is shared within the federal government to provide an appropriate response while
protecting citizens' privacy and civil liberties under the law" (US Federal Bureau of
Investigation, n.d.).

In 2020, the FBI discussed a new strategy to fight cybercrime that would "impose risk and
consequences on cyber adversaries" (Wray, C. 2020). They further stated the following:

_"We've got to change the cost-benefit calculus of criminals and nation-states who_
_believe they can compromise U.S. networks, steal U.S. financial and intellectual_
_property, and hold our critical infrastructure at risk, all without incurring any risk_
_themselves…" (Wray, C. 2020)_

The pillars of this strategy include the following (US Federal Bureau of Investigation, n.d.):

   - **Unique authorities** : Leverage both criminal and counterintelligence authorities to
fight cyber-criminals and foreign threat actors to compromise US networks

_Chapter 8_ 328

**World-class capabilities** : Adapt to cyber-threats by leveraging new, innovative
investigative techniques, developing new tools, and recruiting a world-class workforce

**Enduring partnerships** : Leverage the FBI's strengths to enable their partners to
defend systems, perform attribution, impose sanctions on threat actors, and pursue
adversaries overseas

Of course, other major countries also have ministries, departments, and agencies involved in
law enforcement action resulting from cybercrimes. Most of the governments I advised had
multiple agencies that shared the responsibility of investigating and responding to
cybercrimes. Sometimes it was obvious that there were disagreements between agencies
regarding jurisdictions and the scope of their various cyber operations.

Consequently, the way in which governments organize themselves to fight cybercrime is also
new and evolving. In my experience, it was rare to find a federal or regional law enforcement
organization or regulatory authority that wasn't trying to position itself to be more relevant in
the fight against cybercrime, especially when new government agencies were being created for
this specific purpose. Some open questions in many of these cases seemed to be, are new
agencies needed because the old institutions aren't effective at fighting cybercrime? Do new
approaches to crime require new approaches to law enforcement? How does AI change this?
The answers to these questions are likely to continue to play out well into the future.

I realize I have barely scratched the surface of this subject, and I haven't discussed law
enforcement as a potential cyber-threat yet. I'll discuss this later in this chapter. If you view
governments, and law enforcement more specifically, as a cyber-threat, keep reading!

Next, let's look at governments as defenders.

**Governments as defenders**

The White House published a National Cybersecurity Strategy in March 2023. This strategy
outlines how the federal government, together with its allies and partners, will build a "digital
ecosystem together, making it more easily and inherently defensible, resilient, and aligned
with our values" (The White House, March 2023). The strategy outlines five pillars that include
the following:

Defend critical infrastructure

Disrupt and dismantle threat actors

Shape market forces to drive security and resilience

Invest in a resilient future

Forge international partnerships to pursue shared goals

The strategy states that "criminal syndicates now represent a threat to the nation security,
public safety, and economic prosperity of the United States and its allies and partners" (The

329 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

White House, March 2023). Let's look at three of the functions that governments provide when
playing the role of defender in a cybersecurity context: **public safety**, **national security**, and
**military** .

**Public safety**

Most major national governments have a department or ministry that is responsible for public
safety. Sometimes, public safety is a subset of the work a government department does. Over
the past 25 years, many countries have created national cybersecurity centers that include
public safety, among other things, in their charters. Examples include the **National Cyber**
**Security Centre** ( **NCSC** ) in the UK, the **National Cyber Security Centre of Ireland** ( **NCSC** ),
the **French National Cybersecurity Agency** ( **ANSSI** ), the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security,
the **Cyber Security Agency** ( **CSA** ) of Singapore, the Australian Cyber Security Centre, and CISA
in the US. All of these government organizations are at least in part responsible for driving
awareness of cybercrime and related threats among government departments, industries, and
citizens. Some of them also provide cybersecurity advisory services to government
departments to help protect critical infrastructure. Some of these organizations are responsible
for managing incident response processes and managing **Cyber Threat Intelligence** ( **CTI** )
programs for government departments. Some of these centers were created by merging parts
of **National Computer Emergency Response Teams** ( **CERTs** ), large government departments
with cybersecurity charters, law enforcement, and intelligence agencies together. The
combination of the capabilities that these stakeholder organizations bring together is much
greater than any of them could develop only by themselves. Typically, the one function they
lack within their departments is enforcement, which they partner with law enforcement
agencies to perform.

Additionally, most of these cybersecurity centers offer educational opportunities to public and
private sector organizations and to citizens. The idea here is that a better-educated society will
be able to recognize cyberattacks more readily, report them, and hopefully help mitigate them.
I had the opportunity to attend some of these events, such as the UK NCSC's CYBERUK security
event.

**National security**

Another function governments fulfill in their role as defenders is national security. I've found
this to be a loaded term that means different things to different people. Governments have
been gathering intelligence and practicing military espionage to understand their adversaries'
and allies' military capabilities for as long as governments have existed. Today, this includes
both cyber-offensive and cybersecurity capabilities.

Intelligence gathering is typically a function of national security organizations. Since military
secrets are highly classified, they are typically protected using encryption and key management
technologies and processes. Therefore, intelligence agencies also have deep expertise in signals

_Chapter 8_ 330

intelligence (gathering intelligence by intercepting signals between systems) and
cryptography, so they might intercept and access classified information that they otherwise
would not have access to, as well as protect their own governments' information more
effectively.

Here's how the US **National Security Agency** ( **NSA** ) describes their mission:

_"The National Security Agency/Central Security Service (NSA/CSS) leads the U.S._
_Government in cryptology that encompasses both signals intelligence (SIGINT)_
_insights and cybersecurity products and services and enables computer network_
_operations to gain a decisive advantage for the nation and our allies." (National_
_Security Agency, n.d.)_

The NSA also provides combat support for the US military and its allies. We discussed
governments as standards bodies earlier in the chapter. The NSA is another example of this, as
they "set common protocols and standards so that our military can securely share information
with our allies, NATO and coalition forces around the world. Interoperability is a key to
successful joint operations and exercises" (National Security Agency, n.d.).

The NSA also focuses on cybersecurity:

_"NSA Cybersecurity prevents and eradicates threats to U.S. national security_
_systems, with an initial focus on the Defense Industrial Base (DIB) and the_
_improvement of the nation's weapons' security. At its core, NSA Cybersecurity aims_
_to defeat the adversary through the seven core missions and functions:_

_- Provide intelligence to warn of malicious cyber threats and information U.S._
_Government (USG) policy_

_- Develop integrated Nuclear Command & Control Systems threat, vulnerability,_
_risk, and cryptographic products & services_

_- Release integrated threat, assessment, and mitigation/protection products for the_
_Department of Defense (DoD) and USG customers_

_- Execute high-assurance cryptography and security engineering_

_- Offer combined defense/offence operations with key government partners_

_- Enable the defense of the agency's networks in coordination with NSA's Chief_
_Information Officer_

_- Promote information sharing to support the agency's cybersecurity mission"_

331 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

_(National Security Agency, n.d.)_

Of course, other countries have organizations dedicated to national security as well. In the UK,
domestic intelligence and foreign intelligence services are provided by **Military Intelligence,**
**Section 5** ( **MI5** ) and **Military Intelligence, Section 6** ( **MI6** ), respectively. There are numerous
other stakeholders and participants, including **Government Communications Headquarters**
( **GCHQ** ), the NCSC, and the Home Office.

In Canada, national security organizations include the **Canadian Security Intelligence**
**Service** ( **CSIS** ), the **Royal Canadian Mounted Police** ( **RCMP** ), the **Communications Security**
**Establishment** ( **CSE** ), and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, among others.

The Israeli Intelligence Corps has Unit 8200. This is said to have a similar charter as the NSA in
the US, specializing in **Signals Intelligence** ( **SIGINT** ). Many former Unit 8200 members have
gone on to establish successful cybersecurity start-ups and to lead major companies.

There are also international partnerships that focus on the national security of partner
countries. A great example of this type of organization **i** s the **Five Eyes** . This is an alliance
between Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK, and the US, focusing on intelligence sharing
(Office of the Director of National Intelligence, n.d.). The idea here is that sharing intelligence
across five countries provides these governments with better visibility of potential threats.

One of the reasons governments have national security intelligence programs is to provide
their military forces with information needed to deter war and defend their borders and their
allies. Let's discuss this function next.

**Military**

The US **Department of Defense** ( **DoD** ), is the largest agency in the US government and the

largest employer in the world, employing over 1.3 million people on active duty and 742,000
civilian personnel (US Department of Defense, n.d.). The president requested a $849.8 billion
budget for the DoD in 2025 (Office of the Under Secretary of Defense (Comptroller)/Chief
Financial Officer, March 2024). The armed forces of the US include the Army, Marine Corps,
Navy, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard. There are two reserve components—the Army
National Guard and the Air National Guard. The stated mission of the DoD is to "provide the
military forces needed to deter war and ensure our nation's security." This includes both

_Chapter 8_ 332

offensive and defensive aspects of cybersecurity. With so many people, DoD performs a myriad
of cybersecurity functions.

For example, **USCYBERCOM** is a unified **Combatant Command** ( **CCMD** ) of the DoD. It is
responsible for coordinating military operations involving computer networks and digital
infrastructure to defend DoD networks, support military missions, and protect US national
interests from cyber threats. The DoD has 11 of these unified CCMDs organized around
geographic locations or around specific functions. Cyber is one of those functions.
USCYBERCOM is called a "joint command" because it is composed of several parts of the
armed forces, including the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marines. The NSA is also a partner in
this joint command. The DoD's vision for USCYBERCOM is as follows:

_"Achieve and maintain superiority in the cyberspace domain to influence adversary_
_behavior, deliver strategic and operational advantages for the Joint Force, and_
_defend and advance our national interests." (United States Cyber Command, April_
_2018)_

USCYBERCOM's strategy paper _Achieve and Maintain Cyberspace Superiority Command - Vision_
_for US Cyber Command_ really is a great read. It is very well written and describes the
cybersecurity challenge through a military lens. I think the following two excerpts from this
paper summarize their strategy. The first excerpt describes USCYBERCOM's view of the
challenge that adversaries pose:

_"The security of the United States and our allies depends on international stability_
_and global prosperity. The spread of technology and communications has enabled_
_new means of influence and coercion. Adversaries continuously operate against us_
_below the threshold of armed conflict. In this 'new normal,' our adversaries are_
_extending their influence without resorting to physical aggression. They provoke and_
_intimidate our citizens and enterprises without fear of legal or military_
_consequences. They understand the constraints under which the United States_
_chooses to operate in cyberspace, including our traditionally high threshold for_
_response to adversary activity. They use this insight to exploit our dependencies and_
_vulnerabilities in cyberspace and use our systems, processes, and values against us to_
_weaken our democratic institutions and gain economic, diplomatic, and military_
_advantages…Aggressive non-state actors like terrorists, criminals, and hacktivists_
_pose lesser threats than states but can still damage our military capabilities and_
_critical infrastructure, as well as endanger American lives." (United States Cyber_
_Command, April 2018)_

This second excerpt from the paper focuses on how USCYBERCOM operates to address these
cyber threats to the US:

333 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

_"Superiority through persistence seizes and maintains the initiative in cyberspace by_
_continuously engaging and contesting adversaries and causing them uncertainty_
_wherever they maneuver. It describes how we operate—maneuvering seamlessly_
_between defense and offense across the interconnected battlespace. It describes where_
_we operate—globally, as close as possible to adversaries and their operations. It_
_describes when we operate—continuously, shaping the battlespace. It describes why_
_we operate––to create operational advantage for us while denying the same to our_
_adversaries…Through persistent action and competing more effectively below the_
_level of armed conflict, we can influence the calculations of our adversaries, deter_
_aggression, and clarify the distinction between acceptable and unacceptable_
_behavior in cyberspace. Our goal is to improve the security and stability of_
_cyberspace. This approach will complement the efforts of other agencies to preserve_
_our interests and protect our values. We measure success by our ability to increase_
_options for decision makers and by the reduction of adversary aggression." (United_
_States Cyber Command, April 2018)_

Of course, the US isn't the only military force in the world that has been developing offensive
and defensive capabilities. In 2013, cybersecurity firm Mandiant publicly attributed a series of
cyber-intrusions affecting US organizations to a group it identified as Unit 61398 of China's
**People's Liberation Army** ( **PLA** ), based on its analysis (CBS News, 2013). In 2014, the US
Department of Justice indicted five members of Unit 61398 on charges related to intellectual
property theft.

Unit 61398 is believed to be just one of many such PLA groups in China that focus on
cybersecurity capabilities. Military units of various other countries allegedly conducting cyber
operations have popped up in news feeds ever since. The DPRK (North Korea) and Iran are two
such examples.

I hope that provides a little insight into some of the ways that some countries are leveraging
their military forces for cybersecurity purposes. When viewed through this lens, it becomes
obvious that governments have developed and are using offensive cyber capabilities as part of
their national defense strategies.

Now that we've discussed the roles governments play, this makes conversations about
governments as threats potentially much more productive. I've found that when security
teams can articulate specific threats, only then can specific mitigations be developed with
confidence. A cyberattack by the US military is quite a different risk than a law enforcement
agency serving an organization with a search warrant. Getting specific about the threats and
risks you really need to be concerned with helps you better prioritize resources and avoid
investing in mitigating risks that are ridiculously vague or improbable.

_Chapter 8_ 334

Next, I'll dive into the two specific government cybersecurity threats that I discussed with
CISOs most often: **nation-state threat actors** and **lawful government access to data** . Note
that I'll be discussing legal concepts and mechanisms, regulations, and laws in this section of
the chapter.

###### **Governments as cybersecurity threats**

Governments weren't always viewed as cybersecurity threats by CISOs. However, 2013 was a
turning point. Two widely publicized events happened during that year.

First, in February 2013, Mandiant published the aforementioned report that identified Unit
61398 of the PLA as the source of hundreds of cyberattacks on US companies (CBS News, 2013).
Mandiant labeled the group **APT1**, short for **Advanced Persistent Threat 1** . They attributed
cyberattacks to APT1 going as far back as 2006. They even published pictures of the building
they alleged this group worked in, in Shanghai. Mandiant's report stated that APT1 had stolen
hundreds of terabytes of data from 141 of the organizations they had attacked between 2006
and 2013 (Mandiant, Feb 1, 2013). APT1 maintained access to their victims' networks once they
had it. The report states the following:

_"…we found that APT1 maintained access to the victim's network for an average of_
_356 days. The longest time period APT1 maintained access to a victim's network was_
_at least 1,764 days, or four years and ten months. APT1 was not continuously active_
_on a daily basis during this time period; however, in the vast majority of cases we_
_observed, APT1 continued to commit data theft as long as they had access to the_
_network." (Mandiant, Feb 1, 2013)_

335 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

Another dramatic event occurred in June 2013. At the time, I worked at Microsoft as the
director of trustworthy computing. In those days, customers typically wanted threat
intelligence briefings from me, and to discuss threats to their Windows system networks, but
that all changed in June 2013. That's when Edward Snowden gave a trove of classified
documents to journalists that revealed details about some of the US government's intelligencegathering programs. After the first news stories were published, a global news cycle ensued.
Predictably, numerous large international public and private sector organizations were
suddenly interested in whether their data was safe in the hands of technology companies that
were based in the US. At that time, the underlying question from international customers was
whether US-based companies were obligated to give US intelligence agencies whatever data
they wanted. Since then, many other details of US intelligence agencies' activities have come to
light, and questions about the role of US-based technology firms in these activities have
continued for years.

Fast-forward four or five years, and I was working for AWS, based in London, in the UK. My job
was to advise public sector organizations on how to modernize their cybersecurity strategies
and show them how cloud computing can help. One topic that public sector organizations
across Europe and the Middle East wanted to talk about was government access to data, more
specifically, US government access to data.

Meanwhile, when I'd go back to the US and talk to customers and colleagues there, they were
largely unaware of the debate that had been going on in Europe about the trustworthiness of
US technology providers. They simply didn't think that the US' closest allies in Europe would
be concerned about using their tech products and services. After all, the US' position as the
dominant technology innovation leader in the world meant that they would follow **World**
**Trade Organization** ( **WTO** ) trade rules and never steal intellectual property from other
countries in the way that China was accused of doing. If they crossed that line, they would
have more to lose than any other country in the world. What was the big deal?

Until I lived in London and talked to European-based companies and public sector
organizations every day, I too hadn't fully realized the extent to which the trustworthiness of
the US had been severely tarnished. I came to learn about the collective consciousness among

_Chapter 8_ 336

Western Europeans that resulted from the cumulative impact of a series of revelations about
US intelligence agencies' operations in Europe. Let me give you some examples:

Classified documents leaked by Edward Snowden triggered a series of news cycles
revealing the scope and scale of some US intelligence-gathering programs. The White
House initially defended these programs but later apologized for their overreach
(Gidda, 2013).

Documents disclosed by Edward Snowden and subsequently reported by journalists
prompted widespread scrutiny and criticism of US intelligence surveillance programs,
including their scope and oversight (Ball, 2013).

WikiLeaks published a series of classified reports that they called "Espionnage Élysée."
The reports revealed that the NSA had allegedly intercepted the communications of
three different French presidents, cabinet ministers, and the French ambassador to the
US (James Regan, 2015). WikiLeaks also alleged that "the US has had a decade-long
policy of economic espionage against France, including the interception of all French
corporate contracts and negotiations valued at more than $200 million" (WikiLeaks,
2015).

WikiLeaks published a series of classified documents that they called "Euro Intercepts"
that alleged the NSA had intercepted the communications of senior German
government officials, including the German chancellor at the time, Angela Merkel, her
senior staff, as well as staff of former chancellors going back almost two decades.
According to WikiLeaks, "WikiLeaks so far shows the NSA explicitly targeted for longterm surveillance 125 phone numbers for top German officials and did so for political
and economic reasons, according to its own designations" (WikiLeaks, 2015).

These revelations, and others, damaged the relationship the US had with their European allies.
Unfortunately, this is not limited to Europe; Brazil (WikiLeaks, 2015) and Japan (WikiLeaks,
2015) are two other examples. For US technology companies caught in the middle, this
developed into a quagmire of distrust. Every time I walked into a meeting with a company or a
public sector organization in France, Germany, or Switzerland, I knew this collective
consciousness would be generating serious headwinds. Just how strong were those
headwinds? During some of the public events I spoke at, I'd survey audiences with a question
such as this:

Which one of these threats is your organization most concerned about? Select only one answer.

1.

2.

Attackers from China

Attackers from Russia

337 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

3.

4.

US government access to data using a valid warrant or subpoena

Other

In Western Europe, between 2017 and 2020, typically 80–90% of the people I surveyed
selected answer 3. If this surprises you, you probably live in the US. If you live in Germany,
France, or another location in the EU or the EEA, this likely will not surprise you at all.

The good news for CISOs, their security teams, compliance and risk management
professionals, and other executives is that these dramatic revelations have led to levels of
transparency that can help them quantify and manage the risk associated with government
access to data. I'll explain how to do this, but first, we need to unpack this issue a bit more
because typically, there are a lot of assumptions, generalizations, and misconceptions about it.
In fact, there are a few different scenarios that are typically conflated in conversations about
government access to data; these scenarios do not have the same risk (probability and impact)
for every organization.

Thinking about the US government as a single entity with a single agenda isn't accurate and
typically isn't helpful to CISOs, security teams, and executives who are serious about
understanding and mitigating risks to their organizations. In the thousands of conversations
I've had about governments as threats, many CISOs, security teams, and executives tended to
conflate three different scenarios. Let's look at each of them in depth.

**The signals intelligence scenario**

The SIGINT scenario **i** s where government agencies gather intelligence by intercepting and
analyzing communications and electronic signals, potentially employing cryptanalysis on
encrypted communications. SIGINT programs were the focus of many of the dramatic
WikiLeaks announcements. The reality is that this type of intelligence gathering is employed
by many major governments around the world (Wikipedia, n.d.). The US uses this type of
intelligence gathering to get visibility into its adversaries' evolving military capabilities
(National Security Agency Central Security Service, n.d.). Keep in mind that the US shares
intelligence with the other members of NATO and the Five Eyes SIGINT sharing alliance
(National Security Agency Central Security Service, n.d.).

Many of the executives I met expressed concern about the information leaked by WikiLeaks
because it suggests that some of the targets of SIGINT have been world leaders, their staff, and
the public at large via mass data collection programs. Getting them to put their personal
outrage aside and articulate how they plan to manage the risk that such programs pose to their
organizations was sometimes challenging.

_Chapter 8_ 338

Many executives told me that simply not using US-based technology providers was the way
they planned to mitigate this threat. Since these US intelligence programs, their objectives,
their targets, and their capabilities are all classified, managing such risks with so little
information can be challenging. However, choosing not to use US-based technology providers
would not mitigate the threat that these programs pose in any way because SIGINT doesn't
depend on its targets using technology that is designed, manufactured, or operated by USbased technology firms.

**Nation-state threat actors (unlawful government access to**
**data)**

Nation-state threat actors, also called state-sponsored threat actors, that perpetrate
cyberattacks are involved in unlawful government access to data. Microsoft offers this
definition:

_"Nation-state actor_

_A cyber threat actor sponsored or directed by a government, often targeting other_
_countries for espionage, disruption, or influence." (Microsoft, 2025)_

The US CISA provides this description:

_"As a nation, we are seeing continued cyber and physical threats targeting critical_
_infrastructure Americans rely on every day. Nation-state actors and nation-states_
_sponsored entitiespose [sic] an elevated threat to our national security. On the cyber_
_front these adversaries are known for their advanced persistent threat (APT)_
_activity:_

_The Chinese government—officially known as the People's Republic of China (PRC)_
_—engages in malicious cyber activities to pursue its national interests including_
_infiltrating critical infrastructure networks._

_The Iranian government—officially known as the Islamic Republic of Iran—has_
_exercised its increasingly sophisticated cyber capabilities to suppress certain social_
_and political activity, and to harm regional and international adversaries._

_The North Korean government—officially known as the Democratic People's_
_Republic of Korea (DPRK)—employs malicious cyber activity to collect intelligence,_
_conduct attacks, and generate revenue._

339 _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_

_The Russian government—officially known as the Russian Federation—engages in_
_malicious cyber activities to enable broad-scope cyber espionage, to suppress certain_
_social and political activity, to steal intellectual property, and to harm regional and_
_international adversaries." (CISA, n.d.)_

In this scenario, government agencies or their affiliates perpetrate cyberattacks to steal data
from organizations or their supply chain vendors, as opposed to obtaining a valid court order
to compel such information legally. Military and economic espionage are typical motivations
that are associated with this scenario. Foreign political influence and disinformation
campaigns are also employed in the pursuit of foreign policy objectives to confuse civilian
populations and destabilize governments. In the case of the DPRK (North Korea), it is widely
believed that they are using profits from ongoing cyberattacks to fund their nuclear weapons
program, among other things (NCC Group, June 30, 2022).

Stuxnet is widely attributed by researchers and media reports to the US and Israeli intelligence
agencies, though neither government has formally acknowledged involvement.

Various governments, security researchers, and courts have alleged that state-sponsored actors
linked to China have engaged in cyber-enabled economic espionage, including the
unauthorized acquisition of intellectual property. Of course, there are examples of other
countries allegedly performing acts of espionage as well; examples include France (Ewing,
2014), the United Arab Emirates (Christopher Bing, 2019), Saudi Arabia (Mark Mazzetti, 2019),
Israel (Mehul Srivastava, 2019), and Russia (US Department of Justice, June 28, 2010).

Microsoft has published data on the activities of the numerous nation-state threat actors it
tracks. According to Microsoft, in the 12 months between July 2020 and June 2021, the top
three countries most targeted by nation-state threat actors were the US, Ukraine, and the UK
(Microsoft, October 2021). The most targeted sectors during this time included government,
**Nongovernmental Organizations** ( **NGOs** ), a category called "other," and education. The top
targets changed slightly three years later, in the 12 months between July 2024 and June 2025,
which included the US, Israel, and Ukraine. The most targeted sectors during this period
included IT, research and academia, and government.

Let me break this data down a little further for you, using data published in the Microsoft
