The cloud offers the opportunity to modernize not only technologies and processes, but also
cybersecurity strategies that can be employed. Let's explore this concept a little further and
look at a more modern approach to cybersecurity that I mentioned in _Chapter 10_, called
DevOps.

_Chapter 13_ 634

**DevOps – a modern approach to security in the cloud**

For lack of a better name, let's simply call this approach DevOps. I've also heard some security
professionals refer to it as "immutable short-lived infrastructure" or simply as "re-paving".
This strategy represents a more modern approach compared to the other cybersecurity
strategies that we've examined. It recognizes that development and IT operations disciplines
have been joining forces, partly because, together, these roles are aptly positioned to take
advantage of the power of APIs and automation. Because everything is code in the cloud,
including infrastructure, teams that understand both development and IT infrastructure
operations can take full advantage of all the cloud has to offer. Let's look at some of the ways
that a DevOps-driven security strategy can help security teams protect, detect, and respond to
modern threats in cloud-based environments.

Remember in _Chapter 5_, _The Evolution of Malware_, where I described why the Windows
ecosystem has so much more malware than the Apple iOS ecosystem. The key, it would seem,
is how software has traditionally been distributed in these ecosystems. Microsoft allowed
software developed by anyone to be freely installed by its customers on their Windows-based
systems.

Apple, on the other hand, provides a single source for all applications destined for iOS-based
devices: their App Store. While Windows customers were left to make their own decisions
about the trustworthiness of the software they wanted to run, Apple imposed a security
standard for all ISVs to meet before their apps could be distributed to iOS-based devices. This
difference in software distribution methods, at least partially, explains why the Apple iOS
ecosystem has maintained such a low prevalence of malware.

Let's take this lesson and apply it to our approach to security in the cloud. Leveraging
continuous testing, **continuous integration (CI)**, and **continuous delivery or continuous**
**deployment (CD)** can help minimize the amount of questionable software that makes it into
the cloud-based environments that CSPs' customers build and operate. In their CI/CD
pipelines, they can impose automated (and manual) security and compliance checks. These
ensure that any software or infrastructure that gets deployed into production environments
through these pipelines meets their organizations' security and compliance requirements.

To do this, each step of the CI/CD pipeline will have the appropriate security and compliance
checks automated in it. For example, a DevOps team could develop or procure automation that
looks for issues contained in the OWASP Top 10 (OWASP, 2025). Another common example is
the requirement to perform static code analysis and/or a specific set of functional security
tests. Infrastructure will have to meet the control setting requirements defined by each
organization's compliance team, and this will be verified as items go through the pipeline.

635 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

Implementing such tests is typically done in code and automation, so the number and types of
checks that can be conducted are almost unlimited. Of course, because this can be effective and
fun, once some DevOps teams start developing these checks, they may spend more time on the
development of their CI/CD pipelines than on applications and infrastructure.

If an application or infrastructure item does not pass one of these checks, the pipeline will stop,
the appropriate staff may be alerted, the application or infrastructure will not progress
through the rest of the pipeline, and it will not be introduced into the production environment
as planned. The deficiency in the application or infrastructure item will have to be addressed in
order to pass the check that failed and then go through the entire pipeline again.

This way, only items that pass every security and compliance check in the pipeline will make it
into production. This means Security and Compliance teams can have high confidence that
everything being introduced into their production environment meets all their security and
compliance requirements and that they will not introduce more risks into that environment.
To accomplish this, everything must go through a CI/CD pipeline. Put another way, the only
way to get an application or infrastructure item into production is through a CI/CD pipeline.
For the best chance of success, organizations need to have discipline, as well as the governance
mechanisms, to enforce this requirement. Managing multiple CI/CD pipelines is a predictable
and common outcome, especially for large, distributed organizations. The risk for some
organizations is that the number of CI/CD pipelines proliferates to levels that begin to
compromise the high security and compliance standards that the initial pipelines imposed; too
many pipelines can turn into a governance issue.

Also, note that attackers have clued into the fact that most enterprises are using DevOps and
CI/CD pipelines. This makes the CI/CD pipelines themselves a potential target for attackers.
Understanding the stack of technologies and automations that your organization uses for its
pipelines and taking steps to protect them is important. For some organizations, CI/CD
pipelines can become high-value assets and warrant special attention, as I discussed in _Chapter_
_9_ .

Now that security and compliance teams have confidence in their deployments, how do they
keep those environments in that pristine condition over time? They can use the services and
automation we discussed earlier in this chapter to monitor configuration changes. When
configurations change, they can use automation to bring them back into compliance or initiate
deeper investigations into how and why they changed.

As we discussed earlier, there is a range of options for vulnerability management in the cloud.
Continuing to use the technologies and processes that your organization has used for years in
its on-premises environment is likely one possible option. But as we discussed in _Chapter 3_ and
_Chapter 4, Product Vulnerability Trends_, vulnerability volumes have become so large that even
well-resourced vulnerability management teams are under pressure.

_Chapter 13_ 636

However, using automation, like the Auto Scaling example I provided earlier, has the potential
to simplify and accelerate vulnerability management. Another option is for organizations to
evolve from managing servers and applications themselves to using cloud services higher up
the stack and leaving infrastructure patching to the CSPs. Of course, a combination of all of
these approaches is also permissible. However, if you are going to modernize processes,
technologies, and your strategy, I strongly recommend that you get out of the vulnerability
management game as much as you can. After all, the only way to win that game is not to play
it. Patch a relatively small number of images, not hundreds or thousands of running VMs, and
use managed services where it is possible to delegate vulnerability management to the CSPs.

One of the reasons that Attack-Centric strategies gained such popularity in the industry is that
they can make it hard for "advanced" threat actors to be successful—the so-called **APT** .
However, this is where the power of APIs and high levels of automation can also be helpful. For
example, when organizations thoughtfully shut down subsets of servers running in the cloud
every few hours and replace them with new ones that meet all requirements, it can make it
harder for attackers to get and maintain a foothold in that environment. Short-lived,
immutable systems can leave very little oxygen for attackers to use, unlike systems that remain
running for months or years.

The detection capabilities in the cloud are superior to those found in most on-premises
environments. Remember, the power of APIs and automation in the cloud provides visibility
and control that few on-premises environments can achieve. The cloud can make it easy to log
API calls, network traffic, authentication and authorization operations, encryption and
decryption key operations, and so on. However, one challenge most security teams share,
whether they use the cloud or not, is that the vast amount of data in all these logs makes it
nearly impossible for humans to review and use it in a timely way. This is where the cloud can
also help. AI and ML services can be used to review all of these logs and API activity, instead of
security team members, and identify things that really warrant human attention. This is
possible because AI/ML services can scale as large as needed to churn through enormous log
datasets far, far faster than humans can. As they do this, these services, with the help of
automation, can detect and respond to all sorts of attacks, including DDoS, malware,
exploitation of vulnerabilities, insider threat, and many more.

Let me summarize the characteristics of this strategy I call DevOps, sometimes referred to as
"immutable short-lived infrastructure," and sometimes simply referred to as "repaving":

Automation is used to provision and configure systems and other infrastructure.
Everything that gets released into production cloud accounts or environments must go
through a CI/CD pipeline.

The CI/CD pipeline can employ automated and manual security and compliance checks
and tests to ensure everything that makes it into production meets security and

637 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

compliance standards. If something doesn't meet standards, the pipeline stops and the
deficiencies are remediated.

Systems are designed to be immutable, that is, designed not to change while running in
production. Changes to immutable systems running in production are typically an
indicator of compromise. This makes threat detection easier and faster.

All changes are made to the image(s) that running instances are based on. This
includes scanning for and installing security updates. The images are scanned and
patched, not the running instances. This dramatically reduces the complexity and time
it takes to manage vulnerabilities on large numbers of systems.

To minimize insider threat opportunities, administrators have no direct administrator
access to systems running in production. SSH, RDP, and other remote access software
are prohibited from running on production systems. Administrators are limited to
running tested and pre-approved scripts on systems running in production, except
during break-glass scenarios, which are monitored and audited. MFA is used to
authenticate administrators to the cloud, where they can initiate execution of these
scripts.

Automation is used to thoughtfully shut down production systems every few hours in a
way that will not impact the availability of applications. Auto Scaling or other
automation will restart systems based on the fully patched image(s) as needed. This
reduces and limits the amount of time that compromised systems can be used by
attackers in the production environment. AWS offers a capability built into Auto
Scaling called Instance Refresh for this specific scenario.

Managed services are used to enhance detection and response capabilities instead of
deploying more servers to host security functions. This provides superior detection and
response capabilities and does not increase the attack surface or the number of systems
to manage.

Make use of ubiquitous encryption capabilities to protect data in the cloud and to
protect keys. I'll discuss this later in this chapter.

Note that although I've focused on using virtual machines in this strategy description, an
increasing number of organizations leverage containers and container orchestration software
in very similar ways to achieve better security.

Finally, if all these capabilities fail to protect, detect, and respond to attackers, DevOps and the
cloud can make recovering production environments much easier than in typical on-premises
environments. Since everything is code, rebuilding environments in the cloud can be relatively
easy if some planning and thoughtful preparation have been done. Let's take a quick look at
some **disaster recovery** ( **DR** ) capabilities in the cloud.

_Chapter 13_ 638

**Disaster recovery in the cloud**

As we discussed in _Chapter 5_, targeted attacks that involve extortion (also called ransomware
attacks) are commonplace today. Ransomware is a human-made disaster. Subsequently, most

of the CIOs, CISOs, and security teams I have talked to in the last few years are much more
interested in DR than ever before. In addition to the specter of ransomware, fear of an
increased frequency of extreme weather events due to climate change is also driving interest in
DR.

DR is "the process of providing fast, reliable recovery of IT systems to minimize downtime and
data loss" (Rains, 2022). The traditional approach to DR has led many organizations to build
physical datacenters with specific distances between them. If one datacenter is impacted by a
weather event, power disruption, or human-made disaster, the organization plans to resume
IT operations in another datacenter. The distance between datacenters is arbitrary in that there
is no industry standard—each organization makes its own calculations based on the types of
risks it is trying to mitigate. But generally, the larger the distance between the datacenters, the
less likely a single weather event, earthquake, fire, Internet, or power disruption will impact
them.

In the cloud, as I mentioned earlier, Regions and Availability Zones are used to design highly
available and resilient cloud infrastructures. The distance between datacenters in an
Availability Zone can be large enough to mitigate localized power outages and large-scale
weather events. For organizations that want even more assurance, they can use multiple
Regions and get the advantages of using even more Availability Zones that have greater
distances between them. For example, an organization could use a cloud Region located on the
West coast of the U.S. and plan to use a Region on the East coast for DR. The chances of a single
event disrupting operations on both sides of the country at the same time are very low. Many
large multinational firms use cloud Regions in different countries for various purposes,
including DR. For example, they might leverage a cloud Region on the East coast of the U.S. and
another Region in Ireland for DR purposes. Since there are so many Regions and Availability
Zones available, there are many different options for DR purposes. However, remember that
the speed of light is a constant. The further the distance between the datacenters, the more
network latency will become a limiting factor.

When I worked at AWS, I wrote a blog post about how AWS thinks about distances between
their datacenters and Availability Zones for DR purposes. If you are interested in reading it,
that blog post is titled "The Goldilocks zone for disaster recovery, business continuity
planning, and disaster preparedness." It is available at this URL: `[https://aws.amazon.com/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/publicsector/goldilocks-zone-disaster-recovery-business-continuity-planning-disaster-preparedness/)`

```

planning-disaster-preparedness/

639 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

The cloud offers organizations the ability to leverage all the classic DR architectures, including
backup and restore, Pilot Light, Warm Stand-by, and Multi-Site Active/Active. For example,
implementing a Pilot Light design is relatively easy because everything is code. Duplicating
your production cloud environment, when it's needed, is as simple as using pre-developed and
pre-tested code and automation to reprovision and configure all the existing cloud
infrastructure in a different Availability Zone or Region. Much of it can be sitting in a cloud
account provisioned, but not in a running state. Typically, customers won't pay for this
infrastructure until it is in a running state. Once the infrastructure is up and running as
expected, perhaps as quickly as a few minutes (depending on complexity), the appropriate
DNS records are changed to point to the new infrastructure. This is a bit of an
oversimplification, but it is wildly less complicated and expensive than procuring real estate
for datacenters, conducting construction projects to build datacenters, procuring the
appropriate power and backup power infrastructures, procuring, implementing, and operating
all the IT infrastructure, paying real estate taxes every year, etc.

Rest assured, if you want to implement DR as part of a Protect and Recover strategy, an AttackCentric strategy, a DevOps strategy, or other strategies in the cloud, you have a lot of flexibility
and options at your disposal because of the power of APIs and automation in the cloud. The
key to choosing which DR architecture to use should be based on the **recovery point**
**objectives (RPOs) and recovery time objectives (RTOs)** for each application in scope for
your DR plans. Define these, and then design DR architectures that can achieve them for you.

**Resilience as a security strategy**

Remember resilience as a security strategy that I discussed in _Chapter 10_ . Leveraging this
strategy in the cloud relies heavily on these same DR **c** oncepts and the Well-Architected
Resilience pillar. Instead of planning on a complete failure of a cloud service, they can also be
used to plan for smaller but potentially highly disruptive failures in individual services or
functions. The key is understanding the data flows and the dependencies of the system you are
trying to improve the resilience of. The Reliability pillar of the various Well-Architected
frameworks that the CSPs have published contains best practices to improve the resilience of
your cloud-based solutions.

AWS published a great blog post on this aspect called "Understand resiliency patterns and
trade-offs to architect efficiently in the cloud". It is available at `[https://aws.amazon.com/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/understand-resiliency-patterns-and-trade-offs-to-architect-efficiently-in-the-cloud/)`

AWS also published a resilience lifecycle framework that outlines the following five stages that
can help continuously improve the resilience of systems:

Stage 1: Set objectives - defining resilience objectives, such as RPO and RTO

Stage 2: Design and implement - anticipating failure modes and identifying design
choices

Stage 3: Evaluate and test - test the practices that have been performed in previous
stages and evaluate the results

Stage 4: Operate - deploy application to production and manage customers' experience

Stage 5: Respond and learn - focus on practices that can be implemented to better
respond to disruptive events

You can get all the details on this help framework, including the granular technical controls
they recommend, at `[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/resilience-lifecycle-framework/introduction.html.)`

641 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

**Mitigating ransomware using the cloud**

In addition to the modern **a** pproaches I've discussed in this chapter, I wanted to broach one
more design pattern that can be helpful. One objective every CISO and security team has is to
protect their IT environments from a successful ransomware attack. I outlined the different
flavors of ransomware attacks in _Chapter 5_ . Attackers typically steal sensitive data, sometimes
deny their victims access to their data and infrastructure, and then demand a ransom or
multiple ransoms, promising they'll take specific actions, such as providing a decryption key or
not selling the stolen data.

Let's focus on the data protection aspect and look at a design pattern that makes it harder for
attackers to encrypt or otherwise destroy data. This can be accomplished in both on-premises
environments as well as the cloud. However, it is much easier to accomplish in the cloud given
all the benefits I mentioned earlier in this chapter. I learned about this design pattern while
attending Oracle AI World, so I will leverage **Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI)** in this
example. Oracle describes OCI as "the next-generation cloud designed to run any application,
faster and more securely, for less" (Oracle, n.d.).

_Figure 13.1_ illustrates a high-level design that can help mitigate ransomware and help support
aggressive RPOs and RTOs leveraging OCI (Oracle, August 28, 2025).

_Figure 13.1 – An example of an architectural design leveraging OCI that helps mitigate ransomware and meet_

_aggressive RPOs and RTOs (Oracle, August 28, 2025)._

The design leverages three enclaves, which include a Production enclave, a Vault enclave, and a
Safe Restore enclave. In OCI, an enclave is an isolated operational zone with its own control

_Chapter 13_ 642

plane, identity boundaries, and administrative model, which can be in the same OCI tenancy
or different tenancies. Implementing each enclave in a different tenancy can make it harder for
attackers to compromise all three enclaves after compromising one. Each enclave leverages
different identity providers, different identities, and different **identity and access**
**management (IAM)** policies. This makes it harder for attackers to compromise all three
enclaves using stolen credentials from one enclave. The Vault enclave and Safe Restore enclave
have a relatively small number of administrator accounts compared to the Production enclave,
as access to these enclaves is limited to just the administrators who are involved in backup and
restore related work. There are administrative air gaps between the Production enclave and the
Vault enclave, and between the Vault enclave and the Safe Restore enclave. These
administrative air gaps **e** nforce control-plane separation that ensures no shared administrator
accounts, no shared IAM policies, and no shared automation credentials between enclaves. In
this scenario, it means that even if attackers were able to compromise the Production enclave,
they wouldn't have administrative control over the Vault enclave or the Safe Restore enclave
and wouldn't be able to compromise or destroy the data in them.

With these three enclaves isolated from each other in this fashion, periodic backups are taken
of the production data in the Production enclave and copied into the Vault enclave into
immutable storage. Tampering with these data backup copies is not possible due to the
immutable properties of the storage. Automated data testing can be employed on these
backups to identify data corruption or malware. This results in a catalog of well-known data
backups that can be used to restore the data in the case of data encryption or destruction.

In the Restore enclave, you can do continuous incremental restores of the backups based on the
RTOs and RPOs that were defined. This enclave can be scaled up using automation to
temporarily become the Production enclave in the case of a ransomware incident or other
disaster. This will allow the system to continue to operate while an active incident response
investigation is underway in the Production enclave. After containment and eradication of the
attackers and any infrastructure rebuilding are completed, the Production enclave can be used
to operate the system again or the Safe Restore enclave can become the new Production
enclave. Since system backup and restore operations are constantly being exercised, this
dramatically increases the likelihood that the organization will actually be able to recover from
a ransomware attack and do so within the defined RPOs and RTOs. The separate identities
used in each enclave also increase the odds of success.

This approach is what Oracle refers to as their **Cyber Resiliency Architecture (CRA)** . I've
provided the abridged version of this approach here, but you can find all the details on CRA at

```
https://docs.oracle.com/en/solutions/oci-tenancy-cyber-resilience-architecture/
```

`[index.html](https://docs.oracle.com/en/solutions/oci-tenancy-cyber-resilience-architecture/index.html)` .

643 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

Using the combination of the DevOps strategy I described here, in combination with resilience
as a security strategy and the appropriate DR practices, would represent a major uplift in
cybersecurity and resilience for most of the enterprises I've advised over the years. This would
be hard or impossible for most enterprises to accomplish in their legacy on-premises IT
environments. However, the security story for the cloud gets even better when we layer in its
encryption and key management capabilities. Let's look at those next.
###### **Encryption and key management**

In my experience advising enterprise organizations, most conversations about security in the
cloud conclude by discussing encryption and key management. No matter what topics these
conversations started with, such as vulnerabilities, exploits, malware, internet-based threats,
or government access to data, they concluded by discussing encryption and key management.
This is because encryption is recognized and mathematically proven to be a powerful data
protection control that helps provide confidentiality and integrity for data, whether it's in the
cloud, hybrid environments, or on-premises.

No matter which cybersecurity strategy or combination of strategies organizations pursue,
when the rubber hits the road, protecting the data is the objective. That's what can be so
distracting about the cybersecurity strategies we examined that are proxies for data protection.
Security teams get so focused on protecting endpoints or applications that they can lose sight
of the fact that the underlying objective is to protect data. The proxies I mentioned are
important and must be effectively managed, but don't forget about the data!

The CSPs all know this and offer their customers rich sets of encryption and key management
capabilities. Their goal is to protect data when it is in transit, at rest, and even while it's being
processed. TLS (version 1.3) is the current de facto internet standard for protecting data in
transit. Subsequently, CSPs support TLS, in addition to providing other mechanisms for
protecting data in transit, like VPN connections or directly connecting their cloud
infrastructures to their customers' networks, as examples.

As I discussed in _Chapter 8_, _Friend or Foe? The Roles Governments Play in Cybersecurity_, CSPs offer
a range of encryption options to protect data at rest, enabling their customers to encrypt data
before they put it in the cloud (in some scenarios) and/or after they put it in the cloud.
Remember the difference between client-side encryption and server-side encryption. The
current and recommended encryption standard that CSPs offer for encrypting data at rest **i** s
the **Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)**, using 256-bit key lengths.

If an attacker had access to data (access is typically authenticated and authorized) protected by
AES-256, breaking this type of encryption using brute-force techniques and a large amount of
conventional computing power would likely take far, far more time than the value lifetime of
the data.

_Chapter 13_ 644

An important nuance for security teams to understand is exactly what is being encrypted and
which risks that type of encryption mitigates. For example, if the underlying storage media is
encrypted, but the data being written to the media is not encrypted prior to being written, then
the risks being mitigated are the loss or theft of the storage media. Encrypted storage media
helps mitigate attacks where attackers have physical access to the storage media. If someone
gets physical access to the encrypted storage media but doesn't possess the keys to mount and
decrypt it, the data written on it is protected from unauthorized access. However, if attackers
seek to access the data logically instead of physically, over a network, for example, then
storage-level encryption will likely not mitigate this risk because the data is decrypted as it is
accessed from the network.

In addition to offering data encryption options, CSPs are really providing authenticated and
authorized data encryption. That is, each encryption operation API call is authenticated and
must be authorized; encryption and decryption operations will not occur without being
authenticated and authorized first. Using Identity and Access services this way provides
security teams with a lot of flexibility. For example, one person or group of people can be
authorized to encrypt data but not authorized to decrypt it. Another group can be given
permissions to decrypt data, but not to do both encryption and decryption operations.
Authenticated and authorized encryption enables a separation of duties that can be helpful in
many scenarios.

For many organizations, one of the most challenging parts of encryption can be key
management. The stakes are high because if an organization's keys are damaged, lost, or
stolen, it could have a catastrophic impact on them. CSPs want to make key management easy
and safe for their customers. Google offers Cloud Key Management Service (Google, n.d.),
Microsoft offers Azure Key Vault (Microsoft Corporation, n.d.), and AWS provides the AWS Key
Management Service (AWS, n.d.). Of course, there are third-party vendors that also offer
encryption and key management services, such as Thales, Equinix, and others.

The CSPs' key management services can offer an interesting advantage in that they can be
integrated into their other cloud services. This means that some cloud services can perform

645 _Modern Approaches to Security and Compliance_

encryption and decryption on behalf of users. The advantage here is that the data can be
protected by AES encryption until it's in the physical memory of the servers running the service
that is going to process it. Once processing is completed, the service can re-encrypt the data
again before moving it into storage or other services for more processing. The keys used for
encryption and decryption can be protected in transit between the key management services
and the services that use them. This means that unencrypted data only sees the light of day in
highly controlled environments that are authorized by the data owner. This can help maximize
the number of places and the time that the data is protected with encryption. CSPs' key
management services tend to be designed for low latency and high availability in order to
process billions of requests.

Some organizations want a separation of duties between the vendor they use for compute and
storage and the vendors that provide key management services. Third-party vendors that offer
key management services can play this role, or CSPs' customers themselves can operate and
maintain their own key management infrastructures. The organizations that choose this
option should be comfortable managing their own key management infrastructure or allowing
a third party to do it for them. However, managing **hardware security modules (HSMs)** and
**public key infrastructures (PKIs)** is notoriously difficult. This makes using CSPs' key
management services a popular option.

For organizations that need to keep their keys on-premises but still want to get the benefits of
the cloud, client-side encryption is a potential solution. Using client-side encryption means
that the data owner encrypts the data before they put it into a cloud service. For example, the
data owner has their own on-premises key management infrastructure. Prior to putting data
into a cloud storage service, they generate a key on-premises and then use an application also
running on-premises to encrypt the data using this key. Then, they authenticate and securely
transfer the encrypted data to the cloud storage service. In this scenario, their CSP never had
access to their unencrypted data or the encryption key, as neither left the on-premises IT
environment. To decrypt this data, the data owner authenticates to the cloud storage service,
securely downloads the encrypted data, and uses their on-premises application and onpremises key to decrypt the data. Again, neither the unencrypted data nor the encryption key
was ever shared with the CSP.

We briefly mentioned this in _Chapter 8_ . Client-side encryption isn't limited to storage
scenarios; it can be used with other services, like databases, for example. In this scenario,
client-side encryption is used to encrypt records or individual fields as they are written to a
database service running in the cloud. To do this, an encryption key is retrieved from the onpremises key management system and temporarily used for encryption operations by the
application performing the encryption. Once the record is encrypted as it's written to the
database, the encryption key can be removed from the memory of the application that
performed the encryption operation, thus reducing the time the key is resident on a system

_Chapter 13_ 646

outside of the on-premises key management system. The application performing encryption
and decryption operations on the database records can run on-premises or in the cloud. Since
the CSP's customer has full control of the keys, the CSP cannot get access to the keys unless the
customer grants them access. Indexes and database primary and secondary keys are left
unencrypted so that indexing and searching the database can still be performed. For this
reason, it's important not to put sensitive data into these fields. To decrypt the data, the
appropriate records are retrieved and decrypted after the key is provided from the on-premises
key management system. After the decryption operation, the key can once again be removed
from the memory of the application performing the decryption operation.

There are many different ways to perform client-side encryption and key management.
However, this method can be more complicated and expensive to implement than simply using
the integrated **e** ncryption and key management services that CSPs offer. Some organizations
that start off using client-side encryption with keys kept on-premises, over time, conclude that
using CSPs' key management services mitigates the risks they are most concerned about and
helps to simplify their applications. After all, encryption and decryption operations in the
cloud are performed using API calls that are authenticated, authorized, monitored, and
potentially controlled using automation, as we discussed earlier.

The CSPs want to provide their customers with the confidentiality and integrity that clientside encryption provides, without the extra complexity and costs. After all, moving key
material between on-premises IT environments and cloud environments also has risks
associated with it and doesn't improve application performance, especially at scale. The CSPs
offer sophisticated alternatives to client-side encryption that can also help mitigate insider
threat in many scenarios. The list below contains some examples.

Combining properly implemented encryption and effective key management, along with the
power of APIs and automation in the cloud, helps protect data in ways that would be more
complex to duplicate in on-premises IT environments. Encryption and key management help
protect data from many of the threats we discussed throughout this book; they are powerful
data protection controls that should be part of whichever cybersecurity strategies your
organization pursues.
###### **Summary**

This chapter explored how cloud computing is reshaping cybersecurity and compliance by
enabling organizations to modernize their technologies, processes, and strategies. Moving
from static, on-premises environments to cloud-native models allows security teams to take
advantage of capabilities that fundamentally change how security and compliance are
implemented and operated.

A central theme was the role of **APIs and automation** . In the cloud, nearly all actions occur
through authenticated and authorized API calls, providing consistent visibility, control, and
auditability. When combined with automation, this model reduces human error, limits insider
risk, accelerates detection and response, and enables continuous enforcement of security and
compliance requirements. These capabilities make it easier to mitigate the Cybersecurity Usual
Suspects, including unpatched vulnerabilities, security misconfigurations, weak, leaked, or
stolen credentials, insider threats, and social engineering.

The chapter also examined how the cloud supports multiple cybersecurity strategies.
Compliance as a cybersecurity strategy benefits from continuous monitoring, automation, and
the extensive certifications and attestations maintained by hyperscale cloud providers under a
shared responsibility model. Attack-centric strategies can be implemented using cloud-native
controls and mappings to frameworks such as the Intrusion Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK®.
More modern DevOps-driven approaches, often described as immutable, short-lived
infrastructure, use CI/CD pipelines and automation to ensure that only secure and compliant
systems reach production.

Finally, the chapter highlighted how cloud architectures simplify disaster recovery, resilience,
and ransomware mitigation, and why encryption and key management remain foundational
controls for protecting data. Together, APIs, automation, managed services, and advanced

_Chapter 13_ 648

cryptographic capabilities enable organizations to build security and compliance programs
that are more scalable, resilient, and effective than traditional on-premises approaches.

The next chapter builds on these concepts by examining the role of artificial intelligence in
cybersecurity, including securing AI systems themselves and using AI to improve detection,
response, and overall security effectiveness.

In the next chapter, I'll discuss another topic that has attracted the attention of CISOs and
cybersecurity teams in recent years—how to mitigate "Living Off the Land" techniques.

# 14
##### Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques

_"The greatest danger in times of turbulence is not the turbulence; it is to act with_
_yesterday's logic." (Peter F. Drucker, 1973)_

Regardless of which cybersecurity strategy or combination of strategies CISOs use, they'll still
need to invest time and effort into mitigating attackers' **Living Off the Land (LOTL)**
techniques. Some of these techniques are as old as cyber-attacks themselves, as attackers have
always used them in some form or another as they perpetrated traditional network intrusions.
Some techniques have remained the same, as they continue to be effective after decades of use,
while other new and novel techniques continue to emerge. For attackers who perpetrate
traditional network intrusions, these techniques have become an integral part of their success.
Yet, despite how long these techniques have been in use and how popular they are with
attackers, given their continued success, it seems that relatively few organizations prioritize
the work needed to mitigate them. The **Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency**
**(CISA)** recently noted this:

_"Many organizations do not implement security best practice capabilities that_
_support detection of living off the land (LOTL), so this technique continues to be_
_effective with little to no investment in tooling by malicious cyber_
_actors" (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, 2024)._

In this chapter, you will learn what LOTL techniques are and some of the ways they can be
addressed. First, we will examine the ways attackers leverage legitimate binaries, tools, and
websites during their attacks. Then we will discuss approaches to mitigating such techniques.
Finally, in the "lessons from the trenches" section, I'll offer you some real-world advice on how
to mitigate these techniques based on my own experience. By the end of this chapter, you

_Chapter 14_ 654

should be able to devise a plan of action for your organization to mature its approach to
mitigating LOTL techniques.

The following topics will be covered:

What is Living Off the Land

Mitigating LOTL techniques

Let's get started!
###### **What is Living Off the Land?**

There are more than a few definitions of LOTL available. For example, researchers in
cybersecurity research and response labs who are responsible for endpoint protection and
detection technologies might view LOTL as fileless malware. That is, software with a nefarious
purpose that is never written to local system storage ("to disk"). Their challenge is figuring out
how to detect and block the execution of threats that exist in memory and not "on disk." If the
malware isn't written to disk, it is more challenging for anti-malware software and endpoint
solutions to detect and block it.

Others view LOTL as scenarios where attackers leverage legitimate binaries built into the
operating systems that their victims use to administrate and operate them—so-called **Living**
**Off the Land Binaries (LOLBins)** . These binaries can't readily be detected as malware because
they are included by default with Windows, Linux, and other operating systems commonly
found in enterprise IT environments. The operating systems themselves, IT support teams, and
applications use these binaries in the course of normal operations. For example, attackers are
happy to use cmd.exe, WMI, PowerShell, and Windows Task Scheduler in ways that appear to
be how legitimate administrators use them, but actually to move laterally, further penetrate
the environment, stay persistent, exfiltrate data, and deploy ransomware. It is challenging for
cybersecurity teams to determine whether these tools are being used by administrators for
legitimate purposes or by attackers using administrator credentials to forward their attacks.

Of course, both views are accurate. Cybersecurity teams must be prepared to detect and stop
fileless malware and the malicious use of legitimate binaries if they hope to stop modern-day
attackers in their environments after initial compromise. The US CISA provided this definition,
which I think is very helpful because it is comprehensive and pragmatic.

_LOTL involves the abuse of native tools and processes on systems, especially living off_
_the land binaries, often referred to as LOLBins, to blend in with normal system_
_activities and operate discreetly with a lower likelihood of being detected or blocked_
_because these tools are already deployed and trusted in the environment. Cyber_
_threat actors effectively use LOTL across multiple environments, including in on-_
_premises, cloud, hybrid, Windows, Linux, and macOS environments, in part because_

655 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

_it enables the ability to avoid investing in the development and deployment of_
_custom tools. (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency et al., 2024)_

Besides fileless malware and the malicious use of legitimate binaries, there are some other
techniques attackers use that cybersecurity teams need to be prepared for. In this chapter,
when I refer to LOTL techniques, it includes the following types of potential threats:

**Fileless malware** : Malicious software and scripts that aren't written to disk the way
traditional malware typically is, so they can be more challenging to detect, block, and
disinfect

**Malicious use of legitimate binaries** : Attackers making use of binaries that ship with
operating systems, such as ntdsutil, rundll32, schtasks, ssh, sftp, regedit, wmic,
winword, tar, tftp, telnet, view, vim, and literally hundreds of others

**Malicious use of legitimate websites (URLs)** : Some attackers stage parts of their
attacks from legitimate websites hosted in Internet domains they know enterprises
can't or won't block. They use such websites to host and download their toolkits and
for data exfiltration, among other uses. Leveraging websites hosted on major **content**
**distribution networks (CDNs)**, such as Cloudflare, Akamai, and AWS's Amazon
CloudFront, makes it less likely that outbound access to them will be blocked on their
victims' networks.

**Common IT support tools** : Tools that aren't necessarily included with operating
systems but are ubiquitous in IT environments because of their popularity with IT
teams. Attackers don't need to download or install these tools as IT teams have already
done this. Examples include popular **Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM)**
tools such as TeamViewer, ConnectWise RMM, LogMeIn, and many others.

**Legitimate administrator tools that attackers love:** Legitimate administrator tools
that aren't **b** uilt into operating systems and aren't commonly preinstalled across
enterprise environments, so attackers often bring them in and abuse them during
intrusions. These are tools that, if given the chance, attackers will download and
execute to support different stages of their attacks, including post-intrusion
reconnaissance, exploitation, installation, command and control, and actions on
objectives. Examples include Nmap, Advanced IP Scanner, Metasploit, Burp Suite,
SharpHound, and many others.

**Legitimate developer tools** : Some **a** ttackers are adept at leveraging developer tools
accessible in their victims' environments, including MSBuild, Regsvr32, InstallUtil,
Mshta, C# Compiler, popular interpreters such as Python, Node.js, and Ruby, and
Visual Studio tools, among others. Why download and install executables on victims'

_Chapter 14_ 656

systems that might be detected when you can use victims' developer tools that aren't
monitored to execute code for you?

I realize that this list includes more potential threat types than the strictest definitions of LOTL
permit. Many attackers combine native operating-system binaries with additional malicious or
legitimate tools they deploy inside the victim's environment, along with the use of legitimate
websites to support their operations. Subsequently, in this chapter, I'll take a pragmatic
approach and include all the potential threat types I listed earlier when I refer to LOTL. This
will give cybersecurity teams following this guidance the best chance at detecting attackers
who use only tools that meet the strictest definitions of LOTL, as well as those who do not.

Let's dig into these threat types a bit more to understand why they are so effective for attackers
using LOTL techniques.

**Fileless malware**

Fileless malware is a type of threat that many threat actors use as part of their LOTL toolkits.
There are quite a few definitions of fileless malware available. Let's look at some slightly
different definitions so you get a well-rounded understanding of the concept of fileless
malware.

Fortinet provides a definition that is helpful.

_"Fileless malware is malicious code that works directly within a computer's memory_
_instead of the hard drive. It uses legitimate, otherwise benevolent programs to_
_compromise your computer instead of malicious files. It is "fileless" in that when_
_your machine gets infected, no files are downloaded to your hard drive…Because_
_fileless malware attacks require no malicious files, traditional antivirus tools that_
_perform hardware scans to locate threats may miss them altogether." Fortinet._
_(n.d.)._

CrowdStrike also provides a definition that is a little more tightly linked to LOTL:

_"Fileless malware is a type of malicious activity that uses native, legitimate tools_
_built into a system to execute a cyberattack. Unlike traditional malware, which_
_typically requires a file to be downloaded and installed, fileless malware operates in_
_memory or manipulates native tools, making it harder to detect and remove."_
_CrowdStrike. (November 26, 2024)._

A definition provided by **e** ndpoint security vendor Palo Alto Networks states,

_"Fileless malware attacks are something where attackers are using things that aren't_
_written to disk. So, things that are staying in volatile memory, such as PowerShell_

657 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

_and WMI. And they're doing that because they are much harder to both detect and_
_to find later, because a lot of times, they aren't kept in logs._

_So, you'll see attackers doing things where they're automating a lot of their initial_
_attacks, where they'll use something such as PowerShell or WMI to figure out both_
_where they've landed in the system and do some basic network reconnaissance to_
_decide whether or not they are in a place where they want to be. And those things are_
_very hard to detect via traditional AV vendors, and even without some behavior_
_analytics, they're harder to find." Palo Alto Networks. (n.d.)._

I like Palo Alto Networks' description because it provides a little more context on how attackers
use fileless malware. We will cover PowerShell and WMI in the "Mitigating LOTL Techniques"
section of this chapter.

One final definition from Avast:

_"Fileless malware is malicious code that infiltrates a computer system without_
_leaving an obvious footprint, unlike traditional viruses or other types of malware_
_that typically create trace files. Instead, fileless malware lives entirely in a computer's_
_random access memory (RAM) and weaponizes trusted system tools to execute_
_harmful processes and steal data." Avast. (n.d.)._

There are several techniques that developers of fileless malware use to evade detection and
advance their attacks. Here's a summary of some of them

**Memory** -o **nly malware execution** : No artifacts are left on disk because the malware

runs entirely in memory

**LOTL abuse** : Fileless malware uses trusted, signed system binaries to execute, such as
PowerShell, **Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)**, VBScript, rundll32.exe,
Microsoft HTML Application Host (mshta.exe), among others

**Exploit kits** : Collections of working exploits for unpatched vulnerabilities are used to
compromise systems and inject code directly into memory, thus bypassing writes to
disk

**Registry** -r **esident malware** : Instead of writing malware to a file on the hard drives of
systems, malicious code is stored in the Windows registry. This can make it easier for
fileless malware to restart after a system reboot

**Script** - **based attacks** : Instead of **d** ropping an executable file on the hard drive, fileless
malware leverages batch scripts, WMI, PowerShell scripts, and JavaScript to execute in
memory only

Microsoft has **e** numerated fileless threats and published a helpful taxonomy to understand
them (Type I, II, and III). Type I fileless threats have no file activity (purely memory-resident).

_Chapter 14_ 658

files required to operate, but still uses fileless techniques in parts of their execution chain. _Table_
_14.1_ summarizes the fileless threat taxonomy provided by Microsoft (Microsoft, April 24, 2024).

Industry guidance for mitigating fileless malware is **e** ssentially the same as the guidance for
mitigating LOTL techniques. The same controls recommended for LOTL activity apply directly
to fileless threats. I will provide specific guidance to mitigate LOTL techniques, and
subsequently fileless malware, in the "mitigating LOTL techniques" section of this chapter.

Next, let's take a deeper look at the malicious use of legitimate binaries that attackers use to
LOTL.

**Malicious use of legitimate binaries**

Many attackers use legitimate binaries included by default in operating systems, such as
executables, **Dynamic Link Libraries (DLLs)**, and **d** evice drivers, because they provide several
operational advantages. First, since the binaries are already installed on their victims' systems,
they don't have to risk being detected downloading and installing them. Second, these binaries
are trusted and typically signed by the operating system vendors when they ship them with

_Chapter 14_ 660

their operating systems. Subsequently, anti-malware and endpoint security solutions typically
allow these binaries to execute without scrutiny. Lastly, attackers' use of legitimate binaries
blends into the legitimate use by system administrators, making it harder to detect attackers'
presence. This is especially true when attackers are leveraging stolen administrator credentials
and running legitimate binaries from domain-joined systems. This makes it harder to detect
anomalies.

Some examples of common Windows binaries that are used in LOTL attacks are shown in _Table_
_14.2_ . Some of the examples are binaries found in multiple operating systems from different

_Table 14.2 – Examples of binaries attackers abuse when using LOTL techniques_

Let's dive deeper into that last example in _Table 14.2_ because it's so popular with attackers and
its use can result in network compromises for which recovery is truly aspirational. Remember
the traditional network intrusion attack I described in _Chapter 1_, _How Enterprises Get Hacked_ . A
traditional network intrusion is a targeted attack in which adversaries gain initial access to the

_Chapter 14_ 662

victim organization, establish persistence, escalate privileges, move laterally using stolen
credentials and tools, and ultimately exfiltrate data or deploy ransomware to achieve their
objectives. In my experience, attackers often try to export a copy of their victim's Active
Directory (the ntds.dit file) within seconds of initial compromise when they have
administrator credentials. The number of named threat actors that have reportedly been seen
using `ntdsutil.exe` to get access to credentials is long and includes APT28, APT41, Chimera,
Dragonfly, FIN6, FIN13, Fox Kitten, HAFNIUM, LAPSUS$, Medusa Group, Mustang Panda,
Sandworm Team, Scattered Spider, Volt Typhoon, Wizard Spider, and many others.

If ntdsutil.exe is available on Domain Controllers, attackers can avoid downloading a copy of
ntdsutil.exe or their own tools for this purpose, accelerating the exfiltration of Active Directory
and reducing the risk of being detected during the process. An example of the ntdsutil.exe
command that exports the ntds.dit file is provided below.

```
  ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\temp" q q

```

When run from a command prompt or PowerShell with administrator privileges on a shadow
copy of a domain controller's C:\ drive, this command will result in a file called ntds.dit in the
specified "C:\temp" destination folder.

Attackers will frequently exfiltrate ntds.dit from the victim's network and then extract hashed
passwords from it using a tool such as NtdsAudit, which is available on GitHub. They will
perform offline password cracking on the extracted password hashes using specialized tools
that are also readily available on the internet.

This is where victims' password policies come into play. Relatively short, easy-to-guess
passwords will be revealed in minutes or hours, while relatively long (15 characters), complex
passwords will likely never be cracked except for those that were reused passwords or variants
of old passwords. Instead of guessing passwords randomly, tools like John the Ripper, Hashcat,
and Wordlister enable attackers to use custom rules to generate highly probable variants of
passwords that inform their cracking efforts, simulating how people typically modify words to
create passwords. This dramatically increases the success rate of password cracking attacks.
When a user changes their password using an old password as a part of the new password, it
makes it much easier for attackers to crack using these tools. For example, when a user with an
old password such as "Summer2023!" changes it to "Summer2024!!". This is especially true if
the old passwords were stolen or leaked at some point in the past, giving attackers access to
them. It also turns out that changing a password that uses an old weak password standard,
such as "timrains" for example, to a password using a new stronger password standard, such
as "TimRains123!", is easier to predict than you might think.

663 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

When attackers marry these rule-based mutation capabilities to massive lists of compromised
credentials available on the internet, passwords that have been reused across internet services
and corporate network user accounts become an Achilles' heel. This approach to password
cracking can be startlingly effective even on relatively long passwords, and it highlights how
common human password-selection patterns can weaken security. Given this common human
behavior, it's likely that some passwords in use at large enterprise organizations will always be
crackable despite password length, complexity, and expiration policies.

Cybersecurity teams need to pay attention to popular LOTL binaries such as ntdsutil.exe
because the probability and impact of their malicious use are high. I'll provide some guidance
on how to do this in the _Mitigating LOTL techniques_ section of this chapter.

To maximize the speed and efficiency of their attacks, many attackers have scripted the
commands they need to execute the stages of their attacks. In these cases, attackers have
typically executed the initial stages of their attacks via automation before defenders can detect
them and respond.

There are literally hundreds of binaries included in Windows and Linux operating systems that
attackers use to live off the land. Of course, attackers don't limit themselves to just running
binaries; they will also leverage scripts and libraries that are included with operating systems
too. For example, a Visual Basic script called winrm.vbs is included in Windows. Winrm.vbs is
a VBScript-based command-line tool that **i** s included with Windows as part of **Windows**
**Remote Management (WinRM)** . It provides administrators with examples of how to use
VBScript to interact with the WS-Management protocol. Essentially, this script, if not properly
secured, can enable attackers to move laterally in their victims' environments by executing
processes via WMI on the local host as well as on remote hosts on the network (Red Canary,
May 6, 2025).

An example of a library some attackers have used in the past is called Zipfldr.dll. This is
Microsoft's built-in ZIP file handler. ZIP functionality enables the compression and
decompression of files. Attackers can use this legitimate library, via rundll32.exe, to launch
executables; here's an example of the command.

```
  rundll32.exe zipfldr.dll,RouteTheCall file.exe

```

Fortunately, there are some great resources available that enumerate the binaries, scripts,
libraries, and drivers attackers have used in the past, so you don't have to do this work yourself.
These also include detection guidance in the form of Sigma rules (.yml files):

   - Windows binaries: Living Off The Land Binaries, Scripts, and Libraries (LOLBAS) 
```
    https://lolbas-project.github.io/

```

According to the LOLBAS project webpage, "The goal of the LOLBAS project is to document
every binary, script, and library that can be used for Living Off The Land techniques" (LOLBAS
Project, 2025). At the time of writing, the LOLBAS project page provided details on 228
binaries, including 200 executables, 16 libraries, and 10 scripts that attackers have abused in
the past to support their LOTL techniques (LOLBAS Project, 2025).

The GTFOBins project currently lists 390 Unix binaries (LOLBAS Project, 2025). The purpose of
the GTFOBins project, as stated on its webpage, is

_"GTFOBins is a curated list of Unix binaries that can be used to bypass local security_
_restrictions in misconfigured systems. The project collects legitimate functions of_
_Unix binaries that can be abused to break out restricted shells, escalate or maintain_

_other post-exploitation tasks. " (Pinna, E., & Cardaci, A. (2025)._

Next, let's look at another aspect of LOTL that cybersecurity teams need to plan for: the
malicious use of legitimate websites.

**Malicious use of legitimate websites**

This will come as **a** surprise to no one, but it turns out that the overwhelming majority of
attackers are on the internet. Besides the very small percentage of insiders who abuse their
privileged access either purposely or unintentionally, attackers sit outside their victims'
firewalls. Typically, when attackers successfully perpetrate a traditional network intrusion,
they require outbound internet access from their victim's network to download their tools,
remotely control victims' systems, exfiltrate data, and attack other potential victims using
compromised infrastructure.

Leveraging domains and websites on the internet that are trusted by enterprises implicitly is a
very effective technique to accomplish outbound internet access. That is, even if an
organization does not permit its users unfettered access to the internet, they likely permit
access to github.com, docs.google.com, *.amazonaws.com, *.cloudfront.net,
*.cloudapp.azure.com, youtube.com, slack.com, *.docusign.com, *.doubleclick.net, and many
other legitimate websites. After all, most enterprises leverage software and cloud services from

665 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

these domains and websites and even host their own websites and cloud services in them. In
many cases, their users must have access to these domains and websites in order to do their
jobs.

This is what attackers are counting on. For attackers using LOTL techniques, this means if they
can stage parts of their attacks from trusted domains and websites, it's likely they will have
outbound internet access to them even in relatively secure environments. Exfiltrating data to a
known malicious website might be blocked by their victim's firewalls, but it's highly likely that
legitimate websites hosted in Azure, AWS, and **Google Cloud Platform (GCP)** are accessible.

A great resource to inform such efforts is the **Living Off Trusted Sites (LOTS)** project. The
stated purpose of this project is

_"Attackers are using popular legitimate domains when conducting phishing, C&C,_
_exfiltration, and downloading tools to evade detection. The list of websites below_
_allows attackers to use their domain or subdomain" (mrd0x, n.d.)._

The LOTS project webpage currently lists 175 domains and URLs that are known to be used by
attackers using LOTL techniques. For each URL on the list, they provide tags that describe how
that website was used in past attacks. Tags include phishing, **command and control (C&C)**,
download, and exfiltration. Cybersecurity teams can use this list to inform their approach to
mitigating LOTL techniques and enabling the appropriate internet access for their users.

Additionally, firewall vendors and **Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)** vendors can help block
known malicious websites and provide least-privilege access to both internal and external
websites.

Next, let's look at how attackers use common IT support tools to live off the land.

**Common IT support tools**

Attackers typically make heavy use of IT support tools that aren't necessarily included with
operating systems but are popular with IT teams. Such tools can be deployed broadly across
workstations and servers. This makes it easier for attackers using LOTL techniques to stay
persistent, move laterally, remotely control infrastructure, and exfiltrate data.

Perhaps the best example of such a tool is PSExec.exe. This tool was developed by one of my
former Microsoft coworkers, Mark Russinovich, and is included in the Sysinternals tool suite
available from Microsoft at `[https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/)` . This is a
hugely popular legitimate tool among IT professionals and attackers alike. Mark describes this
tool as follows:

_"Utilities like Telnet and remote control programs like Symantec's PC Anywhere let_
_you execute programs on remote systems, but they can be a pain to set up and require_

_Chapter 14_ 666

_that you install client software on the remote systems that you wish to access. PsExec_
_is a light-weight telnet-replacement that lets you execute processes on other systems,_
_complete with full interactivity for console applications, without having to manually_
_install client software. PsExec's most powerful uses include launching interactive_
_command prompts on remote systems and remote-enabling tools like IpConfig that_
_otherwise do not have the ability to show information about remote systems._

_Note: Some anti-virus scanners report that one or more of the tools are infected with_
_a "remote admin" virus. None of the PsTools contain viruses, but they have been_
_used by viruses, which is why they trigger virus notifications." (Microsoft, April 11,_
_2023)._

From the description, it should be clear why this tool is popular among attackers—it is super
easy to set up and use for remote control of systems. Since this tool is so popular among IT
teams for legitimate IT support use cases, its presence on systems isn't abnormal, and
attackers' use of it can blend into its legitimate uses. Numerous named threat actors, including
some notorious ransomware gangs, have reportedly used PSExec in their attacks. Here are
some examples:

Of course, there are other examples of popular **remote monitoring and management (RMM)**
tools attackers have used, including AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, LogMeIn, and
many others. Attackers are happy to use whatever IT support and management tools are
deployed in their victims' environments.

Similarly, attackers also use legitimate administrator tools in various stages of their attacks.
Let's look at some of these next.

**Legitimate administrator tools**

If attackers can't find the tools of their choice already installed in their victims' environments,
many attackers will simply download them. This isn't strictly LOTL, but attackers use
combinations of legitimate binaries included in operating systems and legitimate
administrator tools they download so often that they are worth mentioning, even in a chapter
on LOTL.

At this point, you might be wondering how cybersecurity teams can mitigate all these LOTL
techniques. Let's discuss this next.
###### **Mitigating LOTL techniques**

Mitigating LOTL techniques is very challenging. This is why they are so popular with attackers
that have the skill to leverage them. Cybersecurity teams must prevent attackers from
accessing the tools and URLs they rely on while still allowing legitimate users to use them.
That becomes especially difficult when attackers and legitimate users may be using the same
credentials. Subsequently, behavioral analysis is often cited as an effective mitigation.

_Chapter 14_ 672

However, when considering the mitigations recommended through the collective wisdom of
cybersecurity subject matter experts and vendors, the list of mitigations is similar to the
combinations of the cybersecurity strategies we examined in _Chapter 10_, _Cybersecurity_
_Strategies_ . That is, there's no silver bullet or easy way to mitigate a diverse set of attack
techniques such as LOTL in large enterprise environments.

Instead, there is a long list of mitigations that in aggregate make LOTL harder for attackers and
make detection more likely for defenders. The themes of these mitigations should be familiar,
as they include the "motherhood and apple pie" of cybersecurity, such as restricting access to
binaries and the internet, effective network segmentation, application control, leveraging the
principle of least privilege, MFA and privileged access management, implementing centralized
logging, auditing access, maintaining behavioral baselines, hardening endpoints, effective
vulnerability management, and conducting continuous threat hunting, among others. In other
words, there are potentially many mitigations cybersecurity teams need to layer into their
environments in order to protect, detect, and respond to LOTL techniques.

One nuance that is worth mentioning in the context of LOTL is the difference between
**indicators of attack (IOAs)** and the **indicators of compromise (IOCs)** I mentioned in _Chapter_
_2, What to Know About Threat Intelligence_ . Remember that IOCs help cybersecurity teams with
post-compromise attacker detection and incident response. They are largely reactive and
artifact-based, although known attacker IOCs can be used to inform red team exercises and
security testing.

IOAs, on the other hand, are proactive, behavior-based, sequence-based, and are detected
ideally in real time, as opposed to after a compromise. IOAs can help cybersecurity teams
detect intent and behavior during an attack. They can help spot attacker behavior such as
privilege escalation, lateral movement, and attacker behaviors to stay persistent. Where IOCs
are used for forensics and incident response, IOAs are used for threat hunting and intrusion kill
chain disruption. Where possible, take advantage of IOAs to detect and disrupt attackers.

Let's look at some specific mitigation guidance from different sources to give you a
comprehensive perspective. Let's start with the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Next, let's look at one tool that advanced threat actors love to use to steal a copy of their
victims' Active Directory.

**NTDSUTIL guidance**

I want to highlight the guidance ATT&CK provides specifically for `ntdsutil.exe`, since
attackers love to use this tool, which is present on every modern Windows Server Active
Directory Domain Controller by default, to get access to hashed passwords for offline cracking.
Once attackers have harvested credentials from the `ntds.dit` file, this will typically enable
them to stay persistent, move laterally, command and control systems, exfiltrate data, and so
on.

677 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

ATT&CK provides four primary mitigations and one detection strategy (MITRE, October 24,
2025):

M1041 – Encrypt sensitive information: secure Domain Controller backups to prevent
offline extraction.

M1027 – Password policies: ensure unique, complex local admin passwords across
systems.

M1026 – Privileged account management: avoid placing domain accounts in local
admin groups; follow tiered admin models to reduce credential exposure.

M1017 – User training: train users/admins not to reuse passwords across accounts.

DET0586 – Detection of `ntds.dit` credential dumping: detects suspicious activity such
as:

Creation of shadow copies

Access to %SystemRoot%\NTDS\ntds.dit

Use of ntdsutil.exe, esentutl, or volume management APIs

      - Unusual file access patterns on Domain Controllers

**WMI guidance**

Similarly, ATT&CK offers guidance on mitigations and detections for attackers seeking to use
legacy **Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI)** as an LTOL technique. Threat actors
abuse WMI to operate across both local and remote systems, applying it in Discovery to gather
system information and in Execution to run commands during intrusions.

ATT&CK provides four primary mitigations and one detection strategy (MITRE, October 24,
2025):

M1040 - Behavior prevention on endpoint: On Windows 10, enable **Attack Surface**
**Reduction (ASR)** rules to block processes created by WMI commands from running

M1038 - Execution prevention: Enable application control configured to block
execution of wmic.exe if it is not required for a given system or network to prevent
potential misuse by adversaries

M1026 - Privileged account management: Prevent credential overlap across systems for
administrator and privileged accounts

_Chapter 14_ 678

M1018 - User account management: Prevent non-administrators from connecting
remotely using WMI by default. Restrict other users who are allowed to connect, or
disallow all users from connecting remotely to WMI.

DET0364 - Behavioral detection strategy for WMI execution abuse on Windows

Analytic ID AN1031: Detects adversarial abuse of WMI to execute local or remote
commands via WMIC, PowerShell, or COM API through a multi-event chain:
process creation, command execution, and corresponding network connection if
remote

WMI is **e** xtremely valuable for administrators of Windows-based systems, but it isn't a feature
that can simply be turned off to prevent attacker abuse. It's a core subsystem relied on by the
Windows operating system and many applications, making it effectively ubiquitous. Disabling
it would break Windows **c** omponents, remote management tools, and **Endpoint Detection**
**and Response (EDR)** agents, among others. ATT&CK's guidance reflects this operational
reality.

In addition to the guidance published as part of the ATT&CK framework, governments have
worked together to publish helpful guidance on LOTL attacks and related topics, such as
securing PowerShell. Let's look at these next.

**Other government guidance**

Governments have been attacked by advanced threat actors for decades and subsequently have
been trying to mitigate LOTL techniques for a long time. Some have shared guidance based on
their research and experiences. There are two helpful publications I want to draw your
attention to related to LOTL.

**LOTL detection and hardening best practices**

Various agencies and **d** epartments of the US government worked with the Australian Signals
Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, the
United Kingdom National Cyber Security Centre, and the New Zealand National Cyber Security
Centre to jointly publish guidance on LOTL techniques. Their publication is called _Identifying_
_and Mitigating Living Off the Land Techniques_ and is available for free download at `[https://](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-03/Joint-Guidance-Identifying-and-Mitigating-LOTL508.pdf)`

679 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

The following is an excerpt from the summary of that guidance:

_"The authoring agencies strongly urge critical infrastructure organizations to apply_
_the following prioritized best practices and detection guidance to hunt for potential_
_LOTL activity. These recommendations are part of a multifaceted cybersecurity_
_strategy that enables effective data correlation and analysis. There is no foolproof_
_solution to fully prevent or detect LOTL activity, but by applying these best practices,_
_organizations can best position themselves for more effective detection and_
_mitigation._

**_Detection Best Practices:_**

_1. Implement detailed logging and aggregate logs in an out-of-band, centralized_
_location that is write-once, read-many to avoid the risk of attackers modifying or_
_erasing logs._

_2. Establish and continuously maintain baselines of network, user, administrative,_
_and application activity, and least privilege restrictions._

_3. Build or acquire automation (such as machine learning models) to continually_
_review all logs to compare current activities against established behavioral baselines_
_and alert on specified anomalies._

_4. Reduce alert noise by fine-tuning via priority (urgency and severity) and_
_continuously reviewing detections based on trending activity._

_5. Leverage user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA)_

**_Hardening Best Practices:_**

_1. Apply and consult vendor-recommended guidance for security hardening_

_2. Implement application allow listing and monitor use of common LOLBins_

_3. Enhance IT and OT network segmentation and monitoring_

_4. Implement authentication and authorization controls for all human-to-software_
_and software-to-software interactions regardless of network location." (CISA, et al.,_
_2024)_
