**PowerShell guidance**

Another highly recommended free publication to consume is called _Keeping PowerShell: Security_
_Measures to Use and Embrace_ . It was published in 2022 by the **National Security Agency (NSA)**,
the **Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)**, the **New Zealand National**
**Cyber Security Centre (NZ NCSC)**, and the **United Kingdom National Cyber Security**
**Centre (NCSC-UK)** . This is a summary of the recommendations from the paper:

Do not disable PowerShell — modern versions provide essential defensive visibility
and controls

Use PowerShell 5.1+ or 7.x and remove PowerShell v2, which lacks security features

Enable full PowerShell logging (module logging, script block logging, transcription)
and centralize logs for detection and forensics

Ensure **Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI)** is active so PowerShell content is
scanned by AV/EDR before execution

Apply **Constrained Language Mode (CLM)** for non-admin users to limit abuse of
powerful language features

Restrict script execution to trusted, signed, or approved sources using Application
Control (WDAC/AppLocker)

Harden PowerShell Remoting with strong authentication, **Just Enough**
**Administration (JEA)**, and restricted endpoints

Monitor PowerShell usage patterns for suspicious behavior (encoded commands,
download cradles, unusual parent processes)

Keep PowerShell and Windows updated to ensure the latest security features and
protections are available

Remove unnecessary modules and features to reduce the attack surface

Enforce least privilege for all PowerShell users and administrators

Use PowerShell as a defensive tool for auditing, IR automation, and system monitoring

- it strengthens, not weakens, security posture

An older publication, updated in October 2021, provides a maturity framework for PowerShell
that I think is a helpful way to approach managing PowerShell in enterprise environments. It

681 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

was published by the Australian Signals Directorate and is available for free download here:

```
https://www.cyber.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/
```

`[Securing%20PowerShell%20in%20the%20enterprise%20%28October%202021%29.pdf](https://www.cyber.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/Securing%20PowerShell%20in%20the%20enterprise%20%28October%202021%29.pdf)` . The
following excerpt from the paper summarizes a maturity framework for PowerShell.

_"Level 0: An organisation uses PowerShell in its default configuration without any_
_consideration of the security risks associated with its use._

_Level 1: An organisation configures a list of approved PowerShell scripts._
_Additionally, the PowerShell script execution policy is configured to run only_
_PowerShell scripts signed by a Trusted Publisher, with any code signing certificates_
_protected from misuse. PowerShell version 5.0 provides greater logging facilities and_
_should be used where possible. Finally, PowerShell-related activity is centrally logged_
_and analysed._

_Level 2: An organisation locks down PowerShell hosts to users performing tasks that_
_require the ability to use PowerShell. This is a form of role-based application control._
_A hardened Windows Remote Management (WinRM) configuration is deployed to_
_make remote PowerShell more secure._

_Level 3: An organisation deploys custom constrained endpoints for PowerShell. This_
_restricts the PowerShell functionality for a given user to a predefined_
_list." (Australian Cyber Security Centre, October 2021)._

Organizations that work to achieve even just Level 1 of this maturity model will make it
incrementally harder for attackers who aspire to use PowerShell scripts in their environments.
However, be aware that even if PowerShell scripts were 100% secure, attackers could still use
the PowerShell console or terminal to run individual commands. Since no PowerShell script is
running, all the rigor around scripts won't apply. Cybersecurity teams' work is never done!

**Lessons from the trenches**

Finally, let me give you some advice based on my own experience working to mitigate LOTL
techniques. I've tried to tackle this challenging problem more than a few times in my career. I
can offer you some advice based on my experience, however imperfect it may be.

**Removing or restricting access to binaries**

Since there are so many legitimate uses for binaries built into operating systems, it is unlikely
you'll realistically be able to restrict access to them in a meaningful way or remove them from
the operating system images in your environment. I've gone down this path myself only to find
that access to these binaries was required by third-party management software or other
software installed in the environment. Removing or blocking these binaries disrupts software

_Chapter 14_ 682

that relies on them for routine functions, causing legitimate management and monitoring
tools to fail. I was surprised to see so many third-party applications call operating system
commands directly. Unfortunately, removing these binaries or dramatically restricting access
to them would have unpredictable consequences in large enterprise environments. Among the
Windows binaries I discovered in this category were pcalua.exe, hh.exe, and bginfo.exe.

**Detect anomalous binary use:** although you likely can't restrict access to all LOTL binaries in
an overly aggressive way, you likely can identify many binaries that are not regularly or actively
used in your environment. Your **Security Information & Event Management (SIEM)**
solution might be a good source for this information. Configuring monitoring and alerting on
the use of these infrequently used LOTL binaries can help detect attackers that leverage them.
Studying their use and the volume of potential alerts before putting them into production is a
good idea. Ensure the proper alerting severity levels are implemented—if `ntdsutil.exe` is
executed, this should be a high priority alert.

**The importance of endpoint security coverage**

Your ability to detect attackers leveraging LOTL binaries in your environment is largely
dependent on how many systems in your environment have endpoint security solutions
installed (EDR/XDR) and are actively reporting data for analysis. My strong recommendation
for cybersecurity teams is to pay attention to the inventory of systems that do not have EDR/
XDR installed on them and/or are not reporting data for analysis. Attackers look for these
systems and stage their attacks from them in order to avoid being detected. Operating
inventories of systems without EDR/XDR actively reporting data gives attackers the
opportunity to use LOTL techniques in their victims' environment. Constantly strive to have
100% coverage on all systems that endpoint agents can be installed on. Bake this into your
reporting requirements for operational awareness.

**Embrace the Principle of Least Privilege:** to the extent that your organization's corporate
culture permits, restrict outbound internet access as much as possible. Not just for outbound
HTTP/HTTPS connections, but all TCP and UDP network traffic. Make it as hard as possible for
attackers to download their tools, command and control compromised systems, exfiltrate large
amounts of data, and achieve their objectives. This includes blocking outbound VPN
connections, SSH, FTP, SFTP, and many other protocols. Outbound internet access for
protocols that are useful to attackers should be granted as an exception, not by default.
Remember, CISOs aren't "Chief Internet Access Officers"; they are responsible for security, not
ensuring everyone has access to the entire internet. At the very least, known malicious
domains and websites should be blocked, along with country code top-level domains (ccTLDs)
that have no legitimate business purpose. After all, if no one in your organization speaks
Russian, Persian, Korean, or a dialect of Chinese, why would they need access to those ccTLDs
on the internet?

683 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

**Restrict access to Living Off Trusted Sites**

Remember the LOTS Project—Living Off Trusted Sites ( `[https://lots-project.com/](https://lots-project.com/)` ). These
are legitimate websites that are challenging for enterprises to block even if they have the desire
to do so. But restricting access to these URLs to just the people who need to access them will
force attackers who are LOTL in your environment to find the identities they can use to access
these URLs or modify outbound access rules for the identities they are already using. This
represents more opportunities to detect their presence in your environment, potentially before
they can deploy ransomware or exfiltrate sensitive data.

**Network visibility**

If you are relying on network detections to help identify attackers on your network, you need to
ensure TLS-encrypted traffic can be inspected. Today, more than 90% of web traffic on
corporate networks is encrypted by TLS. This is great for safeguarding the confidentiality and
integrity of network traffic, but attackers also use it to blend into legitimate network traffic and
conceal their activities. If you aren't inspecting TLS-encrypted traffic, you do not have visibility
into more than 90% of the traffic on your network. In this scenario, those outbound internet
access restrictions I mentioned earlier are even more important, because if you can't inspect
the network traffic before it leaves your network, you shouldn't let it past your firewalls to
sketchy parts of the internet.

**Use cybersecurity vendors' LOTL features**

Major cybersecurity vendors, such as Palo Alto Networks, Cisco, and CrowdStrike, have LOTL
features and functionality built into some of their product offerings. It is prudent to take full
advantage of these features because you need all the help you can get to mitigate this
challenging problem. Here are some pointers to helpful documentation:

**Change is required**

LOTL is the type of problem that will never get better unless organizations change the way
they manage and operate IT systems. "Zero Trust" has become a mantra in our industry, yet we
trust the use of every operating system binary and every non-obvious malicious URL on the
internet implicitly. Attackers are happy to take advantage of this contradiction to continue to
LOTL successfully. CISOs and cybersecurity teams need to lead this change boldly and with a
sense of urgency. The status quo will only sustain LOTL techniques for attackers.

LOTL is a huge topic, and I've only scratched the surface in this chapter. But I hope you benefit
from the analysis and guidance I have provided.

In the next and final chapter of this book, I'll discuss how to secure **artificial intelligence (AI)**
systems and how to use AI to achieve better cybersecurity.
###### **Summary**

This chapter examined why Living Off the Land techniques remain one of the most persistent
and effective approaches used by modern attackers. By abusing native operating-system
binaries, widely trusted tools, legitimate websites, and commonly deployed IT and developer
utilities, attackers are able to blend malicious activity into normal enterprise operations,
significantly reducing the likelihood of detection. The chapter showed that LOTL is not a niche
or emerging technique; it is a core operational model for both criminal and nation-state threat
actors.

A key takeaway is that LOTL succeeds largely because organizations implicitly trust what is
already present in their environments. Fileless malware, LOLBins, trusted cloud-hosted
websites, and administrative tools all benefit from this trust, especially when attackers operate
using valid credentials. This makes traditional, signature-based security controls insufficient

685 _Mitigating "Living Off the Land" Techniques_

on their own and forces defenders to focus more heavily on behavior, context, and intent rather
than artifacts alone.

The chapter emphasized that there is no single control capable of mitigating LOTL techniques.
Effective defense requires a layered approach that combines least privilege, strong identity
controls, application control, network segmentation, centralized logging, and continuous
monitoring. Behavioral detections and IOAs are especially important, as they allow defenders
to identify malicious activity while it is in progress rather than after damage has already
occurred. Guidance from MITRE ATT&CK, CISA, NSA, and allied government agencies
reinforces the importance of focusing on behaviors such as credential abuse, anomalous binary
execution, lateral movement, and misuse of administrative interfaces.

Special attention was given to high-impact tools such as PowerShell, WMI, and ntdsutil.exe,
which are indispensable for administrators but equally valuable to attackers. The lesson is not
to disable these capabilities, but to secure, monitor, and constrain them in ways that preserve
operational value while reducing abuse. Maturity models and published hardening guidance
provide practical paths forward, even in large and complex enterprise environments.

Ultimately, LOTL techniques highlight a broader challenge for cybersecurity teams: balancing
operational necessity with security risk. As long as enterprises continue to implicitly trust
every built-in tool, binary, and widely accessible website, attackers will continue to exploit
that trust. Meaningful progress against LOTL requires intentional change—treating tools,
identities, and network access as privileges rather than defaults and accepting that visibility
and detection are just as critical as prevention.

# 15
##### Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity

_"Who controls the past controls the future. Who controls the present controls the_
_past." — George Orwell, 1949_

Ever since OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022, the world has been obsessed with the
promise of **artificial intelligence (AI)** . AI systems were first seriously contemplated in the
1940s, and development of such systems began in the 1950s. Many enterprises have already
been using various types of AI systems for numerous years; however, OpenAI's generative AI
chatbot demonstrated the potential for AI systems in a way that captured broad attention. The
release of ChatGPT initiated an AI "gold rush," and vendors and organizations started
exploring how they could leverage generative AI, **large language models (LLMs),** and agentic
AI capabilities. The results have disrupted nearly every industry around the world as
developers and vendors embrace new capabilities. This trend is likely to continue indefinitely
as AI is rapidly becoming a foundational component of modern computing.

_Chapter 15_ 690

Given that new AI capabilities are being leveraged across enterprises, many CIOs, CTOs, CISOs,
cybersecurity teams, and vendors are scrambling to understand the risks associated with AI
and how to mitigate them. These new systems share some of the same well-understood
cybersecurity risks as traditional IT systems. After all, they leverage compute, storage, network,
and database resources and services just like traditional systems.

However, generative AI systems differ from traditional enterprise software in that they can
ingest and reason over multiple input types at the same time, spanning far beyond the narrow,
structured formats legacy systems were designed for. Some examples of inputs include:

A range of text inputs including prompts, questions, instructions, partial sentences,
and documents

Structured data such as tables, text in JSON format, and metadata

Images such as pictures, diagrams, PowerPoint slide illustrations, and so on

Audio inputs like audio waveforms or spectrograms (visual representations of sound)

Video inputs like video frames or sequences

Latent space vectors that are compressed, abstract representations of data

Multimodal inputs including text + image, text + audio, image + image, text +
structured data, audio-driven animation, and so on

Because generative AI systems are non-deterministic and capable of producing highly variable
outputs, they introduce new and unpredictable risks that cybersecurity teams must account
for. For example, a generative-AI assistant may refuse a sensitive request nine times in a row
but unexpectedly comply on the tenth, leaking data because its non-deterministic outputs
make harmful behavior appear only intermittently.

Many of the CISOs I've spoken with are skeptical that generative AI can be effectively secured,
and it's not hard to see why. Even the simplest input surface in modern computing, the URL,
has remained one of the most heavily exploited attack vectors for more than three decades. Sir
Tim Berners-Lee published the original URL specification in the 1990s, giving browsers and
servers a formal, tightly constrained input format. Yet browsers that accept essentially one
type of input still generate hundreds of critical and high-severity vulnerabilities every year,
and, as discussed in _Chapter 6, Internet-Based Threats_, attackers send roughly 2.5 billion
phishing emails per month, with more than half weaponizing URLs. In short, a single, wellspecified input type continues to drive both technical exploitation and large-scale socialengineering campaigns.

Against that backdrop, CISOs are understandably skeptical that generative-AI systems, which
must process a far broader and more complex set of inputs, often simultaneously, can be
secured more effectively than web browsers have been. Since generative-AI systems are non

691 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

deterministic, the same input can yield different outputs from one attempt to the next, making
it impossible for users to reliably judge when an answer is trustworthy. It is equally
implausible to assume that attackers will ignore such variability or fail to exploit it. Expecting
these systems to parse every form of content securely or to produce consistently reliable
outputs is unrealistic, and so is believing that adversaries won't leverage their unpredictability
to target consumers and enterprises.

These are just some of the reasons CISOs are concerned about generative AI. These systems are
potentially far more complicated than most of the traditional IT systems that cybersecurity
teams have had to manage in large enterprise environments. By itself, increased complexity
makes it more likely for security incidents to occur. Since enterprises can't simply replace their
older IT systems with new systems all at once, cybersecurity teams will need to manage
security for the decades of legacy IT systems their organizations have invested in, in addition to
the newer, more complicated AI systems. This isn't the first time security teams have been
expected to secure new, rapidly adopted technologies—cloud computing and APIs are the
consummate examples. Given this, it's important that CISOs and cybersecurity teams
understand the new risks associated with these newer technologies.

From an operational cybersecurity standpoint, the CISOs I've spoken with about generative AI,
LLMs, and agentic systems consistently focus, at least initially, on four major categories of risks
and challenges.

1.

2.

3.

4.

Understanding the new risks related to the adoption of new AI capabilities and how
they might increase the attack surface of their organizations

Safeguarding organizational data when third-party AI systems process, store, or
transmit it, whether those systems operate on-premises, in the cloud, or across hybrid
environments

Understanding and defending against cyber-attacks that leverage AI capabilities

Securing AI systems that are developed in-house. These systems share the same
development challenges I discussed in previous chapters, as well as some new ones.

In this chapter, we will explore the first three of these four categories. An entire book could be
dedicated to security development for AI systems—I won't try to do that in a section of one
chapter. I'll endeavor to introduce you to each of the three other aforementioned areas in this
chapter.

We will cover the following topics:

Generative AI safety and cybersecurity risks

Agentic AI and related security risks

Case Study: Security considerations deploying Microsoft Copilot

_Chapter 15_ 692

How attackers leverage AI

Emerging AI security capabilities

Is cybersecurity getting better or worse?

Let's start by examining the risks that accompany the use of generative AI technologies and
LLMs.
###### **Generative AI safety and cybersecurity risks**

CIOs, CTOs, CISOs, and cybersecurity teams are interested in understanding and mitigating
new risks associated with the rapid adoption of generative AI technologies by their
organizations. The stakes are high because, as we've discussed throughout this book, attackers
are relentless and more aggressive now than ever before. Cybersecurity reporting from
governments and major threat intelligence vendors consistently attribute a significant volume
of activity to threat actors operating from DPRK, Iran, China, and Russia, where such actors are
rarely prosecuted. Enterprises face an onslaught of attacks from threat actors based in these
locations as well as throngs of criminals located throughout the Western world. This situation
is pressurized by the necessity for enterprises to evolve IT systems, increase productivity,
reduce costs, and drive consumption and investment.

The adoption of generative AI systems by enterprises has rapidly grown since 2022. There are
plenty of use cases for generative AI and things have been changing rapidly, but some of the
most common are customer service automation and virtual agents, enterprise AI assistants,
document processing and workflow automation, developer productivity / code generation, and
decision-support and analytics assistance (Hadley, L., July 21, 2025). Across these use cases, it
becomes clear that sensitive data is inevitably involved. Take customer service automation for
example. For most enterprises, their customers' personal information is considered sensitive
and is included in the scope of their data protection efforts. This typically includes data such as
names, addresses, phone numbers, genders, birthdates, as well as credit card and banking
information. Data-protection mechanisms for traditional systems have been refined over
decades and are well understood by CISOs. In contrast, the rapid adoption of generative-AI
systems is outpacing the development of comparable safeguards. Developer productivity and
code generation tools are another example. As we discussed in _Chapter 7_, _Application_
_Programming Interface (API) Security_, the mistakes that developers make in development can,
and often do, turn into security incidents in production. Do generative AI coding assist tools
make this challenge better or amplify it? For example, if developers are developing code using
bad programming practices, such as hard coding credentials and keys, does giving AI systems
access to this data exacerbate the problem and increase the risk?

693 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

CISOs and security teams typically have decades of experience securing systems that leverage
traditional computing resources such as compute, network, storage, and databases. Let's
discuss the new risks that specifically accompany generative AI, LLMs, and agentic AI systems.

**AI safety**

Along with their organizations' use of generative AI, one new set of risks that CISOs and
security teams have adopted is collectively referred to as _AI safety_ . AI safety refers to the
principles and practices that help ensure AI systems are developed and used in ways that are
safe and ethical. Where security tends to focus on the confidentiality, integrity, and availability
of data and systems, the concept of AI safety seeks to ensure AI systems are developed and used
with the good of humanity in mind. AI security and safety are dimensions of a broader concept

called _responsible AI_ . Other dimensions of responsible AI include privacy, data governance,
fairness and bias, transparency, and explainability (Nestor Maslej, Loredana Fattorini,
Raymond Perrault, Yolanda Gil, Vanessa Parli, Njenga Kariuki, Emily Capstick, Anka Reuel, Erik
Brynjolfsson, John Etchemendy, Katrina Ligett, Terah Lyons, James Manyika, Juan Carlos
Niebles, Yoav Shoham, Russell Wald, Toby Walsh, Armin Hamrah, Lapo Santarlasci, Julia Betts
Lotufo, Alexandra Rome, Andrew Shi, Sukrut Oak. _The AI Index 2025 Annual Report,_ AI Index
Steering Committee, Institute for Human-Centered AI, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, April
2025).

For most cybersecurity teams, this is a new area of responsibility. Given the dimensions,
responsible AI cuts across numerous corporate functions; CISOs work with **chief privacy**
**officers (CPOs)**, **general counsels (GCs)**, **chief data officers (CDOs)**, and other roles to
provide oversight and guidance on the adoption of AI by their organizations. Many
organizations have pulled these roles together to form AI governance councils or steering
committees.

Failure to take AI safety seriously can result in brand damage for organizations. For example, if
an organization's new generative AI chatbot starts responding to customer inquiries with
extremely inappropriate responses and images, it could lead to dissatisfied customers, loss of
business, regulatory scrutiny, lawsuits, and negative news cycles. Predictably, as more
organizations adopt generative AI, the frequency of AI safety failures has increased. We can get
insight into the scale of these failures from Stanford University's Stanford AI Index Report 2025
—it states the following.

_"The number of AI incident reports continues to increase. According to the AI_
_Incidents Database, the number of reported AI-related incidents rose to 233 in 2024_
_—a record high and a 56.4% increase over 2023" (Maslej et al., 2025)._

There are many recent examples of documented AI safety failures. The following list contains

Given cases such as these, many people are skeptical that generative AI has sufficient
guardrails to protect humanity. Increasing and maintaining trust in these nascent AI systems is
critical to their future success. A loss of stakeholder trust will ultimately undermine the future
potential and adoption of these systems. Although many CISOs remain skeptical, they are
nonetheless charged with addressing the safety and security risks these technologies introduce
as their organizations move quickly to deploy generative AI, LLMs, and agentic systems.

_Table 15.1 – A summary of AI safety risks and their mitigating controls_

Let's take a closer look at a couple of examples from _Table 15.1_ .

First, we'll look at hallucinations. In an AI safety context, hallucinations are a type of
misinformation. A hallucination occurs when a model generates content that appears
confident and coherent but is factually incorrect, fabricated, or unsupported by its training
data or the provided context. It's essentially the model "making something up" while
presenting it as true. For example, a user asks an AI chatbot for a quote attributed to Napoleon,
and the model confidently provides one, even though Napoleon never said it. Another example:
a user asks, "Who won the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics?" and the model confidently replies, "It
was awarded to Stephen Hawking for his work on black hole radiation." This is a hallucination
because Hawking did not win that prize, and the model fabricated a plausible-sounding
answer without any factual basis. The MIT AI Risk Repository describes the risk of such false
and misleading information as "AI systems that inadvertently generate or spread incorrect or
deceptive information, which can lead to inaccurate beliefs in users and undermine their
autonomy. Humans that make decisions based on false beliefs can experience physical,
emotional or material harms" (MIT AI Risk Initiative, 2024). Examples of controls that can
help reduce the frequency of hallucinations include targeted tuning and evaluations, meaning
post-AI model training adjustments specifically focused on improving factual accuracy. This

_Chapter 15_ 698

can involve factual fine-tuning, truthfulness-oriented instruction tuning, counterhallucination training, and domain-specific corrective tuning. Evaluations are structured tests
that measure how often a model hallucinates. Evaluations work by running a model through
curated factuality and adversarial test suites, then measuring how often it produces incorrect
or fabricated answers. Those quantitative scores show whether the model meets safety
thresholds or needs additional tuning to reduce hallucinations. These tests provide
quantitative data to help determine if a model is safe enough for human use or if more tuning
is required. Together, these tools help AI labs improve the performance of their AI models and
reduce hallucinations and misinformation.

Another AI safety risk listed in _Table 15.1_ is the lack of transparency and explainability. Lack of
transparency and explainability refers to situations where an AI system's internal reasoning,
decision pathways, or influencing factors cannot be understood, inspected, or meaningfully
explained by developers, auditors, or end users. This makes it difficult to verify correctness,
detect bias, or ensure the system is behaving as intended. For example, an AI system used in
credit underwriting may issue a loan recommendation without providing any insight into
which variables influenced the outcome or how they were weighted. This opacity prevents
auditors, regulators, and users from understanding the model's reasoning, making it difficult
to assess fairness, accuracy, or compliance. The MIT AI Risk Repository defines this as difficulty
understanding or explaining an AI system's decision-making processes, which can lead to
mistrust, challenges in enforcing compliance or assigning accountability, and an inability to
identify and correct errors (MIT AI Risk Initiative, 2024). To address this, AI labs use
mechanistic and behavioral interpretability together to analyze a model's internal mechanisms
and observable behaviors, helping reveal how the model reasons and where safety risks might
emerge.

_Chapter 15_ 700

Currently, the MIT AI Risk Initiative is likely the best source of information on AI safety risks
and mitigations; at the time of writing, there were "831 mitigations extracted from 13 existing
frameworks and classifications of AI risk mitigations" (MIT AI Risk Initiative, 2024). The Risk
Mitigation Database is available at `[https://airisk.mit.edu/ai-risk-mitigations](https://airisk.mit.edu/ai-risk-mitigations)` .

Next, let's examine new security risks that accompany LLMs.

**New security risks**

At their core, LLMs generate responses by predicting the most likely next piece of text, based on
patterns they learned from the data they were trained on. The frontier AI models developed by
labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are trained on massive collections of text. Their training
process includes randomness, which leads to models that behave probabilistically, generating
language one small step at a time, with each step depending on the one before it. This results
in a learned probability structure that estimates how likely different sequences of words are.
Because these systems are trained on trillions of tokens and contain billions of adjustable
parameters, they can generate a wide range of possible outputs. However, because these
systems learn from large collections of text that include both high-quality information and
low-quality or incorrect material, their responses can reflect that same mix. They generate new
text based on patterns in the data, so the quality of their output depends partly on the quality
of what they were trained on.

According to a paper authored by Mark Russinovich, Ahmed Salem, Santiago Zanella Béguelin,
and Yonatan Zunger, titled "The Price of Intelligence" (2025), these characteristics lead to
these three intrinsic behaviors:

**Hallucination** : the tendency of large language models to occasionally produce answers
that are wrong, fabricated, or nonsensical even when they usually recall the correct
information. In practice, this means a model can retrieve a fact accurately almost every
time yet still fail unpredictably in a small percentage of cases or under slightly different
prompts.

**Jailbreaks** : attempts to manipulate an LLM with carefully crafted prompts so it ignores
its built-in safety rules or ethical constraints. Because these models are trained on
massive, unfiltered text from the internet, which inevitably includes harmful or
undesirable material, attackers can sometimes exploit that knowledge to push the
model into unsafe behavior.

**Indirect prompt injection** : attempts to manipulate an LLM by hiding harmful or
manipulative instructions inside content the user didn't write, such as emails,
documents, or webpages, so the model interprets those hidden instructions as
commands. This happens because current LLMs don't reliably distinguish between

701 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

"data to read" and "instructions to follow," allowing malicious content to influence the
model's behavior in unexpected ways.

These esteemed authors conclude their paper by stating,

_"The future of AI will likely witness the development of more sophisticated LLMs,_
_alongside equally advanced safety mechanisms. For example, the rise of multimodal_
_LLMs that can accept and produce audio, images, and video is already revealing a_
_larger attack vector. By maintaining a balanced approach that harnesses the_
_immense potential of these models while actively addressing their limitations, we_
_can work toward a future where AI systems are not only powerful but also_
_trustworthy and aligned with human values. The journey ahead requires_
_collaboration among researchers, developers, policymakers, and end users to ensure_
_that as LLMs become increasingly integrated into the digital infrastructure, they do_
_so in a manner that is both innovative and responsible." (Russinovich et al., 2025)_

The intrinsic behaviors of LLMs described by these authors aren't simply theoretical, as Red
Teams and security researchers have been proving they can be used to attack AI systems
successfully. Let's dive into these characteristics in a little more detail and look at how
attackers can leverage them.

**Hallucinations**

Hallucinations, instances where an AI system generates false, fabricated, or unjustified
content, are recognized as a core reliability challenge in current mainstream generative models.
As I discussed earlier in this chapter, hallucinations are understood as failures of models to
produce truthful, grounded, or reliable outputs. These failures are due to limitations in training
data, model architecture, or reasoning capabilities. As _Table 15.1_ indicated, mitigations can
include factuality tuning and post-training evaluations to reduce the frequency and severity of
hallucinations. As such, hallucinations are AI model quality issues and, thus, AI safety issues
first and foremost.

However, hallucinations become an AI security issue when they are intentionally induced and
exploited by a threat actor. Through this lens, hallucinations are a "vulnerability surface" that
attackers can leverage to compromise the integrity of AI applications or mislead their users.
Security research reveals that adversarial prompts, indirect prompt injection, and data
poisoning can cause AI models to produce targeted hallucinations that can benefit attackers
(Carlini et al., 2023; Goldstein et al., 2024). In an AI security context, hallucinations typically
involve:

Adversarial prompting to produce harmful or false outputs

Indirect prompt injection (I'll cover this in depth later in the chapter)

_Chapter 15_ 702

AI model manipulation to produce false outputs

Social engineering

We can look to two excellent sources of information to help us understand potential
mitigations and controls for hallucinations in an AI security context—the **Open Worldwide**
**Application Security Project (OWASP)** and MITRE **Adversarial Threat Landscape for**
**Artificial-Intelligence Systems (ATLAS)** . I discussed the OWASP API Security Project in detail
in _Chapter 7_ . There's also an OWASP project focused on AI. The OWASP GenAI Security Project
is a global, open-source effort focused on identifying and reducing the security and safety risks
that come with generative AI systems, including LLMs, agentic AI, and AI-enabled
applications. Its goal is to provide organizations, practitioners, and policymakers with
practical guidance and tools for building, deploying, and governing these systems securely. A
central part of this work is the OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, which
highlights the most critical vulnerabilities found in LLM-based systems. For each AI security
issue in the Top 10, OWASP also includes a description, prevention and mitigation strategies,
examples of attack scenarios, and references. You can find more information at: `[https://](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/)`

`[owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-for-large-language-model-applications/)` .

The MITRE ATLAS is modeled after and complementary to the MITRE ATT&CK framework that
I discussed in detail in _Chapter 11_, _Cybersecurity Strategy Implementation_ . ATLAS is a publicly
available, continuously updated knowledge base that documents how adversaries attack AIenabled systems, drawing on real incidents and realistic red-team demonstrations. It catalogs
the tactics and techniques used against AI models so organizations can better understand, test,
and defend their systems. It currently lists 16 tactics, 147 techniques, 35 mitigations, and 45
case studies. It is accessible at: `[https://atlas.mitre.org/](https://atlas.mitre.org/)` .

Next, let's take a deeper look at another intrinsic vulnerability in LLMs: Jailbreaks.

**Jailbreaks**

An AI jailbreak attack **i** s a technique that manipulates a generative AI system, usually through
crafted prompts, adversarial inputs, or multi-step manipulation, to circumvent its built-in
safety mechanisms, causing the model to violate policies, reveal restricted information, or
execute harmful or unintended instructions. Jailbreaks often leverage prompt injection,
evasion strategies, or model-manipulation methods to override the system's intended
constraints (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2024).

Let's take a deeper look at one type of jailbreak that was identified as an intrinsic vulnerability
of LLMs: indirect prompt injection.

**Indirect prompt injection**

Remember I mentioned earlier that LLM-based chatbots can accept an absurd range of inputs.
Indirect prompt injection attacks are made possible by a core limitation of LLMs—their
inability to reliably distinguish between data and instructions. If attackers can get the system
to execute malicious instructions that are hidden inside data that the system reads, they can
potentially bypass authorization controls, gain access to data, exfiltrate data, stay persistent,
among other illicit actions.

Here's an example of how attackers take advantage of this type of prompt injection

An attacker places a hidden instruction inside something the AI application will later
read, such as a calendar invite, email, document or webpage

The user performs a normal action such as asking the AI application to "summarize my
schedule"

As part of performing the requested operation, the AI application reads the attacker's
hidden instruction and executes it

The execution of the instruction gives the attacker unauthorized access, triggers
actions, or exfiltrates data.

Again, this isn't a theoretical attack. Red Teams and security researchers have demonstrated
indirect prompt injection attacks that work. Here are some recent examples.

In January of 2026, security researchers disclosed details of an indirect prompt injection attack
that enabled attackers to use Google Gemini to bypass authorization guardrails in order to
exfiltrate data using Google Calendar (Lakshmanan, 2026). _Figure 15.1_ illustrates how this

709 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

attack worked. It was also reported that Google addressed this vulnerability to prevent
attackers from using it in the future.

_Figure 15.1 – An illustration of an indirect prompt injection attack using Google Gemini and Google Calendar to_

_exfiltrate private data (Lakshmanan, 2026)_

There is another recent **e** xample of an indirect prompt injection that leveraged ChatGPT to
exfiltrate data and provide a persistent backdoor. In January of 2026, security researchers
revealed new "ZombieAgent" attack techniques that leveraged the Connectors feature of
ChatGPT, which can be used to link the chatbot to third-party services such as email, cloud
storage, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Jira, and GitHub, among others (Constantin, 2026). According
to the researcher Babo (2026), attackers can embed covert instructions within emails or shared
files that, when processed through third-party integrations, cause ChatGPT to execute
unauthorized actions. This mechanism enables zero-click or one-click data exfiltration by
prompting the model to transmit sensitive information to attacker-controlled endpoints,
allowing adversaries to reconstruct the leaked data. The researcher states,

_"We've also demonstrated a method to achieve_ **_persistence_** _, allowing the attacker_
_not just a one-time data leak but ongoing exfiltration: once the attacker infiltrates_
_the chatbot, they can continuously exfiltrate every conversation between the user and_
_ChatGPT._

_In addition, we've demonstrated a new_ **_propagation_** _technique that allows an_
_attack to spread further, target specific victims, and increase the likelihood of_
_reaching additional targets." (Babo, 2026)._

In 2025, security researchers demonstrated prompt injection attacks in popular chatbots, AI
agent platforms, AI-enabled browsers, and AI coding assistants (Constantin, 2025). Given that
this behavior is an intrinsic characteristic of LLMs, it will likely be challenging to fully mitigate
this type of attack in all scenarios and use cases. CISOs, security teams, and the cybersecurity
vendor ecosystem that supports them will need to find ways to detect and block such attacks if
enterprises are going to embrace LLMs with confidence.

_Chapter 15_ 710

Now that we've examined AI safety and security of generative AI systems, focusing on LLMs,
let's take a look at another type of AI system that is becoming popular: agentic AI.
###### **Agentic AI and related security risks**

Generative AI produces content such as text, images, and code. Agentic AI is not a subset of
generative AI the way LLMs are. Instead, these systems are built on top of generative AI models
and add capabilities such as taking actions, using tools, and pursuing goals autonomously.
Agentic AI systems use generative models, including LLMs, as components for planning,
reasoning, and acting. Enterprises that adopt such agents can improve efficiency by
automating repetitive tasks with greater speed and scalability. They can operate under human
supervision or autonomously, depending on the organization's governance and risk
requirements.

An illustrative example of an agentic AI system is a customer-support automation agent that
can read incoming support emails, classify the customer's issue, retrieve relevant knowledgebase articles, draft a response, update the ticket in a **Customer Relationship Management**
**(CRM)** system, and **e** scalate complex cases without requiring a human to manually trigger
each step.

AI agents are developed with five components (Microsoft, 2024):

Generative AI model – agents use models as reasoning engines. In the customersupport automation example, the agent relies on an underlying LLM to read incoming
emails, interpret customer issues, and draft responses—tasks that require language
understanding, summarization, and generation.

Instructions – establish agents' roles, limits, and expected conduct. In this case, the
agent follows predefined instructions that govern how it classifies issues using the
organization's taxonomy and how it applies support-tier escalation rules.

Retrieval – supplies the factual context an agent needs to respond accurately,
minimizing hallucinations. The agent retrieves relevant knowledge-base articles,
customer history from the CRM, and prior ticket context to ensure its responses are
grounded in authoritative enterprise data.

Actions – the APIs, functions, and systems agents rely on to execute tasks. This enables
agents to go beyond information retrieval. The agent performs multi-step actions
across systems, such as updating CRM tickets, attaching knowledge-base links,
sending draft responses, and escalating cases to human agents. These behaviors
represent tool use and system-level execution, core characteristics of agentic AI.

Memory – stores conversation histories and states to ensure continuity across
interactions. The agent maintains short-term and long-term state, including

711 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

conversation history with the customer, the current ticket's workflow status, and prior
classification decisions. This memory enables coherent, multi-turn support without
losing context.

Agentic AI introduces risks that go beyond the generative AI safety and security risks I
discussed earlier in the chapter. Agentic AI systems can act—they aren't just limited to content
generation. The most serious threats involve tool misuse, privilege escalation, unsafe
autonomy, and cascading operational failures. _Table 15.4_ summarizes examples of agentic-AI
risk categories, example threats for each category, and the corresponding mitigating controls
from MITRE ATLAS or MITRE ATT&CK when official mappings exist. Several risk categories do
not yet have associated MITRE mitigations. This reflects the emerging nature of agentic-AI
security; while some attack patterns are well-characterized, many others are still under active
research and have not been formally codified by MITRE, NIST, or other standards bodies.
Mitigations for agentic-AI attacks are expected to evolve rapidly as the field matures.

We've examined AI safety issues and key security risks associated with generative and agentic
AI. Next, we'll look at the security considerations CISOs and security teams must address when
deploying popular AI applications within enterprise environments.
###### **Case study: Security considerations deploying** **Microsoft Copilot**

Microsoft Copilot is an AI assistant embedded across Microsoft 365, Windows, Edge, and Azure
services. It is context-aware and uses natural language to help people create, analyze,
automate, discover, and retrieve information using three core elements:

   - **LLMs:** Copilot uses LLMs to interpret intent, generate content, summarize
information, and orchestrate actions across Microsoft applications

_Chapter 15_ 714

**The Microsoft Graph:** a unified API and data fabric that exposes the relationships
among users, files, messages, identities, devices, and applications across Microsoft 365
core services, Enterprise Mobility and Security services, Windows services, Dynamics
365 Business Central services, and Microsoft Partner Center services (Microsoft, n.d.).
It provides a single programmable interface for querying, analyzing, and acting on
organizational data with consistent security and permissions.

**Copilot users' enterprise data:** Copilot operates on users' content such as emails,
documents, chats, calendars, files, and business data — respecting the same
permissions and security boundaries defined in Microsoft Entra.

_Figure 15.2_ illustrates a high-level architecture to give you an idea of how these elements work
together (Microsoft, n.d.).

_Figure 15.2 – Microsoft 365 Copilot architecture with prompt flow labelled (Microsoft, n.d.)_

The numbered lines in _Figure 15.2_ illustrate how a Copilot prompt flows through the
architecture. The data Copilot uses to generate responses is encrypted in transit using
**transport layer security (TLS)** . The flow is as follows:

1.

2.

From an authorized device, a user enters a prompt into Copilot in a Microsoft 365
application.

Copilot preprocesses the input prompt using grounding and accesses Microsoft Graph
in the user's organization's Microsoft 365 cloud tenant.

Grounding is the process Copilot uses to tie its AI-generated output back to
relevant data sources rather than relying solely on its pre-trained general

715 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

knowledge. This improves the accuracy of responses. There are three types of
grounding (Microsoft, 2024):

1.

2.

3.

**Work Grounding:** Uses **i** nformation specific to the user's organization,
such as emails, files, chats, meetings, and internal web content accessible
through Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Graph

**Web Grounding:** Incorporates current, publicly available data on the
internet.

**Local Data Grounding:** Utilizes **c** ontent the user attached or provided
directly in their prompt, such as files or links

3.

4.

Copilot sends the grounded prompt to the LLM. The LLM uses the prompt to generate a
response that is contextually relevant to the user's task.

Copilot returns the prompt response to the application the user entered the prompt
into in step 1.

Now that you understand how it works from a high level, let's look at security aspects of this
technology in a little more detail. CISOs must grasp a broad set of issues, from the AI
vulnerabilities and attack patterns outlined earlier in the chapter to the wider responsibilities
of governance, compliance, insider-risk management, and related organizational threats.

Most CISOs I've talked to about their Copilot adoption journeys were initially concerned with
two specific risks. First, what happens to their users' prompts? If users enter confidential
information into Copilot, who has access to it? Does Microsoft use that information to train
their AI models, and could that information show up in prompt responses for users outside of
their organization? The prompts, grounding data, and responses remain inside each
organization's Microsoft 365 tenant. Access to data in each organization's tenant is governed
by each organization's own Entra ID permissions, Purview sensitivity labels, **Data Loss**
**Prevention (DLP)** policies, Conditional Access, and Zero Trust controls. Enterprise customer
data is not used to train Microsoft's foundation models, and it remains within the customer's
Microsoft 365 tenant without flowing across tenants (Microsoft, 2024).

The second risk that CISOs are typically concerned about is sensitive data being included in
Copilot prompt responses. This is a result of Copilot enabling enterprise network users to
discover data that they didn't know they had access to, like no other tool before. For decades,
enterprises didn't pay much attention to permission hygiene on their networks. Data
classification was deemed too difficult for users to manage, so the vast majority of content on
their networks remained unclassified, and content was treated like it all had the same value.
The content stored and shared on SharePoint sites and OneDrive accounts was largely
unclassified, and the access permissions for such content were typically overly broad to make
administration easy and to make self-service administration possible for users. After years or

_Chapter 15_ 716

decades of such undisciplined practices, enterprises have vast estates of ungoverned data, and
access permissions to all this data are poorly understood. Most enterprises suffer from overpermissioned identities, and they have failed to follow the principle of least privilege
consistently, if at all.

Suddenly, Copilot becomes available and enables users to easily discover data they had no idea
they had access to. I'm sure many users were stunned when early Copilot queries about
executive compensation and other sensitive HR details surfaced confidential information,
revealing that they unknowingly had access to HR documents they were never meant to see.
The security by obscurity that was traditionally created by a lack of discoverability is now
broken by Copilot's awesome grounding capabilities.

CISOs and security teams now face the difficult task of reversing years, often decades, of weak
or inconsistent data governance. Clearly, Microsoft understands this and has provided tools
and guidance to help enterprises successfully adopt Copilot with effective data protection
processes and controls. I've been involved in a couple of enterprise Copilot deployments, so I'll
share some of the things I've learned.

I suggest deploying Copilot using a phased approach. This will give you control, reduce
surprises, and let you build capabilities and confidence as you make progress. _Table 15.5_
provides a list of deployment phases and their descriptions.

|Deployment Phase|Theme|
|---|---|
|1. Strategic foundations|Establish governance, risk boundaries, and<br>technical prerequisites to set the direction for<br>Copilot|
|2. Data and access hardening|Clean up permissions, labels, and indexing to<br>ensure Copilot accesses only the right data.|
|3. Policy, controls, and guardrails|Implement organizational policies and safety<br>controls to govern responsible Copilot use.|
|4. Pilot, Training, and Adoption|Validate use cases, train users, and roll out<br>Copilot in controlled tranches for safe<br>adoption.|

|Deployment Phase|Theme|

_Table 15.5 – Phases that can be used to deploy Microsoft Copilot in an enterprise IT environment_

Let me provide a little more detail about the objectives and activities in each phase.

In **Phase 1: Strategic Foundations**, the deployment team should establish governance, define
the organization's risk appetite, and fulfill technical prerequisites. The major work items in this
phase include the following:

Establish an **AI Governance Committee (AIGC)** that operates as a cross-discipline
oversight group to guide Copilot strategy, risk decisions, and accountability. It is
typically staffed by senior leaders across Data/AI Operations, IT, Legal, Audit,
Compliance, Cybersecurity, and major business units

Define the organization's risk tolerance and set boundaries for acceptable AI use

Identify potential use cases for Copilot and prioritize business scenarios

Confirm that all licensing and technical requirements are satisfied, ensuring the correct
Copilot licenses, supported application versions, and necessary platform conditions are
established prior to starting the deployment

In **Phase 2: Data & Access Hardening**, the deployment team focuses on data classification and
labeling and addressing excessive permissions. Work items include:

Auditing access controls to identify and remediate excessive permissions and outdated
access patterns

Revisiting your organization's data classification policy and simplifying it if it's too
complicated to be successful. Auditing sensitivity labels that have been applied to data
with this policy in mind. Evaluating data classification coverage and identifying data
that has not been classified or classified properly.

Implementing sensitivity labels with Microsoft Purview or other tools that allow you to
determine the sensitivity of existing data in SharePoint, OneDrive, and other places
where data is stored. Applying and enforcing data labeling policies to enable ongoing
visibility and control of sensitive data.

_Chapter 15_ 718

Validating and optimizing Microsoft Search and content indexing across SharePoint,
OneDrive, Exchange, and Teams to ensure Copilot can retrieve and ground responses in
high-quality organizational data.

Ensuring that core security measures, including MFA, device compliance policies,
Conditional Access rules, and session controls, are properly applied and enforced for all
Copilot users.

**Phase 3: Policy, Controls & Guardrails** focuses on implementing organizational policies and
safety controls for responsible Copilot use. Focus areas in this phase include:

Establishing AI policies and acceptable use guidelines that define clear rules for how
employees should use Copilot and handle sensitive information. Asking users for their
help can be a powerful, scalable control

Deploying data-loss prevention, insider-risk, and compliance safeguards by
configuring Microsoft Purview and associated tools to identify, prevent, and remediate
unsafe or inappropriate data activity

Creating an approval process for evaluating new features and use cases prior to their
adoption

Configuring Copilot safety, governance, and extensibility controls, such as content
filtering, plugin and connector restrictions, and policy-based safeguards to minimize
misuse and align Copilot behavior with organizational requirements

**In Phase 4: Pilot, Training & Adoption**, the deployment team validates use cases, trains
users, and rolls out Copilot in defined tranches. These work items will help accomplish this:

Setting up pilot projects to learn and validate assumptions before scaling

Creating a structured user-training program to drive adoption, effective use, and
overall value, providing role-tailored guidance on prompting techniques, responsible
use expectations, and the specific Copilot features relevant to each group

Recruiting early adopters to accelerate learning and adoption across the organization
by supporting their peers' training and use of Copilot and funneling feedback to the
deployment team and AIGC

Deploying Copilot to users gradually in defined tranches to manage risk, support
adoption, and refine controls between cohorts

719 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

**Finally, in Phase 5: Monitoring, Audit & Continuous Improvement**, monitor Copilot usage
and outcomes so that you can refine the governance process as needed. These activities can
help do this:

Establishing an audit program for Copilot or your wider AI ecosystem that outlines
how usage patterns, data access, and adherence to organizational policies will be
monitored, assessed, and verified

Developing baselines and performing continuous monitoring to help identify data
leakage and governance violations

Assessing Copilot's effectiveness by monitoring adoption trends, analyzing
productivity improvements, and gathering user feedback to understand its overall
business impact

Regularly updating and adjusting your policies, access permissions, and safeguard
controls to keep pace with Copilot's evolution and the emergence of new risks
