So far in this chapter we've focused on some of the safety and security risks associated with
generative and agentic AI systems. We also looked at some of the security risks associated with
Microsoft Copilot adoption and related controls. Next, let's shift gears and discuss how
attackers have been leveraging AI systems in their attacks and examine how AI has changed
threat actors' kill chains.
###### **How attackers leverage AI**

Numerous reports of attackers leveraging AI capabilities in their attacks have been published
over the past few years. During this time, frontier AI labs, such as Anthropic and Microsoft,
have shared insights into how threat actors have been leveraging AI. Security researchers and
Red Teams have also been busy publishing results of their research into how AI can be used to
improve attackers' capabilities.

Perhaps the best way to aggregate and present these various insights is to plug them into the
intrusion kill chain model we discussed in depth in _Chapter 11_ . You might remember this

_Chapter 15_ 720

modified Courses of Action Matrix, illustrated in _Table 15.6_ . Revisit _Chapter 11_ if you do not
remember all the details.

_Table 15.6 – Example of an updated Courses of Action Matrix_

In this section, I introduce an AI-enabled intrusion kill chain that integrates our modified killchain phases with the AI techniques threat actors have leveraged in recent years. I also
reference techniques from both MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE ATLAS. Modern intrusions now
blend traditional cyber tactics with AI-enabled behaviors, and neither of these two frameworks
captures that full picture, but they complement each other nicely. To provide a more complete
view of how attackers operate across the kill chain, this model incorporates both frameworks,
each serving a distinct purpose. ATT&CK anchors the model in well-understood, traditional
adversary behavior, while ATLAS highlights the AI-specific techniques and attack paths that
ATT&CK does not cover. Note that these lists are not meant to be exhaustive, and that attackers
are quickly evolving their use of AI.

Let's start with the Reconnaissance I phase.

**Reconnaissance I (pre-intrusion)**

The Reconnaissance stage of the Intrusion Kill Chain can be divided into two distinct phases
because attackers gather information at different points in a traditional network intrusion.
Before any compromise occurs, they might study potential targets, evaluate weaknesses, and
determine viable attack paths. After gaining an initial foothold, often through one or more of
the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects, attackers typically conduct a second round of
reconnaissance to understand the victim's internal environment, identify High-Value Assets,
and locate sensitive data. Separating these activities into Reconnaissance I (pre-intrusion) and
Reconnaissance II (post-compromise) makes it easier to align defenses with the specific tools,
techniques, and behaviors used at each stage. In both phases, adversaries might rely on either

721 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

low-impact, passive information gathering or more intrusive probing, depending on their
objectives and risk tolerance.

Industry reporting indicates that attackers have increasingly incorporated AI into the
Reconnaissance I phase of intrusions (OpenAI, 2024; Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2024;
Abnormal Security, 2025). One common use involves LLM-assisted research on target
technologies, infrastructure, and publicly available information. Nation-state actors, in
particular, have been observed using large language models to summarize open-source data,
study potential targets, and refine phishing content with greater speed and precision.

Attackers have also relied on AI to translate and summarize **open** - **source intelligence**
**(OSINT)**, enabling them to process large volumes of publicly accessible material more
efficiently. By automating OSINT collection and enrichment, AI tools help adversaries identify
exposed assets, organizational details, and other reconnaissance-relevant insights that would
otherwise require significant manual effort.

Another documented use case involves generating pretexts and synthetic social-engineering
personas. AI systems have been used to craft convincing identities, communication styles, and
tailored narratives that support phishing and other forms of human-targeted reconnaissance.
These capabilities allow attackers to scale social-engineering campaigns while increasing their
believability.

AI has further been applied to automated scanning, enrichment, and profiling of potential
victims. Adversaries have used AI tools to analyze public identity data, summarize employee
roles, and map organizational structures. This automated profiling improves attacker
efficiency by helping them prioritize high-value targets and identify individuals with elevated
access or influence.

In addition, attackers have used LLMs to generate highly tailored phishing lures designed to
increase engagement. These AI-generated emails often exhibit natural language fluency and
contextual relevance, making them more effective as reconnaissance probes and initial access
vectors.

Finally, some threat actors have employed AI-generated deepfake voice techniques during
reconnaissance. By cloning executive voices, attackers have attempted to impersonate senior
leaders in phone-based interactions to extract sensitive information or manipulate employees.
This represents a more intrusive but increasingly accessible form of AI-enabled
reconnaissance.

**Mitigations**

Let's look at how defenders can try to mitigate these techniques by looking at mitigations
provided by ATT&CK and ATLAS (MITRE, n.d.). It's no surprise that both recommend user
training to mitigate these techniques. ATT&CK recommends training users to recognize and

_Chapter 15_ 722

report social engineering and suspicious messages (ATT&CK Mitigation ID 1017 - User
Training).

ATLAS provides more granular recommendations for mitigating these techniques. Its guidance
includes training users to recognize AI-enhanced lures, such as unusual tone, urgency cues, or
stylistic inconsistencies that may indicate synthetic content. It also emphasizes strengthening
identity-verification processes for high-risk interactions to reduce the likelihood of
impersonation or fraudulent requests. In addition, ATLAS recommends requiring secondary
human verification for sensitive or atypical voice-based requests, particularly in scenarios
where attackers may attempt to exploit deepfake audio to manipulate employees or extract
confidential information.

Let's look at the next phase in attackers' kill chains: Weaponization.

**Weaponization**

The Weaponization phase of the intrusion kill chain is where attackers prepare the malicious
payload they will use to compromise the target's network. This might involve building a
weapon, buying a weapon, or partnering with others to build or buy a weapon. In _Chapter 11_, I
removed the Weaponization phase from our modified Courses of Action Matrix because it
typically happens out of the view of defenders. Outside of **c** onsuming **Cyber Threat**
**Intelligence (CTI)** and working with intelligence and law enforcement agencies, defenders
typically don't have controls that can impede attackers during the Weaponization phase.
However, several credible cyber threat intelligence sources have documented how attackers are
incorporating AI into the Weaponization phase of their operations (Anthropic, 2024; Google
Threat Intelligence Group, 2025; KELA Cyber Threat Intelligence, 2025). Reports indicate that
adversaries have used AI models to generate new malware variants and mutate existing
samples in ways that help them evade signature-based detection. AI has also been applied to
exploit development, where models assist in drafting exploit code, refining payloads, and
debugging, thereby accelerating the overall development workflow. In addition, attackers have
leveraged AI to produce multilingual phishing kits, templates, and scripts that closely mimic
corporate branding and communication styles, making downstream delivery more convincing.
Threat actors have also used AI to automate infrastructure setup by generating scripts for
command-and-control configuration, staging servers, and other operational components.
Finally, AI has been employed to assemble social engineering kits that include scripts,
personas, and deepfake media, enabling more sophisticated and scalable phishing and fraud
campaigns.

Clearly, AI is popular with threat actors in this phase because it lowers technical barriers to
entry and accelerates their preparations, thus lowering costs and potentially increasing their
returns on investment. Let's look at mitigations for these AI-enabled techniques.

723 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

**Mitigations**

ATT&CK provides several mitigations relevant to AI-enabled weaponization techniques
(MITRE, n.d.). These include the use of antimalware tools with heuristic and behavior-based
detection to counter malicious code (mitigation ID M1049), as well as exploit-protection
mechanisms such as **Data Execution Prevention (DEP)**, **Address Space Layout**
**Randomization (ASLR)**, and **c** ontrol-flow integrity to reduce exploit success rates (M1050).
ATT&CK also emphasizes user training (M1017), recommending that organizations educate
employees to recognize and report phishing attempts, suspicious messages, and other forms of
social engineering. In addition, network segmentation (M1030) is advised to limit the reach of
compromised accounts or systems and reduce the blast radius of a successful intrusion.

ATLAS offers complementary guidance tailored to AI-specific threats (MITRE, n.d.). Its
recommendations include deploying behavior-based and machine-learning-driven detection
capable of identifying AI-mutated malware samples that may evade traditional signaturebased tools. ATLAS also encourages the use of hardened execution environments that apply
exploit mitigations and secure configurations to reduce exploit reliability. To counter AIgenerated phishing kits, ATLAS recommends enhancing email security with content and
behavior-based detection tuned to synthetic patterns. It further advises restricting automation
tools and scripts to least-privilege network segments to limit misuse. Finally, ATLAS highlights
the importance of AI-aware user training that helps employees recognize AI-enhanced lures,
synthetic personas, and other emerging social-engineering techniques

Let's look at the Delivery phase next.

**Delivery**

The Delivery phase is where attackers send their chosen weapon(s) to the target environment
using vectors such as email, web downloads, removable media, or direct network delivery via a
malicious insider. It represents the moment when the weapon leaves the attacker's control and
is introduced into the victim's environment. Delivery can be highly targeted or broadly
distributed, depending on the attacker's objectives and resources. Defenders often have strong
visibility and controls here, making this one of the most critical phases for defense.

Reports from multiple threat-intelligence sources describe several ways attackers have begun
using AI during the Delivery phase of intrusions (Abnormal Security, 2025; KELA Cyber Threat
Intelligence, 2025; Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2024). Threat actors have used AI to generate
multilingual phishing lures, translating and localizing content to increase credibility across
different regions and language groups. They have also leveraged AI models to produce
malicious attachments, including documents containing embedded macros or scripts designed
to execute upon opening. In addition, some attackers have employed AI-generated or AI

_Chapter 15_ 724

altered deepfake videos to impersonate trusted individuals, enhancing the believability of
scams and increasing the likelihood that recipients will engage with the malicious content.

Let's explore some mitigations for these techniques.

**Mitigations**

MITRE's ATT&CK and ATLAS frameworks each provide relevant mitigations for AI-enabled
delivery techniques (MITRE, n.d.). ATT&CK highlights several controls, including user training
(mitigation ID M1017) to help employees recognize phishing attempts across different
languages and detect manipulated or suspicious media. It also recommends deploying
antimalware tools with heuristic and behavior-based detection (M1049) to identify malicious
content embedded in attachments or delivered through other channels.

Offer complementary guidance tailored to AI-driven delivery threats. Recommendations
include implementing language-agnostic phishing detection capable of identifying malicious
content across diverse languages and encodings, as well as using sandboxing and contentdetonation environments to safely analyze suspicious attachments before they reach end
users. Also advise encouraging verification of unusual or unexpected video-based requests,
particularly in scenarios where attackers may attempt to use AI-generated or altered media to
increase the credibility of their lures.

Next, let's look at how threat actors are using AI in the exploitation phase.

**Exploitation**

The Exploitation phase **i** s where the attacker or victim activates the weapon, such as exploiting
a vulnerability to gain initial execution on the target system. Remember, initial access is always
gained by using one or a combination of the Cybersecurity Usual Suspects. It's the moment
when the malicious content transitions from passive to active, exploiting unpatched
vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or user actions to run code. This phase often relies on
techniques such as exploit kits, malicious links or attachments, drive-by downloads, or
credential-harvesting scripts.

Reports from multiple threat-intelligence sources indicate that attackers have begun using AI
to enhance their activities during the Exploitation phase (Anthropic, 2024; Google Threat
Intelligence Group, 2025; KELA Cyber Threat Intelligence, 2025). Adversaries have leveraged AI
models to assist in generating exploit code, enabling them to draft functional exploits more
quickly and accelerate development timelines. They have also used AI to debug and refine
exploits by feeding crash logs or error outputs into models, allowing the AI to suggest
adjustments that improve reliability. In addition, attackers have applied AI to tailor exploit
payloads to specific operating system versions, configurations, or environmental conditions,
increasing the likelihood of successful execution. Some threat actors have also experimented

725 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

with prompt-injection and model-abuse techniques, crafting malicious prompts designed to
bypass model safeguards or extract confidential information from AI systems themselves.

**Mitigations**

Cybersecurity teams place significant emphasis on halting intrusions at the Exploitation phase
because once an attacker gains execution, the remaining kill-chain actions, such as lateral
movement, persistence, data theft, and destructive activity, can unfold rapidly, dramatically
increasing the effort, time, and cost required for containment and recovery. ATT&CK highlights
several mitigations relevant to this phase (MITRE, n.d.). These include the use of exploitprotection mechanisms (mitigation ID M1050) to reduce the reliability of exploitation
attempts, as well as disabling unnecessary or vulnerable features and services (M1042) to
shrink the attack surface and limit opportunities for initial execution.

ATLAS provides complementary mitigations tailored to AI-enabled exploitation techniques
(MITRE, n.d.). Its guidance emphasizes the importance of hardened execution environments
that apply exploit mitigations and secure configurations to reduce the likelihood of successful
code execution. ATLAS also recommends secure debugging and logging practices to detect
suspicious crash patterns or exception behaviors that may indicate exploit development or
testing. Additional recommendations include reducing the exposed attack surface by
minimizing unnecessary services and APIs and implementing prompt and input validation to
help prevent prompt-injection attacks against AI-enabled systems.

Now let's look at the next phase in our AI-enabled kill chain, the installation phase.

**Installation**

The Installation phase is where the attacker establishes a persistent foothold by placing
malware, backdoors, remote control software, or other execution mechanisms onto
compromised systems. It's the point in the attack where the initial compromise transitions
into a durable presence, often through backdoors, loaders, scheduled tasks, or registry
modifications. Attackers might deploy multiple redundant mechanisms to ensure they can
regain access if one is discovered or removed, making containment more difficult.

At least three CTI sources have reported that attackers can use AI in this phase of their attacks
(Anthropic, 2024; Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2025; KELA Cyber Threat Intelligence,
2025). Threat actors have leveraged AI models to customize malware, modifying code and
generating new variants designed to evade detection. They have also used AI to optimize
implants by tuning configuration settings, persistence mechanisms, and operational
parameters to improve reliability once deployed. In addition, attackers have applied AI to
produce more complex obfuscation and packing schemes, making malicious code harder for
defenders to analyze or detect. Some reports further indicate that adversaries have used AI

_Chapter 15_ 726

models to select and adjust persistence techniques, refining them for durability and stealth
within the compromised environment.

This suggests that attackers with limited technical expertise are now leveraging AI to generate
installation mechanisms that exceed what they could build on their own. Let's look at
mitigations next.

**Mitigations**

ATT&CK provides several mitigations relevant to the Installation phase (MITRE, n.d.). These
include deploying antimalware tools with heuristic and behavior-based detection (mitigation
ID M1049) to identify malicious code introduced during installation, as well as hardening
operating system configurations (M1028) to reduce the likelihood that persistence
mechanisms or configuration-based footholds can be established. Strengthening baseline
configurations helps limit the avenues attackers can use to embed backdoors, loaders, or other
persistence artifacts.

Offer complementary mitigations tailored to AI-enabled installation techniques (MITRE, n.d.).
Its guidance emphasizes the use of behavior-based and machine-learning-driven detection
capable of identifying malware variants that have been customized or obfuscated using AI.
ATLAS also recommends monitoring for unusual or redundant persistence mechanisms, which
may indicate automated implant tuning or AI-assisted persistence selection. Additional
recommendations include using sandboxing and automated unpacking tools to analyze
heavily obfuscated or packed samples, as well as monitoring common persistence locations to
detect unauthorized modifications or newly created footholds.

If attackers succeed in this phase, they can potentially move to the C2 phase—let's examine it
next.

**Command and Control (C2)**

The Command and Control (C2) phase is where the attacker establishes a communication
channel between their infrastructure and the compromised systems. Through this channel,
they can issue commands, move laterally, exfiltrate data, or deploy additional tooling. C2 can
use traditional methods like HTTP(S), DNS, or VPN tunnels, or more covert techniques such as
cloud-based services or encrypted messaging platforms.

Credible reporting indicates that attackers have also begun using AI to enhance their activities
during the C2 phase of intrusions (Anthropic, 2024; Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2025;
Abnormal Security, 2025). Threat actors have used AI models to generate C2 scripts that
automate beaconing, tasking, and other routine communication functions between
compromised systems and attacker infrastructure. They have also leveraged AI to design C2
traffic that mimics legitimate application protocols, making malicious communications harder
for defenders to distinguish from normal network activity. In addition, attackers have applied

727 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

AI to orchestrate and script repetitive C2 workflows, enabling more efficient management of
compromised hosts and reducing the manual effort required to maintain control over an
intrusion.

Again, it appears that AI is lowering the technical barrier for entry into cybercrime and helping
attackers potentially achieve better results, faster. This phase is essential for defenders to
disrupt because once attackers establish C2, they gain stable, ongoing remote access to
compromised systems—access they can leverage to automate malicious tasks, move laterally,
escalate privileges, deploy additional tooling, exfiltrate data, and continue expanding their
control.

Let's look at mitigations for AI-enabled C2.

**Mitigations**

ATT&CK provides several mitigation options that can help defenders disrupt AI-enabled C2
activity (MITRE, n.d.). These include filtering network traffic to and from sensitive systems
(mitigation ID M1037) to limit an attacker's ability to communicate with compromised hosts,
as well as applying network segmentation (M1030) to constrain the reach of C2 channels and
reduce the attacker's ability to move laterally or maintain persistent communication paths.

ATLAS offers complementary mitigations tailored to detecting and constraining AI-driven C2
behavior (MITRE, n.d.). Its guidance emphasizes the use of anomaly-based detection to
identify unusual communication patterns that may indicate AI-generated or dynamically
adapted C2 traffic. ATLAS also recommends establishing protocol fingerprints and behavioral
baselines so deviations from normal application behavior can be identified more readily. In
addition, it advises restricting automation tools and scripts to least-privilege network
segments, reducing the risk that attackers can misuse automated workflows to maintain or
expand control over compromised systems. Once attackers can remotely control systems and
deploy tools, they might want to further explore their victims' networks. Let's see how AI has
been helping them do this.

**Reconnaissance II (post-compromise)**

Reconnaissance II is the post-compromise discovery phase, where attackers explore their
victims' environments. During this phase, they enumerate internal systems, credentials,
network paths, data stores, and security controls. The goal is to understand the organization's
internal topology well enough to plan lateral movement, privilege escalation, or data
collection. This phase often blends automated tooling, using both legitimate software and
malware, with hands-on exploration to map the most valuable paths forward.

At least a couple of credible cyber threat intelligence vendors have reported that attackers are
beginning to use AI to enhance their post-compromise discovery activities during
Reconnaissance II (Anthropic, 2024; Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2024). Threat actors have

_Chapter 15_ 728

used AI models to summarize internal files, logs, and other collected data, allowing them to
quickly understand the environment and determine their next steps. They have also fed
network-scan outputs into AI systems to map internal networks, identify exposed services, and
highlight high-value targets more efficiently than manual analysis alone. In addition, attackers
have applied AI to analyze account roles and permissions, helping them identify potential
privilege-escalation paths and prioritize the most advantageous routes for lateral movement.

This phase can actually work in defenders' favor, since overly aggressive or noisy
reconnaissance tools often expose the attacker. Building strong detections around the tools
adversaries commonly rely on increases the chances of catching them before they deploy
ransomware or take actions on objectives. Here are mitigations from ATT&CK and ATLAS
(MITRE, n.d.):

**Mitigations**

ATT&CK provides several mitigations that can help defenders limit the effectiveness of
attacker activity during the Reconnaissance II phase (MITRE, n.d.). These include regularly
auditing systems, permissions, and access patterns (mitigation ID M1047) to identify misuse or
unauthorized privilege changes, as well as applying network segmentation (M1030) to restrict
an attacker's ability to explore internal systems freely. ATT&CK also recommends strong
privileged-account management (M1026), ensuring that elevated accounts are tightly
controlled, monitored, and limited according to least-privilege principles.

ATLAS offers complementary mitigations tailored to AI-enabled reconnaissance techniques
(MITRE, n.d.). Its guidance emphasizes governing access to internal AI tools so that only
authorized identities and systems can interact with them, reducing the risk that attackers can
misuse AI-assisted capabilities for internal discovery. ATLAS also recommends restricting AIassisted tooling to segmented, least-privilege views so that even if an attacker gains access to
an AI system, the model's visibility is intentionally constrained. In addition, ATLAS advises
enforcing least-privilege AI context, ensuring that any AI system, whether an internal model, a
Copilot-style assistant, or an agentic workflow, receives only the minimum contextual
information, permissions, and data access required to perform its intended function. Critically,
the AI should not inherit the full privileges of a user, service account, or environment unless
absolutely necessary.

If attackers took the time to perform some reconnaissance in their victims' environment, that
represented the last opportunity defenders had to detect them before the final phase in the
attackers' kill chain, Actions on Objectives. Let's look at this phase next.

**Actions on objectives**

The Actions on Objectives phase marks the point where the attacker finally carries out the
purpose of the intrusion, such as stealing data, committing fraud, causing disruption, or

729 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

delivering destructive effects. With their foothold, persistence, and control already in place,
they move into collecting, manipulating, or exfiltrating the information or systems they
targeted. This stage can involve lateral movement to reach high-value systems, staging and
compressing data, or executing ransomware or sabotage. Everything in the earlier phases of
the kill chain has been building toward this moment, where the attacker achieves their
operational goals.

We have at least three credible cyber threat intelligence sources describing how attackers have
begun leveraging AI during the Actions on Objectives phase (Anthropic, 2024; Google Threat
Intelligence Group, 2025; KELA Cyber Threat Intelligence, 2025). Threat actors have used AI
models to triage large volumes of stolen data, summarizing and prioritizing exfiltrated content
to identify what is most valuable or actionable. They have also applied AI to plan follow-on
exploitation, using models to propose next steps based on the nature of the compromised data.
In addition, attackers have relied on AI to support fraud and monetization workflows by
generating scam scripts, social-engineering narratives, and other operational materials. AI has
also been used to organize and compress data for exfiltration, streamlining the staging process
and reducing the time required to move large datasets. Finally, some adversaries have
employed AI to analyze internal topology and recommend lateral-movement routes, helping
them navigate complex environments more efficiently as they work to achieve their
operational objectives.

These examples show how AI is enabling attackers to professionalize and refine the final stages
of their operations. Now we can examine the defensive measures that help disrupt these
techniques.

**Mitigations**

ATT&CK identifies several mitigations that can help defenders reduce the impact of attacker
activity during the Actions on Objectives phase (MITRE, n.d.). These include regularly auditing
systems and data-access patterns (mitigation ID M1047) to detect misuse or unauthorized
retrieval of sensitive information, as well as training users to recognize suspicious financial
activity that may indicate fraud or monetization attempts (M1017). ATT&CK also recommends
encrypting sensitive information both in transit and at rest (M1041) to limit the value of any
data an attacker manages to access or exfiltrate and applying network segmentation (M1030)
to constrain lateral movement and reduce the attacker's ability to reach high-value systems.

ATLAS provides a complementary set of mitigations tailored to AI-enabled activities in this
phase (MITRE, n.d.). Its guidance emphasizes monitoring for large or unusual data-access
patterns through data-access analytics, which can help detect AI-accelerated data triage or
staging. ATLAS also recommends requiring human-in-the-loop review for high-risk data
operations to prevent automated misuse of sensitive information. Additional mitigations
include applying fraud analytics and transaction-monitoring capabilities to identify

_Chapter 15_ 730

anomalous monetization behaviors, deploying data-loss-prevention and egress-control
mechanisms to detect or block staged exfiltration, and minimizing available lateral-movement
paths by reducing and monitoring access routes within the environment

I've really only scratched the surface here. Security researchers, Red Teams, and threat actors
are just getting started with AI. Their use of AI and their attacks on AI systems will continue to
evolve for the foreseeable future. Subsequently, it is important for CISOs and security teams to
stay informed of the evolving threat landscape. Next, I'll share some resources that will help
you do that.

That wraps up our examination of how adversaries are exploiting AI and some of the defensive
measures available to counter their techniques. It's clear that attackers will continue evolving
their use of AI to streamline and strengthen their operations, and defenders must respond with
equally innovative AI-driven capabilities. With that in mind, we can now turn to emerging AI
security capabilities.
###### **Emerging AI security capabilities**

Any cybersecurity product vendor that wants to remain competitive is investing heavily in AI.
For example, LLMs, **Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)**, and **e** arly agentic-AI systems are
increasingly reducing the industry's reliance on traditional **machine learning (ML)**
components **a** nd RegEx-based pattern-matching. RegEx is a syntactic tool designed for exact
pattern matching, while LMMs function as semantic engines capable of interpreting meaning
across varied and inconsistent formats. As a result, LMMs are beginning to replace RegEx in
workflows such as log parsing, entity extraction, alert enrichment, ticket analysis, screenshot
interpretation, and unstructured data processing. Products such as Microsoft Security Copilot,
CrowdStrike Charlotte AI, SentinelOne Purple AI, Google Security Operations (Chronicle +
Gemini), and Palo Alto Networks Precision AI increasingly use LLM/LMM-based semantic
analysis for tasks that historically relied on RegEx. While these systems do not eliminate RegEx
entirely, they reduce dependence on brittle pattern-matching by introducing contextual and
semantic understanding.

The cybersecurity industry has been at the forefront of adopting agentic-AI capabilities. Vinay
(2025) outlines a five-generation taxonomy that captures this rapid evolution, and _Figure 15.3_

_Chapter 15_ 734

visualizes the timeline across which these generations emerged. Vinay (2025) describes these
generations as follows:

G1 — Single LLM Reasoners: Text-only LLMs used for summarization and basic
reasoning; no tool use or grounding

G2 — Tool-Augmented Agents: LLMs connected to structured tools (log search, intel
lookups) for more reliable, auditable workflows

G3 — Distributed Multi-Agent Systems: multiple cooperating agents handling triage,
investigation, intel research, and reporting

G4 — Schema-Bound Tool Ecosystems: multiple agents operating inside constrained,
typed, validated tool ecosystems for stronger safety and reproducibility

G5 — Early Semi-Autonomous Pipelines: agents plan, act, observe, and iterate across
multi-step investigations with partial autonomy and human oversight

_Figure 15.3 – Evolution of agentic AI in cybersecurity across five generations (G1–G5), adapted from Vinay (2025),_

_showing how capabilities progressed from single-model reasoning to early semi-autonomous pipelines._

The evolution of **a** gentic AI in cybersecurity shows a steady progression from basic reasoning
models to coordinated, tool-augmented, and partially autonomous systems. Each generation
expands the scope of what AI can safely and reliably handle within security operations.
Although today's systems still require human oversight, the trajectory points toward

735 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

increasingly capable pipelines that can accelerate detection, investigation, and response at
enterprise scale.

From an operational cybersecurity perspective, AI-driven innovation has accelerated across
security alert triage, vulnerability analysis, threat-intelligence research, incident response
planning and reporting, and the emergence of tool-augmented and agentic LLMs within
**security operations center (SOC)** platforms. Beyond triage and incident-response workflows,
AI, LLMs, and agentic-AI systems have also transformed detection engineering, malware
analysis, identity security, cloud-configuration analysis, attack-surface management,
adversary simulation, and even governance and compliance functions.

Over the next couple of years, the most significant AI and agentic-AI innovations are expected
in detection engineering automation, incident-response workflows, and cloud-identity
security analysis—areas where multi-step reasoning, tool orchestration, and operational scale
create strong demand for **a** gentic capabilities.

That's the end of this chapter and the book. One final thought...
###### **Is cybersecurity getting better or worse?**

I often get asked, "Are things getting better or worse in cybersecurity?" After doing the research
necessary to write the 15 chapters in this book, including all the up-to-date data, I'm sorry to
report that things have definitely gotten worse. I don't want to sound negative, but the data
I've shared in this book overwhelmingly supports this view.

Consider that the industry hasn't seen a reduction in annual vulnerability disclosure counts
since 2016, when there were 50 fewer CVEs disclosed than in 2015. In 2015, there were 6,504
CVEs disclosed, while, at the time of writing, 48,448 were disclosed in 2025 (7.5 times more).
The annual rate of growth in CVE disclosures has been increasing, not decreasing.

In the 10 years between 2015 and 2024, the average growth in new malware samples was
approximately 102.6 million per year (AV-Test Institute, August 25, 2025). Metaphorically
speaking, if malware were a country, it would become the most populated country in the
world, overtaking India and China in the next two years.

The largest **distributed denial of service (DDoS)** attacks in 2018 generated 126 million
packets per second, compared to large attacks in 2025 that generated 10.6 billion packets per
second. 10.6 billion is 84 times more packets per second than 126 million.

One major cloud provider observed more than 311 billion attacks on web applications and APIs
in 2024. That's an average of more than 850,000,000 attacks per day. If we extrapolate this
data by assuming that the number of attacks observed by other major cloud providers is
similar, the number of attacks each year on web applications and APIs is certainly several

_Chapter 15_ 736

hundred billion, if not more. These numbers are poised for potential explosive growth as new
AI services further the proliferation of APIs.

The data is very clear that CISOs and cybersecurity teams are being challenged more than ever
before to identify, protect, detect, respond, and recover. This is consistent with my own
professional experience working in the cybersecurity industry for decades.

The good news is that CISOs and security teams have never had a bigger or better ecosystem
supporting them. The future looks bright regardless of the ever-increasing volume of attacks.
Marcus Aurelius (121–180 CE) wrote that "what stands in the way becomes the way" (Aurelius,
2002). Few ideas resonate more strongly with the challenges we face today.

I sincerely hope you found this book to be educational and helpful.
###### **Summary**

The rapid adoption of generative and agentic AI since 2022 has fundamentally reshaped
enterprise computing, productivity, and the cybersecurity landscape. While these systems
unlock new efficiencies and capabilities, they also expand the attack surface, introduce nondeterministic behavior, and create entirely new classes of safety and security risks that
traditional controls were never designed to manage. Because AI systems ingest and reason over
diverse inputs, often simultaneously, and can act autonomously through tools and
integrations, they amplify both the scale and unpredictability of potential failures and attacks.
CISOs and cybersecurity teams now face the dual challenge of securing legacy IT environments
and increasingly complex AI-driven systems in parallel, all while threat activity continues to
accelerate.

This chapter examined AI risk through multiple lenses, beginning with AI safety and
responsible AI, which focus on ensuring systems behave ethically, transparently, and in
alignment with human values. Risks such as hallucinations, bias, over-reliance, and unsafe
deployment are no longer theoretical; real-world incidents demonstrate how these failures can
produce legal, financial, and reputational harm. At the same time, intrinsic security
vulnerabilities in large language models, including hallucinations, jailbreaks, and indirect
prompt injection, create new opportunities for adversaries to manipulate AI systems, exfiltrate
data, or bypass safeguards. Frameworks such as OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications and
MITRE ATLAS provide essential structure for understanding these risks and mapping them to
practical mitigations.

As organizations move beyond content generation toward agentic AI systems capable of taking
actions, new threat categories emerge. Tool misuse, privilege escalation, memory poisoning,
unsafe autonomy, and cascading operational failures extend AI risk beyond misinformation
into direct business and security impact. These risks demand stronger governance, least

737 _Artificial Intelligence: Security of AI Systems and Using AI for Better Cybersecurity_

privilege design, human-in-the-loop controls, and lifecycle-wide security practices that evolve
alongside rapidly maturing agent frameworks. The deployment of enterprise AI assistants such
as Microsoft Copilot illustrates both the promise and the challenge: AI can dramatically
improve discoverability and productivity, but it also exposes long-standing weaknesses in data
governance, access hygiene, and organizational discipline that can no longer be ignored.

The chapter also demonstrated how attackers are already leveraging AI across every phase of
the intrusion kill chain, from reconnaissance and social engineering to malware development,
command and control, and data exfiltration. AI lowers barriers to entry, accelerates attacker
workflows, and enables more personalized and scalable operations. Defenders must respond in
kind, combining traditional security controls with AI-driven detection, analytics, and
automation, while maintaining strong human oversight. Although the data shows that
cybersecurity outcomes are worsening in terms of attack volume, sophistication, and scale, the
ecosystem supporting defenders has never been stronger.

Ultimately, AI does not change the fundamental goals of cybersecurity, but it does change the
terrain. CISOs and security teams that treat AI as just another technology risk will fall behind.
Those who invest in governance, disciplined deployment, continuous monitoring, and AIaware security practices can turn these challenges into an advantage. As history has shown
repeatedly, what stands in the way becomes the way, and the responsible, secure adoption of
AI will be one of the defining tests of modern cybersecurity leadership.
